title: Can We Read the Query in the Order We Explain the Job?
openingTitle: Filter the Jobs, Then Add Their Minutes
opening: Botie needs pumps whose completed maintenance has consumed more than fifty minutes. Open jobs contain estimates that should not enter this report. A long nested query can make it difficult to see whether those estimates were excluded before the total was calculated.
We can give the qualifying jobs a name, then give the per-pump totals another name. Each stage describes a relation we can inspect.
blurb: Use common table expressions to name meaningful query stages while keeping grain, scope and execution assumptions explicit.

history.title: Names Made Intermediate Relations Easier to Review
blocks: Nested queries let one operation use another’s result, but deeply nested expressions can be awkward to inspect. Common table expressions give those intermediate relations names inside one statement. SQLite added CTE support in its February 2014 release.

This is a language feature for expressing dependencies. Naming closed_jobs does not permanently create a table or promise a particular execution strategy. Its value for our report is that the next stage clearly receives completed work rather than every job in the system.

parts.title: 1. Name a useful intermediate result
paragraphs: WITH closed_jobs AS (...) places a name before the main query. Inside the parentheses is a SELECT describing the relation. Later stages and the final SELECT can refer to that name during this statement.
Start by selecting from closed_jobs directly. If open estimates remain, repair that boundary before adding aggregation.
interpretation: A CTE is scoped to its statement. The next separate statement cannot assume that name still exists.

interpretation: The NULL duration remains unknown. The filter changes which jobs qualify, not the meaning of their duration cells.

parts.title: 2. Let the next name depend on the earlier one
paragraphs: Separate CTE definitions with commas. The totals stage can read closed_jobs and group by asset_id. Its output is now one row per asset with at least one qualifying job.
Give the aggregate a useful column alias such as total_minutes. That name lets the final filter describe the question without repeating the aggregate expression.
interpretation: The same statement can contain several named stages without creating permanent objects.

interpretation: The large open estimate never enters P7’s completed total. P9’s unknown total does not pass the numeric threshold.

parts.title: 3. Use the names to explain the row meaning
paragraphs: At closed_jobs, job_id would still identify a row if we retained it. At totals, several job IDs have contributed to one asset row. Joining totals to another job-level table could multiply that summary again.
Write down the grain beside each stage when reviewing a query. A name such as data2 does little to help another person notice that the row meaning changed.
interpretation: CTEs make a grain change visible; they do not prevent an incorrect later join.

parts.title: 4. Keep filters on the side of aggregation they belong to
paragraphs: The status condition describes individual jobs, so it belongs before their durations are added. The total threshold describes grouped assets, so it follows aggregation.
A direct GROUP BY with HAVING could express this same report. The named version is useful when we want to inspect or extend the intermediate relations. It is not automatically more correct or faster.
interpretation: Compare the results of alternative forms on the same changed fixtures before deciding whether a rewrite preserves meaning.

parts.title: 5. Do not confuse naming with storing
paragraphs: An ordinary CTE is a query expression. Depending on the engine and the query, it may be folded into surrounding work or materialised as an intermediate result. Referencing its name twice is not a portable promise that expensive work runs exactly once.

SQLite documents MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED hints, but these affect planning rather than changing the logical result. Begin without hints. Use the query plan and measurements before trying to force a strategy.
interpretation: When a result must persist across statements, that is a different design involving a table or view.

parts.title: 6. Test the stage that a new record should enter
paragraphs: Insert a large open job and predict that the completed report stays unchanged. Close that same job and predict that its asset can now pass the threshold.

The workshop keeps filtering, grouping and the final threshold on separate components. Inspect the output of the first component when the wrong jobs enter the total rather than trying to repair the final number.
interpretation: The useful structure follows the question’s dependencies. Additional CTEs are helpful when they name a real intermediate meaning.

quiz.prompt: That alone does not guarantee the engine materialises it exactly once.

title: How Far Does the Failed Supply Line Reach?
openingTitle: The Next Connection Is in Another Row
opening: Supply node 1 feeds nodes 2 and 3. Those nodes feed other equipment. When the supply fails, Botie needs to follow the connections far enough to identify the affected equipment. A single join only follows one connection.

We could write another join for every level, but we do not know the depth of every installation in advance. A recursive query applies the same step to the rows discovered by the previous step. We also need a stopping rule, because a bad record can point back to equipment we already visited.
blurb: Follow a hierarchy or dependency graph using an anchor, a repeated join and explicit safeguards against cycles and excessive traversal.

history.title: Repeated Relationships Needed More Than a Fixed Join

sources.title: SQLite WITH and recursive query examples
PostgreSQL recursive queries and cycle detection

blocks: A parts list, reporting hierarchy or network can contain an unknown number of levels. Recursive CTEs let a query start from a known row and repeatedly follow a relationship. The database documents describe that repeated expansion explicitly, including examples where a cycle would otherwise keep producing work.

The maintenance question is the same one: which records can we reach from this starting point? Our path guard rejects a return to a node already on the current path. A separate depth limit bounds how far this particular report is allowed to explore.

reading.experimentTitle: Follow the supply connections
reading.experimentIntro: Seed a starting node, expand its outgoing links, and keep the shortest discovered depth for each reached node.
reading.connectionTitle: Each recursive step consumes a discovered node
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Trace the bounded dependency report
reading.outputLabel: Reached node IDs and minimum depths
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: Expand the frontier before writing the recursion
intuition.explanation: The links are 1→2, 1→3, 2→4 and 3→4.

scene.caption: The final report keeps node 4 once with depth 2. Paths and reached nodes are different grains.

parts.title: 1. Keep the relationship in an edge table
paragraphs: An edge row stores parent_id and child_id. The pair says which node supplies another node; it does not contain all descendants. A graph can have several parents for the same child, as node 4 does here.

Decide whether the question wants paths, distinct reached nodes, or quantities propagated along paths. Removing repeated node IDs is suitable for our affected-equipment list, but could destroy useful information in a parts-quantity calculation.
interpretation: The output grain determines whether two routes to node 4 should remain separate.

parts.title: 2. Choose the anchor before repeating anything
paragraphs: The anchor SELECT creates node 1 at depth 0. Its path text is /1/. It runs without reading the recursive result. The recursive term then receives discovered rows and joins their node IDs to the edge table’s parent_id.
UNION ALL preserves newly discovered paths. We increment depth and append each child ID so later expansion can inspect the route already taken.
interpretation: The anchor answers where to begin. The recursive term answers how to take one more step.

parts.title: 3. Run the bounded traversal
paragraphs: The query below expands rows only while their current depth is below 3. It therefore includes discoveries at depth 3, then stops expanding them. The path check separately prevents revisiting a node on the current route.

After traversal, grouping by node_id and taking MIN(depth) can produce one reached-node row with the shortest depth among the paths explored. First inspect the paths themselves. The final ORDER BY controls display order; recursive processing order is not the report’s order.
interpretation: The cap defines a bounded report. It does not prove that no equipment exists beyond the cap.

examples.title: Inspect the paths before combining reached nodes
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE edges(parent_id INTEGER NOT NULL, child_id INTEGER NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO edges VALUES (1,2),(1,3),(2,4),(3,4);
examples.code:
WITH RECURSIVE walk(node_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT 1, 0, '/1/'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.child_id, w.depth + 1, w.path || e.child_id || '/'
  FROM walk AS w JOIN edges AS e ON e.parent_id = w.node_id
  WHERE w.depth < 3
    AND instr(w.path, '/' || e.child_id || '/') = 0
)
SELECT node_id, depth, path FROM walk ORDER BY depth, node_id, path;
paragraphs: Node 4 appears through two routes in the internal walk. The challenge will combine them into one reached-node row.
interpretation: Both routes to node 4 are visible. The starting node has depth zero because no edge was followed to reach it.

parts.title: 4. A cycle changes the stopping problem
paragraphs: Suppose a mistaken edge points from node 4 back to node 1. Without a guard, repeated UNION ALL expansion can revisit the same equipment indefinitely. The slash-delimited path lets instr search for the complete integer ID rather than confusing node 1 with node 11.

Changing UNION ALL to UNION is not a universal cycle repair. If the recursive row contains increasing depth or changing path text, each new row can still be distinct. Deduplication compares whole rows.
interpretation: Our integer-ID path representation is a teaching choice. Arbitrary text identifiers need a representation whose delimiters cannot be confused with the identifier itself.

parts.title: 5. Separate cycle prevention from a resource bound
paragraphs: A path guard prevents one route from looping. It does not prevent a graph with many branches from containing a very large number of simple paths. A maximum depth, execution budget and an operational row limit can still be necessary.
If the limit is reached, label the result as bounded or incomplete. Quietly treating a truncated report as the full dependency closure could leave affected equipment out of a shutdown plan.
interpretation: The workshop caps depth and total expanded rows to keep the demonstration responsive. Those limits are not a proof that a real installation is small.

parts.title: 6. Inspect the intermediate paths when the result surprises you
paragraphs: Temporarily select node_id, depth and path from walk to see why a node was reached. If node 4 is missing, check the edge direction. If it appears twice, decide whether you forgot the final node-level summary or whether the task actually needs both routes.
Recursive CTE syntax and built-in cycle facilities differ between engines. This example uses SQLite-compatible string paths rather than assuming another database’s SEARCH or CYCLE syntax.
interpretation: A final MIN(depth) is a report over discovered paths. It does not repair an incorrect edge direction or missing source records.

quiz.prompt: What can the report honestly claim?
options: It reports nodes found within the allowed depth
It proves that the deeper child does not exist
It is the complete graph because cycles were blocked
quiz.because: A depth bound limits exploration and therefore the completeness of the result.

given.data: The traversal permits depth 0 through 3. An unvisited child exists at depth 4.

quiz.prompt: Node 4 should appear once with depth 2.
quiz.because: That final aggregation deliberately changes path grain to reached-node grain.

given.data: Two acyclic paths reach node 4 at depths 2 and 3. The output is one row per node with MIN(depth).

practice.title: Which nodes are reachable within three connections?
practice.question: Which nodes are reachable within three connections?

sql.setup:
CREATE TABLE edges(parent_id INTEGER NOT NULL, child_id INTEGER NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO edges VALUES (1,2),(1,3),(2,4),(3,4);

task: Start at node 1 with depth 0. Follow parent_id to child_id through edges, including discoveries up to depth 3.
Prevent revisiting a node already on the current path. Return node_id and minimum discovered depth, one row per reached node, ordered by node_id. Keep the starting node.
practice.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE walk(node_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT 1, 0, '/1/'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.child_id, w.depth + 1, w.path || e.child_id || '/'
  FROM walk AS w JOIN edges AS e ON e.parent_id = w.node_id
  WHERE w.depth < 3
    AND instr(w.path, '/' || e.child_id || '/') = 0
)
SELECT node_id, MIN(depth) AS depth
FROM walk GROUP BY node_id ORDER BY node_id;
hints: Join the current node to edges.parent_id, then emit edges.child_id.
Store a delimiter around each integer ID in the path. Test the child before appending it.
Group the discovered paths by node_id after recursion.

title: Keep Every Reading While Looking at Its Neighbours
openingTitle: The Average Alone Has Lost the Reading We Need
opening: Botie has several readings for each pump. A grouped average can describe each pump, but the technician also needs the latest individual reading and wants to compare it with the one before it. Grouping everything into one average loses those individual rows.

A window function calculates across related rows while keeping a result attached to each row. We will first decide which rows belong together, then put those rows in an order that gives “latest” a precise meaning.
blurb: Partition and order individual records for row numbers, ranks and previous-reading comparisons without collapsing them into groups.

history.title: Analytical Queries Needed to Keep Their Detail
blocks: Ordinary aggregation answers questions about groups by producing fewer rows. Analytical reports often need a group calculation beside the original rows instead. Window functions provide that arrangement. SQLite added window-function support in September 2018.

For the technician, this means a reading can retain its timestamp and identity while receiving a position within its pump’s history. That position is meaningful only after we define the partition and its ordering.

reading.experimentTitle: Select each pump’s latest complete row
reading.experimentIntro: Order each pump’s readings, number them within the pump, and retain position one.
reading.connectionTitle: The window annotates rows before selection
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Return the latest recorded reading
reading.outputLabel: One latest reading row per asset
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: Number inside each pump rather than across the file
intuition.explanation: All timestamps are UTC. More recent readings come first.

scene.caption: The latest P8 value is NULL. A missing value does not make the older reading the latest record.

parts.title: 1. Partition the comparison before choosing the function
paragraphs: PARTITION BY asset_id means each pump has its own window population. Without it, one global numbering could select the latest reading in the whole table and omit other pumps.
Unlike GROUP BY, the window annotation leaves each reading row available. Its value, ID and timestamp remain connected to the same observation.
interpretation: Partitioning determines which rows may influence each other. It does not sort the final report.

parts.title: 2. Give latest a deterministic order
paragraphs: ROW_NUMBER assigns one position per row within the window order. We order measured_at descending, then reading_id descending. If two readings share a timestamp, the larger ID wins under this lesson’s explicit policy.
The ID is a tie breaker, not proof that the physical measurement happened later. A production system should choose a rule that matches its event identity and revision policy.
interpretation: Window ORDER BY establishes row positions. The outer ORDER BY independently controls the displayed report.

examples.title: Inspect every row’s assigned position
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE readings(reading_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, measured_at TEXT NOT NULL, value INTEGER);
INSERT INTO readings VALUES (1,'P7','2026-01-01 08:00:00',20),(2,'P8','2026-01-01 08:00:00',50),(3,'P7','2026-01-01 09:00:00',24),(4,'P8','2026-01-01 09:00:00',NULL);
paragraphs: The CTE keeps the window result available for a later filter. Here we inspect all positions before choosing the winners.
interpretation: P8’s latest row receives position one even though its value is unknown. Filtering value first would instead ask for the latest known reading.

parts.title: 3. Filter a window result in a later query stage
paragraphs: Window functions operate after the input rows have passed the relevant WHERE and grouping stages. SQLite does not let WHERE in the same query directly filter ROW_NUMBER(). Put the annotation in a CTE or subquery, then filter its result.

Be careful with filters placed before the window. Restricting the source to a recent day changes what LAG can see at that day’s first reading. If the previous reading must come from earlier history, compute it before restricting the displayed rows.
interpretation: The stage where a filter runs changes the rows available to the window.

parts.title: 4. Choose what a tie should mean
paragraphs: ROW_NUMBER gives tied rows different positions. RANK gives peers the same position and leaves gaps after ties. DENSE_RANK gives peers the same position without those gaps. With values 90, 90 and 70 in descending order, RANK gives 1, 1 and 3; DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1 and 2.

For a competition-style value rank, order by the value alone if equal values should remain peers. Adding a unique ID to that ranking order breaks the tie. For selecting one latest row, that deterministic tie break is exactly what we want.
interpretation: The function and ordering must express the requested tie policy together.

parts.title: 5. Read the previous observation without joining the table to itself
paragraphs: LAG(value) reads an earlier row in the partition’s order. It is useful for a reading-to-reading comparison. The first row has no predecessor and receives NULL unless a default was supplied.
An earlier row can itself contain NULL, so a NULL lag value does not always mean “there was no previous record.” Keep the previous reading’s ID too if the distinction matters.
interpretation: Subtracting a previous value measures change between observations. It is not automatically a rate per hour.

examples.title: Expose the previous reading beside each value
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE readings(reading_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, measured_at TEXT NOT NULL, value INTEGER);
INSERT INTO readings VALUES (1,'P7','2026-01-01 08:00:00',20),(2,'P8','2026-01-01 08:00:00',50),(3,'P7','2026-01-01 09:00:00',24),(4,'P8','2026-01-01 09:00:00',NULL);
paragraphs: Here the window runs forward through each pump’s history.
interpretation: The first P8 row does not borrow a previous value from P7. Partitioning keeps those histories separate.

parts.title: 6. Try a tied timestamp before trusting the latest-row query
paragraphs: A MAX(measured_at) query joined back to the original table can return two rows when two readings share the maximum time. That might be correct for a request for all latest-time observations, but not for this one-row-per-pump contract.
The workshop first sorts complete records, then adds a row number and selects position one. New timestamps and ties should change the winner through those operations, without hard-coded reading IDs.
interpretation: Inspect the sorted records when a winner looks wrong. The numbering cannot repair the wrong order.

parts.title: 7. Keep frame-sensitive calculations for an explicit frame
paragraphs: Row numbers, ranks and LAG describe positions or neighbours. Running totals and rolling averages also need a decision about which range of nearby rows contributes to each answer.
That range is a window frame. The next lesson will use tied timestamps to show why an implicit frame can produce a result different from the row-by-row total we expected.
interpretation: A partition defines the group of related rows. A frame can select a smaller portion of that partition for the current calculation.

title: Which Readings Belong in This Rolling Total?
openingTitle: The Total Jumps Before We Reach the Second Reading
opening: Two usage readings arrive with the same timestamp. Botie expects a running total to increase after each record, but both records suddenly display the total after both readings. The database has followed its frame rule; we had not actually specified the row-by-row rule we intended.
A window frame names the rows allowed to contribute to the current answer. We will compare a running total with a two-reading total, then decide what a tied timestamp and a missing day should do.
blurb: Choose ROWS, peer groups and time ranges deliberately so rolling calculations include the observations the question actually describes.

history.title: An Ordered Group Still Needed a Boundary
blocks: Adding an order to an analytical calculation makes questions such as “so far” possible, but it leaves another choice: how many neighbouring rows should contribute? Window frames make that boundary part of the query. Default frame rules can include all peers sharing the current ordering value.

That explains our apparent jump. If timestamp alone defines peers, both records at that timestamp can enter a cumulative frame together. A physical-row frame and a complete ordering express a different, equally deliberate calculation.

scene.caption: The final frame contains two observations despite the gap in calendar days.

parts.title: 1. Separate the partition, order and frame
paragraphs: The partition selects the pump’s history. The ordering puts that history in sequence. The frame selects the portion of that ordered history used for the current aggregate.

These choices answer different questions. Correctly partitioning by asset does not make a two-day frame equivalent to a two-reading frame. Correctly ordering by time does not say whether all earlier records should contribute.
interpretation: Say the calculation aloud before choosing its frame: current observation plus one preceding observation.

parts.title: 2. See the default peer behaviour directly
paragraphs: With an ordered aggregate and no explicit frame, SQLite uses a RANGE frame from the partition’s start through the current row’s peers. When timestamp alone orders the window, equal timestamps are peers.

In this example, the two 08:00 readings therefore both receive 5. This is useful when simultaneous readings should share a cumulative result. It is surprising if we expected event-by-event accumulation.
interpretation: The outer event_id ordering displays the rows consistently without changing the window’s timestamp-only peer groups.

examples.title: Compare peer-aware accumulation with explicit row accumulation
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE usage(event_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, measured_at TEXT NOT NULL, amount INTEGER);
INSERT INTO usage VALUES (1,'P7','2026-01-01 08:00:00',2),(2,'P7','2026-01-01 08:00:00',3),(3,'P7','2026-01-03 08:00:00',7),(4,'P8','2026-01-01 08:00:00',10);
examples.code:
SELECT event_id,
 SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY asset_id ORDER BY measured_at) AS peer_total,
 SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY asset_id ORDER BY measured_at, event_id
                   ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS row_total
FROM usage WHERE asset_id='P7' ORDER BY event_id;
paragraphs: The two sums deliberately use different window orders and frames.
interpretation: Neither total is random. The first includes the tied peer immediately; the second follows the chosen event-ID order.

parts.title: 3. Write the two-reading boundary explicitly
paragraphs: ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes the previous ordered record and the current one. The first row has no predecessor, so its frame contains only itself.

A second ordering column makes the sequence deterministic when timestamps tie. SUM ignores NULL amounts; if the entire frame is unknown, its result is NULL. We do not replace missing measurements with zero without a separate decision.
interpretation: A two-row frame can contain fewer than two known values.

examples.title: Compare a wider three-record frame
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE usage(event_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, measured_at TEXT NOT NULL, amount INTEGER);
INSERT INTO usage VALUES (1,'P7','2026-01-01 08:00:00',2),(2,'P7','2026-01-01 08:00:00',3),(3,'P7','2026-01-03 08:00:00',7),(4,'P8','2026-01-01 08:00:00',10);
paragraphs: This worked query allows two preceding rows, while the challenge asks for only one. P8 still begins its own partition.
interpretation: The third P7 frame includes all three amounts and totals 12. Reducing it to one preceding row would remove the first amount and leave 10.

parts.title: 4. Do not turn a record count into a duration by renaming it
paragraphs: ROWS counts physical rows. GROUPS counts peer groups defined by the ordering values. RANGE defines a value-based boundary, with engine-specific rules for its ordering expression and offsets.

If the task asks for the preceding 24 hours, sparse measurements make a fixed row count unsuitable. Use an explicitly defined time-range calculation and verify its boundary and timestamp representation. In SQLite, a numeric timestamp expression can support suitable RANGE offsets; it should not be improvised by subtracting from arbitrary text.
interpretation: The next date lesson makes missing calendar days and half-open time boundaries visible.

parts.title: 5. Check the frame before using LAST_VALUE
paragraphs: LAST_VALUE returns the last value inside its frame, which is not necessarily the last row of the entire partition. Under a cumulative default, the frame often ends at the current peer group.

For the last value over the complete ordered partition, specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING with a deterministic order. By contrast, LAG and LEAD use relative row positions and do not use the frame to limit their lookup in SQLite.
interpretation: A function’s name does not override its documented frame behaviour.

parts.title: 6. Change the spacing and missingness independently
paragraphs: Move the third P7 observation a week later. A two-observation calculation should still combine it with the second observation. Set both amounts in one frame to NULL and predict an unknown total.
These tests separate what the frame counts from what SUM does with values inside it. When the output is wrong, inspect the ordered rows and frame membership before changing the arithmetic.
interpretation: The workshop’s preceding-row count is adjustable, but it always counts observations rather than elapsed time.

title: Where Did the Quiet Day Go?
openingTitle: The Report Has Skipped Tuesday
opening: Botie groups recorded incidents by day and draws a chart. Monday has two incidents and Wednesday has one. Tuesday disappears entirely, which makes the chart look as though Wednesday immediately followed Monday.

The event table records things that happened. It cannot supply a row for a day when nothing happened. We need a calendar to define the days we intend to report, plus a precise rule for assigning each event to one day.
blurb: Define UTC timestamps, half-open reporting intervals and a calendar spine so missing days do not disappear or midnight events get counted twice.

history.title: Event Logs and Calendars Answer Different Questions
blocks: Time values have to represent both instants and calendar conventions. SQLite supports date calculations over defined text and numeric representations rather than a dedicated date/time storage type. That makes a consistent representation an application responsibility.

A daily report needs more than a timestamp function. It needs a set of expected days. Joining a calendar to an event log preserves days that have no matching event, just as an asset register preserves pumps that have no visit.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep every requested calendar day
reading.experimentIntro: Read each event’s UTC day, count events by day, and left join those counts onto the requested calendar.
reading.connectionTitle: The calendar defines the report’s rows
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Count events without losing quiet days
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: The calendar has a row the event log cannot supply
intuition.explanation: The requested report includes January 1, 2 and 3.

scene.caption: Midnight on January 3 belongs to January 3 only. A missing day and a missing timestamp are different problems.

parts.title: 1. Agree on the timestamp representation
paragraphs: These fixtures store UTC timestamps as fixed-width YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS text. In that one representation, text order follows chronological order. Mixed offsets, inconsistent widths or a mixture of seconds and milliseconds would invalidate that shortcut.
Store or validate the format at ingestion, and document the unit for numeric timestamps. A column named occurred_at does not by itself guarantee a timezone or a unit.
interpretation: SQLite’s date functions support particular representations. They are not a substitute for deciding what the source field means.

parts.title: 2. Give adjacent days boundaries that do not overlap
paragraphs: We assign an event to a day when its timestamp is at least the start of that day and strictly less than the start of the next day. This half-open interval includes the starting midnight and excludes the next midnight.

BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Using it with the two midnights would count a boundary event in both adjacent days. Guessing a final instant such as 23:59:59 also ties the query to a precision that may change.
interpretation: Use the next interval’s start as the exclusive upper bound.

examples.title: Inspect January 1’s exact interval
examples.code:
SELECT event_id FROM events
WHERE occurred_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND occurred_at < '2026-01-02 00:00:00'
ORDER BY event_id;
paragraphs: The event at midnight on January 3 lies outside this first-day interval.
interpretation: The two January 1 events qualify without guessing the final supported fractional second.

parts.title: 3. Put the calendar on the preserved side of a left join
paragraphs: The calendar table lists the days we want, including those with no event. LEFT JOIN keeps those calendar rows. Put the event-time conditions in ON so an unmatched day still survives.
Count the non-NULL event_id, not COUNT(*). A left join supplies one placeholder row for an unmatched day; COUNT(*) would incorrectly turn that placeholder into one incident.
interpretation: The fixture’s event_id is always known on a real event, so it is a reliable counted match.

examples.title: Inspect the calendar’s unmatched placeholder
examples.code:
SELECT c.day, e.event_id
FROM calendar AS c LEFT JOIN events AS e
  ON e.occurred_at >= c.day || ' 00:00:00'
 AND e.occurred_at < datetime(c.day, '+1 day')
ORDER BY c.day, e.event_id;
paragraphs: Before counting, inspect which event IDs were attached to each requested day.
interpretation: January 2 survives with no event ID. The challenge turns these matches into daily counts without counting that placeholder as an incident.

parts.title: 4. Decide when a missing count really means zero
paragraphs: A calendar left-joined to precomputed daily counts also works. In that arrangement, an absent count is NULL and COALESCE can deliberately convert it to zero. That is the arrangement used by the workshop.

This assumes the log is complete enough for “no recorded events” to be useful. If the sensor system was offline, zero records does not prove zero real incidents. Keep ingestion coverage or service status separately when the distinction matters.
interpretation: Replacing missing data with zero is a statement about the report’s meaning, not a general cleanup rule.

parts.title: 5. Keep UTC reporting separate from local business days
paragraphs: Our day boundary is midnight UTC. A maintenance team may instead ask for days in a named timezone or shifts beginning at 07:00. Those are different boundaries and can cross UTC dates.

Use a timezone-aware system to construct the intended interval boundaries. Daylight-saving changes can make a local day shorter or longer than twenty-four hours. SQLite’s host-local conversion is not a general named-timezone database for arbitrary sites.
interpretation: Once the correct UTC boundaries are known, the same inclusive-start/exclusive-end comparison can assign events consistently.

parts.title: 6. Measure elapsed time using numeric instants
paragraphs: For elapsed seconds in this second-precision fixture, subtract unixepoch values. A calendar label alone is not an elapsed duration, and months are not a fixed number of seconds.

For fractional precision, choose a representation and conversion that preserve the required resolution. Functions available in newer SQLite releases may not exist in the browser’s runtime; these examples use functions supported by the lesson environment.
interpretation: Round only for display when the underlying precision matters.

examples.title: Measure a ninety-minute repair
examples.code: SELECT unixepoch('2026-01-03 09:30:00') - unixepoch('2026-01-03 08:00:00') AS seconds;
paragraphs: Both inputs explicitly use UTC, so timezone transitions do not change this elapsed interval.
interpretation: The numeric difference is elapsed seconds, rather than a formatted clock time.

parts.title: 7. Test the beginning, the boundary and the empty interval
paragraphs: Insert an event exactly at the next midnight. It must enter the next day only. Add an event outside the requested calendar range and verify that no extra report day appears. Remove every event and verify that every requested calendar day still appears with zero.
These cases catch reporting mistakes that a busy day full of ordinary timestamps can hide.
interpretation: The requested calendar is part of the query input. Do not derive it only from days that happened to have records.

title: Why Did a Pump Search Return the Wrong Equipment?
openingTitle: That Underscore Is Part of the Name
opening: The maintenance import contains “ PUMP_7 ”, “pump_9” and “pumpX8”. Botie searches for codes beginning with pump_ and unexpectedly includes pumpX8. In a LIKE pattern, the underscore has a special meaning: it matches any single character.
Before searching text, we need to decide how names should be cleaned and which characters in the search are literal. A query can run successfully while still applying the wrong naming policy.
blurb: Clean and compare text under an explicit identifier policy, with literal pattern characters, NULL handling and honest Unicode limits.

history.title: Matching Text Required Rules Beyond Its Appearance
blocks: Text processing in SQL includes both exact comparisons and pattern matching. Those operations developed different conventions: a pattern can reserve characters to stand for something else, while comparison rules decide which text values count as equal.

For imported identifiers, the useful lesson is to name the convention. We use ordinary surrounding spaces, ASCII letter case and a literal underscore. That limited rule is easy to demonstrate and test without pretending it solves every language’s text behaviour.

reading.experimentTitle: Normalise the code before applying a literal prefix
reading.experimentIntro: Trim surrounding ordinary spaces, lowercase ASCII letters, and retain codes beginning with the literal pump_ prefix.
reading.connectionTitle: Text cleanup is an explicit policy
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Select the intended pump codes
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: Distinguish a literal underscore from a wildcard
intuition.explanation: The desired prefix contains the actual underscore character.

scene.caption: SQLite’s default lower handles ASCII case conversion. It does not turn Ü into u.

parts.title: 1. Separate the original record from the comparison form
paragraphs: Keep the original imported code if it matters for audit or display. Add a derived normalised value for the specific matching policy. Silently overwriting an external identifier can make it difficult to reconcile later records.
Our rule removes ordinary spaces from both ends and lowercases ASCII letters. It leaves internal spaces and non-ASCII characters alone. Empty text remains different from NULL.
interpretation: A cleanup rule should describe what changes and what remains meaningful.

parts.title: 2. Use trim and lower with their actual limits
paragraphs: SQLite trim(code) removes ordinary space characters at the ends by default. It does not promise to remove every Unicode whitespace character or internal spacing. Its default lower function converts ASCII letters.

A multilingual name-matching system needs a deliberate Unicode normalisation and case-folding policy, often with additional library support. Test that policy before using it in a unique key or deduplicating people.
interpretation: A simple identifier lesson should not imply that all visually similar names are interchangeable.

examples.title: Inspect cleanup without filtering anything
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE codes(record_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT);
INSERT INTO codes VALUES (1,' PUMP_7 '),(2,'pumpX8'),(3,'pump_9'),(4,NULL),(5,'PÜMP_2');
examples.code: SELECT record_id, lower(trim(code)) AS normalised FROM codes ORDER BY record_id;
paragraphs: The unmodified unusual character and missing value remain visible.
interpretation: The output makes the rule inspectable before it influences which records are returned.

parts.title: 3. Escape characters that should be literal in a pattern
paragraphs: LIKE uses percent for any sequence of characters and underscore for one character. Our pattern must escape the underscore but retain the final percent wildcard. ESCAPE declares which character introduces that literal interpretation.

A literal prefix can also be expressed with an appropriate substring comparison. Parameter binding protects query structure, but it does not automatically turn pattern wildcards in a parameter into literal characters. Escape them according to the search contract.
interpretation: SQL injection safety and wildcard interpretation are separate responsibilities.

examples.title: Inspect both pattern interpretations
paragraphs: The first expression treats the underscore as a wildcard. The second uses it literally.
interpretation: The escaped pattern excludes pumpX8 while retaining pump_8. The challenge applies that rule to cleaned source records.

parts.title: 4. Know which comparison is controlling equality
paragraphs: A collation determines how text is compared for operations such as ordering and equality. SQLite BINARY compares its encoded text representation; built-in NOCASE folds ASCII letter case rather than providing universal linguistic equality.

LIKE has its own documented matching behaviour, so attaching a collation is not a general way to rewrite its wildcard or Unicode rules. If case sensitivity matters, verify the exact operator and database configuration used by the query.
interpretation: Do not assume one comparison rule governs every text operation in every database.

parts.title: 5. Inspect missing pieces before concatenating a label
paragraphs: The || operator concatenates text in SQLite. A NULL operand normally makes that concatenation NULL. Use COALESCE only when you have chosen a real fallback meaning, such as a displayed “unknown” marker.

substr can select a segment and instr can locate a substring. SQLite positions in these functions are one-based; instr returns zero when the substring is absent. Explicit examples help avoid importing Python’s zero-based indexing assumptions.
interpretation: A display label is not a reliable replacement for separate structured identifier fields.

examples.title: Locate the separator and preserve an unknown value
examples.code: SELECT instr('pump_7', '_'), substr('pump_7', 6), 'pump_' || NULL;
paragraphs: These small expressions isolate position and missing-value behaviour.
interpretation: The suffix starts at position 6. The unknown concatenated suffix does not silently become an empty string.

parts.title: 6. Do not let cleaning invent identity
paragraphs: Two different raw codes can become equal after cleanup. That is useful only if the domain says those forms represent the same equipment. Preserve a stable internal key and review collisions before enforcing uniqueness on the derived value.

The challenge deliberately returns record IDs beside cleaned text. If two matching records clean to the same code, both records remain. It is a selection exercise, not an unrequested deduplication policy.
interpretation: Use examples with literal underscores, missing text and unfamiliar characters to test the policy you actually promised.

quiz.prompt: Should the query automatically remove one?
options: No, both records remain unless deduplication is requested
Yes, the smaller ID is always incorrect
Yes, normalised text proves both rows are the same event
quiz.because: Cleaning a value does not establish that separate source records are duplicate events.

given.data: Two raw rows clean to pump_7, but their record_id values differ. This query selects matching imported records.

quiz.prompt: Parameter binding by itself makes that underscore literal.
quiz.because: Binding protects SQL structure. Pattern metacharacters still need a literal-search policy.

given.data: A bound LIKE parameter contains an underscore.

practice.question: Which imported records have the literal pump_ prefix?

title: Is That Temperature a Number or Just Text?
openingTitle: The Payload Looks Familiar, but Its Types Have Changed
opening: One sensor sends temperature as the number 42. Another sends the text “42”. A third sends no temperature at all, and an interrupted upload is not valid JSON. Botie must not treat these records as interchangeable just because a person can guess what some of them meant.

JSON lets a row carry a structured payload, but extraction still needs a contract. We will validate the text, inspect the property’s JSON type, then accept only the numeric values this report promises to use.
blurb: Extract structured payloads with explicit JSON validity and type checks while preserving the distinction between missing, null, text and numeric data.

history.title: Structured Messages Entered Relational Queries

sources.title: SQLite JSON functions and their inclusion since 3.38.0

blocks: Services commonly exchange structured messages as JSON, while analysis often happens in relational tables. Database JSON functions let queries inspect those messages without first flattening every property into a permanent column. SQLite made its JSON functions built in by default in version 3.38.0 in February 2022.

That convenience does not erase the payload’s types. A numeric property, a text property and an absent property still mean different things. Our report uses that distinction before it allows a value into a temperature calculation.

reading.experimentTitle: Inspect the payload before accepting its temperature
reading.experimentIntro: Read only valid numeric temperature properties, filter the unknown extraction results, and preserve record identity.
reading.connectionTitle: The type gate belongs before numeric analysis
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Extract genuine numeric temperatures
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: Similar-looking payloads take different routes
intuition.explanation: The report accepts only a JSON integer or real at $.temperature.

scene.caption: Rejecting a record from this report does not mean deleting it from the source or concealing its data-quality issue.

parts.title: 1. Separate valid JSON from the right schema
paragraphs: json_valid asks whether the text follows the supported JSON syntax. A valid array, object or scalar can pass that check while still being the wrong structure for a sensor record.

Our contract expects a top-level temperature property whose JSON type is integer or real. It does not parse units from strings or convert booleans into readings. Production ingestion should also impose size limits, a schema and a policy for duplicate property names.
interpretation: Syntax validation is the first boundary. It is not proof that the message has a useful meaning.

parts.title: 2. Read a path and inspect the JSON type
paragraphs: The path $.temperature addresses the temperature property at the root. json_type reports a type label such as integer, real, text or null; an absent path returns SQL NULL. json_extract returns a corresponding SQL scalar for a single scalar path.

A JSON null property and a missing property can both extract as SQL NULL, so retain the type result when that distinction matters. A boolean can extract numerically, which is why extraction alone is not the temperature check.
interpretation: Check the JSON type before trusting the extracted SQL value.

examples.title: Distinguish null from absence
paragraphs: These expressions use valid payloads so the missing-value distinction is isolated.
interpretation: The string label null identifies an explicit JSON null. The final 1 represents a JSON boolean, not a valid temperature under our contract.

parts.title: 3. Guard extraction with a lazy CASE branch
paragraphs: Calling JSON functions on malformed text can raise an error. The nested CASE first checks json_valid, then checks the property type, then extracts the accepted value. SQLite evaluates only the required CASE branch.
Do not assume arbitrary AND conditions will always execute left to right to protect a failing expression. Put the protection into an expression with the required evaluation semantics.
interpretation: The invalid payload follows the unknown extraction route without crashing the whole report.

examples.title: Inspect the extraction for every source record
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE telemetry(record_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT);
INSERT INTO telemetry VALUES (1,'{"temperature":42}'),(2,'{"temperature":"42"}'),(3,'{}'),(4,'{"temperature":null}'),(5,'broken'),(6,'{"temperature":true}');
examples.code:
WITH extracted AS (
 SELECT record_id,
   CASE WHEN json_valid(payload) THEN
     CASE WHEN json_type(payload, '$.temperature') IN ('integer','real')
          THEN json_extract(payload, '$.temperature') END
   END AS temperature
 FROM telemetry
)
SELECT record_id, temperature FROM extracted
ORDER BY record_id;
paragraphs: This query retains rejected records as NULL extractions so the type boundary is visible.
interpretation: The text 42 and boolean true follow the rejected route even though a loose conversion could produce numbers. The challenge selects only accepted rows.

parts.title: 4. Choose what to do with rejected payloads
paragraphs: This teaching report omits invalid or unsuitable temperatures. A real pipeline should count and investigate those omissions, preserve a safe reference to the original event and avoid filling them with invented zero readings.

Range and unit checks would follow the type check. A valid numeric value is not necessarily a plausible Celsius measurement, and the same number can mean a different physical quantity under a different unit.
interpretation: The worksheet tests type extraction. It does not claim to validate a complete sensor contract.

parts.title: 5. Expand arrays without forgetting the new row grain
paragraphs: json_each returns one row for each top-level array element or object member. When joined to a source row containing an array, it can multiply that row. Carry the original record ID and the element key or position if you need to identify each result.
Do not sum an original invoice total after expanding its line-item array unless the intended aggregation accounts for that repetition. The same fan-out issue from relational joins appears here.
interpretation: An array expansion changes the output grain from payload to payload element.

examples.title: Inspect one sensor’s tagged components
examples.code: SELECT key, value FROM json_each('["bearing","seal"]') ORDER BY key;
paragraphs: For an array, json_each supplies zero-based positions in key.
interpretation: Those two rows are two elements from one message, not two independent messages.

parts.title: 6. Promote stable fields when they become part of the core contract
paragraphs: Keeping an original JSON payload can be useful for occasional details. Frequently filtered or joined properties often deserve typed columns, constraints and an indexing strategy that fits the database. Otherwise every query repeats parsing and policy decisions.

Avoid assuming JSON syntax is portable across engines. The functions here use SQLite JSON text support available in the lesson runtime, rather than newer JSONB features or another database’s operators.
interpretation: The representation should make the contract easier to enforce and the common queries easier to inspect.

parts.title: 7. Test zero, negatives and lookalike types
paragraphs: Zero and negative numbers are still numbers. Whether they are physically valid is a later domain rule. The extraction should therefore retain zero and negative numeric values while excluding the strings that resemble them.

The workshop makes the typed property extraction a visible component, followed by a NULL filter. Inspect that intermediate result to see which records were rejected before changing the downstream analysis.
interpretation: A truthiness check would lose a legitimate zero reading. Use the declared type and missing-value policy.

quiz.prompt: What should be returned?
quiz.because: Zero is a numeric value and must not be lost to a truthiness check.

given.data: The payload is {"temperature":0}. The extraction contract accepts numeric values and has no range restriction.

quiz.prompt: The expanded output still necessarily has one row per source record.
quiz.because: The output grain can become one row per element.

given.data: One source row contains a JSON array of four elements and is expanded with json_each.

practice.title: Which payloads contain a genuine numeric temperature?
practice.question: Which payloads contain a genuine numeric temperature?

sql.setup:
CREATE TABLE telemetry(record_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT);
INSERT INTO telemetry VALUES (1,'{"temperature":42}'),(2,'{"temperature":"42"}'),(3,'{}'),(4,'{"temperature":null}'),(5,'broken'),(6,'{"temperature":true}');

task: Return record_id and the numeric $.temperature value for valid JSON payloads whose property type is integer or real. Order by record_id.
Safely exclude malformed JSON, missing properties, JSON null, booleans and numeric-looking strings. Retain zero and negative numbers.
practice.starter: SELECT record_id, payload FROM telemetry ORDER BY record_id;
practice.solution:
WITH extracted AS (
 SELECT record_id,
   CASE WHEN json_valid(payload) THEN
     CASE WHEN json_type(payload, '$.temperature') IN ('integer','real')
          THEN json_extract(payload, '$.temperature') END
   END AS temperature
 FROM telemetry
)
SELECT record_id, temperature FROM extracted
WHERE temperature IS NOT NULL ORDER BY record_id;
hints: Use CASE to guard JSON operations behind json_valid.
Check json_type before extracting. Filter SQL NULL only after that controlled extraction.

title: What Could the Model Have Known at That Moment?
openingTitle: Yesterday’s Prediction Has Been Given Tomorrow’s Evidence
opening: Botie is preparing training rows for a model that will help prioritise pump inspections. Each row represents a decision made at noon. A temperature was measured at 11:00, but the device did not upload it until 13:00. Today’s database contains that measurement. The person making the noon decision did not have it.

If we include the late upload in the noon feature, the training example describes a better-informed system than the one we can actually deploy. We need to reconstruct the information available at each decision, not simply gather every record whose event time looks old enough.
blurb: Build one feature row per historical decision using event time, availability time and explicit label boundaries, without leaking later evidence into the inputs.

history.title: Training Data Needed a Memory of What Was Available

sources.title: Feast point-in-time joins and created-timestamp filtering

blocks: Feature-store systems address the problem of joining historical features to the time of each training example. Feast documents point-in-time retrieval relative to each entity timestamp, including a bounded lookback. Its current documentation also distinguishes event time from when a value became available.

That distinction explains our late upload. Filtering event time alone cannot exclude data that arrived after the decision. This lesson expresses both boundaries directly in SQL so their meaning remains visible regardless of the feature-store framework used later.

reading.experimentTitle: Reconstruct the observations available at each decision
reading.experimentIntro: Match events to decisions by asset, enforce both time boundaries, then summarise and reattach the results to every decision.
reading.connectionTitle: The decision row defines the information boundary
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Build the historical feature table
reading.outputLabel: Decision IDs with eligible means and counts
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: Read the noon decision from the evidence it actually had
intuition.explanation: D1 concerns P7 at January 2, 12:00 UTC, with a 24-hour lookback.

scene.caption: The accepted mean is 20 from two observations. D2 concerns P8, which has no eligible measurement.

parts.title: 1. Start with a table of decisions
paragraphs: A training row needs a stable identity and a stated prediction time. Here decision_id identifies the row, asset_id identifies the pump and cutoff is the instant at which we imagine making the prediction. The same pump can have several decision rows at different times.
Do not group only by asset_id when the task has repeated decisions. That would merge information boundaries that must remain separate.
interpretation: One row per decision is the grain of the feature table, even when many events contribute to it.

parts.title: 2. Record when an event happened and when it became usable
paragraphs: event_at describes when the measurement occurred. available_at describes when that value became usable by the decision system. Ingestion, validation or publication can make availability later than the physical measurement.

These timestamps require trustworthy pipeline semantics. A warehouse load time is not automatically the moment a production service could read the value. If availability was never recorded, a query cannot reliably recover it from wishful assumptions.
interpretation: The feature contract needs the availability of the actual value used, including later corrections.

parts.title: 3. Apply both boundaries in the join
paragraphs: The lookback includes events at the start of the preceding 24 hours and excludes events at the cutoff itself. The availability condition allows values usable no later than the cutoff. These inclusivity choices are part of this lesson’s contract.
All event conditions belong in the LEFT JOIN matching rule. That preserves decisions with no eligible event. AVG then remains NULL for those decisions, while COUNT of a real event ID is zero.
interpretation: Event time prevents future observations. Availability time prevents later-arriving past observations.

examples.title: Calculate the mean before adding its coverage count
examples.code:
SELECT d.decision_id, AVG(m.value) AS feature_mean
FROM decisions AS d LEFT JOIN measurements AS m
  ON m.asset_id=d.asset_id
 AND m.event_at >= datetime(d.cutoff, '-24 hours')
 AND m.event_at < d.cutoff
 AND m.available_at <= d.cutoff
GROUP BY d.decision_id ORDER BY d.decision_id;
paragraphs: The value 90 is older by event time but newer by availability time, so it cannot contribute.
interpretation: D2 stays in the output with an unknown mean. The challenge adds a count so each mean’s evidence basis remains visible.

parts.title: 4. Inspect the eligible event rows before trusting their mean
paragraphs: When a feature value looks surprising, select the joined event IDs and timestamps before aggregating them. That reveals a late arrival or a boundary event directly. An aggregate alone hides which records were admitted.

The workshop exposes this relation as a separate component. Its summaries are then left-joined back to the decision list, because filtering joined event rows first can otherwise remove decisions with no remaining matches.
interpretation: Preserve the intended decision population separately from the population of eligible events.

examples.title: Show the two records supporting D1
examples.code:
SELECT d.decision_id, m.event_id, m.value
FROM decisions AS d JOIN measurements AS m ON m.asset_id=d.asset_id
 AND m.event_at >= datetime(d.cutoff, '-24 hours')
 AND m.event_at < d.cutoff AND m.available_at <= d.cutoff
ORDER BY d.decision_id, m.event_id;
paragraphs: This query inspects evidence membership instead of calculating a summary.
interpretation: The first event sits exactly on the lower boundary and is correctly included.

parts.title: 5. Keep the answer’s future window separate from the input window
paragraphs: A failure label might describe whether the pump failed in the next seven days. That future information is the target being learned, not an input available at noon. Its source records and join conditions should remain separate from the feature calculation.

A decision made two days before the dataset ends has not necessarily completed a seven-day outcome window. Treating its absent failure record as a negative label can introduce censoring errors. Define when labels have matured, how failures are observed and how incomplete follow-up is handled.
interpretation: A clear label definition includes its horizon and observation coverage as well as the outcome event.

parts.title: 6. A correction needs its own historical version
paragraphs: Suppose an old value is corrected after the decision. If the original row was overwritten, filtering its old event time does not reconstruct what the model originally saw. Preserve versions or an as-of history with availability for each value revision.

Use a documented revision-selection rule when several versions of one logical event are eligible. Do not count those versions as independent physical measurements. Our small table deliberately contains one immutable row per event so that the timing rule can be studied first.
interpretation: Point-in-time reconstruction depends on data history that the storage design actually retains.

parts.title: 7. Check joins for multiplication before calling the output a feature
paragraphs: A measurement joined to several maintenance notes can appear several times before averaging. Some averages may accidentally remain the same while counts and weighted summaries change. Aggregate each relation to the intended grain before combining independent one-to-many histories.

Check uniqueness of decision_id in the final result. Compare counts of eligible event identities as well as numerical summaries, and retain a versioned feature definition so a changed rule is not silently mixed into old training sets.
interpretation: A time-correct join can still be wrong because of record multiplication.

parts.title: 8. Keep training and live feature rules aligned
paragraphs: The live service and historical query need compatible units, windows, missing-value handling and availability rules. A notebook calculation that uses a different cutoff or quietly fills missing means with zero will train a different input distribution.

Feast’s documented created-timestamp filter is one available mechanism when supported by the selected offline store and backed by a meaningful timestamp. Framework support does not decide the correct timestamp semantics or repair missing version history for us.
interpretation: Verify the deployed feature values against independently reconstructed historical examples.

parts.title: 9. A time-respecting feature does not replace an evaluation split
paragraphs: This lesson prevents one source of leakage within each row. Training and evaluation still need a split suited to the deployment question, which may involve later time periods, held-out equipment or both. Reusing related outcomes across the split can still make results look better than they will be on new work.
Keep preprocessing fitted only on the appropriate training data. The SQL table is an input to that learning process, not evidence that the entire modelling workflow is free of leakage.
interpretation: The database boundary and the model-evaluation boundary solve different problems.

parts.title: 10. Test the rows that almost belong
paragraphs: Move availability from 13:00 to exactly noon and predict that the 11:00 event becomes eligible. Move an event to exactly the decision cutoff and predict that it stays excluded. Add a second decision for the same pump and calculate its boundaries independently.
These changes test the information the model was allowed to have. They are more revealing than checking only whether the base mean happens to equal twenty.
interpretation: A useful historical feature test states both what entered and why other plausible-looking evidence stayed out.

quiz.prompt: What must be considered before assigning a negative label?
options: Whether the outcome window and observation coverage are complete
Whether the current feature mean is low
Whether the SQL query has an ORDER BY
quiz.because: No observed failure in an incomplete horizon is not automatically a confirmed negative.

given.data: The label is failure within seven days, but the dataset ends two days after a decision with no recorded failure.

quiz.prompt: An event-time predicate alone can reliably reconstruct the original served value.
quiz.because: Reconstructing historical knowledge requires the value versions and their actual availability.

given.data: The source overwrote an old reading with a correction received after the decision. No original value history remains.

practice.title: Build features using only what each decision could know
practice.question: Build features using only what each decision could know
task: For each decisions row, average measurements.value from the same asset whose event_at is in the preceding 24 hours, including the lower bound and excluding cutoff. Require available_at <= cutoff.
Return decision_id, feature_mean and n, counting eligible event IDs. Preserve decisions with no eligible measurements as NULL mean and zero count. Order by decision_id.
practice.starter: SELECT decision_id, asset_id, cutoff FROM decisions ORDER BY decision_id;
practice.solution:
SELECT d.decision_id, AVG(m.value) AS feature_mean, COUNT(m.event_id) AS n
FROM decisions AS d LEFT JOIN measurements AS m
  ON m.asset_id=d.asset_id
 AND m.event_at >= datetime(d.cutoff, '-24 hours')
 AND m.event_at < d.cutoff
 AND m.available_at <= d.cutoff
GROUP BY d.decision_id ORDER BY d.decision_id;
hints: Keep the time restrictions in the left join’s ON condition.
Both event time and availability time are checked against each decision’s cutoff.
Count event_id rather than the unmatched placeholder.

title: What Does One Equipment Record Promise?
blurb: A column called cost can hold cents, pounds or an unexplained string. Give the maintenance team a table whose identities and units mean the same thing on every row.
openingTitle: P7 Is an Identifier. Why Did the Import Treat It as a Measurement?
opening: Botie receives a spreadsheet of equipment. One file uses asset labels, another uses row positions, and the cost column has no unit. We can write a SELECT over those values, but it cannot decide what the authors meant.
A schema records what a row represents and what its fields promise. We will design an equipment table, then use the database to reject records that violate that promise.

history.title: Keeping the Meaning of a Record Separate from Its Storage
blocks: Codd’s 1970 paper argued for a relational description of data that did not make users depend on physical storage arrangements. A logical table needs a stable interpretation even when the database changes how it stores its rows. Our equipment register uses that distinction: an asset identity should survive a new sort order or index.

SQLite later made a deliberate choice to support flexible value typing. Its STRICT table option, introduced in version 3.37.0 in 2021, provides stronger type enforcement for applications that want it. The browser exercises use SQLite 3.39-compatible syntax and make those dialect choices explicit.

reading.experimentTitle: Which incoming records fit the declared fields?
reading.experimentIntro: Connect the field contract before deciding which record IDs need repair.
reading.connectionTitle: A schema makes the row’s meaning testable
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Create the equipment register
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Decide what each column means before picking a type
intuition.explanation: One row represents one equipment asset, including retired assets.

scene.caption: An identifier can contain digits without being a quantity to average.

parts.title: 1. Choose the row’s grain and identity
paragraphs: Our equipment table has one row per asset. A visit table would instead have one row per visit. Putting several visits into extra columns on an equipment row would mix those grains and make another visit require a schema change.

Choose a key that identifies the asset across imports. A spreadsheet row number changes when rows are sorted. A serial number may be a useful natural key if the business guarantees its uniqueness and stability. A generated surrogate key can provide stable internal identity while a separate unique constraint preserves a business identifier.
interpretation: A generated key does not remove the need to define which real-world duplicates are forbidden.

parts.title: 2. Write the unit into the contract
paragraphs: Cost in cents can be stored as an integer when the business works in one currency and fixed minor units. A currency field is needed if that assumption changes. A temperature needs a unit and a measurement time. Neither choice follows from calling a column REAL.

Decide how unknown values differ from zero, and which values may be absent. A retired asset is still an asset, so retaining its row preserves references from earlier inspections. Our retired flag records that state without reusing its identity for another pump.
interpretation: The schema is an agreement about meaning as well as storage.

parts.title: 3. SQLite affinity is not a general type guarantee
paragraphs: In an ordinary SQLite table, a declared type usually gives the column an affinity that guides conversion. It does not generally forbid another storage class. STRICT tables narrow the allowed declared types and require compatible values, although lossless conversions may still occur.

Use TEXT for our identifiers, INTEGER for the flag and cents, and explicit NOT NULL where absence is invalid. REAL is floating point, so it does not provide exact decimal-money arithmetic. PostgreSQL has different type rules and offers NUMERIC for exact decimal quantities. Porting a schema requires reviewing those differences.
interpretation: We use STRICT here because the exercise asks the database to reject incompatible values. The workshop checks already-decoded values without simulating SQLite conversion.

examples.title: Give a small asset register declared types
paragraphs: Create one row and ask SQLite how it stored its values.
interpretation: The identifier remains text while cents remain an integer. Type still does not tell us which currency the cents represent.

parts.title: 4. Declare the complete table
paragraphs: CREATE TABLE lists each column and its constraints. PRIMARY KEY identifies a row; NOT NULL forbids a missing required field. CHECK adds the domain rule that the retired flag is either zero or one and that cost is nonnegative.

SQLite has historical exceptions around nullable primary keys in ordinary rowid tables. Use explicit NOT NULL for portable intent rather than depending on that behaviour. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY has special rowid behaviour in SQLite and can generate an ID when NULL is inserted. Our text asset key is supplied by the application.
interpretation: Use an explicit INSERT column list. It documents the mapping and makes later schema changes less likely to reorder values silently.

parts.title: 5. Inspect a schema instead of guessing it
paragraphs: PRAGMA table_info(equipment) reports declared columns in SQLite, while sqlite_schema contains schema definitions. Other engines provide information_schema or their own catalogues. These are useful when diagnosing an import that worked against an older schema.

CREATE TABLE AS SELECT can be convenient for an analytical copy, but it does not preserve the original table’s keys and constraints in SQLite. A copied dataset and a durable application table can therefore have very different guarantees even when their visible rows match.
interpretation: The challenge tests future inserts as well as the initial displayed rows.

parts.title: 6. Treat schema changes as data changes
paragraphs: Adding a required field to a populated table raises a question: what value belongs on existing rows? A default is only appropriate when it represents a defensible meaning. Inventing zero to satisfy NOT NULL can corrupt later analysis.

Plan a migration that adds or rebuilds the structure, converts and checks existing data, and updates readers and writers in a controlled order. Keep a recovery path and test with representative old records. A fresh empty exercise database avoids deployment concerns; it does not demonstrate a safe migration on a live service.
interpretation: Botie can now reject an incompatible record, but we still need rules connecting one table to another.

quiz.because: Matching data does not establish matching schema guarantees.

quiz.prompt: The type declaration alone guarantees exact decimal-money arithmetic.

title: Can a Job Refer to a Pump We Have Never Recorded?
blurb: A row can have the right types and still contain an impossible reference. Put identity, domain and relationship rules at the database boundary.
openingTitle: The Job Exists, but Its Asset Does Not
opening: The maintenance team opens an inspection for P99. The job has a valid-looking ID and duration, but P99 is absent from the equipment register. A later join quietly loses the job.

We need the database to preserve the relationship while accepting writes from every application that uses it. Constraints make those rules part of the table rather than a convention in one import script.

history.title: Preserving Relationships Across Several Writers
blocks: Relational tables let records be connected through values instead of application-specific pointers. That independence makes relationship rules important: any writer can otherwise introduce a child record whose parent is absent. Foreign keys put that relationship check in the database.

SQLite’s documentation records foreign-key enforcement beginning in version 3.6.19 in 2009. It must be enabled for each connection in the configuration used here. The browser runner enables it before executing your statements. Merely seeing REFERENCES in a schema is insufficient evidence that a particular connection enforces it.

reading.experimentIntro: Check duration and parent identity together, then retain the failing job IDs.
reading.connectionTitle: A valid field can still point to a missing parent
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Protect job records with constraints
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Different constraints answer different questions

records.label: CHECK
cells: Is duration in the allowed domain?

scene.caption: A positive duration does not establish an asset reference.

parts.title: 1. Let the database check every writer
paragraphs: A form can validate an asset ID, but a batch importer may bypass the form. A constraint checks the data at the shared write boundary. It also protects against two writers that both passed a preliminary application check before either committed.

Keep friendly validation in the interface so users can repair mistakes. Treat database constraint failures as expected error outcomes too. The interface cannot safely assume that the state remained unchanged between its first check and its write.
interpretation: The database rejects the violating change; the application still needs to explain which request failed.

parts.title: 2. Separate missing values from invalid values
paragraphs: A CHECK expression rejects a row when it evaluates to false. An unknown result from NULL does not act like false in this setting. CHECK(minutes >= 0) therefore needs NOT NULL when every job must have a duration.

A UNIQUE constraint handles duplicate keys, but null treatment varies by dialect and declaration. Specify the intended null policy separately. Our job IDs and asset references must always exist, so both are explicitly not null.
interpretation: A constraint is a precise predicate. Read its NULL behaviour rather than relying on the wording of the column name.

parts.title: 3. Make the parent key explicit
paragraphs: REFERENCES assets(id) connects the child’s asset_id to the parent’s declared unique identity. Insert the parent before an immediately checked child. The child column’s type and representation should match the identifier contract.

The SQLite runner enables PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON before starting learner work. Changing this pragma inside an active transaction does not enable enforcement for that transaction. Production connections need deliberate initialisation and a verification check.
interpretation: A foreign key establishes existence. It does not establish that the current user is allowed to use that asset.

examples.title: Attach an inspection to an existing asset
examples.setup: CREATE TABLE assets(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL); INSERT INTO assets VALUES('P7'),('P8');
paragraphs: The child row stores the parent identity once.
interpretation: The join can resolve the reference because the parent was inserted first.

parts.title: 4. Decide what deleting a parent should mean
paragraphs: Deleting an asset with historical jobs may need to be forbidden. ON DELETE RESTRICT expresses that policy here. CASCADE can be appropriate when dependent rows have no independent meaning, but it can also erase useful history if chosen casually.

SET NULL requires a nullable child reference and changes the meaning of the relationship. Often an equipment register should mark an asset retired rather than delete it. Choose based on the records’ lifetimes and audit requirements.
interpretation: A referential action is a business decision that the database executes automatically.

parts.title: 5. Some rules involve more than one row
paragraphs: A row-level CHECK can validate minutes or a status. Rules such as one active assignment per asset may need a unique or partial unique index. More complex cross-row conditions can require carefully designed transactions or triggers.

Do not hide a lookup of another table inside an apparently local check and assume every future change will revalidate it. Use the database mechanisms whose enforcement scope matches the invariant. PostgreSQL and SQLite differ in supported forms, so inspect the chosen dialect.
interpretation: Constraints are strongest when their intended scope is easy to state and test.

parts.title: 6. Test the rejected writes as well as the accepted one
paragraphs: The exercise inserts one valid job, then its tests try a missing parent, a duplicate key, a negative duration and a null duration. Each failure reveals a different missing constraint.

After a failed statement, inspect transaction state before deciding whether to continue or roll back. Engines and conflict policies differ. Our test harness isolates each attempted invalid insert in a savepoint so a rejection does not contaminate the next test.
interpretation: A display containing one good row cannot prove that the next bad row will be rejected.
