title: Why Must a Pump Move Be Edited on Every Job?
blurb: Repeated asset details make updates disagree. Find which identity determines each fact and give that fact one deliberate home.
openingTitle: P7 Is in Two Places According to the Same Database
opening: The maintenance spreadsheet repeats each pump’s model and site on every job. When P7 moves, one row is updated and another still says the old site. Which row should Botie trust?
We can separate facts about an asset from facts about an inspection. The useful question is what determines each value, not how many tables we can create.

history.title: Reducing Facts That Have to Be Updated Together
blocks: Relational design made it possible to describe data independently of a file’s arrangement. It also raised a design problem: several table layouts can represent the same apparent facts while behaving differently under updates. Work on dependencies and normal forms addressed those redundancies.

Our repeated pump-site example shows an update anomaly directly. Splitting the records helps only if the decomposition preserves the facts and supports the rules the application must enforce. A smaller table is not automatically a better design.

reading.experimentTitle: Which asset has conflicting site facts?
reading.experimentIntro: Group site values by asset identity, check whether each group has one value, and retain the conflicting IDs.
reading.connectionTitle: Use dependencies to choose where a fact belongs
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Separate assets from their jobs
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: The same asset fact appears on several job rows
intuition.explanation: A site update changes only one repeated copy.

scene.caption: If the table means current site, the two P7 rows disagree. If it means site at inspection time, the differing sites may be correct and need explicit timestamps.

parts.title: 1. First decide whether the repeated fact means now or then
paragraphs: An asset’s current site belongs to its current register entry. Its site at the time of an inspection is a historical fact about that event. Moving an asset should not rewrite history.

We assume the repeated site column in this lesson means current site. That makes its disagreement a problem. If the intended meaning were site at inspection, the design would need an event-time snapshot or a versioned history instead. Normalisation cannot resolve an ambiguous business definition for us.
interpretation: Name the temporal meaning before deciding whether values are redundant.

parts.title: 2. A determinant identifies the dependent fact
paragraphs: Within our stated rules, asset_id determines model and current site. We write that dependency as asset_id → model, site. Job_id determines asset_id and minutes. These are rules about all permitted records, not claims established by a lucky small sample.

The workshop groups site values by asset ID. Several distinct values refute the current-site dependency in that sample. Finding only one value does not prove the dependency for future data; the domain contract and constraints still matter.
interpretation: A dependency explains why changing one asset fact should not require editing several unrelated job rows.

parts.title: 3. Separate the asset facts from the job facts
paragraphs: Create assets with one row per asset and jobs with one row per job. Store asset_id in jobs as a foreign key. A join reconstructs the current display when it is needed.

The exercise copies distinct consistent asset facts from flat_jobs, then copies the job-specific facts. If source rows disagree about an asset, blindly choosing MIN(site) would conceal the disagreement. Repair or quarantine the conflict before migration. A primary-key violation during the copy is a useful signal that the assumption needs investigation.
interpretation: The decomposition must reconstruct every original job without inventing combinations or losing rows.

examples.title: Observe one repeated asset fact
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE flat_jobs(job_id TEXT,asset_id TEXT,model TEXT,site TEXT,minutes INTEGER);
INSERT INTO flat_jobs VALUES('J1','P7','M2','north',20),('J2','P7','M2','north',30),('J3','P8','M3','south',15);
examples.code:
SELECT asset_id,COUNT(DISTINCT site) AS site_values
FROM flat_jobs GROUP BY asset_id ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: Group by the determinant and count distinct current-site values.
interpretation: This sample does not contradict the dependency. We still need the business rule that site means current site.

parts.title: 4. Understand the anomalies the split removes
paragraphs: An update anomaly occurs when repeated copies disagree. An insertion anomaly occurs when an asset cannot be recorded without inventing a job to hold it. A deletion anomaly occurs when removing its final job also removes the only record of the asset.
Separate asset and job tables address those problems in this example. The asset can exist before its first job and after its last one. Its current model and site have one maintained location.
interpretation: The benefit is clearer ownership of facts, not a ritual of splitting every column into a table.

parts.title: 5. Use normal forms to examine dependencies
paragraphs: First normal form asks for a relation with values in the chosen domains rather than repeating groups of job columns. With a composite key, second normal form addresses non-key facts depending on only part of that key. Third normal form also addresses inappropriate transitive dependencies; its formal condition allows a dependency when its determinant is a superkey or its dependent attribute is prime. Boyce-Codd normal form requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey.

For our job table, asset_id is not the job key, yet it determines current site. Moving site into assets removes that dependency from jobs. Complex schemas need candidate keys and all relevant dependencies before a normal-form claim is justified.
interpretation: Do not infer a normal form merely by counting tables or noticing an integer primary key.

parts.title: 6. Can the separated tables reconstruct the same facts?
paragraphs: Imagine splitting a job into one table containing job_id and asset_id, and another containing job_id and minutes. If job_id is unique in both, joining on it can reconstruct the original job. If we instead join tables using a repeated status such as open, unrelated jobs can combine and invent records. This is why a decomposition needs a lossless join, not merely fewer repeated words.

For our assets/jobs split, the shared asset_id identifies one asset row. Each job therefore finds exactly its own asset facts, provided the foreign key is enforced. Also ask whether the original dependencies can still be checked in the new tables. A decomposition that requires a large join to enforce a common write rule may introduce a practical cost even if it removes redundancy.
interpretation: Reconstructing the current sample is a useful test. Keys and dependencies explain why reconstruction remains correct for future permitted records.

parts.title: 7. Denormalise for a measured purpose
paragraphs: An analytical feature table can deliberately repeat asset information to avoid repeated joins or to freeze a training snapshot. Document who builds that table, when it refreshes, and which source/version it represents.

A derived snapshot should not become another independently edited source of truth. Materialised views, caches and warehouse tables need refresh and reconciliation rules. The cost of repetition is acceptable when its maintenance and temporal meaning are explicit.
interpretation: The later feature and incremental lessons connect this design decision to reproducible model data.

title: Change the Requested Jobs Without Rewriting the Rest
blurb: New inspections arrive, existing ones change, and cancelled drafts leave the queue. Give each write a precise target and preserve newer information.
openingTitle: One Status Change Updated the Entire Queue
opening: Botie was asked to close J1. An UPDATE without a WHERE condition closed every job. The SQL was valid, but its target set was wrong.

Writing data requires the same care about row selection as reading it, with a more consequential result. We will add new jobs, accept newer revisions, and delete only the cancelled empty drafts specified by the policy.

history.title: Describing a Set of Rows to Change
blocks: The early SEQUEL work described composable operations over tabular data. That set-oriented approach also means an update can target many records at once. The useful question becomes which rows satisfy the write’s predicate.

Modern dialects add ways to handle duplicate identities during insertion. SQLite’s UPSERT follows PostgreSQL-style ON CONFLICT syntax, with its own details. Our revision rule is an application policy layered on that mechanism; the database does not know which imported status is newer unless we specify it.

reading.experimentTitle: Does the update preserve unselected jobs?
reading.experimentIntro: Select the intended records, replace their fields, then merge them back by identity.
reading.connectionTitle: A write is a selection followed by an effect
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Merge newer job revisions
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Keep selection visible before applying a change
intuition.explanation: Closing the chosen job should not alter the other records.

rows.label: Original queue
items: J1 open; J2 open; J3 done

rows.label: Merge by ID
items: J1 done; J2 open; J3 done

scene.caption: Previewing a selector helps inspection; a live transaction still needs protection against concurrent changes.

parts.title: 1. Inspect the set you intend to change
paragraphs: Start with a SELECT using the same intended predicate. Include the primary key and fields that will change. Check whether zero, one or several rows would be expected.

A preview is useful evidence, but another writer can change data after the preview. Keep critical preconditions in the actual UPDATE or DELETE, and use transactions or version checks when the operation depends on previously read state.
interpretation: A WHERE condition is part of the business operation, not optional punctuation.

parts.title: 2. Insert with an explicit field mapping
paragraphs: INSERT INTO jobs(id,status,minutes,revision) names the destination fields. VALUES adds literal records; INSERT ... SELECT copies records calculated from another table. Constraints apply to the resulting rows in both cases.
An omitted field may receive a default. Explicit NULL has a different meaning from asking for that default. Avoid inserting a full row positionally when schema changes could reorder the fields.
interpretation: The incoming table is a staging area. Its rows are proposals until the application’s conflict policy accepts them.

parts.title: 3. Update selected rows from their current values
paragraphs: UPDATE jobs SET minutes = minutes + 5 WHERE id = ... expresses an increment relative to the stored value. Fetching a value into the application, adding there, then writing the result can lose a concurrent update.

For status changes, include the expected state when the transition requires one. Check affected-row counts in the application and treat an unexpected zero as a conflict or missing record, rather than announcing success.
interpretation: The concurrency lesson will make an expected version part of the predicate.

examples.title: Close one selected job
examples.code:
UPDATE jobs SET status='done' WHERE id='J1' AND status='open';
SELECT id,status FROM jobs ORDER BY id;
paragraphs: The predicate leaves other jobs alone.
interpretation: The displayed IDs make the target set visible.

parts.title: 4. Handle repeated identities with an explicit policy
paragraphs: UPSERT handles a uniqueness conflict during insertion. excluded names the proposed row in SQLite’s DO UPDATE clause. Our rule accepts it only if its revision is greater than the stored revision. An older arrival therefore cannot overwrite a newer status.

SQLite INSERT ... SELECT may need a WHERE clause before ON CONFLICT to disambiguate its parser; WHERE true is sufficient when no source filtering is needed. An equal revision with different content is a source-contract error to quarantine, not a reason to pick whichever arrival happened last.
interpretation: ON CONFLICT handles uniqueness conflicts. It does not excuse violated foreign keys or CHECK constraints.

parts.title: 5. A replacement is not always an update
paragraphs: SQLite INSERT OR REPLACE can delete a conflicting row before inserting a replacement. That can interact with references and other database behaviour differently from updating selected fields. Use a deliberate UPSERT when the intended operation is an update.

Our delete policy removes only cancelled jobs with zero minutes. A completed inspection is historical data and remains. Hard deletion, soft deletion and retention rules need to match the records’ purpose.
interpretation: Never use a convenient conflict keyword without checking which effect it actually performs.

parts.title: 6. Make repeated delivery predictable
paragraphs: A source can replay the same batch after a failure. A stable primary key and revision comparison make our merge leave the same final rows on a replay. Repeating an unconditional increment would instead add the value again.

Idempotency belongs to the operation’s semantics. It is not a property of every SQL statement. Use operation identities for repeated business effects and keep the transaction boundary aligned with what the application reports as committed.
interpretation: The last lesson will combine this merge with a durable ingestion checkpoint.

parts.title: 7. Review write results before reporting success
paragraphs: RETURNING can expose changed rows in supported dialects, including the SQLite version used here. An application can also inspect affected-row counts and query the committed result. Choose the method that fits the driver and transaction policy.

Keep errors visible. Do not catch every constraint failure and announce that the batch succeeded. If a batch deliberately quarantines rejected rows, record which ones failed and why so the import can be reconciled.
interpretation: The challenge’s final SELECT is a visible result. Its tests also replay data and add records the original example did not contain.

quiz.prompt: Which merge rule avoids applying the same revision again?
options: Update only where incoming revision is greater
Increment every stored duration on every arrival
Delete every row before each insert
quiz.because: The newer-version predicate makes replayed records no-ops under the stated source contract.

given.data: The same batch is delivered twice. Its stable IDs and revisions are unchanged.

quiz.prompt: It is always equivalent to updating a few selected fields.
quiz.because: Replacement can delete the conflicting row before insertion, so its effects differ.

given.data: SQLite INSERT OR REPLACE is used for a row referenced elsewhere.

title: Move Spare Parts Without Losing Half the Transfer
blurb: A transfer changes two stock balances and its audit record. Make those changes one unit of work, and learn what a rollback can actually undo.
openingTitle: The Parts Left the North Store but Never Reached the South Store
opening: Botie subtracts three replacement seals from the north store. The next statement fails before the south store is updated. The database now describes missing stock even though the intended transfer was one operation.

A transaction gives these related changes a boundary. We can publish them together or abandon the database changes together. We will also use a savepoint to undo an optional part of a larger operation.

history.title: Making a Business Operation Survive a Failure
blocks: Transaction-processing research addressed operations whose meaning spanned several low-level writes. Jim Gray’s 1981 paper described the transaction concept and its limitations. The problem was practical: interruptions should not leave half of an intended database operation visible as a completed result.

Our spare-parts transfer is an invented example of that boundary. It updates database records only. Sending a delivery truck or an email involves another system whose effects are not automatically reversed by a SQL rollback.

reading.experimentTitle: Would the complete transfer leave valid balances?
reading.experimentIntro: Stage both changes, check the resulting balances, then select all staged rows or all original rows.
reading.connectionTitle: Treat the related database changes as one decision
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Commit a valid stock transfer
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: The intended operation changes both stores
intuition.explanation: A transfer should preserve the total stock in this example.

scene.caption: The middle row is an incomplete business operation, even though each written value is a valid integer.

parts.title: 1. Choose the transaction’s business boundary
paragraphs: The transfer consists of validating the request, recording it, subtracting source stock and adding destination stock. Committing only the subtraction would report a result the business never intended.

Keep the boundary as small as possible while preserving that invariant. Long transactions can hold resources and delay other writers. Avoid waiting for a person or an unrelated network call while a transaction is open.
interpretation: A transaction boundary follows the operation’s meaning, not an arbitrary number of statements.

parts.title: 2. Separate atomicity from the rest of correctness
paragraphs: Atomicity concerns all-or-nothing database effects. Consistency means the transaction should preserve declared invariants; the application must still express those rules correctly. Isolation governs interaction with other transactions. Durability concerns retaining committed changes under the database’s documented configuration and failure assumptions.
A transaction containing an incorrect unrestricted UPDATE can commit perfectly and still damage every row. Transactions do not discover the intended predicate or business policy.
interpretation: We will study isolation separately because concurrent work creates failures that a single-session example cannot display.

parts.title: 3. Use BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK deliberately
paragraphs: BEGIN starts the explicit unit. COMMIT publishes its successful database changes. ROLLBACK abandons its uncommitted changes. The SQL worksheet does not automatically commit between your statements, so these boundaries can be exercised directly.

Driver defaults matter outside the worksheet. Python sqlite3 versions and connection settings affect implicit transactions, and executescript has special transaction behaviour. Read the driver contract and keep application exception handling responsible for rolling back a failed unit.
interpretation: A failed statement does not necessarily roll back every earlier statement in the transaction. Check the engine and conflict policy.

parts.title: 4. Mark an optional part with a savepoint
paragraphs: A savepoint names a position within the current work. ROLLBACK TO returns to that position while keeping the savepoint active; RELEASE removes the savepoint boundary. Releasing an inner savepoint is not the same as durably committing the outer transaction.
This is useful when an optional batch item may be abandoned while the application deliberately keeps earlier valid work. It should not hide a failure that invalidates the whole business operation.
interpretation: Nested BEGIN transactions are not how SQLite provides this behaviour.

examples.title: Undo a tentative stock adjustment
paragraphs: Only the edit after the savepoint is abandoned.
interpretation: The north adjustment preceded the savepoint. The tentative south value did not survive rollback to it.

parts.title: 5. Keep validation and its writes in the same unit
paragraphs: The challenge has exactly one proposed transfer and an initially empty transfers table. It first inserts an audit row only if both stores exist, the amount is positive, the stores differ and the source has enough stock. Both stock updates then follow that accepted row.

A live multi-writer implementation also needs a concurrency strategy. For SQLite a deliberately acquired write transaction may be appropriate; PostgreSQL can use row locks or carefully designed conditional updates. A read performed outside the write transaction is not a reservation of stock.
interpretation: The browser fixture demonstrates a transaction’s logical effects, not simultaneous users or crash recovery.

parts.title: 6. A rollback has a boundary too
paragraphs: A database rollback cannot unsend a message already accepted by another service. If a committed transfer must trigger an external message, an outbox record written in the same database transaction can support reliable later delivery. The delivery process still needs deduplication and recovery.
A cancellation after commit requires a new compensating business operation when reversal is allowed. Preserve the audit trail instead of claiming the original transfer never occurred.
interpretation: Treat a commit result that was lost over a connection as an uncertain outcome to reconcile, rather than blindly repeating a consequential operation.

quiz.prompt: What does RELEASE establish here?
options: The savepoint is removed; the outer transaction still controls commit
Every earlier database write is durably committed
The entire outer transaction was rolled back
quiz.because: Releasing an inner savepoint does not commit the outer transaction.

given.data: An outer transaction contains SAVEPOINT extra, an optional write, ROLLBACK TO extra, and RELEASE extra.

quiz.prompt: Its uncommitted database changes should not become a successful partial transfer.
quiz.because: That is the intended atomic boundary, subject to the database’s guarantees.

given.data: A database transaction is rolled back before commit and its only effects were database writes.

practice.title: Can both stores agree on one accepted transfer?
practice.question: Can both stores agree on one accepted transfer?
task: The setup has one request and an empty transfers table. Within one explicit transaction, record the transfer only when amount is positive, source differs from destination, both stores exist and the source has enough units. Apply both stock changes only for that accepted transfer. Commit, then return stock id and units ordered by id. An invalid request must leave both stock and transfers unchanged.

title: What If Someone Changes the Job While Botie Is Reading It?
blurb: Two valid edits can overwrite each other. Make stale assumptions visible, and distinguish version checks from the database’s isolation guarantees.
openingTitle: The Second Save Quietly Erased the First Edit
opening: Two technicians read J1 at version 4. One assigns a replacement specialist and saves version 5. The other closes the earlier copy, unaware that the job changed. A blind save can overwrite work that happened after the read.
We will first use an expected version to reject a stale edit. Then we will examine what snapshots, write locks and isolation levels can guarantee in a real database.

history.title: Coordinating Readers and Writers Without Losing Work
blocks: Shared databases needed to coordinate transactions whose operations overlapped. Locking and multi-version approaches provide different ways to control which state a transaction can observe and change. These mechanisms developed to support concurrent applications, long before a model could issue SQL.

SQLite and PostgreSQL expose different concurrency models. SQLite serialises writers, while WAL mode lets readers keep an earlier snapshot as a writer commits. PostgreSQL offers several isolation levels with their own anomaly and retry rules. Our one-connection exercise illustrates an optimistic version predicate, not either engine’s full scheduler.

reading.experimentTitle: Does the edit still match the version it was based on?
reading.experimentIntro: Compare the proposal with the stored version before applying its replacement status.
reading.connectionTitle: Keep stale assumptions in the write predicate
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Apply an optimistic version check
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Two edits began from the same record
intuition.explanation: A later save must notice that its original view is old.

scene.caption: The version mismatch asks the second editor to reload and reconsider the change.

parts.title: 1. A read is an observation, not a reservation
paragraphs: Reading a row tells the application what was visible at that moment under its transaction rules. Another transaction may commit before the application writes. A user thinking about an edit can make that gap quite long.

Carry the observed version with the proposed change. The application should explain a conflict and show the current state when the version no longer matches. Automatically reapplying the old decision can be wrong even if the SQL is retried successfully.
interpretation: The conflict concerns the meaning of the edit, not merely a temporary database error.

parts.title: 2. Put the expected version in the UPDATE
paragraphs: Match both the primary key and expected version in the same UPDATE predicate. If it matches, update the fields and increment the version. A stale proposal affects zero rows. The application must inspect that outcome instead of reporting a successful save.

This protects against a lost update for cooperating writers that follow the version protocol. It does not independently enforce a condition involving several different rows. Every write path that can change the relevant state must maintain the version.
interpretation: The version is a concurrency token. It need not be a timestamp, and clock ordering is unnecessary for this comparison.

parts.title: 3. Try a successful edit and then replay the stale one
paragraphs: The supplied edit expects version 4. The first application of the statement can produce version 5. Replaying the same proposal must leave version 5 untouched because the expectation is still 4.

An application that wants another edit obtains the new record and creates a new deliberate proposal. It should not silently replace expected_version with whatever is current just to make the UPDATE succeed.
interpretation: The exercise has one edit row. The key and version predicate generalise when the driver binds a different proposal.

examples.title: A stale editor cannot close the changed job
paragraphs: Change the stored version first, then apply the old expected version.
interpretation: The old proposal matched no row. The other job also remains untouched.

parts.title: 4. What SQLite serialises
paragraphs: SQLite permits only one writer at a time. Its journal mode affects reader/writer interaction: WAL readers can keep a snapshot while a writer commits. A read transaction may be unable to upgrade to a writer when its snapshot is no longer current.

BEGIN IMMEDIATE requests the write transaction earlier and can fail when another writer holds it. It does not make multiple SQLite writers execute their writes simultaneously. Set bounded busy handling and keep transactions short. The in-browser worksheet uses one isolated connection, so it cannot demonstrate real lock contention.
interpretation: Sequentially replaying a stale edit is a controlled illustration of an application precondition, not a concurrency benchmark.

parts.title: 5. What PostgreSQL isolation levels change
paragraphs: At PostgreSQL Read Committed, a statement reads a snapshot established for that statement, with documented rules for concurrent updates. Repeatable Read gives a transaction a stable snapshot but still permits some anomalies that Serializable prevents. Serializable execution may reject a transaction so that the application retries the complete unit.

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE can lock selected rows when pessimistic coordination is appropriate. It does not automatically lock every possible future row that could satisfy an arbitrary business rule. Choose the isolation and locking strategy from the invariant, and test the exact interleaving that could break it.
interpretation: A generic claim that transactions prevent all races hides the isolation level that actually governs them.

parts.title: 6. One row version cannot protect a rule across several rows
paragraphs: Suppose two engineers must never both leave the on-call rota. Each reads a snapshot showing the other still on call, then updates only their own row to off call. Both individual row versions can match even though their combined result breaks the rota rule. This is a write-skew pattern: the writes affect different rows, but both decisions relied on a shared condition.

Protect the condition at the database boundary. Depending on the engine and schema, the solution can use a common row that competing decisions lock, a suitable constraint, or serializable transactions with retry handling. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read uses snapshot isolation and can permit serialization anomalies of this kind; Serializable can reject a conflicting execution instead. SQLite permits one writer at a time, but an application that reads outside its eventual write transaction can still act on stale decisions. The transaction boundary is part of the design.
interpretation: Our versioned job edit solves a single-row stale overwrite. It does not claim to enforce every rule involving a set of jobs.

parts.title: 7. Retry the whole decision when its read assumptions changed
paragraphs: A serialization failure can require retrying the transaction from the beginning with fresh reads. Repeating only the final UPDATE preserves stale calculations. Keep retries bounded and make external effects replay-safe.

For an optimistic user-edit conflict, asking the user to reconcile may be preferable to automatic retry. Record the conflict and current state. Avoid a loop that continually overwrites newer work until one write finally succeeds.
interpretation: The next lessons improve query cost; they should preserve these correctness requirements while changing execution plans.

quiz.prompt: What does a correct retry generally need?
options: Repeat the transaction’s decision with fresh reads
Retry only its last statement using old calculations
quiz.because: The invalidated assumptions may come from earlier reads in the unit.

given.data: A PostgreSQL Serializable transaction fails because its reads and writes conflict with concurrent work.

quiz.prompt: Its sequential version-check exercise proves how a live multi-user server schedules transactions.
quiz.because: It illustrates the predicate only. Live isolation and contention require separate multi-connection tests.

title: Find One Pump’s Readings Without Checking Every Pump
blurb: The reading table keeps growing. Arrange useful lookup keys so the database can find a small candidate region, then account for the cost of maintaining that structure.
openingTitle: Why Read Every Sensor Record to Find P7’s Morning?
opening: The team asks for P7’s readings within a short time range. The table also contains years of measurements from other assets. Checking every row works, but the work grows with data the question does not need.
An index keeps an additional structure organised by selected values. We will examine what its ordering makes easy, then create a composite index without changing the query’s answer.

history.title: Letting the Database Choose an Access Path

sources.title: Selinger and colleagues: Access path selection, 1979

blocks: SQL lets a caller describe desired records without specifying their physical traversal. System R’s 1979 access-path paper described choosing routes for queries, including joins. Indexes provide candidate routes that the optimiser can compare with reading a table.

Our pump-and-time example gives a physical intuition: equal leading keys occupy a region of an ordered index. The widget lays out records directly; it does not implement database pages, B-tree balancing or disk I/O.

reading.experimentTitle: Which records occupy the selected index prefix?
reading.experimentIntro: Order records by the declared keys, find the leading-key region, then expose the candidate IDs.
reading.connectionTitle: The key order determines which region is contiguous
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Add an index for an asset’s time range
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Compare two useful orderings
intuition.explanation: Both contain the same records. Their leading key groups different questions together.

records.label: asset, time
cells: One asset then a time range

records.label: time, asset
cells: Filtering one asset inside that range

scene.caption: An index is an additional access structure. It does not change the table’s logical row set.

parts.title: 1. An index stores a route back to the records
paragraphs: A typical B-tree index arranges key values so a search can narrow to a relevant region rather than inspect every table row. Leaf entries connect that region to stored row identities or values, depending on the database and index structure.
The database must still retrieve or verify the requested data. If most rows match, a sequential scan can be cheaper. Small tables may also favour scanning because an index lookup adds overhead.
interpretation: The existence of an index does not require the optimiser to use it.

parts.title: 2. Read a composite index from its leading key
paragraphs: For an index on asset_id, recorded_at, rows for one asset are grouped before their times are ordered. Equality on the asset and a time range can therefore narrow a contiguous region.

A condition on a later column alone does not generally provide the same direct leading-prefix lookup. Some engines can use additional strategies such as skip scans, so avoid the absolute claim that later columns can never help. Inspect the chosen plan for the actual database and data.
interpretation: Choose the index order from recurring predicates and ordering needs, not alphabetical column names.

parts.title: 3. Keep a range predicate usable by the index
paragraphs: A direct range on recorded_at lets an ordinary index on that column represent the bounds. Wrapping it in a function can prevent that particular access path unless an appropriate expression index or optimiser transformation applies. This property is often called sargability: whether a predicate can be used as a search argument.

Use a half-open time interval with an inclusive start and exclusive end when that matches the domain. It avoids inventing the last fraction of a second in a day. Our fixture uses consistently formatted date text; mixed offsets or formats require a stronger time representation.
interpretation: An efficient rewrite must return the same boundary records as the original intended question.

examples.title: Create the lookup order and inspect its columns
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE readings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,asset_id TEXT NOT NULL,recorded_at TEXT NOT NULL,value REAL NOT NULL);

parts.title: 4. An index can also cover a result
paragraphs: If an index contains all values needed by a query, an engine may avoid some visits to the base table. Such a covering access path trades additional index size and write maintenance for less reading. The exact columns implicitly available depend on the database and table structure.

Do not append every column to every index. Measure representative queries and inspect whether table lookups are a real cost. Sensitive columns in duplicated storage also remain part of the data-management responsibility.
interpretation: Covering is a property of an index relative to a query, not a universal property of the index name.

parts.title: 5. Every write maintains the additional structure
paragraphs: Inserts add index entries, deletes remove them, and updates to indexed values move or replace entries. Indexes consume space and can increase write latency. Several overlapping indexes may provide little extra value while multiplying that cost.
Uniqueness indexes also enforce correctness and cannot be discarded merely because one read benchmark is faster without them. Review constraints and workload together before changing an index set.
interpretation: Read optimisation and invariant enforcement can share a structure while serving different purposes.

parts.title: 6. Verify with the plan and a representative workload
paragraphs: Create the candidate index, confirm that answers remain correct, then inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in SQLite. Use representative row counts and value distributions when measuring. A four-row exercise is useful for syntax and semantics but cannot establish production speed.

Database statistics help the optimiser estimate selectivity. Keep their maintenance appropriate to the engine and version, and investigate skewed values separately. The next lesson compares planned work and observed work without treating either as a promise.
interpretation: The challenge tests the index’s declared key order and query results. It does not demand an unstable exact plan string.

title: Why Does a Short Query Repeat So Much Work?
blurb: A compact query can scan the same table repeatedly. Read the access plan, preserve the answer, and compare work on data that resembles the real job.
openingTitle: Botie Counts the Entire Visit Table Again for Each Pump
opening: The report needs visit counts and minutes for every asset. A convenient query asks two correlated subqueries for every asset. With a small register that looks harmless; a growing visit history can make the repeated work expensive.

We will group the visit data once at the required grain and join it to the register. The larger lesson is how to inspect a plan and test a rewrite without confusing a shorter SQL statement with a faster or correct one.

history.title: Choosing Work from a Declarative Request
blocks: The System R work showed how a database could choose access paths for a declarative request instead of requiring the caller to prescribe every step. That freedom creates several possible plans for the same logical result. Estimating their costs depends on what the engine knows about the data.

EXPLAIN facilities make some of those choices visible. Their formats and meanings are engine-specific, and SQLite warns that its query-plan output can change. We will inspect plan structure without treating exact display text as an application API.

reading.experimentTitle: Which measured plan did less comparable work?
reading.experimentIntro: Check answer identities before counting repeated scan visits, then choose the smaller measured count.
reading.connectionTitle: A faster wrong answer is still the wrong report
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Aggregate visits before joining the register
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Repeated work can hide behind a small node
intuition.explanation: The numbers are invented scan measurements.

scene.caption: Counted row visits are one diagnostic measure. CPU, I/O, memory and elapsed time can still differ.

parts.title: 1. Read the plan as operations on rows
paragraphs: A plan describes operations such as scanning a table, searching an index, joining inputs and sorting results. Follow where rows come from and how often an operation is repeated. A nested operation can be cheap once and expensive when executed for every outer row.

SQLite’s EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN gives a high-level tree. Its SCAN and SEARCH descriptions help distinguish broad traversal from a constrained lookup, but interpretation depends on the chosen access path. An index scan can still visit many entries.
interpretation: The query text describes the result; the plan describes a route the engine currently chooses.

parts.title: 2. Verify the answer before measuring speed
paragraphs: Our report includes assets with zero visits. An inner join would discard them and may look faster because it returns less information. A rewritten aggregate must preserve both the row grain and the intended treatment of missing matches.

Write result tests for empty visit groups, additional assets and repeated visits. Check tie ordering only where the report requires it. Comparing a fast wrong query with a correct one is not a useful optimisation result.
interpretation: The workshop refuses a measured plan whose answer IDs differ before comparing its scan counts.

parts.title: 3. Pre-aggregate at the join grain
paragraphs: Group visits by asset_id so the derived table has one row per asset. Join that table to the asset register with LEFT JOIN, then replace missing count and minute totals with zero under this report’s policy.

A CTE names the intermediate result so its grain is easy to see. It does not universally force materialisation or guarantee that the engine scans the source only once. Optimisers can inline or transform it. Inspect the actual chosen plan rather than inferring execution from the presence of WITH.
interpretation: An appropriate index can also help a correlated query. Evaluate alternatives instead of declaring one syntactic form universally best.

examples.title: Inspect the aggregate before adding assets with no visits
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE assets(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL); INSERT INTO assets VALUES('P7'),('P8'),('P9');
CREATE TABLE visits(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,asset_id TEXT NOT NULL,minutes INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO visits VALUES(1,'P7',20),(2,'P7',30),(3,'P8',10);
examples.code:
SELECT asset_id,COUNT(*) AS visits,SUM(minutes) AS minutes
FROM visits GROUP BY asset_id ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: The intermediate result has one row per asset that appears in visits.
interpretation: P9 is absent here because it has no visit. The outer register join must restore its report row.

parts.title: 4. Distinguish estimates from observed execution
paragraphs: An optimiser estimates row counts and costs before running the query. Statistics, parameter values and correlated columns can make those estimates inaccurate. A large estimate error near the beginning of a plan can lead to poor downstream choices.

PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement and reports observations such as actual rows and loops. For a write statement, it can therefore perform writes. Use a deliberate transaction and rollback where appropriate, remembering external effects may not be reversible. SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN does not provide the same runtime analysis.
interpretation: Do not copy an ANALYZE command into a production write path as if it were a harmless formatter.

parts.title: 5. Measure representative conditions
paragraphs: Timing one warm-cache query on a tiny database tells us little about a larger workload. Compare realistic distributions, common and rare parameter values, repeated runs, and the resource pressure the service normally sees. Preserve result checks alongside timing.

Refresh or inspect database statistics when estimates look implausible. Also check temporary sorting, spilling and repeated lookups. The workshop’s row-visits metric isolates one concept; it is not an optimiser cost model or a substitute for elapsed-time and resource measurements.
interpretation: A smaller measured row count is evidence about that run, not a universal speed guarantee.

parts.title: 6. Keep a plan improvement explainable
paragraphs: Record the query version, schema/index changes, data scale and measurements used to justify an optimisation. Verify that write costs and other important queries did not regress. A new index or materialised result can move work elsewhere rather than remove it.

Plans can change after a database upgrade or a data-distribution shift. Monitor the user-visible outcome and investigate plan changes when they matter. Tests should protect query semantics and deliberate schema contracts rather than exact unstable plan text.
interpretation: The challenge accepts any equivalent report query. To inspect your route, prefix the final SELECT (including its WITH clause, if present) with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN and choose Run code. Remove that prefix before Run tests so the challenge receives report rows rather than plan rows.

title: Let a Search Value Stay a Value
blurb: A search box should select an asset, not rewrite the query or change whose records are visible. Keep values, query structure and permissions at separate boundaries.
openingTitle: An Asset Search Should Not Become a New SQL Command
opening: A technician types an asset name into a search box. The application pastes it into a SQL string. A quote in that name can change how the database reads the statement instead of remaining ordinary text.

We will bind values through the database driver, keep the tenant scope supplied by trusted application state, and expose only the fields the interface needs. The SQLite exercise demonstrates a scoped view; a deployed service also needs real database and application permissions.

history.title: Separating Query Structure from Supplied Data
blocks: Database applications needed to reuse a query while supplying different values. Driver parameter interfaces separate those values from SQL structure. That same boundary prevents a value containing SQL punctuation from being reinterpreted as part of the query when used correctly.

Database access control developed alongside shared data systems because syntactically valid queries can still access the wrong records. Parameter binding and authorisation solve different problems. Botie’s maintenance search needs both, even though our isolated browser database has no production users or server roles.

reading.experimentTitle: Does the selected asset belong to the trusted tenant?
reading.experimentIntro: Filter the record set by trusted tenant scope before matching the supplied asset value.
reading.connectionTitle: Parameter binding does not grant permission
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Expose the permitted job fields
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: Keep the source of each input visible
intuition.explanation: Two values enter the query from different trust boundaries.

scene.caption: A user-supplied tenant field cannot replace the authenticated scope simply because it is safely parameterised.

parts.title: 1. Keep a query’s shape separate from its values
paragraphs: The query structure says which table and fields are involved and how rows are filtered. The asset name is a value placed into that fixed structure. Driver placeholders preserve that distinction.

Manually adding quotation marks or escaping a few characters is easy to get wrong across dialects and encodings. Use the driver’s binding API. A parameter containing a quote or SQL-looking text is then compared as a value rather than becoming a new predicate.
interpretation: The exercise uses a local database and harmless fixture strings. It does not connect to any external service.

parts.title: 2. Trusted scope must come from the application
paragraphs: Binding tenant and asset values prevents them from changing SQL syntax. It does not prove that the caller may choose any tenant. Obtain the tenant from authenticated server-side context and enforce access again at the data boundary appropriate to the service.

Do not place database credentials in a browser worksheet or give a model unrestricted SQL access because its outputs pass a schema check. A model-generated query is still code whose available operations and data access need deliberate limits.
interpretation: The workshop shows exact record matching. It does not interpret strings as SQL commands.

parts.title: 3. Bind values through Python sqlite3
paragraphs: Python sqlite3 accepts placeholders such as ? and a separate parameter sequence. A single parameter still needs a one-item sequence. fetchall returns a list of row tuples in the requested order.

The programming exercise writes find_jobs(connection, tenant, asset). Its tenant argument represents scope already established by the caller; the function does not implement login or authorisation. The SQL string remains fixed while the parameters change.
interpretation: Placeholder spelling varies between database drivers. Follow the driver used by the application.

examples.title: A quoted identifier remains ordinary data
paragraphs: This complete local program searches for a value containing a quote.
examples.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE assets(id TEXT)")
connection.execute("INSERT INTO assets VALUES(?)", ("P'7",))
print(connection.execute("SELECT id FROM assets WHERE id = ?", ("P'7",)).fetchall())
interpretation: The quote belongs to the stored value and does not alter the SQL statement.

parts.title: 4. Identifiers need a different choice mechanism
paragraphs: A value placeholder does not generally substitute a table name, column name or sort-direction keyword. If the interface offers a sort order, map its allowed choices to known query fragments or use the driver’s supported identifier-composition API.

Do not convert an arbitrary submitted string into a column identifier and assume value binding elsewhere protects it. Keep the list of accessible fields narrow. The safe design depends on which parts are data and which parts would change executable structure.
interpretation: An allowlist chooses among known structural options. It is not an attempt to sanitise arbitrary SQL.

parts.title: 5. Expose a smaller read surface
paragraphs: Our SQL exercise creates a view containing only north’s open jobs and the fields used by the queue. It demonstrates projection and a stable predicate in one named relation. Inspecting the view makes accidental private_note inclusion easy to notice.

SQLite does not provide PostgreSQL-style server users and GRANT privileges. A local caller with direct access to this database can still read the underlying table. In a server database, appropriate roles and grants can restrict access to the view or approved operations; application checks and, where suitable, row-level security add separate controls.
interpretation: A view is not an authentication system.

examples.title: Return only the fields needed for the queue
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE jobs(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,tenant TEXT NOT NULL,asset_id TEXT NOT NULL,status TEXT NOT NULL,private_note TEXT);
INSERT INTO jobs VALUES('J1','north','P7','open','private A'),('J2','south','P8','open','private B'),('J3','north','P9','done','private C');
examples.code: SELECT id,asset_id,status FROM jobs WHERE tenant='north' AND status='open' ORDER BY id;
paragraphs: This fixed projection leaves internal notes out of the result.
interpretation: The result includes the permitted row and omits private_note. The exercise turns that relation into a named view.

parts.title: 6. Give the service only the operations it needs
paragraphs: Use separate credentials or roles for migrations, application writes and read-only reporting where the architecture supports them. A report process rarely needs permission to change schemas. Revoke unnecessary inherited or public grants and inspect effective privileges rather than only the most recent GRANT statement.

PostgreSQL row-level security can constrain visible rows under defined policies, with important ownership and privileged-role exceptions. Treat it as a configured database feature to test, not a promise made by a WHERE clause in one code path.
interpretation: The browser examples do not configure production roles or claim to demonstrate complete tenant isolation.

parts.title: 7. Bound the query even when its values are safe
paragraphs: A parameterised query can still be expensive or return too much permitted data. Apply pagination, response-size limits and bounded execution appropriate to the service. Avoid logging secrets or unnecessary row content while retaining enough identifiers to investigate access decisions.

Test a literal quote, an SQL-looking asset name, an absent asset, and the same asset ID in another tenant. Those cases check binding and scoping separately. Operational testing must additionally exercise the actual deployed role and every exposed endpoint.
interpretation: Correct syntax handling is one necessary boundary in a larger access design.

options: Map allowed choices to known column/order fragments

Paste the submitted string without restriction
quiz.because: Identifiers and keywords need deliberate structural composition rather than ordinary value binding.

quiz.because: A narrower projection needs actual access restrictions on the surrounding data surface.

title: Which Sensor Records Should Reach the Training Table?
blurb: A query can run successfully over duplicate identities, missing readings and impossible timestamps. Turn the dataset’s assumptions into visible checks before building model features.
openingTitle: The Training Query Ran, but the Input Was Wrong
opening: Botie builds a feature table without a SQL error. Later we discover a repeated sensor message, a reading linked to an absent pump and a temperature with the wrong scale. Successful query execution did not establish useful training data.

We will inspect a raw staging table, report every failed contract per reading identity, and keep rejected data available for repair. The rules are explicit so a reader can see what a clean report does and does not establish.

history.title: Checking the Facts Before Combining Them

sources.title: TensorFlow Data Validation: Detecting schema and distribution problems

blocks: Relational constraints supplied ways to keep declared identities and relationships consistent. Analytical pipelines also receive raw data that must be inspected before it is admitted to those curated tables. A staging area makes it possible to report failed records rather than losing the evidence at the first rejected insert.

Machine-learning data tools later added schema and distribution comparisons to that practice. Our SQL audit addresses selected deterministic rules for invented sensor records. It cannot establish that labels are correct or that a dataset represents the population a model will encounter.

reading.experimentTitle: Which reading identities fail the declared contract?
reading.experimentIntro: Check known assets, required readings, range and timing, then expose the failing identities.
reading.connectionTitle: A successful SELECT does not validate its inputs
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Report every reading-contract violation
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: A plausible number can still belong to a bad record
intuition.explanation: Each row carries identity and timing as well as its measured value.

records.label: Absent asset
cells: Features attach to no registered entity

scene.caption: The fixture assumes event and ingestion counters share the same clock. Real clock skew needs a documented tolerance.

parts.title: 1. Keep raw evidence separate from accepted records
paragraphs: A raw table preserves what arrived and its source identity. A curated table contains records that satisfy the declared contract after any justified transformation. A quarantine or issue table records what failed and why.

Do not silently drop failed rows and report the remaining count as if the original batch were complete. Record accepted and rejected counts, source batch IDs and the rule version. A downstream feature query should know whether a missing interval means no events or an unresolved ingestion failure.
interpretation: The audit output is part of the dataset, not an incidental debug message.

parts.title: 2. Check identity before computing aggregates
paragraphs: Duplicate event identities can count the same physical observation twice. Distinct identities with equal temperatures are different observations and should not automatically collapse. Define which source fields identify an event before applying deduplication.

A duplicate ID with conflicting payloads is a different problem from an exact replay. Choose a policy based on source revisions or quarantine the conflict. Taking the first row the database happens to return is not a reproducible rule.
interpretation: The exercise reports a duplicate identity once, while retaining all issue categories it violates.

parts.title: 3. Report each violated rule independently
paragraphs: Our audit returns id and issue. Separate SELECT branches identify duplicates, unknown assets, missing values, out-of-range values and future events. UNION makes each identity/reason pair appear once. A single CASE expression would stop after one branch and could hide a second problem on the same record.
The range is an invented accepted interval in one declared unit. It is inclusive at both ends. NULL is checked separately because ordinary numeric comparisons with NULL do not return true.
interpretation: Explain the boundary values and clock assumptions beside each rule.

examples.title: Find orphaned asset references
examples.code:
SELECT DISTINCT r.id,r.asset_id FROM raw_readings r
LEFT JOIN assets a ON a.id=r.asset_id WHERE a.id IS NULL ORDER BY r.id;
paragraphs: A left join keeps the raw record even when the register has no match.
interpretation: The raw row survives for diagnosis. An inner join would hide it from this report.

parts.title: 4. Check time relative to the decision being modelled
paragraphs: Event time describes when something happened. Ingestion time describes when the pipeline received it. Prediction time determines whether the information was available for a training example. A historical event that arrived later can be valid raw data while being unavailable to an earlier prediction.

The simple future-event check only verifies consistency under a shared-clock assumption. It is not a point-in-time feature join. Use the earlier feature-table lesson’s availability conditions when assembling model inputs, and keep label availability separate from feature availability.
interpretation: A clean range-and-identity audit does not rule out target leakage.

parts.title: 5. Look beyond individual rows
paragraphs: A batch can satisfy every row constraint while losing half the expected sensors. Monitor freshness, volume, null rates and distribution changes at meaningful groups such as site or device family. Compare these with documented expectations and investigate changes rather than automatically declaring every shift wrong.

A real equipment upgrade can change the measurement distribution. A stale ingestion job can leave a perfectly shaped but obsolete table. SQL summaries provide evidence for these checks; deciding what action to take requires the application’s context.
interpretation: Choose thresholds from observed operating requirements, and record the uncertainty behind them.

parts.title: 6. Keep validation reproducible
paragraphs: Store the SQL or rule version, source snapshot, accepted units and data cutoffs with the validation report. Rebuilding a model from today’s corrected table may differ from the data used by the original run. Preserve a versioned snapshot or a reproducible change history when that distinction matters.

Test the audit with simultaneous failures, boundary values and an empty batch. A no-issue output for zero records should not automatically be labelled a healthy delivery. The pipeline also needs a separate completeness expectation.
interpretation: The incremental lesson will preserve source change position so repairs and replays can be reconciled.

practice.title: Can the audit report every problem without hiding a second failure?
practice.question: Can the audit report every problem without hiding a second failure?
task: Return distinct (id, issue) pairs ordered by id then issue. Issue names: duplicate when an ID occurs more than once; unknown_asset when asset_id has no match; missing_value for NULL; out_of_range outside inclusive [0,100]; future_event when event_seq exceeds ingest_seq. Report every applicable issue. The counters share a clock in this fixture. Preserve raw rows.
practice.starter: -- Combine independent issue queries and order the report.
practice.solution:
SELECT id,'duplicate' AS issue FROM raw_readings GROUP BY id HAVING COUNT(*)>1
UNION
SELECT r.id,'unknown_asset' FROM raw_readings r LEFT JOIN assets a ON a.id=r.asset_id WHERE a.id IS NULL
UNION
SELECT id,'missing_value' FROM raw_readings WHERE value IS NULL
UNION
SELECT id,'out_of_range' FROM raw_readings WHERE value<0 OR value>100
UNION
SELECT id,'future_event' FROM raw_readings WHERE event_seq>ingest_seq
ORDER BY id,issue;
hints: Use separate branches when one row may violate several rules.
UNION removes duplicate identity/reason pairs. It does not remove different reasons for one ID.

title: Pick Up New Changes Without Losing Late Readings
blurb: Repeated full imports become expensive, but a naive timestamp filter misses corrections and deletions. Track source change position, merge versions and commit the checkpoint with the result.
openingTitle: Yesterday’s Reading Arrived After Today’s Import Finished
opening: Botie’s pipeline remembers the latest event time and asks for anything newer on the next run. A delayed sensor message arrives with yesterday’s event time, so it never enters the training source. A later correction has the same problem.
We need to track when the source exposes a change, as well as when its measured event happened. The lesson builds a versioned merge and a checkpoint that can be replayed after a failure.

history.title: Remembering a Change Position Instead of Recopying Everything
blocks: Databases maintain change information to recover and coordinate writes. Change-data-capture systems can expose committed changes to downstream consumers instead of forcing every consumer to recopy the full source. PostgreSQL logical decoding is one documented implementation with its own restart, retention and delivery responsibilities.

A consumer still needs a recoverable position and a replay policy. Our source supplies a strictly increasing ingestion sequence and per-record versions. These are explicit teaching contracts; an arbitrary timestamp column does not automatically provide the same guarantees.

reading.experimentTitle: Apply the new source changes and keep their checkpoint
reading.experimentIntro: Select changes after the committed cursor, merge each identity by version, then keep resulting state and cursor together.
reading.connectionTitle: A checkpoint must describe the data that was actually committed

intuition.explanation: A late event can be a newly delivered change.

cells: Update R1 to its newer version
Insert R3 even if its event time is old

scene.caption: The cursor follows source delivery order. Per-record version decides whether a payload is newer.

parts.title: 1. Separate event time, arrival order and record version
paragraphs: Event time belongs to the measured phenomenon. Arrival order describes when a change becomes available to the pipeline. Version orders successive states of one identity. A late event can have an old event time and a new arrival sequence.

Our source guarantees unique increasing sequence values and monotonic versions per identity. A production source must document its ordering, transaction and retention behaviour. A poll over updated_at needs careful tie handling and cannot detect hard deletions unless another mechanism records them.
interpretation: Do not turn MAX(event_time) into a reliable ingestion cursor by naming it a watermark.

parts.title: 2. Define exactly what the checkpoint means
paragraphs: The checkpoint is the last source change position whose effects are committed in the sink. Read only later positions for the next batch. If the sink commits data but loses the checkpoint update, a replay can occur. If the checkpoint commits first, a crash can skip data that was never written.

Commit both in one transaction when they share a database. Across systems, use a delivery protocol and idempotent merge that tolerate replay, and reconcile partial outcomes. Exactly-once claims require specifying the entire boundary and its assumptions.
interpretation: The exercise’s checkpoint table and current table share one SQLite transaction.

parts.title: 3. Merge identities by version
paragraphs: A stable primary key identifies the record. A newer version replaces its stored payload; an older version does not. Replaying an equal version with the same payload leaves the result unchanged.

The exercise assumes equal versions always carry equal payloads because conflicting records have already been quarantined. A real pipeline must check that contract. Choosing a random last arrival for equal conflicting versions destroys reproducibility. The workshop rejects that conflict explicitly.
interpretation: Source position and record version solve different ordering problems.

examples.title: Keep a newer value when an old revision arrives
paragraphs: A delayed old payload should not replace the current row.
interpretation: The old version is ignored even though it was delivered now.

parts.title: 4. Represent deletion as a versioned change
paragraphs: If a deleted identity simply disappears from a snapshot, an incremental consumer may never learn what to remove. A deletion event or tombstone tells the sink that this identity was deliberately removed at a particular version.

Retaining that tombstone prevents an older late update from recreating the deleted record. Our current_readings table stores deleted as 0 or 1 and keeps a NULL value for a tombstone. Readers of active data must explicitly filter deleted=0. Tombstone retention needs to cover the source’s replay and late-arrival assumptions.
interpretation: A deletion is data about an identity. It is not equivalent to a missing sensor value.

parts.title: 5. Advance over ignored old versions too
paragraphs: A batch may contain an arrival whose version is older than the current record. Its payload is ignored, but its source position was still processed. Advance the cursor past it once the batch commits. Otherwise the consumer may read the same obsolete change indefinitely.

An empty batch leaves the cursor unchanged. Never move a checkpoint backwards because an old source extract was supplied. The SQL exercise uses the greater of the previous checkpoint and the maximum available change sequence.
interpretation: The resulting cursor describes processed delivery positions, not only rows whose values changed.

parts.title: 6. Bound a batch without skipping changes that share a timestamp
paragraphs: A busy source can keep producing changes while the consumer works. Capture a source-supported upper position for the batch, then read positions after the committed cursor up to that bound. Commit the result before starting the next interval. The source must retain the interval and expose complete changes within it; reading an arbitrary MAX from a changing business table does not establish those properties.

Timestamp polling adds another problem. If two rows share the final timestamp and a row limit splits them, resuming with only updated_at greater than that timestamp skips the remaining row. An ordered timestamp-and-identity cursor can paginate a stable set, but it still cannot detect a later change that reuses an earlier timestamp. Reliable polling needs a source contract, an overlap-and-deduplication policy where suitable, or a change log. Our teaching input uses unique source sequence numbers so that these assumptions are visible.
interpretation: The exercise receives a complete finite extract. A production reader must additionally define how it obtains and retains a complete bounded interval.

parts.title: 7. Plan for backfills and late corrections
paragraphs: A historical backfill may revisit a time range already represented in features. Give it a declared source snapshot and transformation version, and merge by stable identity or rebuild a partition deliberately. Do not mix a backfill cursor into the live stream unless its ordering contract supports that.

Corrections can invalidate previously built aggregates or training examples. Decide whether to recompute affected partitions, keep immutable historical snapshots, or publish a new dataset version. Retain enough lineage to explain which source revisions produced a model’s features.
interpretation: Idempotent row merging does not automatically refresh every derived aggregate downstream.

parts.title: 8. Notice when the source no longer has the required history
paragraphs: Suppose the sink stopped at change position 100, but the source has already discarded everything before 150. Resuming at 150 would silently omit an interval. The consumer needs to detect that its checkpoint is older than the retained history and take a documented recovery path.

A new full snapshot can rebuild the sink, but the snapshot and following change stream need a consistent handoff position. Otherwise changes that occur during the copy can be missed or duplicated. Preserve the old dataset version while rebuilding when it is needed for model reproducibility. Reconcile the rebuilt state before directing readers to it.
interpretation: A successful connection does not prove that the source can still replay the interval the sink needs.

parts.title: 9. Reconcile the incremental result with a complete view
paragraphs: Periodically compare record counts, keys and selected aggregates against a trusted source snapshot. Missing change retention, a broken cursor or a source schema change can produce a plausible but incomplete sink. Monitor lag and checkpoint progress separately from job success messages.
The final challenge replays a batch, introduces an older version after a deletion, and tests an empty source extract. These are ordinary recovery cases to design before the first production outage.
interpretation: The pipeline is ready for the next lesson when its checkpoint and data tell the same story after a restart.

title: Which Records Does the Technician Need Together?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A pump screen, a recent-reading lookup and a site report ask different questions of the same records. Start with those requests before choosing how to store the data.
openingTitle: The Pump Screen Keeps Asking for the Same Visits
opening: Botie already has an asset register and a table of inspections. A technician opens P1 and expects its recent visits. Another screen needs the latest temperature for P1. The weekly report needs totals across every pump at a site. Those requests use the same information in different ways.

Before choosing another database, write down exactly what each request knows and what it must return. That gives us something to judge a design against. A convenient record layout for one screen can make another question harder.

history.title: A Shopping Cart Had to Survive a Busy Service
blocks: Amazon’s 2007 Dynamo paper describes services such as shopping carts that needed highly available reads and writes. Its interface retrieved an object by a key. Concentrating on that access pattern let the designers make different tradeoffs from a system intended to answer arbitrary relational queries. Dynamo is a particular distributed design; its choices do not define every database called NoSQL.

Our invented maintenance service is much smaller, but we can ask the same first question: what operation must remain practical? The pump screen supplies an asset ID and wants its visits. Grouping visits under that identity makes the requested association visible. We still have to decide how writes keep the grouping current.

parts.title: 1. Describe the read before naming a database
paragraphs: An access pattern is a particular way the application reads or changes data. “Show recent visits for this pump” tells us the lookup identity and the records we need together. Add the required ordering, the largest plausible result and how fresh it must be.

Ask about writes too. A new inspection arrives while somebody is viewing the history. Does the next refresh need to show it immediately? Can the screen tolerate a short delay? Those are application requirements, and a data model cannot choose them for us.
interpretation: A useful design note names an operation and its constraints. “We need something scalable” leaves the important questions unanswered.

parts.title: 2. Keep the meaning of a record intact
paragraphs: The asset table has one row per asset. The inspection table has one row per visit. If we create a dictionary keyed by asset ID and assign a single visit to each entry, a later visit replaces the earlier one. The code has changed the meaning of the data.

A bucket of visits is different: the asset ID selects a list, and that list retains separate visit identities. This gives the pump screen what it asked for without pretending each pump has only one inspection.
interpretation: Row grain from SQL still matters when the container is a dictionary or a document.

parts.title: 3. Build a lookup while keeping repeated keys
paragraphs: A Python dictionary maps a key to a value. Here each value is a list. Read a visit, find or create its asset’s list, and append the visit. We perform the grouping once in this demonstration, then retrieve a selected list.
Constructing the grouping scans the input. Keeping an equivalent structure in a real service also costs storage and update work. We have made the read simple by doing work elsewhere.
interpretation: This dictionary is an inspectable model of grouping, not an implementation of distributed storage.

examples.title: A repeated pump adds to its list
paragraphs: Use setdefault to create each list only when its key first appears.
interpretation: The first lookup retains both visit identities. The second has no bucket and returns the application’s chosen empty result.

parts.title: 4. Compare the families by the operations they expose
paragraphs: A key-value store starts with a key and returns its associated value. A document database can inspect fields inside a stored record. Wide-column systems organise records around keys and related columns, often with query patterns tied closely to their partitioning. Graph databases make relationships and traversals central to their interfaces. Products vary within each family.

Relational databases can also store JSON and maintain indexes for targeted lookups. A JSON-shaped request alone does not establish that we need a document database. Compare the integrity rules and operational burden of the actual candidates.
interpretation: NoSQL names a broad collection of approaches. It does not promise a particular consistency model, transaction boundary or performance result.

parts.title: 5. Account for the copies a faster read creates
paragraphs: Suppose visits remain in the SQL system of record while a service keeps a pump-history document. Now an inspection write may need to reach both representations. A failed second write can leave them disagreeing. We need a rebuildable projection, a reliable change feed, or another explicit update process.

A screen-specific copy is useful when its freshness contract permits that process. The same copy is a poor authority for a decision that requires the newest committed safety status. Say which store owns each fact and how other representations catch up.
interpretation: Before adding a second representation, write down what happens when only one copy changes.

parts.title: 6. Test the request when the data stops being convenient
paragraphs: The workshop first contains one visit per pump, so assigning a single record might appear sufficient. Then a second visit for the requested pump arrives. Your grouping must retain both. A request for an unseen asset needs an explicit empty response.

Use this failure to challenge a proposed model before measuring speed. Once the answers are correct, investigate the workload with a real database and realistic record sizes. Our in-memory counts cannot predict network latency or server capacity.
interpretation: The next lesson follows the lookup key itself. Two sites can both call their pump P1.

title: Which P1 Did the Lookup Mean?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: Two sites use the same short asset ID. Build keys that preserve the full identity, and distinguish a missing entry from a stored zero.
openingTitle: North and South Both Have a Pump Called P1
opening: North reports no outstanding inspections for P1. South reports seven. Botie stores each answer under the key P1, and the second write replaces the first. The storage service did exactly what it was asked to do. Our key did not describe the thing we meant.
A key is the complete name used by a lookup. We need to decide which parts make that name unique, how those parts are encoded, and what an absent name means to the caller.

history.title: Small Operations Around Explicit Keys
blocks: Redis began in 2009 under Salvatore Sanfilippo. Its string commands illustrate a small interaction: set a value under a key, then retrieve that key. A server can implement that interface without interpreting the application meaning of a pump name.

That division gives the application responsibility for a naming convention. Our site and asset pair is an invented example. The key must carry enough identity before a key-value service can return the intended record.
