title: Why Did the Repair Disappear When Botie Read It Back?
blurb: Copies can disagree while an update is travelling. Define what a particular read must guarantee before deciding which replica may answer it.
openingTitle: The Save Succeeded, but the Next Screen Shows the Old Status
opening: A technician marks a job complete. One copy records the change, but the next screen reads a replica that has not received it yet. The update may still be safe in storage while the screen gives the user an older view.

Replication creates several copies; a consistency contract says what their readers may observe. We will first preserve one session’s known revision, then separate that promise from stronger global ordering.

history.title: Keeping a Service Usable When Copies Cannot Communicate

sources.title: Dynamo: Amazon’s highly available key-value store (2007)
Gilbert and Lynch: Perspectives on the CAP theorem

blocks: Dynamo made explicit choices about accepting operations and reconciling versions when replicas were unavailable. Gilbert and Lynch’s work on CAP explains why a replicated read/write service cannot guarantee both linearizable responses and a response to every request at a non-failing node under an arbitrary network partition.

A disconnected replica cannot discover which remote write completed. Returning its local value can preserve a response while violating the stronger read contract. Waiting or rejecting the operation preserves that contract at the expense of CAP availability for that request. This is a failure-time constraint, not a rule that every database must always choose two letters.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep a read from moving behind this session
reading.experimentIntro: Filter reachable replicas, require the session revision, and retain a wait result when no eligible copy is available.
reading.connectionTitle: Name the promise before selecting a replica
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Route a read using a session floor
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: The same session has already observed revision seven
intuition.explanation: The network observations below belong to an invented single-record version sequence.

scene.caption: A version floor preserves known progress. It cannot reveal a later write that the session has never observed.

parts.title: 1. Copying data and deciding when to answer are separate choices
paragraphs: A primary can accept writes and send them to followers. Other systems permit several writers or require coordination among replicas before an operation completes. The replication topology alone does not tell us which acknowledgements count as success or where a subsequent read is allowed to go.
Ask what was acknowledged, which failures the durability promise covers, and what the chosen read mode returns. A successful write and a fresh read are related concerns with different contracts.
interpretation: Do not infer a database’s behaviour from the label NoSQL.

parts.title: 2. State the read guarantee in terms a user can observe
paragraphs: Read-your-writes means a session does not read a state older than its own completed writes, within the system’s specified scope. Monotonic reads prevent that session from moving backwards after observing a newer state. Neither promise alone gives every user the same latest value.

Linearizability gives operations the appearance of taking effect at one instant between invocation and response, respecting real-time order. A read starting after a completed write must reflect that write or a later one for the object. Eventual consistency instead describes convergence once updates stop and communication succeeds; it is not a fixed staleness deadline.
interpretation: Our version-floor model illustrates a session property on one totally ordered record, not a complete implementation of any distributed protocol.

parts.title: 3. Represent what this session actually knows
paragraphs: The Python input contains replica IDs, visible revisions and reachable booleans. minimum is the greatest revision this session is required to preserve. We remove unreachable copies, then remove visible revisions below that floor.

Among eligible copies, the example chooses the highest visible revision and breaks ties by replica ID. If none qualify it returns wait. Real systems may use session tokens or route to a suitable leader rather than exposing revision numbers to the caller.
interpretation: Selecting the maximum from a supplied list is not evidence that an unseen replica has no newer value.

examples.title: An available copy can still be too old
paragraphs: Check the two independent conditions for one observed copy.
examples.code:
replica = {"id":"west", "version":6, "reachable":True}
minimum = 7
print(replica["reachable"])
print(replica["version"] >= minimum)
interpretation: The connection works, but returning this version would break the session’s declared floor.

parts.title: 4. A partition forces a choice for the affected operation
paragraphs: If the replica with a completed update cannot communicate with the replica receiving the read, the reader cannot learn the update from that unavailable path. A service requiring the stronger ordering may stop or fail the affected read. An application permitting a stale result may return one with appropriate semantics.

CAP availability is a formal property that every request at a non-failing node eventually receives a valid response. It is not the same as an uptime percentage, and an error response is not a successful read of the specified register. When the network works, latency and coordination costs still matter, but CAP is not a general two-out-of-three purchasing checklist.
interpretation: Choose per operation where the system permits it. A repair history screen and an exclusive stock reservation may need different contracts.

parts.title: 5. A quorum count is not the entire consistency proof
paragraphs: A read set and write set can intersect when their quorum sizes are chosen appropriately for a fixed replica set. That intersection is useful, but the protocol must also handle concurrent writes, version order, failed acknowledgements and recovery. Sloppy quorums that use replacement nodes change the intersection assumptions.

Cassandra exposes consistency levels for operations and has separate mechanisms for lightweight transactions. Treat each documented guarantee as scoped to its protocol and configuration. Counting two answers out of three cannot, by itself, prove linearizability.
interpretation: The workshop intentionally avoids turning replica counts into a promise stronger than the model can establish.

parts.title: 6. Read the mode supported by the actual access path
paragraphs: DynamoDB documents eventually consistent reads as its default. Its tables and local secondary indexes also support strongly consistent reads, while global secondary indexes and streams do not provide that same read option. Global tables now have distinct multi-Region eventual and multi-Region strong consistency modes.

Review the selected mode and supported region/configuration requirements rather than transferring a statement about one path to another. A transaction, a table lookup and a secondary-index query can have different boundaries.
interpretation: The source links document the current implementation. The local exercise does not contact DynamoDB.

parts.title: 7. Make stale and unavailable outcomes visible to the application
paragraphs: A read can return a permitted older view, wait, fail, or fall back to another source. Decide which outcomes the screen can explain accurately. A bounded timeout may be necessary even when the formal contract permits waiting; timing out does not mean the remote write never happened.

For an optimistic edit, preserve the expected revision and check it atomically when writing. A stale screen should not silently overwrite another technician’s later repair. The next lesson uses that condition to protect a concrete stock reservation.
interpretation: The changed workshop case restores connectivity without weakening the session’s revision requirement.

parts.title: 8. Test the history of observations, not a single result
paragraphs: A freshness test should include the write receipt, subsequent reads, replica lag and a recovery path. Record which session and key each observation belongs to. A test that begins after every replica caught up cannot expose the disappearing-write experience.

Use the local model to reason about allowed routes, then use fault-aware integration tests against the chosen database to verify its real contract. Do not treat the Python function’s deterministic output as evidence about a live network.
interpretation: We can now say exactly why a reachable replica may still be unsuitable for this read.

title: Two Technicians Cannot Both Reserve the Last Kit
blurb: A successful read does not reserve the stock it showed. Put the expected version and remaining-stock rule inside the actual write.
openingTitle: Both Screens Say a Kit Is Available
opening: Two technicians open the same stock record. Each sees enough parts and submits a reservation. If each program writes a quantity calculated from its earlier screen, one reservation can overwrite the other.
The decision needs to be checked where the change happens. Botie will combine the record version with the stock rule, then apply the update only if that complete condition still holds.

history.title: Testing the Precondition at the Write Boundary
blocks: A read followed by an unconditional write leaves a gap in which another writer can change the record. Conditional updates address that gap by making the check part of the write operation. DynamoDB condition expressions and MongoDB update filters are concrete database interfaces for this idea.

This is the same concurrency problem encountered in the SQL versioned update. The syntax changes, while the reasoning stays useful: the application states which existing state would make its proposed action valid, and the database checks that condition atomically within the operation’s supported scope.

reading.experimentTitle: Reserve against the record that was actually read
reading.experimentIntro: Check identity and revision on one branch, sufficient stock on another, then connect their joint decision to the update.
reading.connectionTitle: An earlier screen is a proposal, not a reservation
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Apply a conditional stock change
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: The request carries the assumptions behind its action
intuition.explanation: This invented request reserves three kits.

scene.caption: A matching version does not excuse a request larger than the remaining stock.

parts.title: 1. Separate a precondition from the proposed effect
paragraphs: The precondition asks whether this is the intended stock record, whether its version still matches, and whether enough units remain. The effect decreases units and increments the version. These are separate pieces even when one database command evaluates them together.
Our local function returns an accepted flag and a record. On rejection it keeps the entire old record. That makes the outcome inspectable without pretending a rejected reservation succeeded.
interpretation: In the real service, the check and effect must share the database’s atomic write boundary.

parts.title: 2. A version identifies the state the caller used
paragraphs: The request carries expected_version from the read that informed the technician’s decision. A successful change advances the record’s version. An old request then fails even if its proposed quantity would be legal in isolation.

Every writer participating in this protocol must advance the version consistently. A maintenance script that updates units without doing so can invalidate the assumption. Blindly replacing expected_version with the latest one turns a conflict into an unreviewed new decision.
interpretation: A version check is useful only when all relevant writes follow its contract.

parts.title: 3. Build the guarded change with ordinary records
paragraphs: Python dictionaries let us inspect the components independently. Check the identifier and version, then compare requested units with available units. Combine the booleans before changing a copied dictionary.

The browser runs one function invocation at a time. It demonstrates the state transition and rejection behaviour, but the function itself is not an atomic database write and is not safe as a concurrent inventory service.
interpretation: The challenge asks for the transition model so we can test what an accepted or rejected command should mean.

examples.title: Keep a stale proposal from changing a record
paragraphs: The current stock has moved to revision five while the proposal still expects four.
interpretation: There are enough kits, but that fact does not repair the proposal’s stale assumption.

parts.title: 4. Send a fixed update expression and bound values
paragraphs: The server should construct the permitted operation. The caller supplies validated values, not an arbitrary update expression or a dictionary of database operators. Tenant scope comes from authenticated application context and must be checked before issuing the storage command.

Use a service role limited to the necessary table and operations. Attribute-name placeholders and value bindings keep expression structure separate from values; they do not replace authorisation. A partition key containing north cannot prove the requester belongs to north.
interpretation: The following reference performs a real write only in an explicitly prepared external development table.

references.title: A DynamoDB reservation guarded at the service
description: The table has the string partition key id and an existing seal-kit item with numeric version and units.
references.code:
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name="us-east-1").Table("maintenance_stock_dev")
try:
    result = table.update_item(
        Key={"id": "seal-kit"},
        UpdateExpression="SET #u = #u - :amount, #v = #v + :one",
        ConditionExpression="#v = :expected AND #u >= :amount",
        ExpressionAttributeNames={"#u":"units", "#v":"version"},
        ExpressionAttributeValues={":amount":3, ":one":1, ":expected":4},
        ReturnValues="ALL_NEW",
    )
    print(result["Attributes"])
except ClientError as error:
    if error.response["Error"]["Code"] == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
        print("Re-read and reconcile the reservation")
    else:
        raise
setup: External setup: install boto3, create a disposable development table and seed the named item.
Use an authorised development role through the SDK credential chain. Do not place AWS credentials in the browser exercise or source file.
interpretation: Only an explicit conditional rejection takes the reconciliation path. Transport failures require separate outcome handling.

parts.title: 5. A missing response is different from a rejected condition
paragraphs: If the server applies the update but the response is lost, the client cannot conclude that nothing happened. Repeating an unconditional decrement can reserve twice. Repeating the original versioned request will fail after a successful first application, but that failure alone cannot tell the client whether its own first attempt or another writer changed the record.

A production reservation needs a stable operation identity and a documented receipt or idempotency mechanism, with its scope and retention understood. Reconcile an unknown result before presenting another reservation as a new action.
interpretation: The exercise has no transport and no persistent receipts. Its accepted flag describes only this local invocation.

parts.title: 6. Name the boundary of the invariant
paragraphs: A single-item condition can protect that item’s stock. It does not automatically reserve a kit in one record and book an engineer in another as one unit. Multi-item invariants require a supported transaction mechanism or an explicit workflow with compensation and visible partial states.
Test a repeated request, insufficient stock and an incorrect identity. Then test the actual server operation with concurrent callers before relying on it in production.
interpretation: The next lesson considers operations whose replicas can merge safely after disconnected work.

title: How Can Two Offline Teams Keep Both Inspection Counts?
blurb: Choosing the last arriving total can lose someone’s work. Give each replica an owned contribution and derive a merge whose repeated delivery does not inflate the count.
openingTitle: East and West Both Counted Inspections While the Link Was Down
opening: Each maintenance team finishes inspections while disconnected. When their tablets reconnect, replacing one total with the other loses work. Adding the two totals can also count shared history twice.

We need to preserve enough information to tell which contribution belongs to which writer. A grow-only counter gives each replica its own component. That small change lets us derive a repeatable merge instead of guessing which total to trust.

history.title: Choosing Merge Rules That Fit the Operation

sources.title: Dynamo: Amazon’s highly available key-value store (2007)
Preguiça, Baquero and Shapiro: Conflict-free replicated data types (2018)

blocks: Dynamo described preserving divergent object versions so application logic could reconcile them. Later conflict-free replicated data type research examined data structures with precisely defined merge rules that converge under stated delivery assumptions. Redis Active-Active is one product family that uses CRDT ideas; this does not mean every Redis deployment has those semantics.

Our counter is a teaching instance of a state-based grow-only counter. We derive its merge from ownership and monotonic updates. It is suitable for accumulated inspections under those assumptions, not for every mutable document or bounded stock balance.

reading.experimentTitle: Combine replica contributions without adding a replay twice
reading.experimentIntro: Merge each component with maximum, then compute the total from the merged component map.
reading.connectionTitle: Choose a merge from the meaning of the operation
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Merge grow-only inspection counts
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: Each component belongs to one writer
intuition.explanation: The replicas hold different observations of the same component map.

records.label: east
cells: East has advanced beyond the state B last saw

records.label: west
cells: West has advanced beyond the state A last saw

scene.caption: Keeping the larger value for each owner preserves both advances. Adding the entire snapshots would repeat their shared history.

parts.title: 1. A last-write rule chooses a winner, not a combined meaning
paragraphs: A last-write-wins policy uses an ordering, often involving a timestamp and a tie-breaker, to choose one value. It can be useful for a replaceable preference, but it can discard an independent update to an inspection total. Wall clocks can also disagree, so a later timestamp does not necessarily identify the later real-world action.
Different fields may need different treatment. A technician’s note should not automatically be merged with the same rule as a set of completed inspection IDs or a stock reservation.
interpretation: Convergence describes agreement after merging. It does not establish that the chosen value preserves the application’s intent.

parts.title: 2. Keep one component per writer
paragraphs: The counter state is a dictionary from replica ID to its nonnegative count. East increments only east’s component; west increments only west’s component. A replica may copy the whole map, but it must not independently invent increments for another owner.

Counts only increase. A replica that loses its local state cannot safely reset its old component to zero and continue under the same identity. Recovery must restore that state or introduce a new unique writer identity under a documented policy.
interpretation: The ownership and no-reset assumptions make maximum a meaningful merge.

parts.title: 3. Derive the merge one component at a time
paragraphs: For each owner, the larger observed count includes at least the progress represented by the smaller one. Retain that maximum. A missing component represents zero progress in that snapshot. After merging all owners, sum their retained contributions.

Use a dictionary for named components rather than a list whose positions silently depend on the order writers joined. Sorting the names only gives a repeatable display; it does not change the mathematical state.
parts.calculation:
merged[owner] = max(left.get(owner, 0), right.get(owner, 0))
total = sum(merged.values())
interpretation: This formula performs a merge of states, not a replay of increment commands.

examples.title: Replaying one component does not create another increment
paragraphs: Compare two observed values belonging to the same writer.
examples.code:
earlier = 2
later = 5
merged = max(earlier, later)
replayed = max(merged, earlier)
print(merged)
print(replayed)
interpretation: The earlier observation adds no new progress after the later one is already retained.

parts.title: 4. Check the properties that permit reordering and replay
paragraphs: Merging a state with itself leaves it unchanged: idempotence prevents duplicate snapshots from inflating the result. Swapping the two inputs gives the same state: commutativity removes dependence on arrival order. Grouping successive merges differently also gives the same state: associativity allows intermediate replicas to combine updates.

Those properties help when valid states eventually reach the replicas that need them. They do not deliver messages, authenticate writers or guarantee that every offline device will reconnect. The application still has to satisfy the communication and identity assumptions.
interpretation: The challenge tests these properties on concrete component maps instead of treating one displayed total as sufficient evidence.

parts.title: 5. A decrement needs a different representation
paragraphs: A grow-only counter cannot represent removing an inspection. One extension keeps separately owned positive and negative components and subtracts their totals, with its own rules. Sets with removal also need information about which additions were observed; deleting a value from a plain union can be undone by a delayed copy.
Do not implement removal by decreasing a component in this counter. A remote replica holding the previous larger value would restore it at the next maximum merge.
interpretation: A new operation can require a new data type and a new proof of its merge behaviour.

parts.title: 6. Convergent counts do not reserve the last kit
paragraphs: Two disconnected teams can each decrement a local available-stock estimate and later agree on a negative total. The merge can be internally consistent while violating the business invariant that stock must never be oversold.

Coordination, preallocated spending rights or another specialised design is needed when the invariant requires it. Our earlier conditional write intentionally took a different approach for a single authoritative stock item.
interpretation: Choose availability and merging only where the permitted outcomes match the maintenance task.

parts.title: 7. Keep conflict evidence when no safe merge is known
paragraphs: A document can contain two incompatible repair decisions that no automatic rule should erase. Retain the relevant versions, actors and source evidence, then route the conflict for reconciliation. The resolver’s decision becomes a new recorded action.
Choose a policy before an outage produces competing writes. A deterministic arbitrary winner makes failures reproducible, but it does not make a lost repair note acceptable.
interpretation: Botie’s changed counter case tests repeated and older observations. It does not claim a universal conflict resolver.

title: Why Does the Dashboard Still Count a Job That Was Closed?
blurb: A source record changes while a dashboard keeps its own count. Build a projection from versioned job images and make repeats, moves and deletions visible.
openingTitle: The Repair Record Is Correct. Its Dashboard Is Behind.
opening: Botie closes J1 in the job store. The asset dashboard is a separate read view, so its open-job count still includes J1 until that change reaches it. Updating both places with two unrelated writes creates a gap if one succeeds and the other fails.

A change stream can carry source changes to a projection, a derived representation built for a particular read. We will retain the latest image of each job and derive the asset counts from that state.

history.title: Letting a Committed Change Feed Another Read View
blocks: Database logs and change notifications allow downstream systems to follow committed changes instead of repeatedly scanning a source for differences. DynamoDB Streams and MongoDB change streams expose such changes through different APIs and retention contracts. They are examples of the mechanism, not interchangeable delivery protocols.

A stream can close the application’s source-write/notification gap when its guarantees match the design. It still leaves the consumer responsible for applying changes, recovering its position and handling its own side effects. Our local projection focuses on those applied-state semantics.

reading.experimentTitle: Repair the open-job view from the latest images
reading.experimentIntro: Merge job versions first, count only current open jobs by asset, and retain the images alongside the derived result.
reading.connectionTitle: A projection must reflect replacement, not just arrival
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Rebuild the open-job view
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: An update replaces a job’s previous contribution
intuition.explanation: The dashboard counts current open jobs, not every message it has seen.

scene.caption: Counting arrivals would inflate the dashboard when a consumer resumes and sees a message again.

parts.title: 1. Give the projection a declared source of truth
paragraphs: The job store owns job state. The dashboard owns a derived count that can be rebuilt from it. Users should not independently edit the same job status through both stores without a conflict policy.

A projection can be a document, an index, a search view or another table. Its useful difference is a read shape suited to the dashboard. That convenience comes with a freshness lag and a repair responsibility.
interpretation: The dashboard should expose enough freshness information to avoid presenting old counts as a new source decision.

parts.title: 2. Decide what information a change contains
paragraphs: A change may contain a full document image, changed fields, a deletion key, or before and after images depending on the system and configuration. Applying a patch requires the state it expects. A delete needs enough identity to remove the previous contribution.

Our exercise deliberately uses full images with id, asset, version and status. A deleted status is a retained tombstone in this toy protocol. Actual stream event formats and image options must be read from their source documentation.
interpretation: The explicit image contract lets us reason about replay without inventing a database event format.

parts.title: 3. Retain the latest version before counting
paragraphs: A dictionary keyed by job ID keeps one current image per identity. A greater version replaces the old image, a smaller version is ignored, and an equal version with an identical image is a replay. Conflicting images for the same identity and version anywhere in the supplied state and batch violate the input contract and raise an error, including older images already superseded by a newer version. The model cannot inspect historical images that were not supplied.

We then count open images by asset. Because we recompute from retained state, a moved job stops contributing to its old asset. This is a deliberately small rebuild, not a claim that every production dashboard should rescan its full state on each event.
interpretation: The stored images make the count’s explanation available.

examples.title: See why counting messages is the wrong quantity
paragraphs: Two identical messages describe one job state.
examples.code:
images = [{"id":"J1","asset":"P7","status":"open"},
          {"id":"J1","asset":"P7","status":"open"}]
by_id = {row["id"]:row for row in images}
print(len(images))
print(len(by_id))
interpretation: This small example identifies repeated identity. The challenge adds version ordering and explicit conflict checks.

parts.title: 4. A moved job must leave its old group
paragraphs: Suppose J2 was assigned to P7 and is corrected to P8. An incremental count needs to retract the old contribution before adding the new one. Without the old image or equivalent maintained state, the consumer cannot know which group to decrement.

Our rebuilt view handles the correction by counting only J2’s latest retained image. In a larger incremental projection, test retractions, deletes and reclassification explicitly. A system tested only on inserts can produce plausible counts long after its first correction.
interpretation: The changed workshop case moves a job rather than merely adding another arrival.

parts.title: 5. Checkpoint the applied result, not just the received message
paragraphs: A consumer can receive a message, update its view, then lose its response before saving progress. Resuming can repeat application. Saving the source position before the view update risks skipping an unapplied effect.

Use an atomic sink/checkpoint operation where the architecture supports it, or a replay-safe consumer and a documented recovery protocol. The versioned full-image merge here makes repetition harmless to this derived state. It does not make an unrelated email or stock decrement replay-safe.
interpretation: A stream’s delivery wording does not establish exactly-once effects across arbitrary downstream services.

parts.title: 6. Treat a resume token as a source-owned position
paragraphs: MongoDB change streams provide resume tokens and require enough retained history to resume. Keep the token with its stream configuration; do not parse it into an application timestamp or reuse it with a different pipeline casually. DynamoDB Streams uses a different shard-based interface and retention contract.

A consumer falling behind retention needs a snapshot-and-stream recovery procedure with a consistent handoff. A success message from the last process run cannot prove that every required change remains available.
interpretation: The browser input is a finite supplied batch. It does not emulate a resumable network cursor.

parts.title: 7. Repair the view and verify what readers will see
paragraphs: Rebuild a damaged projection into a separate destination when appropriate, compare identities and counts against the source, then switch readers deliberately. Keep a version for the projection logic so a transformation change is distinguishable from new business data.

Bound retries and watch processing lag, not only worker uptime. A worker can stay alive while a malformed event prevents later events from applying. Preserve that event for diagnosis instead of silently advancing its checkpoint.
interpretation: The next lesson makes a representation change explicit so old and new documents can be read without guessing their fields.

quiz.prompt: What must the resulting current-state projection do?
options: Remove its P7 contribution and add its P8 contribution
Count neither because its ID is unchanged
quiz.because: The identity persists while its grouping field changes.

given.data: J2 changes asset from P7 to P8 while remaining open.

quiz.because: The email effect is outside the image merge and needs its own delivery policy.

title: The New Sensor Sends a Different Document
blurb: Some readers still expect temp_c while a new device sends a value and a unit. Introduce an explicit representation version and a reader that can explain both.
openingTitle: A Number Called Temperature No Longer Tells Us Its Unit
opening: The first sensors stored temp_c. A new device sends temperature as a nested value-and-unit record. Both documents can fit in a collection, but the old code does not suddenly understand the new shape.

We will make the representation version explicit, read each known shape deliberately, and produce a consistent Celsius view for Botie. The original documents stay available so a conversion can be checked.

history.title: Letting Old and New Records Coexist During a Change
blocks: Document databases permit records with different shapes, which can make a gradual rollout possible. MongoDB’s schema-versioning pattern documents an explicit version field and readers that understand the relevant shapes. The ability to store both versions is a mechanism; compatibility still has to be implemented.

The maintenance problem is a units change as well as a field move. An adapter can connect both representations to the same interpreted measurement while keeping their original meaning visible. Guessing from whichever field happens to exist would hide malformed or future records.

reading.experimentTitle: Read the declared shape before converting units
reading.experimentIntro: Decode supported document versions, then convert their declared measurements into the common Celsius view.
reading.connectionTitle: Flexible storage still needs a representation contract
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Adapt mixed sensor documents
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: Two documents, one physical quantity
intuition.explanation: These invented documents differ in both shape and unit.

scene.caption: The adapter uses the declared version and unit. It does not infer a unit from the magnitude.

parts.title: 1. Separate schema version from business revision
paragraphs: A schema version describes how to interpret a document’s fields. A business revision describes successive states of one record. A version-2 schema document can still have its own revision 17. Reusing one number for both roles makes update and migration logic difficult to reason about.
Our input uses schema only for representation. We do not claim that a version-2 measurement was taken later than a version-1 measurement. Event time belongs in its own field when it matters.
interpretation: Version names should identify the question they answer.

parts.title: 2. Publish the old and new field contracts
paragraphs: Version 1 has id, schema and temp_c. Version 2 has id, schema and a temperature dictionary containing value and unit. The supported units are C and F. An unknown version or missing field is an error, not a zero reading.

Choose a policy for extra fields. Our reader emits only the declared measurement view, so it does not preserve unrelated metadata in its output. That makes it an adapter for reading, not a complete in-place migration of every stored document.
interpretation: Retain the raw document if later repair or audit needs fields outside this view.

parts.title: 3. Decode structure before performing the conversion
paragraphs: First use schema to select the field path. Then validate the numeric value and unit. Only a declared Fahrenheit value receives the conversion. Celsius passes through unchanged. Round the output to the stated display precision after the conversion.

The same output shape can be passed back to the adapter because it is a supported version-2 Celsius document. This repeatability helps test a rollout where old and new readers may encounter already adapted records.
parts.calculation: celsius = (fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9
interpretation: Changing a field name without converting its value would produce a structurally readable but physically incorrect measurement.

examples.title: A nested measurement makes its unit readable
paragraphs: Read a value and unit before deciding whether conversion is necessary.
examples.code:
doc = {"schema":2,"temperature":{"value":68,"unit":"F"}}
measurement = doc["temperature"]
print(measurement["unit"])
celsius = (measurement["value"] - 32) * 5 / 9
print(round(celsius,3))
interpretation: The conversion follows the explicit unit. The new field location alone would not establish it.

parts.title: 4. Validate stored records at the shared write boundary
paragraphs: An application adapter protects its own read path. Other writers can bypass it, so configure server-side validation for the permitted shapes when the database supports it. During a transition, the validator may allow both known versions while refusing unknown or malformed ones.

MongoDB validation can use JSON Schema features with BSON-specific type names. Choose enforcement settings deliberately and test rejected writes. A bypass privilege should not be part of an ordinary application role. Existing invalid records and migration behaviour need review as well as new inserts.
interpretation: The reference validates the common envelope only. Add the complete version-specific field rules before using it as the collection’s full contract.

references.title: Enable explicit envelope validation in MongoDB
description: This administrative example requires the existing development collection. It deliberately shows only the shared id and schema fields.
setup: External setup: install pymongo and use an authenticated MongoDB development service with a readings_dev collection.
MONGODB_URI belongs in the external process environment. Use a migration role authorised for collMod; the browser does not run this command.
interpretation: An envelope rule does not check units or nested measurement fields. The local exercise tests that fuller reader contract.

parts.title: 5. Roll out readers before relying on the new shape
paragraphs: A staged rollout can first deploy readers that understand both representations, then introduce new writers, then backfill old records where appropriate. Old readers may still exist in batch jobs or mobile clients, so inventory the consumers instead of checking only the newest web page.

A persistent backfill must avoid overwriting concurrent business changes. Use version conditions or another supported migration protocol and preserve progress so it can resume. Test that rerunning a migrated record leaves its meaning unchanged.
interpretation: The local adapter never writes back to storage. Its repeatability is one useful property, not a complete migration procedure.

parts.title: 6. Retire compatibility only after measuring what remains
paragraphs: Track the versions still being read and written, malformed-document rates and any differences between old and new interpretations. Update indexes and queries if fields move; an index over the old field path does not automatically cover the new one.

Keep the conversion version with derived training data. A later correction to an adapter can change a dataset even when the raw sensor documents did not change. Preserve enough source history to rebuild and compare those results.
interpretation: Botie’s changed fixture asks for a real unit conversion rather than merely recognising a different key.

quiz.prompt: What else may need to change?
options: Queries and indexes that address the old path
quiz.because: Storage flexibility does not automatically redirect path-specific queries or indexes.

title: The Bad Update Reached Every Replica. What Can We Restore?
blurb: Replication faithfully copies a mistake too. Recover a known snapshot through a complete log interval, then verify the recovered service before switching readers.
openingTitle: Every Copy Now Agrees on the Wrong Stock Balance
opening: A faulty importer sets north’s stock to zero. Replication does its job and sends that change to the other copies. Botie can reach the service, but every reachable view now contains the mistake.
We need history from before the damage, not merely another current copy. A backup snapshot and retained changes can reconstruct a chosen state if their recovery contract covers the required interval.

history.title: Retaining an Earlier State After the Current Copies Change

sources.title: DynamoDB restore to a new table

blocks: Database backup mechanisms preserve earlier data so operational mistakes and storage failures need not destroy the only recoverable state. Different products expose different units: Cassandra documents snapshots and incremental backups; DynamoDB provides managed backup and point-in-time restore mechanisms. Neither is reproduced by our local dictionary.

The useful recovery idea is a boundary. A snapshot establishes a known earlier state; a valid replay interval brings that state to a chosen later point. The target must fall inside the history the backup system can actually recover.

reading.experimentTitle: Restore the stock record before the faulty import
reading.experimentIntro: Check the replay interval, apply its replacements to a snapshot copy, then label the recovered state with its target position.
reading.connectionTitle: A recoverable point needs complete supporting history
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Replay a bounded recovery log
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: Stop before the known bad change
intuition.explanation: This teaching log uses consecutive positions and full replacement values.

scene.caption: Real database log positions need not be consecutive integers. Completeness must come from that system’s recovery protocol.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish surviving a failure from undoing a mistake
paragraphs: Replicas can help keep a service running after a node fails. They commonly receive validly committed mistakes as well as intended writes. A backup protects a different need: recovering a previous state or a separate durable copy under its retention policy.

A backup on the same compromised account or storage boundary may share the incident’s failure mode. Choose isolation, retention and deletion controls according to the failures the maintenance service must recover from.
interpretation: A healthy replica is useful, but it is not automatically a historical backup.

parts.title: 2. Define the recovery point and the recovery time
paragraphs: The recovery point objective describes acceptable data loss, often expressed as how far back the restored state may be from the incident. The recovery time objective describes how long the service can remain unavailable or degraded while recovering. These are requirements, not outcomes established by enabling a setting.

Measure both in restore drills. Include locating the backup, obtaining authorised keys, restoring data, checking application configuration and making the service usable. A quick file copy can be a small part of the complete recovery time.
interpretation: The exercise’s target sequence illustrates a chosen point, not a measured RPO or RTO.

parts.title: 3. Check that the replay interval is complete
paragraphs: Our teaching snapshot contains seq and a dictionary of inventory balances. Each log record gives the next consecutive sequence and a full replacement for one balance. To restore a target, select positions after the snapshot up to that target and require every intervening position.

A missing event stops the operation. Publishing the remaining records would create a plausible image whose history is incomplete. Real recovery logs may have gaps in numeric positions, so their completeness checks use the database’s documented mechanism rather than this invented consecutive-integer rule.
interpretation: The local function is a deterministic restore calculation, not a database backup tool.

examples.title: Inspect the required replay positions
paragraphs: The target lies after the snapshot and before a later faulty update.
examples.code:
snapshot_position = 10
target = 12
required = list(range(snapshot_position + 1, target + 1))
print(required)
print(13 in required)
interpretation: The later operation is excluded because it is outside the selected recovery interval.

parts.title: 4. Replay into a separate state and verify the result
paragraphs: Copy the snapshot before applying changes so a failed attempt does not destroy the starting point. Replaying full replacements in sequence gives the state at the target under this fixture’s contract. A new key can appear in the replay even if the snapshot did not contain it.

After recovery, compare expected identities and balances and run application-level checks. Restoring bytes is not proof that indexes, access policies, credentials and application configuration are ready. Some services restore into a new resource that needs its settings reapplied.
interpretation: DynamoDB documents restoration into a new table and lists settings that need separate attention.

parts.title: 5. Protect backup access and the keys needed to read it
paragraphs: Backups can contain the same sensitive tenant data as the live service. Restrict who can list, read, restore or delete them. Use the supported encryption mechanism and retain access to its keys for the entire recovery period. A perfectly intact encrypted backup is unusable if the recovery team cannot obtain the required key permissions.

Use separate development restore destinations and appropriately scoped roles during drills. Verify that a restored copy does not accidentally expose production data through a broadly accessible test service.
interpretation: Recovery permissions should allow the planned procedure without becoming ordinary web-application privileges.

parts.title: 6. Decide what happens to legitimate work after the target
paragraphs: Restoring before the faulty import can also remove legitimate changes that happened afterward. Identify which later operations can be safely replayed, reconciled or re-entered. Keep evidence of external actions, such as deliveries already dispatched, because moving the database backwards does not undo them.

Freeze or route writes during cutover according to a documented plan. Otherwise the old and restored services can both accept new stock changes and diverge while the team believes recovery is complete.
interpretation: Choosing a point is a business recovery decision as well as a storage operation.

parts.title: 7. Prove the procedure before the incident
paragraphs: Run a restore drill with representative size and application checks. Record which backup was used, its recoverable interval, the measured elapsed time and any settings that were missing. Test a missing-history case so the process refuses an unsupported target.
Repeat after material schema, encryption or infrastructure changes. A recovery document that nobody has exercised can preserve an obsolete assumption for months.
interpretation: The workshop’s later target includes the faulty change deliberately. Inspect the target before treating a successful replay as the desired repair.

Move the snapshot label forward without replay

The teaching log is consecutive. Require every position after snapshot.seq through target, apply its full replacements in sequence to a copy, and return {"seq": target, "state": mapping}. Ignore records outside that interval after validating their shape. Preserve inputs.

title: A Fast Feature Lookup Still Has to Mean the Right Thing
blurb: A model needs the right entity, feature definition and available measurements in a fixed order. Use a serving document for that contract while keeping historical training evidence separately.
openingTitle: The Model Received a Reading Quickly. Was It the Right Reading?
opening: Botie’s fault model expects temperature followed by vibration. A fast key lookup returns the fields in a different order, using an older feature definition. The storage request succeeded, but the input no longer means what the model was trained to interpret.
The database choice follows the task. We will assemble a serving record only when its identity, definition and freshness match the model request, and retain an explicit fallback when they do not.

history.title: Separating Fast Current Lookups from Reproducible Training History
blocks: Feature-store systems separate concerns that otherwise get mixed into one table: serving inputs quickly by entity and retaining information for training or analysis. SageMaker documents online and offline storage modes with distinct update and history behaviour. They are one implementation of this separation, not a requirement that every model use a specialised store.

Our maintenance system already has historical SQL feature logic. Here we decide what a current serving lookup must return and which checks belong between that lookup and the model. The storage format is useful only if it preserves the feature contract.

reading.experimentTitle: Check the document before handing values to the model
reading.experimentIntro: Match the entity and feature definition, check decision-time availability and age, then assemble the names in the model’s required order.
reading.connectionTitle: A storage success is only the start of an input check
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Assemble a permitted feature vector
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: The same values in the wrong positions are different model inputs
intuition.explanation: The model contract names the positions explicitly.

scene.caption: Object field insertion order is not the model’s feature specification.

parts.title: 1. Choose a store from the operation you need
paragraphs: A keyed serving record can be useful when the request already knows the tenant and asset and needs a small fixed set of inputs quickly. A document can keep related feature values and their metadata together. A relational table can also serve keyed reads; measure the existing system before introducing another database.
A fleet-wide historical training join has a different access pattern. Keep the source of truth, derived feature view and serving copy distinct in the design so each has an owner and a rebuild path.
interpretation: The exercise does not rank database brands. It exposes the contract that any chosen serving path must meet.

parts.title: 2. Name the feature definition that produced the values
paragraphs: A feature name can remain the same while its meaning changes. Vibration might move from a raw reading to an average over a different time window. Units, missing-value rules and preprocessing can also change. Record a version or digest for the definition expected by the deployed model.

The feature definition version is separate from the document schema and source record revision. Compatible field shapes do not prove compatible model inputs. Reject or adapt a mismatch under an explicit policy instead of treating every readable dictionary as usable.
interpretation: Our request requires bearing-v2 exactly. The fixture does not implement semantic version negotiation.

parts.title: 3. Keep observation time and availability time visible
paragraphs: Event time tells us when the measurement describes the asset. Availability time tells us when that value became usable by this serving path. An old event can arrive after the decision it is meant to support.

The earlier SQL lesson showed historical point-in-time selection. This lesson checks one retrieved document against a decision time and a maximum measurement age. It cannot reconstruct an overwritten historical value; if the current record fails, the route stays fallback unless another authorised source supplies suitable evidence.
interpretation: A lookup of today’s latest document is not a historical training query.

examples.title: Check a late arrival against an earlier decision
paragraphs: The event existed in the world before the decision, but the serving path received it afterward.
examples.code:
event_time = 100
available_time = 115
decision_time = 110
print(event_time <= decision_time)
print(available_time <= decision_time)
interpretation: The measurement’s event time alone would admit information the service did not yet have.

parts.title: 4. Assemble by the declared names, never by dictionary order
paragraphs: The model supplies an ordered feature-name list. Read each required name from the document in that order. Check for absent, nonnumeric and nonfinite values before constructing the vector. Extra document fields should not silently become model inputs.

A missing value policy belongs to the model’s definition. If training used a particular imputation rule, serving must use the compatible rule. Our exercise has no trained imputer, so it falls back rather than inventing a zero.
interpretation: The vector’s positions are part of its meaning, even when all its entries are valid numbers.

parts.title: 5. Scope the lookup and retain its actual read contract
paragraphs: The authenticated service establishes tenant scope and builds the permitted key. It should use credentials limited to the needed records and operations. A browser should call the application boundary rather than receive broad storage credentials.

The read mode must suit the operation. A stronger table read can reduce one kind of staleness, but it cannot refresh a feature pipeline that has not produced a new document. Check the measurement metadata even when the storage read succeeds.
interpretation: This external reference obtains a document. It deliberately leaves the application’s feature checks as a separate step.

references.title: Read a development serving document by its complete key
description: The prepared table has string partition key pk. Trusted tenant and asset values must come from the authorised application context.
references.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name="us-east-1").Table("maintenance_features_dev")
response = table.get_item(
    Key={"pk":"tenant:north:asset:P7"},
    ConsistentRead=True,
)
item = response.get("Item")
print(item is not None)
setup: External setup: install boto3 and provision a disposable development table with the stated key and an example feature item.
Use an authorised SDK role with the required read permission. The browser challenge performs no network calls.
interpretation: A found item still needs entity, definition, availability, age and value checks. Key encoding also needs a collision-free production convention.

parts.title: 6. Keep an explicit outcome when the feature contract fails
paragraphs: A missing document, wrong feature version or stale measurement should not silently proceed to prediction. Decide whether the application can use a documented baseline, request a fresh measurement, or ask for human inspection. That decision depends on the task’s consequences.

Our function returns fallback with an empty vector. A production interface should record the reason without leaking another tenant’s data, and should make clear when it is showing a baseline rather than the requested model result.
interpretation: A fallback is an application outcome. It is not evidence that the asset is healthy.

parts.title: 7. Retain enough evidence to reproduce the prediction
paragraphs: A compact serving record often keeps only the latest state. Retain an appropriate prediction log or immutable references that identify the model, feature definition and input data used, subject to privacy and retention requirements. An offline store can support historical reconstruction if its time and revision semantics are understood.

Compare training and serving transformations with shared cases. A correct training query cannot compensate for a serving adapter that changes units or feature order. Monitor missing inputs, age and version mismatches alongside model performance.
interpretation: The record checks test input compatibility, not the accuracy or fairness of the trained model.

parts.title: 8. Change the feature system without losing its reconstruction path
paragraphs: A new feature definition may require a new serving namespace or an explicit versioned rollout. Backfill the required entities, compare representative predictions, and switch the model and feature contract together. Keep the earlier version long enough for the agreed rollback and audit needs.

If another database is added, account for its projection lag, rebuild process and access boundary. A smaller inference lookup can be worth that work, but a second current copy also creates another place whose freshness must be explained.
interpretation: Botie now has a concrete boundary between finding a document and using it as model input.

quiz.prompt: Which outcome matches this lesson’s contract?

Rename the version without changing the values

given.data: The requested model expects bearing-v2, but the current serving document is bearing-v1.

quiz.prompt: Strong read consistency alone makes that measurement fresh.
quiz.because: Storage freshness relative to committed writes and measurement age are different properties.

practice.question: Does this document satisfy the model’s input contract?
task: Write serving_vector(record, request, fields). request contains nonblank tenant, asset and feature_version plus nonnegative integer as_of and max_age. fields is a nonempty list of distinct nonblank names. record and request must be dictionaries. Reject malformed request structure with ValueError. Booleans are not numeric fields or timestamps.

Return {"route":"predict","vector": values in fields order} only if record matches all three identifiers, has nonnegative integer event_time <= available_time <= as_of, and as_of minus event_time is at most max_age. Every required feature must be a finite number in record.features. Otherwise return {"route":"fallback","vector":[]}. Preserve inputs.
hints: Check identity and definition before using feature values.
Use the ordered names to collect the vector; do not iterate over the feature dictionary’s values.

title: Which Equipment Depends on This Supply?
openingTitle: The Pump Record Does Not Contain the Whole Answer
opening: P7 depends on supply S1. Another pump, P8, depends on P7. Botie needs to distinguish the supply P7 needs from the equipment that needs P7. A list of asset names cannot express that difference.

We need to store the connection itself, including what it means and which way it points. A graph makes those connected records explicit. We can then ask a question by following the relationships that matter to it.
blurb: Represent equipment and its directed dependencies as nodes and relationships before choosing how to query the connections.

history.title: Relationships Became Part of the Stored Model

sources.title: Cypher authors on the historical data-model problem

blocks: The Cypher authors describe Neo4j’s early data-model work in a media asset management system around 2000. Its changing structures, relationships and access-control views made variable-length connection queries useful. This is one documented route into modern property graphs, rather than a claim that Neo4j invented graphs. A property graph gives entities nodes and stores typed relationships with properties of their own.

This changes how we express a dependency question. The relationship is a stored fact we can follow from a known starting asset. It does not make every query faster, and relational tables can represent the same facts with keys and joins.

intuition.title: Read the arrows as dependency statements
intuition.explanation: The arrow means the source requires the target. Follow only the direction the question asks for.

scene.caption: P7 directly depends on S1. P8 directly depends on P7. The arrow convention must be stated before interpreting a path.

parts.title: 1. Give each entity a node
paragraphs: A node represents one entity whose identity matters. P7 and S1 are separate assets even if both have the display name “Main unit.” An asset category can be a label, while its status or installation date can be properties.
A label groups nodes; it is not the node’s identity. A node can have several labels in a property graph. Our Python records use kind for one teaching category and id for a stable identifier.
interpretation: Begin with the things the application must distinguish, rather than turning every cell into a node.

parts.title: 2. Make the relationship a record too
paragraphs: A relationship connects a source node to a target node and has a type such as DEPENDS_ON. Its direction expresses our modelling convention. Properties on that relationship can describe the connection, such as when the dependency became active.
Two relationships may connect the same nodes for different reasons, or represent separate events. Removing them as duplicates without a domain rule can lose information.
interpretation: The source and target describe the relationship, not which object is more important.

parts.title: 3. Ask a one-hop question before following a chain
paragraphs: For “what does P7 depend on directly?”, find outgoing DEPENDS_ON relationships from P7 and read their target nodes. For “what depends on P7?”, match the incoming direction.
Cypher writes node patterns in parentheses and relationship patterns in brackets. The arrow preserves the convention we drew. RETURN chooses the information to display.
interpretation: A direct neighbour is one relationship away. It is different from every node reachable through a longer chain.

references.title: Read P7’s direct dependencies
description: This is an external Cypher query over the setup graph.
references.code:
MATCH (:Asset {id:$asset})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s:Asset)
RETURN DISTINCT s.id AS dependency
ORDER BY dependency
setup: In a fresh Neo4j test database, run CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}), (s:Asset {id:'S1'}), (q:Asset {id:'P8'}), (p)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s), (q)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(p).
Supply parameter asset as the string P7. Use a read-only database role for the query.
interpretation: S1 is the result. Reversing the arrow would answer a different question.

parts.title: 4. Represent the same mechanism with ordinary records
paragraphs: The graph dictionary contains a nodes list and an edges list. Each edge names its source and target by ID. We can inspect the relevant edge records without needing a database server.
This program shows the matching edge identities. The challenge takes the next step and returns distinct dependency IDs instead.
interpretation: These loops demonstrate the model; database storage and query planning remain separate topics.

examples.title: Inspect the outgoing edge records
paragraphs: Only the edge whose source is P7 matches.
examples.code:
edges = [{"id": "d1", "source": "P7", "target": "S1", "type": "DEPENDS_ON"}, {"id": "d2", "source": "P8", "target": "P7", "type": "DEPENDS_ON"}]
print([e['id'] for e in edges if e['type']=='DEPENDS_ON' and e['source']=='P7'])
interpretation: The incoming d2 relationship does not describe a resource P7 requires.

parts.title: 5. Choose graphs because the relationships matter
paragraphs: A graph representation is useful when questions repeatedly follow connected entities, especially through changing numbers of hops. A simple tabular report may be clearer and cheaper in a relational database.

The learning task is to preserve identity, direction and relationship meaning. Storage products differ in constraints, transactions and indexing, so a picture of connected circles is not a complete architecture decision.
interpretation: We will keep the maintenance question stable while adding the machinery needed to answer it reliably.

quiz.prompt: Can they always be merged into one edge?
options: Only if the names are short
quiz.because: Relationship type and identity can distinguish facts with the same endpoints.

given.data: Two relationships connect the same pumps but have different types.

quiz.prompt: Choosing a graph model does not prove that every query will run faster.
quiz.because: Query shape, storage and indexing still determine performance.

given.data: Equipment dependencies can also be represented by relational tables and keys.

title: Are These Two Pumps Actually the Same Pump?
openingTitle: Both Plants Called Their Pump P7
opening: Two plants send Botie a record named P7. Both display names say “Main pump.” If we merge on either field, the graph will connect inspections from two different physical machines.
Identity is the rule that tells us when records refer to the same thing. Before importing relationships, we need an identifier whose scope is clear and whose meaning survives a renamed label.
blurb: Separate durable identity from names, qualify external IDs by their source and detect collisions before merging records.

history.title: A Graph Needed Stable References Beyond Display Names

sources.title: RDF identity and shared resource descriptions, W3C 1999

blocks: Sharing descriptions between systems made identity a practical problem for early web metadata. W3C’s 1999 RDF recommendation addressed exchangeable resource descriptions, where common references matter more than a displayed name. Our property-graph import has a related problem at a smaller scale: local pump IDs need enough scope to refer to the intended entity. The mechanisms differ, but neither model can safely equate entities from matching display text alone.

A source-qualified equipment code makes the scope visible. It prevents an import from treating identical local names as global identifiers, while allowing a later display-name change on the same entity.

intuition.title: Keep the plants’ identities separate
intuition.explanation: The same local code belongs to different source systems.

scene.caption: Matching the display name would incorrectly connect these separate maintenance histories.

parts.title: 1. Ask what makes an entity the same over time
paragraphs: A display name can change, be misspelled or be shared. A source system’s local ID may be stable only inside that system. Use a documented application key, and retain the source ID used to resolve imports.
Database internal identifiers are implementation references, not a substitute for a durable cross-system business key. Avoid persisting assumptions about their reuse across deletion or export/import.
interpretation: The question is which physical or logical thing this record refers to.

parts.title: 2. Qualify a local identifier by its namespace
paragraphs: Treat system and external_id as a pair. Concatenating raw text with an unescaped delimiter can collide when either value contains that delimiter. A structured pair or a carefully encoded identifier preserves the boundary.
Our exercise serialises the pair as compact JSON text. That is a teaching key, not an attempt to choose the permanent identifier scheme for every production system.
interpretation: east/P7 and west/P7 remain distinct even when their display names match.

examples.title: Inspect the qualified keys
paragraphs: The same local code is scoped by a different system.
interpretation: The pair remains unambiguous even if a field later contains punctuation.

parts.title: 3. Merge on identity and set mutable properties separately
paragraphs: MERGE matches the pattern supplied. Including a mutable name in the identity pattern can create a new node after a rename. Match the stable key, then update the appropriate properties.

A uniqueness constraint backs the intended key under concurrent writers. MERGE by itself is not a general promise of global uniqueness. Resolve conflicting source records explicitly before applying updates.
interpretation: A repeated import and a changed entity identity are different events.

references.title: Keep a rename out of the identity pattern
description: This writes only in a disposable database after the stated constraint is installed.
references.code:
MERGE (a:Asset {system:$system, external_id:$external_id})
SET a.name=$name
RETURN a.system, a.external_id, a.name
setup: Use a test database. Run CREATE CONSTRAINT asset_source_key IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Asset) REQUIRE (a.system, a.external_id) IS UNIQUE. This enforces uniqueness of complete pairs; it does not require both properties to be present.
Supply system east, external_id P7 and name Renamed pump as parameters.
interpretation: The stable pair locates the entity. The name is updated after matching. Required-key presence is a separate policy.

parts.title: 4. Do not merge two entities just because a similarity model suggests it
paragraphs: Entity resolution may propose that two vendor codes refer to the same equipment. Keep the proposed mapping and its evidence separate from a confirmed identity merge. A mistaken merge can redirect every attached relationship.
Define who approves ambiguous mappings and how a merge can be audited or reversed. Confidence scores are useful evidence, but they do not define identity by themselves.
interpretation: Identity errors propagate through traversals even when the query syntax is correct.

parts.title: 5. Detect duplicate scoped keys before accepting a batch
paragraphs: Two rows with the same qualified key need a replay or conflict policy. A renamed display field may be a valid update, while differing immutable serial numbers may require review. The challenge only reports repeated keys so a later stage can decide.
Do not let dictionary overwrite order silently make that decision. Keep both source records available until the conflict has been interpreted.
interpretation: A collision report identifies work for a policy; it does not prove the duplicate is fraudulent or incorrect.

quiz.because: A key collision needs interpretation before relationships are redirected.

quiz.prompt: Its use alone is not a general guarantee of unique keys under concurrent updates.
quiz.because: The database constraint and application identity policy are separate parts of the design.

given.data: MERGE is used without a supporting uniqueness constraint.

title: Who Inspected This Pump?
openingTitle: The Technician Is Two Relationships Away
opening: The pump points to an inspection record. That inspection points to the technician who performed it. Botie must keep those connections together: a technician attached to another pump’s inspection is not an answer.

A pattern describes the connected shape we want to find. Its variables remember which node filled each position, so the next relationship continues from the same inspection rather than starting an unrelated search.
blurb: Match a connected pattern and preserve variable bindings across steps instead of accidentally combining unrelated records.

history.title: A Query Could Describe the Connected Shape It Wanted

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018

blocks: Cypher developed inside Neo4j as a declarative property-graph language. Its 2018 language paper explains pattern matching as producing rows of variable bindings: each row records which entities satisfy a connected pattern.

That is why the inspection variable matters. Once a row binds it to I1, the technician relationship must extend from I1. The drawing-like syntax makes this connection visible while leaving physical execution to the database.

intuition.title: Follow the same inspection through both links
intuition.explanation: The two pump histories are separate connected patterns.

scene.caption: A search starting at P7 reaches T1 through I1. T2 belongs to the other branch.

parts.title: 1. Make the starting entity specific
paragraphs: Bind a to the Asset whose stable ID is P7. The start is part of the question, not a detail to discard once expansion begins. A useful index can help locate it, but the query must still state the identity condition.
Our workshop binding keeps origin as P7 while current moves to the endpoint reached by each relationship. The path list is evidence of how that row was obtained.
interpretation: A starting ID and a type condition prevent unrelated records from becoming candidates.

parts.title: 2. Extend one binding at a time
paragraphs: The first expansion binds i to an inspection connected to a. The second expansion uses that same i to find t. Several inspections can produce several valid binding rows.

If we instead collect every inspection and every technician independently, a cross-product can pair unrelated records. Reusing a variable expresses a shared entity, just as matching a key constrains a relational join.
interpretation: Keep the connecting inspection ID visible while learning the pattern.

examples.title: Inspect the first-hop inspection IDs
paragraphs: This program stops after the first relationship rather than answering the full technician question.
examples.code:

parts.title: 3. Read the Cypher pattern from left to right
paragraphs: MATCH describes the required graph shape. Variables a, i and t name the bound nodes; relationship types describe which links may connect them. RETURN DISTINCT t.id changes the output from one row per matching route to one row per technician.
DISTINCT is appropriate because the question asks which technicians, rather than how many inspections they performed. For an audit of individual visits, retain the inspection identity instead.
interpretation: Projection and duplicate policy determine the report’s grain.

references.title: Find technicians through the bound inspection
description: The parameter supplies the starting asset without rewriting query structure.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i:Inspection)
      -[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(t:Technician)
RETURN DISTINCT t.id AS technician
ORDER BY technician

interpretation: T1 is returned. A second P7 inspection by T1 would still return that technician once.

parts.title: 4. Pass values through parameters
paragraphs: User-controlled asset IDs belong in driver parameters such as $asset. Do not paste them into a Cypher string. Keep query structure under application control and use reviewed templates for supported questions.

Dynamic labels, property keys and relationship-type syntax depend on the database version. If an application lets a user choose a structural option, validate it against a deliberate allowlist or use the documented supported parameter mechanism. String escaping is not a general substitute for that boundary.
interpretation: Parameter binding preserves query structure; it does not authorise the requested asset.

parts.title: 5. Keep access rules on the path, not only the final result
paragraphs: A tenant restriction on the returned technician is insufficient if the match traverses another tenant’s inspection to get there. Restrict the starting node and every relevant intermediate entity and relationship according to the application’s permissions.
Use least-privilege database roles and an application authorisation layer. Hop limits and result limits control work; they do not grant permission to read a node.
interpretation: The Python exercise uses a fully permitted fixture so the matching mechanism remains clear. The retrieval lesson adds an explicit scope before traversal.

parts.title: 6. Know which route repetitions the language permits
paragraphs: A two-hop pattern and a variable-length traversal have different scopes. Cypher has documented rules for reusing relationships in a match, and newer versions provide additional match modes. Do not assume an arbitrary Python loop exactly implements every Cypher mode.
Our workshop refuses to reuse a relationship already present in a binding’s route. It demonstrates this fixed connected pattern, with complete edge identities visible for inspection.
interpretation: The lesson’s mechanism is a small specified subset, not a browser implementation of the query language.
