title: How Many Inspections Were Actually Completed?
openingTitle: A Repeated Link Has Doubled the Report
opening: P7 has one completed inspection. An import has accidentally recorded two relationships to that same inspection. Botie’s first count says two. The query counted matching relationships, while the maintenance team asked for distinct completed inspections.
Before adding numbers, we need to decide what a matched row represents. We can inspect status on the bound inspection, then remove repeated asset/inspection pairs before counting them.
blurb: Filter bound properties and aggregate at the intended grain, distinguishing paths, relationships and distinct inspection identities.

history.title: Graph Matches Still Produce Rows That Need a Grain
blocks: Pattern matching can produce many binding rows from one starting node. Cypher combines those rows using aggregate functions and explicit intermediate stages such as WITH. The result depends on what is counted and which bindings remain as grouping keys.

Our duplicate link shows the practical consequence. The graph can contain two matched relationships while representing one inspection entity. Counting the entity once requires an identity-based duplicate policy.

intuition.title: Two relationship records point to one inspection
intuition.explanation: The duplicate edge IDs are separate records, but the target inspection identity is the same.

scene.caption: The completed-inspection count is one. Counting relationship matches would answer a different question.

intuition.title: Follow the row meaning through the count
intuition.explanation: These are the duplicate-link records drawn above, inspected stage by stage.

records.label: Closed Inspection filter
cells: Two routes still refer to one inspection

records.label: Distinct asset/inspection pairs
cells: Relationship ID is no longer part of the counted grain

scene.caption: Removing duplicates before deciding which fields define the entity can change the answer.

parts.title: 1. Filter the property of the bound inspection
paragraphs: The status belongs to the inspection node. Require the endpoint to have kind Inspection as well as status closed. A mistyped HAS_INSPECTION edge to a technician is a data-quality failure, not completed inspection work.

Inspect the node reached by each binding, then require status closed. An absent status does not pass that equality condition. Decide separately whether missing statuses should trigger a data-quality report.
interpretation: Relationship meaning and node state are different facts.

parts.title: 2. Write down what one matched row represents
paragraphs: After expansion there is a row for each matched asset/relationship/inspection combination. Two edges to I1 therefore produce two rows. If the desired count is distinct inspections, reduce each row to the asset ID and inspection ID before deduplication.
Deduplicating only the inspection ID globally would lose which asset the count belongs to. Some domains legitimately associate the same inspection with several assets.
interpretation: The distinct pair preserves the grouping identity and the counted entity.

examples.title: Collapse repeated asset/inspection pairs
paragraphs: This small program demonstrates the grain change before aggregation.
examples.code:
pairs=[('P7','I1'),('P7','I1'),('P8','I2')]
print(sorted(set(pairs)))
interpretation: The two P7 matches become one pair while P8 keeps its own association.

parts.title: 3. Keep the grouping variable beside the aggregate
paragraphs: In Cypher, non-aggregate returned expressions define grouping keys. Returning a.id with count(DISTINCT i) gives one count per asset. WITH can name that count for a later condition.
If a later relationship match multiplies the rows, an already computed count can also be repeated. Inspect intermediate cardinality before summing a summary again.
interpretation: The group boundary deserves the same attention in Cypher as in SQL.

references.title: Count inspection entities rather than matched links
description: Only assets with at least one completed match appear in this required-pattern query.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i:Inspection)
WHERE i.status=$status
WITH a, count(DISTINCT i) AS completed
RETURN a.id AS asset, completed
ORDER BY asset
setup: In an empty Neo4j test database, run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7'}),(b:Asset {id:'P8'}),(i:Inspection {id:'I1',status:'closed'}),(j:Inspection {id:'I2',status:'open'}),(t:Technician {id:'T1'}),(u:Technician {id:'T2'}),(a)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i),(b)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(j),(i)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(t),(j)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(u).
Bind status to closed.
interpretation: P7 has one completed inspection. P8 is absent because its inspection is open.

parts.title: 4. Do not manufacture zero rows after a required match
paragraphs: If no completed inspection matches an asset, that asset has no binding row in this query. Grouping cannot produce a group for an entity that vanished earlier.

If the report must show zero, preserve the asset population before matching optional inspections. That will be the next lesson’s problem. Replacing a missing number at the end cannot recreate a missing asset row.
interpretation: Absent groups and groups with zero counts are different query results.

parts.title: 5. Filter before aggregation only when the question calls for it
paragraphs: Closed status qualifies individual inspections, so it belongs before the count. A requirement such as at least two completed inspections belongs after that grouped count has been calculated.
Counting all inspections and then asking whether any status is closed mixes two different questions. Keep row-level conditions and group-level conditions on the stages where their inputs exist.
interpretation: Read the count as a statement about a specific population of distinct inspection identities.

title: Keep the Pumps That Have No Completed Inspection
openingTitle: The Asset Most in Need of Attention Has Disappeared
opening: Botie’s report correctly counts completed inspections, but P8 is missing. P8 only has an open inspection. The maintenance team needs to see that zero, because it is precisely the pump that may need attention.
A required pattern keeps only successful matches. We need to retain each asset even when its qualifying inspection pattern has no match.
blurb: Use optional graph patterns without losing the starting population or mistaking an unmatched placeholder for a real inspection.

history.title: Absence Became a Result Worth Preserving
blocks: Cypher OPTIONAL MATCH extends pattern matching with NULL bindings when the requested pattern has no match. This resembles an outer join: existing input rows can survive without a related record.
That behaviour lets an asset register define the report population. A missing completed inspection is then visible as absence, instead of causing the asset itself to disappear.

intuition.title: An open inspection does not satisfy the closed-work pattern
intuition.explanation: Both assets remain in the report, but only one has a qualifying target.

scene.caption: Preserving P8 does not relabel I2 as closed. Its qualifying optional match is absent.

parts.title: 1. Begin with the complete asset population
paragraphs: MATCH (a:Asset) establishes every asset that belongs in the report. The next match is allowed to be absent, but the original a remains bound.
In Python, initialise an empty inspection set for every asset before examining edges. That small ordering decision is what keeps a pump with no relationships at all.
interpretation: The output population must exist before optional evidence is attached.

examples.title: Start a count entry for an isolated asset
paragraphs: No inspection edge is required to establish a report row.
examples.code:
nodes=[{'id':'P7','kind':'Asset'},{'id':'P9','kind':'Asset'}]
print({n['id']:set() for n in nodes})
interpretation: Each empty set can later produce a count of zero.

parts.title: 2. Make the qualifying condition part of the optional pattern
paragraphs: The closed-status condition describes which inspection is an acceptable match. In Cypher, a WHERE associated with OPTIONAL MATCH participates in that pattern’s matching conditions.
Moving the condition to a later WITH/WHERE stage can instead remove a row whose optional inspection is NULL. The resulting query may again omit the asset we meant to preserve.
interpretation: The position of the predicate expresses whether it qualifies a match or filters an already preserved result.

parts.title: 3. Count matched identities rather than preserved rows
paragraphs: count(i) ignores NULL bindings, while count(*) counts rows. An asset with no qualifying inspection has an optional placeholder row, so count(*) can produce one even though no inspection exists.
Use count(DISTINCT i) when repeated relationships should not multiply the same inspection. The grouping asset remains in the output with zero.
interpretation: The placeholder preserves the asset. It is not an inspection.

references.title: Keep zero-completion assets
description: The status predicate belongs to the optional pattern.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset)
OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i:Inspection)
WHERE i.status=$status
RETURN a.id AS asset, count(DISTINCT i) AS completed
ORDER BY asset
setup: In an empty Neo4j test database, run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7'}),(b:Asset {id:'P8'}),(i:Inspection {id:'I1',status:'closed'}),(j:Inspection {id:'I2',status:'open'}),(t:Technician {id:'T1'}),(u:Technician {id:'T2'}),(a)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i),(b)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(j),(i)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(t),(j)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(u).
Bind status to closed.
interpretation: P7 appears with 1 and P8 with 0.

parts.title: 4. Distinguish no inspection from an inspection with unknown properties
paragraphs: An actual inspection node may lack its completion date or status. That is different from having no inspection relationship. Inspect the node identity when diagnosing missing values.
A report can preserve both facts by returning inspection IDs and their properties separately. Do not use a nullable descriptive field as proof that no node matched.
interpretation: NULL in one property is not evidence that the whole related entity is absent.

parts.title: 5. Keep independent optional branches from multiplying each other
paragraphs: Suppose an asset has two inspections and three manuals. Matching both branches can produce six combinations. Counting inspections after that multiplication requires an explicit distinct policy or separate aggregation of each branch.
OPTIONAL MATCH preserves absence; it does not eliminate fan-out. Work through one small asset with multiple matches on both sides before trusting a dashboard total.
interpretation: The workshop has one optional branch so we can observe its preserved row directly.

parts.title: 6. Build the qualifying edge set before optional expansion
paragraphs: Our components first identify closed inspection targets and retain only relationships pointing to those targets. Optional expansion then preserves a binding whose source has no qualifying relationship.
The resulting NULL current value is excluded by count values. The distinct origin/current pair prevents repeated links from adding another inspection.
interpretation: This record mechanism mirrors the question’s matching boundary without pretending to parse OPTIONAL MATCH syntax.

quiz.because: A nullable property is not a reliable match sentinel.

quiz.because: Optionality preserves missing matches but does not remove combinations of present matches.

title: Follow a Dependency Without Following It Forever
openingTitle: The Dependency List Points Back to the Pump
opening: P7 requires S1, S1 requires S2, and a later import says S2 requires P7. Botie’s recursive search keeps returning to the same equipment. Even if the cycle describes a real feedback dependency, our list of affected entities should not repeat forever.

We need to decide what the traversal is collecting and when a node has already been dealt with. For distinct reachable assets, a breadth-first search can remember visited IDs and stop expansion at a stated depth.
blurb: Separate reachability from path enumeration, handle cycles explicitly and interpret bounded traversal results without promising complete discovery.

history.title: Unknown-Length Connections Needed Repeated Expansion

sources.title: Cypher authors on variable-length traversal needs

blocks: The early Neo4j use case described by the Cypher authors included access through variable-length relationships. A fixed sequence of joins or pattern segments cannot express every unknown chain length conveniently. Graph query languages therefore provide bounded or variable-length path matching.

The repeated step does not decide the answer’s grain. A list of reachable nodes, every distinct path and the shortest path are different questions. Our teaching traversal collects nodes once, which gives the visited set a clear purpose.

intuition.title: A cycle returns to an already discovered node
intuition.explanation: P7, S1 and S2 form a directed cycle. S3 lies one step beyond S2.

scene.caption: With maximum depth 2, the report includes S1 and S2, excludes the starting P7, and makes no completeness claim about deeper dependencies.

intuition.title: Watch the frontier meet the cycle

records.label: If depth were three

scene.caption: The return edge to P7 cannot restart the search. S3 is outside the depth-two answer, rather than proven unreachable.

parts.title: 1. Choose whether the answer contains nodes or routes
paragraphs: Reachability asks whether a node can be reached at all. Path enumeration retains the route, so two different paths to S2 can both be useful results. A global visited set is suitable for our distinct reachability answer, but would suppress alternative routes if we were trying to enumerate them.
State this before writing a recursion. The same graph can legitimately produce different answers under different output contracts.
interpretation: The challenge returns distinct reachable IDs, excluding the starting ID.

parts.title: 2. Keep a queue of nodes still to explore
paragraphs: Breadth-first search begins with the starting node at depth zero. Remove the oldest queued entry, inspect its outgoing dependency edges and add unseen targets at the next depth. Mark a target visited when it is queued so two frontier nodes do not enqueue it repeatedly.
Because each step has equal hop cost, the first discovery gives the minimum number of relationships from the start. Weighted cost is a different question.
interpretation: The queue is work still to do; the visited set records identities already discovered.

examples.title: Expand the first frontier
paragraphs: This program only inspects the first step. The exercise must keep expanding safely.
interpretation: The next frontier comes from outgoing edges of the current frontier, not every edge in the graph.

parts.title: 3. Bound a real path query deliberately
paragraphs: The Cypher range *1..3 requests paths from one through three relationships. DISTINCT on the returned node removes repeated endpoints from different matching paths. The query below also excludes the starting node if a cycle returns to it.

Cypher’s relationship-reuse rules and a global-visited BFS are different mechanisms. For this bounded reachability question their intended endpoint set aligns, but the path rows and search work need not be identical.
interpretation: A hop bound says how far the query may explore; it does not certify the graph has no deeper nodes.

references.title: Ask for dependencies within three hops
description: This uses established variable-length relationship syntax; newer quantified syntax is another documented option.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..3]->(d:Asset)
WHERE d <> a
RETURN DISTINCT d.id AS dependency ORDER BY dependency
setup: In an empty test database run CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}),(a:Asset {id:'S1'}),(b:Asset {id:'S2'}),(c:Asset {id:'S3'}),(p)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(a),(a)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(b),(b)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(p),(b)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(c).
Bind asset to P7.
interpretation: The result includes S1, S2 and S3. The chosen three-hop cap is part of the report’s scope.

parts.title: 4. Interpret the depth boundary honestly
paragraphs: At depth two, S2 has been discovered but its outgoing edges are not expanded. S3 is therefore absent from the two-hop result. Calling that result “all dependencies” would overstate what was checked.

A depth cap also does not bound the number of nodes tightly in a high-degree graph. Add operational time and result-size limits, and report truncation or failure rather than presenting partial results as a complete answer.
interpretation: The workshop caps the reachable set to protect responsiveness and reports a limit error rather than silently trimming it.

parts.title: 5. Filter allowed relationships before expanding them
paragraphs: An edge type restriction prevents unrelated meanings from entering the traversal. A tenant or access restriction serves a different purpose: it determines which data the caller may use at all. Apply those restrictions before or during expansion, including intermediate nodes.
A shallow traversal can still read forbidden data. Treat depth and output limits as resource controls, never as permission checks.
interpretation: The fixture is fully permitted. Later retrieval applies a scoped graph before either dependency or document expansion.

parts.title: 6. Inspect cycles as domain evidence as well as an algorithm concern
paragraphs: A cycle in a supply dependency may be an impossible import or a real mutually dependent system. A visited set makes our computation terminate, but it does not decide whether the cycle is valid in the domain.

Keep enough edge identity and provenance to investigate it. If the application requires a directed acyclic hierarchy, enforce or audit that separate invariant rather than assuming the traversal repaired the data.
interpretation: Algorithmic termination and domain correctness solve different problems.

title: The Route with Fewer Stops Takes Longer
openingTitle: Two Hops Are Slower Than Three
opening: The maintenance cart can reach B directly from A in nine minutes. Going through C takes four minutes. A search that chooses the fewest relationships selects the direct route, even though the crew asked for the quickest one.

We need to define what “shortest” measures. Hop count treats every edge equally. Travel time assigns a cost to each edge, so the route choice must compare accumulated costs rather than the number of connections.
blurb: Distinguish minimum-hop paths from minimum-cost paths and implement Dijkstra’s nonnegative-cost frontier with explicit unreachable and tie semantics.

history.title: Shortest Routes Needed a Cost-Aware Search

sources.title: Dijkstra, A note on two problems in connexion with graphs, 1959

blocks: Dijkstra’s 1959 paper described a procedure for finding the shortest route between nodes in a weighted graph. The useful step is to separate tentative distances from settled ones: with nonnegative lengths, the least tentative distance cannot later be improved by taking a detour through a more expensive unsettled node.

Dijkstra’s shortest-path method is used to find minimum accumulated cost in graphs with suitable nonnegative weights. Neo4j’s Graph Data Science documentation exposes that method separately from simple hop-count path matching. The algorithm keeps the cheapest unsettled distance visible rather than committing to the first route discovered.

For our cart, that distinction allows a route with an extra stop to win. The Python exercise implements a small nonnegative-weight version so we can inspect why the earlier expensive route is replaced.

intuition.title: Compare route costs rather than counting arrows
intuition.explanation: Each edge label is travel time in minutes.

scene.caption: The cheapest A-to-D route goes through C and B. More relationships can still mean less total time.

intuition.title: Replace a tentative route when a cheaper one appears
intuition.explanation: The pending column shows the heap entries after each expansion, including entries that later become stale.

records.label: D at 5
cells: The stale B 9 entry cannot improve the answer

scene.caption: A tentative cost is replaced only by a cheaper route. With nonnegative edge costs, the cheapest current candidate can be settled.

parts.title: 1. Choose the quantity to minimise
paragraphs: Minimum hops answers how many links must be followed. Minimum travel time answers how much edge cost accumulates. Neither is inherently the correct question; the operational objective decides.
A directed route can be traversable in one direction only. If a corridor is bidirectional, represent both permitted directions or use a graph projection whose orientation is deliberately defined.
interpretation: Our route graph is directed, and every minutes property uses the same unit.

parts.title: 2. Replace first discovery with the best known cost
paragraphs: B is first discovered with cost nine through the direct edge. When C is expanded, the route through C offers a lower cost to B. The algorithm updates B’s best value rather than treating its first discovery as final.

A priority queue makes the lowest current candidate the next one to process. Older queued entries for a node can become stale after an improvement, so the code checks them against the best-known distance.
interpretation: The visited-on-discovery rule from unweighted BFS does not implement this weighted objective.

examples.title: Compare the two routes to B
paragraphs: This isolates the accumulated-cost comparison before implementing a search.
examples.code:
direct=9
via_c=2+2
print({'direct':direct,'via_C':via_c})
interpretation: The longer-in-hops route has the smaller time cost.

parts.title: 3. Use the heap to revisit a tentative choice
paragraphs: A Python heap stores the candidate with the smallest first tuple value at its front. heappush adds a candidate; heappop removes the cheapest one. The second tuple item is the node ID, which also provides a deterministic tie break for these string IDs.

We do not need to find and delete an old heap entry when a better route appears. Update best and push the cheaper candidate. When the old entry eventually comes out, compare its cost with best and skip it if they differ. The program below isolates that mechanism before the challenge adds graph traversal.
interpretation: The heap remembers candidates. The best dictionary records the current best estimate for each node.

examples.title: Replace B’s nine-minute candidate
paragraphs: Suppose A has already produced candidates C at two and B at nine. Expanding C finds a cheaper way to B.
examples.code:
import heapq
best={'B':9,'C':2}
pending=[(2,'C'),(9,'B')]
heapq.heapify(pending)
cost,node=heapq.heappop(pending)
proposed=cost+2  # C to B takes two minutes.
if proposed < best['B']:
    best['B']=proposed
    heapq.heappush(pending,(proposed,'B'))
while pending:
    cost,node=heapq.heappop(pending)
    if cost != best[node]:
        print('skip',node,cost)
        continue
    print('use',node,cost)
interpretation: The old entry remains in the heap but cannot overwrite the improved estimate. This example teaches one relaxation, not the full shortest-path function.

parts.title: 4. Why nonnegative weights matter
paragraphs: Once the cheapest candidate is settled, nonnegative future edges cannot produce a cheaper route by leaving that settled frontier and later subtracting cost. That property supports Dijkstra’s decision rule.

Negative weights require another algorithm and careful treatment of negative cycles. A missing weight is not automatically zero. Validate the graph projection’s weight field and units before running the method.
interpretation: The exercise accepts zero-cost edges but rejects negative or nonfinite costs.

parts.title: 5. Do not mistake Cypher shortestPath for weighted optimisation
paragraphs: A hop-oriented shortestPath pattern does not automatically minimise a minutes property just because the relationship contains it. Weighted algorithms such as GDS Dijkstra use an explicitly projected weight.

For the tiny setup below, the reference query enumerates bounded paths and orders their summed cost. It exposes the objective in ordinary Cypher, but it is not a scalable replacement for a dedicated weighted algorithm.
interpretation: This reference is limited to a tiny acyclic graph with all relevant paths within three hops.

references.title: Inspect accumulated route costs on the tiny graph
description: The small bounded enumeration is for explanation, not a production path planner.
references.code:
MATCH p=(a:Location {id:$start})-[:ROUTE*1..3]->(b:Location {id:$target})
WITH p, reduce(total=0, r IN relationships(p) | total+r.minutes) AS cost
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.id] AS route, cost
ORDER BY cost, route
LIMIT 1
setup: In a fresh test database run CREATE (a:Location {id:'A'}),(b:Location {id:'B'}),(c:Location {id:'C'}),(d:Location {id:'D'}),(a)-[:ROUTE {minutes:9}]->(b),(a)-[:ROUTE {minutes:2}]->(c),(c)-[:ROUTE {minutes:2}]->(b),(b)-[:ROUTE {minutes:1}]->(d),(c)-[:ROUTE {minutes:20}]->(d).
Bind start A and target D. Use GDS Dijkstra with an appropriate projection for larger weighted problems.
interpretation: The route A,C,B,D has cost 5. The LIMIT does not prevent the preceding enumeration from doing substantial work on a different graph.

parts.title: 6. Keep unreachable and zero-cost answers distinct
paragraphs: If the destination cannot be reached, return no distance, represented by None in the exercise. If start equals target, the empty route has cost zero. A reachable route can also legitimately have zero total cost.
Do not replace absence with zero. That would make a disconnected workshop look as though the cart were already there.
interpretation: The challenge returns the minimum cost only, so equally cheap paths do not require a route-selection tie break.

parts.title: 7. A computed route is only as current as its allowed edges
paragraphs: A closed corridor or a restricted area must be removed before routing. Applying permission checks only after choosing the cheapest path can select an unusable route and obscure valid alternatives.

Travel times may change while the cart moves. A graph snapshot provides an estimate under stated conditions, not a guarantee about the physical journey. Validate operational safety separately from minimising cost.
interpretation: The workshop filters ROUTE edges and computes costs from the supplied snapshot.

title: Which Rules Must Every Asset Write Preserve?
openingTitle: The Second P7 Broke the Meaning of Every Match
opening: A query that used to locate one P7 now finds two nodes. Some relationships point to one copy and some to the other. Botie cannot repair that ambiguity by choosing whichever match appears first.

The application needs a durable identity rule enforced at the write boundary. An index can help find an asset, but a constraint is what rejects a forbidden duplicate. Those responsibilities are related without being interchangeable.
blurb: Separate key presence, uniqueness and lookup performance, then audit existing data before installing graph constraints.

history.title: Flexible Records Still Needed Shared Invariants

sources.title: Neo4j constraint creation and backing indexes

blocks: Property graphs let applications evolve node properties without requiring every category to have an identical record shape. As those graphs became application databases, shared write rules remained necessary. The Cypher language paper includes schema-definition capabilities alongside queries and updates; current Neo4j constraints make selected identity and property requirements enforceable.

The purpose here is narrower than making every node identical. All Asset nodes need an unambiguous application identity, while different kinds of equipment can still have different optional properties.

intuition.title: Duplicate node identities split the maintenance history
intuition.explanation: The display shows two different stored nodes with the same forbidden application key.

scene.caption: A uniqueness constraint prevents new duplicate keys. Existing conflicting nodes need review before the constraint can be created.

parts.title: 1. Separate presence from uniqueness
paragraphs: A uniqueness rule prevents repeated known key values. It does not necessarily require every node to carry that key. A node with no application ID can remain difficult to address even when all present IDs are unique.

For this import audit, a valid ID is a nonempty string. Count missing, blank or nonstring IDs separately from duplicate known IDs. Production databases may offer key, existence and type constraints with edition-specific availability.
interpretation: Passing the duplicate check does not establish that every record has a usable identity.

parts.title: 2. Audit the existing records first
paragraphs: Creating a constraint over conflicting data can fail. Inspect the duplicate groups and missing keys, decide which nodes are genuine duplicates, and preserve their attached relationships while repairing them.

Do not delete a duplicate-looking node simply because its ID repeats. Its relationships may contain the only copy of an inspection association. A migration needs a reviewed reconciliation rule and a recovery path.
interpretation: The exercise reports problems without changing the records.

examples.title: Count missing key values separately
paragraphs: These rows have no duplicate valid ID, but one lacks any ID.

parts.title: 3. Install the identity constraint deliberately
paragraphs: The first statement below creates uniqueness for Asset.id. Neo4j backs property uniqueness constraints with an index, so it can also support the identity lookup. This does not turn every other property into a constrained field.

Property existence and type constraints, and node-key constraints, have edition/version requirements. Validate required fields at ingestion and use the database-supported rule set for the deployment; do not advertise a uniqueness-only rule as mandatory-key enforcement.
interpretation: A query plan and a data invariant answer different questions.

references.title: Create and inspect an asset identity constraint
description: Run schema changes with an authorised administrative role in a disposable test database.
setup: Use an empty Neo4j test database or first repair duplicate Asset.id values.

This uniqueness constraint does not require id on every Asset. For deployments that support it, CREATE CONSTRAINT asset_id_required IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Asset) REQUIRE a.id IS NOT NULL adds an existence rule; check the edition requirement before running it.
interpretation: The installed constraint rejects duplicate known IDs. Missingness remains a separate obligation.

parts.title: 4. Use indexes for the predicates that actually locate nodes
paragraphs: An index on a label/property combination can help a selective starting lookup. It does not automatically speed every relationship traversal or every expression applied to that property.
Inspect the plan for the actual query and representative parameters. Extra indexes consume storage and add write work, so create them around measured access patterns rather than every possible field.
interpretation: Index presence is not proof that a particular query uses it.

parts.title: 5. Keep application rules alongside database rules
paragraphs: A uniqueness constraint does not verify that an asset belongs to the caller’s tenant or that a proposed dependency is physically sensible. The database may enforce some structural rules while application policy checks the rest.
Document which boundary owns each rule and test writes through every supported path. A bulk loader that bypasses an application check can otherwise reintroduce the same problem.
interpretation: The workshop’s independent duplicate and missing-ID branches are an audit, not an installed database constraint.

practice.solution:
def key_issues(nodes):
    from collections import Counter
    usable=[n.get('id') for n in nodes if isinstance(n.get('id'),str) and n['id']]
    counts=Counter(usable)
    return [sorted(k for k,n in counts.items() if n>1),len(nodes)-len(usable)]

print(key_issues([{"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P8", "kind": "Asset"}]))

title: The Graph Changed While the Approval Was Waiting
openingTitle: An Approved Plan Is Now Based on an Old Record
opening: Botie prepared a change for P8 when its revision was three. While a person reviewed that proposal, another technician updated P8 to revision four. Applying the old plan without checking would overwrite a decision made with newer information.

We need to separate preparing a change, approving it and committing it against current state. A snapshot check can reveal an obviously stale request, but only the database transaction can protect the final write from concurrent changes.
blurb: Treat approvals and snapshot checks as preparation, then use authorised, parameterised transactions with explicit conflict and retry behaviour.

history.title: Connected Updates Needed a Transaction Boundary
blocks: A graph update can change an entity and several attached relationships together. Transaction support provides a boundary within which the database either commits the unit of work or rolls it back. Modern Neo4j drivers also retry selected transient failures, which makes the behaviour of the transaction function part of the application’s correctness.

The maintenance approval adds another boundary: a person approves a particular action against particular evidence. Rechecking that evidence at commit time prevents an old approval from silently becoming authority for a materially different state.

intuition.title: Approval belongs to a particular proposed change
intuition.explanation: The stored asset has advanced beyond one proposal’s expected revision.

scene.caption: Only P7 passes the snapshot comparison. Passing it still does not commit the change or protect against a later concurrent write.

parts.title: 1. Keep the request separate from the stored entity
paragraphs: A proposal should identify its target, intended change, caller and the state it was based on. The approval should be tied to that proposal rather than a general reusable “yes.”

Our exercise deliberately selects eligible target IDs only. It does not apply status changes, validate arbitrary payloads or claim to perform an atomic update. Those responsibilities belong to the eventual authorised executor.
interpretation: A useful preflight result says which requests need further execution checks.

parts.title: 2. Require explicit approval and the expected snapshot
paragraphs: Only boolean true counts as approval in the example. A string such as “true” is not the same typed value. Compare expected_revision with the target’s current snapshot revision, and exclude missing targets.
A stale request should return to review or be recalculated according to policy. Quietly changing expected_revision to the latest number would remove the protection the field was meant to provide.
interpretation: Approval and freshness are independent conditions.

examples.title: Inspect the revision mismatch
paragraphs: This program reports the two revisions rather than applying a change.
interpretation: The approved request used older state. A new plan may need new approval.

parts.title: 3. The commit must enforce the concurrency rule
paragraphs: Between a browser preflight and a server write, another update can occur. Use a database-supported transaction and locking or conditional-update strategy whose isolation semantics have been checked for the deployed database.

A read in one transaction followed by an unconditional write in another is not optimistic concurrency control. Even a predicate and write in one statement need the engine’s documented concurrent-update semantics; do not assume a snapshot comparison creates a lock.
interpretation: The workshop intentionally stops before commit and cannot establish transaction isolation.

parts.title: 4. Parameterise the approved write and verify its result
paragraphs: The external example demonstrates the simpler unit: update one uniquely identified asset inside an application-managed transaction, then verify exactly one target was returned before committing. It does not implement the revision conflict policy by itself.

Use an authorised driver session, a parameterised reviewed query and explicit rollback when the matched target count violates the contract. Do not execute arbitrary Cypher generated by a user or model as the writer role.
interpretation: Application validation, authorisation and concurrency control remain required around this query.

references.title: A parameterised write inside the executor transaction
description: This query must be run inside the transaction described in setup, not pasted into an unrestricted production console.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})
SET a.status=$status
RETURN a.id AS updated
setup: In a disposable database, create unique Asset.id values and install the uniqueness constraint from the preceding lesson.
Use a Neo4j driver transaction. Bind asset P7 and a validated status. Read the returned rows, require exactly one, and roll back on mismatch before commit.
For revision-sensitive requests, add a tested locking/conditional-update protocol at that same transaction boundary. This snippet does not supply that protocol.
interpretation: The query changes one validated field. The transaction determines whether that change commits.

parts.title: 5. Retries must not repeat outside effects
paragraphs: A driver-managed transaction function may be invoked again after a transient failure. Sending an email, charging a service or issuing a physical maintenance action inside that retried function can repeat the effect even if the database transaction rolled back.

Keep external actions out of automatically retried database callbacks. Where an action must follow a commit, use a durable outbox or another explicit delivery design with idempotency keys and reconciliation. A database rollback cannot undo an email already sent.
interpretation: Exactly-once business effects require more than calling MERGE or retrying a transaction.

parts.title: 6. MERGE and DELETE need their own identity and scope rules
paragraphs: MERGE matches or creates the supplied pattern. Match stable identity separately from mutable fields and back required uniqueness with constraints. A replayed logical request should have a stable idempotency identity if its outcome must be reconciled.

DELETE of a node with relationships and DETACH DELETE have different consequences. Broad deletion patterns can remove connected history. Preview the exact target identities and use least-privilege permissions; the lesson’s preflight does not authorise a deletion.
interpretation: Read the write pattern as a description of everything it may affect.

parts.title: 7. Test stale, missing and ambiguously typed requests
paragraphs: The challenge checks explicit approval, known target and matching integer revision. It retains each eligible target ID once for this report. Real executors still need per-request identity, payload validation and conflict handling when several proposals target the same node.
That limited output makes the lesson’s claim testable: the records qualify for further execution checks under this snapshot. It never says those changes have been safely committed.
interpretation: Keep the displayed result at the same level of authority as the mechanism that produced it.

The database always rolls back the email
quiz.because: External effects do not share the database rollback boundary.

title: A Replayed Import Must Not Create Another Relationship
openingTitle: The Loader Lost Its Response and Tried Again
opening: Botie imports a dependency file, but the connection drops before the loader receives a success response. Retrying every row with CREATE can add another copy of relationships already committed. Some rows also refer to assets that have not been imported.
We need stable identities for imported relationships and an explicit route for records that cannot be applied. An import is a reconciliation process, not simply a loop that draws every edge it sees.
blurb: Stage graph imports by stable identity, distinguish exact replays from conflicts and preserve rejected records instead of silently losing relationships.

history.title: Bulk Data Exchange Had to Survive Partial Progress
blocks: Graph loaders need to resolve source identities to stored nodes before creating their relationships. Neo4j’s documented import workflows combine row-oriented input with matching and merge operations, while transaction batching changes the unit of rollback.

The operational problem is older than any one loader: a response can be lost after work commits. Stable source identities and a recorded checkpoint make replay a question of recognising prior work rather than assuming every arrival is new.

intuition.title: One new edge is resolvable and another has no endpoint
intuition.explanation: The source batch contains an already known relationship and an unresolved asset reference.

scene.caption: A rejected relationship stays in an import report. Creating a mystery endpoint would invent an asset unless that policy was explicitly chosen.

parts.title: 1. Load or resolve entity identities before connecting them
paragraphs: A relationship requires both endpoints. Import node identities first or resolve them against a known registry. An unmatched endpoint should enter a rejection or deferred-resolution queue with its source row identity.
Silently skipping a MATCH failure can make a loader appear successful while losing relationships. Inventing missing nodes with MERGE can be equally misleading when an ID is misspelled.
interpretation: Choose whether unresolved endpoints are rejected, deferred or explicitly created; do not let query structure choose by accident.

parts.title: 2. Give each imported relationship a replay identity
paragraphs: A stable source relationship ID can identify a logical record across retries. The same ID with the same complete payload is a replay. The same ID with different endpoints, type or properties is a conflict under this lesson’s immutable-import policy.

If the source supports revisions, add a documented version rule rather than treating every changed payload as a harmless repeat. A relationship’s minutes or observation time can matter as much as its endpoints.
interpretation: Identity equality and payload equality are separate checks.

examples.title: Notice a property conflict on a reused ID
paragraphs: The endpoints are identical, but the stored payload is different.
interpretation: A replay check that compares endpoints alone would conceal the changed travel-time fact.

parts.title: 3. Use a parameterised batch to expose the import operation
paragraphs: UNWIND turns a bound list parameter into rows. Matching both endpoint nodes resolves the relationship’s meaning before MERGE uses its stable ID. The example deliberately uses one approved relationship type rather than accepting arbitrary user query structure.

The executor must validate unique IDs and detect changed payload conflicts before this write. It must also compare processed-row counts with the staged batch so unmatched endpoints do not disappear unnoticed.
interpretation: A successful query response does not prove every source row was imported.

references.title: Apply a prevalidated dependency batch
description: Run this only after rejecting unresolved endpoints and reused-ID conflicts.
references.code:
UNWIND $rows AS row
MATCH (a:Asset {id:row.source}), (b:Asset {id:row.target})
MERGE (a)-[r:DEPENDS_ON {import_id:row.id}]->(b)
RETURN row.id AS imported ORDER BY imported
setup: Use a disposable current Neo4j database supporting relationship property uniqueness constraints. Run CREATE CONSTRAINT import_asset_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Asset) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE. Then run CREATE CONSTRAINT dependency_import_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR ()-[r:DEPENDS_ON]-() REQUIRE r.import_id IS UNIQUE. These uniqueness constraints do not require property presence; the importer validates it.
Create the complete stored fixture: CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}),(q:Asset {id:'P8'}),(s:Asset {id:'S1'}),(p)-[:DEPENDS_ON {import_id:'a'}]->(s).

Bind rows to [{id:'a',source:'P7',target:'S1'},{id:'new',source:'P8',target:'S1'}] through the driver. This particular write schema has only immutable endpoint identities and the fixed DEPENDS_ON type; reject additional fields rather than silently ignoring payload properties.

Run in a transaction after source and endpoint validation. The first row matches the stored relationship and the second creates one. Running the same batch again should match both. A reused import ID on different endpoints must fail the uniqueness constraint and enter conflict handling. Reconcile returned IDs against the staged input so an unmatched endpoint is not silently lost.
interpretation: The two import identities are returned on the first and repeated run. Endpoint uniqueness and relationship import-ID uniqueness back this deliberately narrow immutable schema. A richer mutable payload requires its own version/conflict protocol; the workshop demonstrates full-payload classification without committing a database write.

parts.title: 4. Make batch atomicity and checkpoints explicit
paragraphs: A large import may commit in batches to control memory and transaction size. If batch three fails, batches one and two may already be durable. The loader must resume from a checkpoint that corresponds to committed work, not merely rows read from the file.
Record batch IDs, source versions, accepted counts and rejection counts. Keep checkpoints and sink updates consistent through an appropriate transaction or recovery protocol.
interpretation: Batching reduces the rollback unit; it does not make the whole source file one atomic transaction.

parts.title: 5. Validate properties before they become graph facts
paragraphs: CSV text needs explicit type conversion and missing-value rules. A blank date is not an arbitrary default instant, and an invalid cost must not enter a weighted path algorithm. Parameter binding protects query structure but does not validate the values’ domain meaning.
Reject or quarantine malformed records with enough non-sensitive context to repair them. Keep credentials, personal data and restricted payloads out of casual loader logs.
interpretation: Import quality directly changes the answers later traversals can produce.

parts.title: 6. Distinguish the admission list from the import audit
paragraphs: The exercise returns IDs of new resolvable edges only. The workshop exposes a richer classification before selecting ready rows: repeat, conflict, dangling and invalid records remain inspectable in the intermediate output.
Both mechanisms preserve the original graph. They stage work for a real importer rather than pretending a browser result has committed anything.
interpretation: Inspect the classification component when an expected ID does not reach the ready list.

title: Why Did One More Hop Make the Query So Expensive?
openingTitle: A Small Result Can Hide a Large Search
opening: Botie returns three equipment IDs, but the query takes seconds. It began at every asset, followed broad relationship types and only then filtered to P7. The small final answer does not show how many candidates the database inspected.

We need to look at where the search starts and how intermediate rows grow. An index can narrow the start, while selective patterns and early justified predicates can limit expansion. We should measure the plan instead of judging work from the final row count.
blurb: Read query plans, reason about candidate expansion and compare access paths without confusing a toy operation count with measured database performance.

history.title: Declarative Graph Queries Needed Physical Execution Plans
blocks: A declarative pattern describes the answer, leaving the database to choose how to find it. The Cypher authors describe Neo4j’s cost-based planning and physical execution operators. This separation lets equivalent logical queries use different access paths.

For our maintenance graph, locating one asset before expanding relationships can avoid unrelated work. The improvement is a claim to verify in a real plan, because cardinality estimates, indexes and graph degree all affect execution.

intuition.title: An anchored question should not begin from every component
intuition.explanation: Only the outgoing relationships of P7 are candidates for its one-hop question.

scene.caption: The workshop counts candidate checks under two specified algorithms. Those counts are not milliseconds or a prediction of Neo4j’s optimiser.

intuition.title: Count the work that the teaching model actually measures
intuition.explanation: The fixture has two DEPENDS_ON edges: P7 to S1, and P8 to P7. The adjacency lookup already exists.

scene.caption: Both strategies deduplicate starts. The comparison excludes building the lookup and makes no latency claim.

parts.title: 1. Locate the start before explaining the expansion
paragraphs: An equality predicate on a constrained Asset.id can provide a selective starting point. A label narrows the entity category; a property condition narrows the instance. A traversal from a huge unfiltered population asks a different amount of work even if the final WHERE keeps one asset.
The optimiser may reorder compatible operations. Write clear predicates, then inspect the physical plan rather than assuming text order is execution order.
interpretation: The logical query and the physical access path are connected but different descriptions.

parts.title: 2. Count candidate checks in a deliberately small model
paragraphs: A naive one-hop loop scans every edge for each distinct start. An already built adjacency lookup inspects only outgoing edges for those starts. Comparing these counts makes the access-path idea tangible.
Building and maintaining the adjacency lookup costs work and memory too. Our counter excludes that setup and is not an estimate of database latency, cache behaviour or storage I/O.
interpretation: State what the measured quantity includes before interpreting the result.

examples.title: Build one adjacency bucket
paragraphs: This example constructs the lookup rather than the later comparison report.
interpretation: The bucket gives the outgoing edge candidates after the lookup structure has been built.

parts.title: 3. Use EXPLAIN before PROFILE
paragraphs: EXPLAIN shows a planned execution without executing the query. PROFILE executes it and reports actual operator statistics, so profiling a write can perform that write. Begin with read-only queries against representative test data.

Look for starting scans or seeks, expansion operators, estimated versus actual rows and substantial intermediate multiplication. Compare DB hits and timing carefully; warm caches, parameter values and server load can change results.
interpretation: A final LIMIT does not necessarily remove upstream expansion, sorting or aggregation work.

references.title: Inspect an anchored dependency query
description: The same typed pattern is visible beside its plan request.
references.code:
EXPLAIN
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(d:Asset)
RETURN DISTINCT d.id AS dependency
setup: In a fresh Neo4j test database, run CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}), (s:Asset {id:'S1'}), (q:Asset {id:'P8'}), (p)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s), (q)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(p).
Install an Asset.id uniqueness constraint or suitable index, then bind asset P7.
For actual statistics, run the same read-only query with PROFILE in a controlled test environment.
interpretation: Inspect whether the plan locates P7 selectively before expansion. A three-node fixture demonstrates syntax, not a meaningful production benchmark.

parts.title: 4. Watch degree and repeated branches at each hop
paragraphs: A node with many outgoing relationships can produce a large frontier even when the starting lookup is fast. Several hops can combine many routes to the same endpoint. DISTINCT removes repeated output rows but may still require processing many prior matches.
Constrain relationship types, justified properties and path length according to the actual question. Avoid enumerating all paths when you only need existence, reachability or a shortest-path result.
interpretation: The operation you ask for determines how much route information must be retained.

parts.title: 5. WITH controls scope as well as aggregation
paragraphs: WITH a, count(i) AS n carries only a and n into the next stage. A variable omitted from that projection is no longer available in the ordinary following scope. WITH DISTINCT can deliberately change cardinality before later matches.
Do not drop the identity needed to connect the next branch correctly. An optimisation that accidentally changes grouping or optional-match semantics is a different query, even if it runs faster.
interpretation: Preserve meaning first, then measure the equivalent alternatives.

parts.title: 6. Apply workload limits and monitor production behaviour
paragraphs: Set timeouts, result-size limits and controlled query templates appropriate to the service. A high-degree tenant or newly imported relationship type can change a previously cheap workload. Monitor latency distributions and failure rates, with enough plan context to investigate regressions.
Performance bounds do not replace tenant access checks. They protect capacity while the authorisation boundary determines which records may be touched.
interpretation: The workshop compares one-hop candidate checks so its interpretation stays narrow and testable.

    # Work through the record relationships here.

practice.solution:
def candidate_counts(graph, starts):
    selected=[e for e in graph['edges'] if e['type']=='DEPENDS_ON']
    starts=set(starts)
    return [len(selected)*len(starts),sum(e['source'] in starts for e in selected)]

print(candidate_counts({"nodes": [{"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "S1", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P8", "kind": "Asset"}], "edges": [{"id": "d1", "source": "P7", "target": "S1", "type": "DEPENDS_ON"}, {"id": "d2", "source": "P8", "target": "P7", "type": "DEPENDS_ON"}]}, ['P7']))

title: Can Two Teams Describe the Same Resource?
openingTitle: Two Files Agree on a Name and Mean Different Things
opening: One supplier calls a pump P7. Another uses P7 for a spare motor. Meanwhile, two teams describe the same supply under different display names. Botie cannot combine these records safely by comparing their text labels.

We need identifiers whose meaning survives the move between datasets, and a shared way to state a relationship. RDF expresses a statement using a subject, a predicate and an object. SPARQL asks which assignments to variables make patterns of those statements match.
blurb: Distinguish resource identifiers from literals, read RDF statements and build SPARQL patterns without confusing RDF with the property-graph model.

history.title: Web Resources Needed Descriptions That Could Travel
blocks: W3C’s 1999 RDF recommendation addressed machine-readable descriptions of Web resources. Shared identifiers and statement structure let descriptions from different applications be combined without agreeing on one table layout. The later RDF 1.1 and SPARQL 1.1 recommendations specify the graph model and its query language.

That helps our two maintenance teams state which resource a claim concerns. Agreement on identifiers and predicates still requires modelling work. Publishing a statement in RDF does not establish that it is correct.

intuition.title: A predicate gives the arrow its meaning
intuition.explanation: The full resource identifiers distinguish entities even when the diagram uses short display names.

scene.caption: Here ex: abbreviates https://fitlab.example/. Changing the abbreviation while retaining the same full IRI does not change the resource.

parts.title: 1. Read a statement before choosing a database
paragraphs: In the statement P7 dependsOn S1, the subject is P7, the predicate is dependsOn and the object is S1. RDF identifies predicates with IRIs too, so two independently invented properties with the same short name need not mean the same thing.
A resource IRI is an identifier, not a promise that fetching its URL will return a useful page. Choose and document identifiers that remain stable when a display name changes.
interpretation: The full identifier, rather than the label drawn beside a node, controls matching.

parts.title: 2. An object can be a resource or a literal
paragraphs: A resource object can participate in more statements. A literal is a value, such as a name, a date or a number. A literal whose characters look like an IRI is still a literal. Datatype and language tags carry meaning that a plain string comparison can lose.

Our compact Python fixture uses kind to distinguish IRI objects from literals. It deliberately omits blank nodes and datatype processing. Blank nodes represent resources without a global IRI; their local labels are not durable cross-file business keys.
interpretation: The workshop projects only resource-to-resource statements. It is not a general RDF parser.

examples.title: Keep an identifier separate from its written text
paragraphs: The characters match, but the object categories differ.

objects=[{'kind':'iri','value':'https://fitlab.example/S1'},{'kind':'literal','value':'https://fitlab.example/S1'}]
print([o['kind'] for o in objects])
interpretation: Selecting a resource relationship must check the kind as well as the characters.

parts.title: 3. Let a variable occupy the unknown position
paragraphs: In SPARQL, ?asset names a variable. A triple pattern with that variable as subject asks which resources have the stated predicate and object. PREFIX only abbreviates IRIs in the query text; SELECT chooses the variables returned.

The braces contain the graph pattern. Several patterns sharing ?asset must agree on the same resource binding. FILTER can constrain a bound value, while OPTIONAL adds bindings when a pattern exists without requiring it for every row.
interpretation: The same variable-binding idea from Cypher appears in a different graph data model.

references.title: Find resources depending on S1
description: Run this against an RDF store or SPARQL engine containing the Turtle fixture below.
references.code:
PREFIX ex: <https://fitlab.example/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?asset
WHERE { ?asset ex:dependsOn ex:S1 . }
ORDER BY ?asset
setup: Load this complete Turtle into a disposable dataset: @prefix ex: <https://fitlab.example/> . ex:P7 ex:dependsOn ex:S1 . ex:P8 ex:dependsOn ex:S1 . ex:P9 ex:dependsOn "https://fitlab.example/S1" . ex:P7 ex:near ex:S2 .
The expected resources are ex:P7 and ex:P8. Bind external values using your chosen RDF client’s supported RDF-term/query-binding mechanism; do not concatenate unchecked query fragments.
interpretation: P9 has a literal object. Its text looks like the resource IRI, but it does not match the resource object ex:S1.

parts.title: 4. Separate graph statements from query-result duplicates
paragraphs: An RDF graph is a set of triples, so repeating an identical triple does not add another graph statement. A query can still produce repeated projected bindings through several matching combinations. DISTINCT applies to the projected query result, not to an imagined duplicate edge identity.

In a property graph, two separately identified relationships can have the same endpoints and type. That difference matters when importing visit events. Do not mechanically convert each event into an identical RDF triple and expect its identity to survive.
interpretation: Model an event as an identified resource when the event itself needs its own properties or evidence.

parts.title: 5. Missing information is not automatically false
paragraphs: If the dataset has no dependsOn statement for P9, we know that this dataset did not produce a match. We have not proved that P9 has no physical dependency. RDF’s open-world interpretation leaves room for information that has not been recorded.

Inference is also an explicit choice. A SPARQL store does not necessarily apply every ontology rule automatically. Know the configured entailment regime before interpreting a query that relies on inferred types or relationships.
interpretation: State whether the report concerns recorded statements, inferred statements or a verified complete inventory.

parts.title: 6. Keep statement evidence when combining sources
paragraphs: A short RDF triple does not by itself say who asserted it or which source document supported it. Named graphs and explicit provenance models can retain source context, but their interpretation must be documented.
Our next lesson keeps claims separate from the sources that support them. That gives Botie somewhere to look when the two teams disagree instead of silently treating the latest import as the truth.
interpretation: Interoperable syntax makes disagreement easier to represent; it does not resolve it.

title: Where Did This Maintenance Claim Come From?
openingTitle: The Graph Contains Two Conflicting Answers
opening: One document says P7 is overdue for inspection. A later log says the inspection is current. If Botie stores one unqualified status on the asset, whichever import runs last can erase the disagreement.

Keep the claims and their supporting records visible. We can then ask who supplied a claim, when it became usable and whether it still applies. Choosing evidence for review is different from declaring one source correct.
blurb: Represent claims and their sources, retain contradictions and apply explicit time boundaries before using graph evidence.

history.title: Derived Results Needed a Traceable History
blocks: W3C’s 2013 PROV recommendations gave applications a shared way to describe the entities and activities involved in producing information, including who was responsible. A chart could be linked to the dataset and transformation that produced it rather than circulating without that history.

Our maintenance claims have the same need on a smaller scale. A recorded source helps us inspect a disagreement or withdraw a superseded claim. Provenance explains how information arrived; it is not a certificate of truth.

intuition.title: Keep each assertion attached to its evidence
intuition.explanation: Two statements concern P7 without being collapsed into one status property.

scene.caption: Both claims can remain visible during review. Their sources and applicability times determine what can be considered at a particular decision time.

parts.title: 1. Make the assertion an identifiable record
paragraphs: A Claim node can contain its statement, subject and stable claim ID. Separate relationships connect it to the asset and source document. This lets several claims concern the same asset without overwriting each other.

Retain enough source detail to locate the supporting passage or inspection event. A document title alone is often insufficient when revisions change its contents. Prefer a stable document/version identifier plus a specific locator.
interpretation: Claim identity keeps disagreement inspectable instead of turning import order into an evidence policy.

parts.title: 2. Distinguish source permission from source reliability
paragraphs: The requested reader may be allowed to use only particular source documents. That access check must happen before evidence is exposed. A separate quality policy decides which sources are acceptable for the task.

Our workshop receives a permitted-source list and retains only those claim records. Inclusion means the claim passes this supplied policy, not that its statement is verified. Real source permissions belong in the server-side access boundary.
interpretation: The browser fixture demonstrates selection over invented data and is not an access-control system.

parts.title: 3. Draw the interval during which a claim applies
paragraphs: For this exercise, observed_at is the hour the claim became available to this decision process. valid_until is the first hour at which we stop treating it as applicable; null means no stated end. All values use one invented integer-hour clock.

At hour eight, a claim with valid_until eight has expired. A claim first available at hour nine cannot justify an hour-six decision. In real systems, keep event time, ingestion time and validity intervals separate when those meanings differ.
interpretation: We require availability at or before the requested time and an end strictly after it, when an end exists.

examples.title: Inspect an exclusive end boundary
paragraphs: The claim was available at hour two and expires at eight.
examples.code:
observed_at=2
valid_until=8
for at in [7,8]:
    print(observed_at <= at and at < valid_until)
interpretation: The exact end hour belongs to the next state, preventing overlapping interpretations at the boundary.

parts.title: 4. Retrieve evidence without hiding a disagreement
paragraphs: Apply the source and time predicates to claim records, then return their identities and source links. If two surviving claims contradict each other, return both for the defined review process. Do not let a dictionary keyed only by asset discard one.
A later stage may resolve conflicts using an approved policy, but that decision should leave an audit trail. A confidence score alone is not proof that an unsupported claim beats a documented one.
interpretation: The query below uses a property-graph claim model inspired by provenance practice; it is not a PROV-O RDF serialisation.

references.title: List current permitted claims about P7
description: All fixture times are integer hours, so the boundaries can be checked by hand.
references.code:
MATCH (c:Claim)-[:ABOUT]->(a:Asset {id:$asset}),
      (c)-[:WAS_DERIVED_FROM]->(d:Document)
WHERE d.id IN $allowed_sources
  AND c.observed_at <= $at
  AND (c.valid_until IS NULL OR $at < c.valid_until)
RETURN c.id, c.statement, d.id
ORDER BY c.id
setup: In an empty test database run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7'}),(d:Document {id:'manual-A'}),(e:Document {id:'log-B'}),(c:Claim {id:'C1',statement:'inspection overdue',observed_at:2,valid_until:8}),(f:Claim {id:'C2',statement:'inspection current',observed_at:4}),(c)-[:ABOUT]->(a),(c)-[:WAS_DERIVED_FROM]->(d),(f)-[:ABOUT]->(a),(f)-[:WAS_DERIVED_FROM]->(e).
Bind asset P7, allowed_sources [manual-A, log-B] and at 6 as driver parameters. Enforce access to every matched entity and relationship according to the service policy.
interpretation: Both C1 and C2 survive. The query reports current permitted evidence, including its disagreement.

parts.title: 5. Retain derivation when a model extracts the claim
paragraphs: An extraction model can misread a sentence or associate it with the wrong asset. Record the source span, extraction version and review status so the graph statement can be checked against the original. A citation pointing to an entire unrelated manual is weak evidence.

When a source is withdrawn, investigate derived claims and downstream summaries that used it. Preserve the minimum audit evidence needed under the retention policy rather than copying sensitive source text into every log.
interpretation: Provenance gives a route for correction, provided downstream results retain their dependencies.

parts.title: 6. Keep uncertainty visible to the answerer
paragraphs: A graph can contain stale, contradictory or incomplete evidence. The response may need to say that available records disagree, or request inspection rather than assert a status. That behaviour can be tested using deliberately conflicting fixtures.
The coding task stops at eligible claim IDs. It does not infer truth, apply natural-language contradiction detection or call a language model.
interpretation: A narrow evidence-selection result is useful because its meaning can be inspected and tested.

quiz.because: Selection preserves the disagreement rather than hiding it.

title: Which Connected Records Can the Assistant Use?
openingTitle: A Relevant Manual Can Still Be the Wrong Evidence
opening: The assistant has found P7, but its own manual does not explain a supply fault. Botie could follow P7’s dependency to S1 and retrieve the supply’s manual too. That connected context might explain what the isolated document misses.

There are limits. One route passes through another tenant’s asset, and one manual was uploaded after the decision we are evaluating. Relevance alone does not make either route acceptable. We need an explicit retrieval policy before handing records to a model.
blurb: Build bounded graph retrieval with access and time boundaries, then preserve evidence and measure whether the added context actually helps.

history.title: Some Questions Needed Connections Across Retrieved Passages
blocks: The 2024 GraphRAG paper studied questions that require a broad view of a document collection. Its method builds an entity graph and community summaries to support query-focused summarisation. It addresses a different failure from simply finding a nearby text passage.

Our maintenance example uses a smaller local retrieval mechanism: start from a known asset and follow approved dependency types to related manuals. It is not a reproduction of that paper’s community-summary pipeline. The common motivation is that useful evidence may be connected across records.

intuition.title: A route has to remain usable all the way through
intuition.explanation: The request belongs to tenant red and is evaluated at hour six.

scene.caption: D2 is future information. D3 is red, but this route crosses blue asset X. Filtering only the final document would miss that boundary violation.

parts.title: 1. Choose the starting entity before collecting neighbours
paragraphs: The request concerns P7. Entity resolution must connect that mention to a stable permitted asset, rather than treating a similar display name as sufficient. Vector search can suggest candidates, but an approximate similarity score does not establish identity or access.

For this lesson the starting ID is already supplied. We also receive the tenant, decision hour and maximum dependency depth. Those inputs define the retrieval question; the model does not get to silently widen them.
interpretation: A known start keeps this exercise focused on connected evidence rather than language-based entity resolution.

parts.title: 2. Apply the scope to intermediate nodes and relationships
paragraphs: Construct the permitted graph before expanding. Keep nodes in the requested tenant and only relationships whose endpoints both remain. This prevents a route through an excluded asset from revealing an otherwise permitted endpoint.

Real policies can also restrict relationship types, individual records or properties within a tenant. The browser receives invented multi-tenant fixtures so we can see the failure. In a deployed system, enforce the policy on the server before forbidden records are exposed to the client or model.
interpretation: A traversal depth limit controls work. It does not grant permission.

parts.title: 3. Keep dependency expansion separate from document lookup
paragraphs: Require the start and every intermediate dependency node to have kind Asset. Starting at P7, follow DEPENDS_ON up to the chosen depth and retain each reached asset once. Include P7 at depth zero so its own manual remains eligible. Then follow HAS_MANUAL from those assets to document records.

This separation prevents a general “follow every edge” search from wandering through technicians, unrelated claims or other relationship types. Inspect the reached asset IDs before inspecting document content.
interpretation: Each stage has a different row meaning: assets reached, document IDs attached, then eligible evidence.

examples.title: Inspect what remains after applying the tenant boundary
paragraphs: Only edges whose two endpoints are in red remain.
interpretation: The cross edge and m3 disappear because X is excluded, even though D3 itself belongs to red.

parts.title: 4. Use only evidence available by the decision time
paragraphs: The supply manual D2 becomes available at hour eight. It cannot support a response evaluated as of hour six. Check availability after resolving document records, and retain version information so a later revision does not leak backward into an old evaluation.

For training features, apply the same point-in-time discipline to graph edges and node properties. A future relationship can leak an outcome even when the final label column is absent. This exercise assumes the graph topology is the authorised snapshot for the decision and varies document availability only.
interpretation: Real historical evaluation needs the graph snapshot and evidence versions that existed at the time.

parts.title: 5. Express the same narrow retrieval policy in a database query
paragraphs: The bounded path begins at the asset, permits zero dependency hops and then matches a manual. all over nodes(p) checks the tenant of every asset along that path. The document has its own tenant and availability predicates.

These query conditions illustrate the policy. A server must derive the permitted tenant from authenticated context and enforce its full access rules. Never accept an arbitrary user-selected tenant as authorisation.
interpretation: The example fixes a two-hop query template and parameterises data values.

references.title: Retrieve manuals through a scoped dependency route
description: This reads a disposable property graph; it does not run in the Python challenge.
references.code:
MATCH p=(a:Asset {id:$asset,tenant:$tenant})-[:DEPENDS_ON*0..2]->(x:Asset)
MATCH (x)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(d:Document)
WHERE all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n:Asset AND n.tenant=$tenant)
  AND d.tenant=$tenant AND d.available_at <= $at
RETURN DISTINCT d.id AS document
ORDER BY document
setup: In an empty test database run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7',tenant:'red'}),(s:Asset {id:'S1',tenant:'red'}),(x:Asset {id:'X',tenant:'blue'}),(d:Document {id:'D1',tenant:'red',available_at:2}),(e:Document {id:'D2',tenant:'red',available_at:8}),(f:Document {id:'D3',tenant:'red',available_at:1}),(a)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s),(a)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(x),(a)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(d),(s)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(e),(x)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(f).
Bind asset P7, tenant red and at 6 through the driver. Use server-enforced permissions appropriate to every traversed record.
interpretation: Only D1 is returned. At hour eight, D2 also qualifies. D3 remains unreachable through the permitted graph.

parts.title: 6. Give the model evidence with its limits attached
paragraphs: Return source IDs and relevant passages, rather than an unlabelled bundle of graph text. The answer should cite support for its claims and acknowledge missing or conflicting evidence. Documents can contain hostile instructions; retrieved content remains untrusted data rather than instructions to the application.

Bound expansion, document count and context size using documented policies. If a bound truncates potentially useful evidence, expose that limitation rather than claiming a complete search. A graph makes relationships available; it does not guarantee a factual model response.
interpretation: Graph retrieval and graph neural network training are separate uses of graph data.

parts.title: 7. Evaluate the retrieval decision as well as the generated answer
paragraphs: Use held-out maintenance questions with known supporting records. Check whether required evidence is retrieved, whether forbidden or future evidence is excluded and whether citations support the answer actually given. Include an unresolved question where the correct behaviour is to ask for more information.

Compare this retrieval policy with a simpler document search on the same questions. Measure latency and failure cases alongside answer quality. More connected context can add irrelevant material or repeated claims, so improvement needs evidence.
interpretation: The workshop tests the evidence-selection mechanism. It makes no claim to evaluate a live language model.

task: Implement context_docs(graph,start,tenant,as_of,max_depth). Keep only nodes in tenant and edges with both endpoints permitted. If start is absent or is not an Asset, return []. Follow DEPENDS_ON only through Asset nodes for at most max_depth hops, including start at depth zero. Follow HAS_MANUAL from reached nodes, and return sorted distinct Document IDs with available_at <= as_of.
max_depth is a nonnegative integer. Document availability values and as_of are integer hours; this is an already time-appropriate graph snapshot.
