topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
title: Is the Model Wrong, or Is the Record Wrong?
blurb: A suspicious label deserves a closer look. Use out-of-fold disagreements to organise review while preserving original records and the boundary around the final assessment.
openingTitle: The Fault Label Describes the Wrong Inspection
opening: Botie repeatedly predicts a fault for a pump labelled healthy. We inspect the record and discover that its label came from an earlier visit. Changing model settings would not fix that timestamp.
Other disagreements will be genuine model mistakes. We need a review process that can tell those cases apart without treating the model’s own opinion as the answer.

history.title: Looking for Problems in the Labels

sources.title: Northcutt, Jiang and Chuang: Confident Learning

blocks: Datasets are often treated as a fixed answer key even though their labels may contain mistakes. Confident Learning developed methods for estimating label uncertainty and identifying likely label issues using predicted probabilities under stated assumptions.

Our review queue is a simpler teaching rule, not an implementation of Confident Learning. It flags strong disagreements for investigation. The original observation and an independent review remain the evidence for any correction.

reading.experimentTitle: Request review without rewriting the answer
reading.experimentIntro: Keep eligible development records before applying the disagreement threshold.
reading.connectionTitle: A suspicion needs evidence
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Build a label review queue
reading.exampleNote: Invented records with supplied out-of-fold positive scores. The browser does not infer true labels or run a label-noise estimation method.

intuition.title: The same disagreement can have different causes
intuition.explanation: The score concerns the probability of a fault; the label records the reviewed outcome.

records.label: A
cells: Does the label belong to this visit?

records.label: B
cells: Did the model confuse harmless vibration with a fault?

scene.caption: A high score does not decide which record is wrong.

intuition.title: Keep an audit trail for a correction
intuition.explanation: A reviewer needs the original evidence and a defined target.

rows.label: Revision
items: Refit and evaluate under the declared split

scene.caption: Never silently replace a label with the model prediction.

parts.title: 1. Check the target and the join first
paragraphs: A record may join a sensor reading to the wrong pump, an inspection to the wrong day, or a label to an event that was unavailable when prediction was supposed to happen. Inspect identifiers and timestamps before diagnosing model capacity.

Write the target in operational terms. “Fault present at inspection” differs from “maintenance performed within a month”. A team’s maintenance decisions may depend on the existing model, so those labels can reflect the policy as well as the condition.
interpretation: An accurate calculation on misjoined records still answers the wrong question.

parts.title: 2. Look for duplicates across the split
paragraphs: Exact duplicates can place the same example in training and assessment. Near duplicates, repeated patients and multiple views of one event can do the same less obviously. Group related observations before splitting when they share the information the model could memorise.

Deduplication itself needs a definition. Two pumps with equal temperature readings are not automatically duplicate events. Preserve event identity and domain context instead of dropping equal numeric rows indiscriminately.
interpretation: A data audit can change the split plan, not only the label values.

parts.title: 3. Use predictions made without fitting that record
paragraphs: A model fitted on an example can memorise its label, making agreement uninformative. Out-of-fold predictions come from models that did not train on the evaluated fold. They provide a more useful disagreement signal for development review.

Respect group and time boundaries inside those folds. Keep label review on the development side; do not feed final test answers back into training while retaining the old test score as independent evidence.
parts.calculation:
For a recorded label 0: disagreement score = p(fault)
For a recorded label 1: disagreement score = 1 - p(fault)
interpretation: An overconfident model can produce strong but mistaken flags. The queue is a prioritisation aid.

parts.title: 4. Make the review rule explicit
paragraphs: Our teaching rule flags eligible records when disagreement confidence reaches a threshold above one half. Threshold inclusion is deliberate: a score equal to the threshold enters the queue.

Review records in a stable order and keep unique IDs. A real queue might combine disagreement with group coverage or expected correction value. Sample some unflagged cases too; otherwise you may never see errors the model confidently agrees with.
parts.calculation:
Record A: label 0, score 0.95, threshold 0.90 → review
Record B: label 1, score 0.95, threshold 0.90 → no disagreement flag
interpretation: The rule does not estimate how many labels are wrong, and unflagged does not mean verified.

parts.title: 5. Keep correction provenance and unresolved cases
paragraphs: A reviewer should see the evidence needed for the target, with a written annotation policy. Record the previous label, new label if any, reason and data version. Where feasible, independent or blinded review reduces the chance of simply agreeing with the model.
Some cases remain ambiguous. Keep that status rather than manufacturing certainty. Agreement rates between reviewers, adjudication rules and sampling design help explain what the revised labels mean.
interpretation: If a final evaluation label really is wrong, correct it transparently and report the changed assessment version. Do not silently tune on it and continue calling it untouched.

parts.title: 6. Filter records without mutating them
paragraphs: The review function returns IDs only. It should not rewrite labels, reorder source records or substitute predictions. That separation makes an accidental automatic relabelling harder to hide.
interpretation: The challenge adds eligibility, threshold and duplicate checks around this inspection.

examples.title: Read the evidence behind one flag
paragraphs: This example computes a disagreement score without changing its record.
examples.code:
record = {"id": "P4", "label": 1, "p": 0.08}
disagreement = 1 - record["p"]
print(round(disagreement, 2))
print(record["label"])
interpretation: The label remains 1. A score of 0.92 requests review; it is not a replacement label.

parts.title: 7. Test the dataset revision as a change
paragraphs: After corrections, refit the same procedure first so the comparison can isolate the data revision. Record any additional feature or algorithm change separately. Keep prior difficult cases in regression tests and assess on evidence outside the correction process.

Report how many records were reviewed, corrected, retained and unresolved. A model may improve because labels became more consistent, because the task definition changed, or because difficult cases were removed. Those explanations have different implications.
interpretation: A cleaner development dataset is useful. It still needs an assessment that represents the intended use.

quiz.prompt: What should the audit retain?
options: An unresolved status with the original evidence
quiz.because: Unresolved evidence belongs in the report. Forced labels and silent deletion hide uncertainty.

given.data: A reviewer cannot determine whether the inspection label applies to the current visit.

practice.question: Can Botie request review without editing the labels?

Return development IDs whose disagreement score is at least threshold, preserving record order. Require 0.5 < threshold <= 1 and raise ValueError for invalid inputs. Empty input returns []. Do not alter records.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
def review_queue(records, threshold):
    raise NotImplementedError

print(review_queue([{'id':'A','split':'development','label':0,'p':.95},
                    {'id':'B','split':'test','label':0,'p':.99}], .9))
hints: Filter by declared split; confidence does not change eligibility.
For label 1, disagreement uses one minus p. Preserve the label itself.

tests.name: Both disagreement directions
tests.code:
rows=[{'id':'x','split':'development','label':1,'p':.05},{'id':'y','split':'development','label':0,'p':.9}]
assert review_queue(rows,.9)==['x','y']
assert rows[0]['label']==1

tests.code:

assert review_queue([{'id':'x','split':'test','label':0,'p':1}],.9)==[]

tests.name: Reject duplicate IDs and thresholds

build.problem: Strong disagreement may identify a mistaken label or a mistaken model.
build.challenge: Keep development records, then return IDs whose disagreement reaches the supplied threshold. Do not rewrite labels or include test records.

cases.name: The strongest flag belongs to the test set

build.why: Eligibility is determined before disagreement strength. The output requests review without treating the model as an answer key.
build.limitation: This simple rule is not Confident Learning, an automatic correction method or proof that unflagged records are correct.

topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
title: When Should the Model Ask for Help?
blurb: Sending uncertain cases to a person changes both the error rate and the workload. Measure what the model handles and what it leaves for the review team.
openingTitle: The Review Desk Has Only So Much Time
opening: Botie classifies pump inspections, but a person can review cases it is unsure about. That seems helpful until almost every inspection lands on the desk. We have reduced the model’s workload by giving it to someone else.
We need to measure two things together: how much work the model accepts and how often it is wrong on that accepted work. Then we can check whether the remaining queue is manageable.

history.title: Allowing a Classifier to Decline a Decision

sources.title: Geifman and El-Yaniv: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks, 2017

blocks: Selective classification studies predictions with a reject option: the system can decline some cases and trade coverage for lower error on accepted cases. Geifman and El-Yaniv developed a method for deep networks with risk control under their stated procedure.

Our threshold exercise measures empirical coverage and error on supplied cases. It does not implement that paper’s guarantee. The useful intuition is that refusing a case changes the population whose errors we report.

reading.experimentTitle: Watch both sides of the handoff
reading.experimentIntro: Threshold the supplied confidence, then count accepted errors and cases sent for review.
reading.connectionTitle: The rejected cases still exist
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Measure what the model accepts
reading.exampleNote: Invented confidence scores and observed error flags. Confidence is a supplied selection score, not a verified probability of correctness.

intuition.title: Acceptance changes the denominator
intuition.explanation: An error flag of 1 means the frozen model’s predicted class was wrong.

scene.caption: The review queue contains C even though the recorded prediction happened to be correct.

intuition.title: A confident mistake can survive a stricter rule
intuition.explanation: Now A is the error. Raising the threshold keeps that wrong prediction.

scene.caption: Confidence thresholding does not guarantee that the accepted error rate decreases on every sample.

parts.title: 1. Separate the prediction from the decision to use it
paragraphs: The classifier produces a predicted label. A selector decides whether the application should accept that label or request review. These are distinct decisions. For a binary probability, confidence might be the larger class probability, but a different selection score can be trained or calibrated.

Our inputs already contain confidence and an observed error flag for each frozen prediction. A low positive-class probability is not necessarily low confidence: it may express confidence in the negative class.
parts.calculation:
Binary p(fault) = 0.05
Predicted class = healthy
Maximum class probability = max(0.05, 0.95) = 0.95
interpretation: Do not reuse a positive-class alert threshold as a confidence threshold without changing its meaning.

parts.title: 2. Measure coverage and the errors left inside it
paragraphs: Coverage is the fraction of all cases accepted by the selector. Selective risk, for zero-one loss, is the error fraction among accepted cases. Rejected cases do not enter that error denominator, but they remain in the workload report.
If nothing is accepted, selective risk is undefined. Reporting zero would make a system that refuses every task look flawless.
parts.calculation:
At threshold 0.75:
Accepted = 2 of 3
Coverage = 2 / 3
Accepted errors = 1
Selective risk = 1 / 2
interpretation: A lower accepted error rate can accompany a much larger review queue.

parts.title: 3. Test the confident mistakes
paragraphs: Raising the threshold changes which cases remain. It often removes difficult examples when the selection score is useful, but overconfident mistakes can stay. Examine them directly and report the coverage-risk tradeoff across development thresholds.

Calibration of probabilities and ranking of correctness are related questions with different answers. A system can order cases usefully while overstating their probabilities, or be well calibrated in broad bins while still failing in an important subgroup.
interpretation: Freeze a chosen selector before assessing it on new cases. Repeatedly tuning against the final assessment reuses its evidence.

parts.title: 4. Treat review as part of the system
paragraphs: Count arrivals and service capacity over time, not only a daily total. Cases can arrive in a burst while the reviewer is unavailable. Decide what happens when the queue is full and how urgent cases are prioritised.

Human review is not automatically correct. Measure reviewer agreement, turnaround time and downstream outcomes. If the model’s label is shown to reviewers, consider whether it anchors their decisions.
parts.calculation:
100 cases arrive in a shift
Coverage = 0.70
Review arrivals = 100 × (1 - 0.70) = 30
Review capacity = 20
Unserved cases in this simplified shift = 10
interpretation: This count ignores arrival timing and existing backlog. A deployment plan needs those details too.

parts.title: 5. Check who is being referred
paragraphs: Compare acceptance rates and accepted errors across relevant groups. A model could look better overall because it sends nearly every case from an underrepresented group to a slower manual route.

Report outcomes for all incoming cases where they can be obtained, including rejected ones. Labels collected only for accepted cases create a selective observation problem: the missing outcomes can hide failures in the selection policy.
interpretation: A useful selector needs an evaluation of the complete service, not only its easiest accepted cases.

parts.title: 6. Use the mask on the errors, not on the denominator twice
paragraphs: The acceptance mask selects the observed error flags. Averaging those flags gives accepted risk. Averaging the mask gives coverage because its zeros and ones refer to every incoming case.
interpretation: The challenge must handle the empty accepted set explicitly.

examples.title: Inspect accepted cases
paragraphs: This example demonstrates the mask on a different three-case batch.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
confidence = np.array([.9,.4,.8])
errors = np.array([0,1,1])
accepted = confidence >= .8
print(errors[accepted].tolist())
print(int((~accepted).sum()))
interpretation: The rejected error remains part of the workload to resolve. It is excluded only from the accepted-error metric.

quiz.prompt: What does the result establish?
options: The accepted model subset improved, but review capacity is unresolved
quiz.because: The deferred work remains part of the task and must be assessed.

topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
title: Should This Change the Prediction?
blurb: The same measurement can arrive in different units or a different batch. State the behaviour that should survive those changes, then test the actual prediction pipeline.
openingTitle: The Sensor Started Reporting Fahrenheit
opening: A greenhouse sensor update changes its output from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The physical temperature has not changed. If our prediction service feeds the new number into the old feature position, Botie sees a much hotter greenhouse.

A random test split may never contain that deployment change. We need tests built around a relationship we understand: after the correct unit conversion, the same physical input should produce the same result from a deterministic frozen pipeline.

history.title: Testing Behaviour That a Single Score Misses

sources.title: Ribeiro and colleagues: Beyond Accuracy, CheckList, 2020

blocks: A held-out average can miss a specific behaviour that users rely on. CheckList applied behavioural testing ideas to language models, including tests of capabilities and expected responses to input changes.

We use that testing perspective for a temperature service. Our unit and batching checks are examples of declared relationships between inputs and outputs, not a claim to implement the CheckList software or certify robustness.

reading.experimentTitle: Test a declared relationship
reading.experimentIntro: Compare each transformed run with its expected output and a stated absolute tolerance.
reading.connectionTitle: Choose the transformation before declaring invariance
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Report each behavioural check
reading.exampleNote: The workshop uses recorded expected and observed outputs. The worked Python program runs a real unit conversion; no trained model is called in the workshop.

intuition.title: Equivalent measurements should remain equivalent
intuition.explanation: The adapter converts the incoming value into the feature unit expected by the frozen pipeline.

scene.caption: The adapter needs the unit label. Guessing from the magnitude is not a reliable contract.

intuition.title: Some changes should matter
intuition.explanation: Define the expected relationship before constructing a test.

records.label: Reorder batch rows
cells: Same outputs after restoring row order

scene.caption: Changing a feature value is not automatically an invariance test.

parts.title: 1. Name the behaviour we rely on
paragraphs: An invariance test changes representation while preserving something the task should treat as equivalent. A unit conversion is one example. A metamorphic test describes a relationship between multiple runs even when we do not know an exact answer for every input.

Begin with the intended use. Flipping a photo may preserve its object label but change the meaning of left and right. Removing “not” from a sentence should often change its meaning. A convenient transformation is not automatically a valid test.
interpretation: Write the expected relation and the conditions under which it holds.

parts.title: 2. Keep the adapter inside the tested pipeline
paragraphs: A model receives numbers in a particular schema. Test from the input boundary through the adapter to prediction. A unit test of the coefficient multiplication alone will not catch a wrong conversion before it.
Keep named feature order as part of the contract. If temperature and heater setting swap columns, a matrix still has the right shape while representing the wrong input.
parts.calculation:
Fahrenheit to Celsius:
C = (F - 32) × 5 / 9
For F = 68:
C = (68 - 32) × 5 / 9 = 20
interpretation: Reject unknown units rather than silently assuming the training unit.

parts.title: 3. Use a tolerance that fits the output
paragraphs: Floating-point calculations can differ slightly across implementations. For a deterministic numerical pipeline, compare differences with a justified absolute or relative tolerance. State the units and avoid a tolerance so broad that a real bug passes.
Our workshop uses an absolute tolerance. Equality at the limit passes. NumPy isclose also supports relative tolerance; if you use it, understand how both terms combine.
parts.calculation:
pass = abs(observed - expected) <= absolute_tolerance
Expected: 20; observed: 20.25; tolerance: 0.25 → pass
interpretation: A stochastic generator needs repeated-distribution or task-level checks, not an assumption that every run produces identical text or pixels.

parts.title: 4. Test batches without mixing up identities
paragraphs: For a row-independent deterministic predictor, predicting records individually should agree with predicting them as a batch. Permuting rows should permute outputs in the same way. Restore IDs before comparing.

Some models legitimately use context across records, such as sequence models. Their batching and ordering contracts need different tests. State that dependency instead of treating every order effect as a bug.
interpretation: A test can reveal a contract mismatch even when the model’s ordinary benchmark remains unchanged.

parts.title: 5. Try plausible corruptions and measure degradation
paragraphs: Sensor noise, missing fields and delayed measurements deserve separate tests. These can change the available information, so identical outputs may be the wrong requirement. Check degradation against a task-specific allowance or require a clear rejection of unsupported inputs.
Record corruption severity and why it is plausible. Test important slices too. Passing a few perturbations does not establish resistance to arbitrary adversarial inputs or unseen distribution shifts.
interpretation: Use failures to create specific regression tests. Keep a fresh assessment to check whether the resulting repair generalises.

parts.title: 6. Run the conversion before comparing results

topic: Build and Check a Model Revision
title: Repair the Night-Shift Model Without Breaking the Day Shift
blurb: Diagnose a missing condition, fit a revised predictor and compare it with the baseline. Botie then checks whether the overall gain survives group and runtime requirements on a fresh shift.
openingTitle: The Same Heater Setting Produces Different Nights
opening: We have enough evidence to try a specific repair. Botie’s temperature baseline uses the heater setting, but its night readings are consistently underpredicted. The night indicator is available before prediction, so we can test whether adding it helps.

Keep the original model as a reference. We will fit both versions using the same training records, compare their predictions on development data, and write down what the candidate must satisfy before a limited trial. The next shift will challenge those requirements.

history.title: A Fitted Equation Needs an Evaluation Record

sources.title: Mitchell and colleagues: Model Cards for Model Reporting

blocks: Least-squares fitting provides coefficients that minimise squared training discrepancies for a specified linear model. It does not decide whether the inputs are appropriate or whether a revised model is useful for its intended population.

This project brings fitting together with explicit evaluation and reporting. The greenhouse is invented, and the small exact training relation makes the mechanics visible. We still keep the distinction between fitting a relation and collecting enough evidence to use it.

reading.experimentTitle: Give the revision a fair trial decision
reading.experimentIntro: Compute both error arrays from shared observations, inspect group changes, then enforce the declared policy.
reading.connectionTitle: A repair needs a record of what changed
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Fit both versions without reading the answers early
reading.exampleNote: Workshop predictions and runtime are supplied measurements for an invented comparison. The Python challenge actually fits both least-squares models on training data.

intuition.explanation: The heater setting alone cannot distinguish these day and night records.

scene.caption: The night indicator is known at prediction time. These four exact values are a teaching construction, not a field dataset.

intuition.title: Carry a specific hypothesis into the comparison

parts.title: 1. Write the hypothesis before changing the code
paragraphs: Our hypothesis is that a missing night condition contributes to the residual pattern. The candidate adds a night indicator and keeps the rest of the fitting procedure unchanged. Save the dataset version, split IDs and baseline first.

An indicator can capture an association without identifying its physical cause. It may stand in for ventilation or other scheduled changes. If that schedule changes, the association may fail. The diagnosis gives us a useful experiment, not a causal proof.
interpretation: Confirm the new feature is available at prediction time and uses the same definition in training and serving.

parts.title: 2. Represent both models with visible columns
paragraphs: The baseline has a constant column and heater setting. The candidate adds the night column. Each row is an observation; each coefficient multiplies its matching column.

NumPy column_stack combines the one-dimensional columns into those matrices. The leading ones let the fitted coefficient represent an intercept. The candidate design must have independent columns to identify all three coefficients in this exercise.
parts.calculation:
Baseline row:  [1, heater]
Candidate row: [1, heater, night]
Prediction = design row @ coefficients
interpretation: Keep column names and order with the saved model. A two-column input matrix should not silently accept a swapped schema.

parts.title: 3. Fit on training records, then freeze the coefficients
paragraphs: linalg.lstsq returns a least-squares solution. We use its first returned item, the coefficient vector, and multiply a separate evaluation design matrix by those coefficients. Evaluation outcomes enter only after the predictions exist.
The model is fitted by squared error while this task reports MAE. That is deliberate: the fitting objective and the operational report need not be identical, but their difference should be stated.
parts.calculation:
For the exact training table:
Baseline coefficients: [12, 2]
Candidate coefficients: [10, 2, 4]
New rows: [[2, 0], [2, 1]]
Baseline predictions: [16, 16]
Candidate predictions: [14, 18]
interpretation: The exact candidate fit was designed for teaching. Real data include noise and may not support this simple relation.

parts.title: 4. Use a small fitting program before the full comparison
paragraphs: The example below fits one intercept-and-slope model. Inspect the design matrix and prediction before building both versions in the challenge.

The reusable challenge returns predictions as well as scores. That allows a test to change evaluation labels and verify that the predictions do not move. If they do, the fitting step has leaked evaluation information.
interpretation: Rank checks here produce a clear teaching failure instead of silently fitting an unidentified candidate.

examples.title: Fit one frozen rule
paragraphs: This example uses one input feature and a different dataset. The challenge adds a candidate feature and evaluation checks.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0., 1., 2.])
y = np.array([3., 5., 7.])
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
weights = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y, rcond=None)[0]
print(weights.round(4).tolist())
print(round(float(np.array([1.,3.]) @ weights),4))
interpretation: The new input uses the fitted coefficients. No outcome for that new input was needed to produce its prediction.

parts.title: 5. Compare the repair where it was meant to help
paragraphs: Calculate both absolute-error arrays on the same development observations. Report mean gain and group changes. A night repair that damages daytime performance deserves another look even if it meets an overall target.

Keep a ledger of attempts: hypothesis, changed feature or setting, observations used, outcome and next decision. Use paired uncertainty analysis at the appropriate independent unit when the data support it. Do not select one lucky seed and omit the other runs.
parts.calculation:
Group increase = candidate group MAE - baseline group MAE
Worst group increase = maximum over declared groups
Overall improvement = baseline MAE - candidate MAE
interpretation: A negative worst-group increase means every observed group improved. Small or absent groups still limit the evidence.

parts.title: 6. Declare the policy before the fresh shift
paragraphs: For the workshop, require at least the specified overall gain, no group increase above its allowance, and runtime no greater than its limit. Preserve every failure reason. A faster candidate does not compensate for a failed error requirement unless the policy explicitly allows that trade.

Real runtime assessment needs a defined hardware and workload distribution, often including tail latency. A single supplied runtime in this fixture only teaches how an independent requirement enters a decision.
parts.calculation:
Teaching policy:
minimum MAE gain: 0.5
maximum group MAE increase: 0.25
maximum recorded runtime: 10 ms
interpretation: Passing this small gate means eligible for a limited trial under these rules. It does not establish safety or justify automatic broad deployment.

parts.title: 7. Let a fresh shift challenge the repair
paragraphs: The investigation keeps the overall improvement but moves the candidate’s errors into the night group. Predict which requirement will reject it before running the construction. Then test the slow candidate, where errors improve but the runtime limit fails.

Retain both failures as regression cases. If either changes the model or policy, obtain new independent assessment data for the resulting candidate. Repeatedly repairing against one “fresh” set eventually makes it another development set.
interpretation: The learner’s actual comparison graph must explain which requirement failed; a memorised decision cannot handle the changed cases.

parts.title: 8. Keep the evidence with the model that enters a trial
paragraphs: Save the feature schema, fitted parameters, data version, evaluation IDs and metric definitions. Record the trial limits and how to revert to the baseline. Monitor delayed outcomes as well as input changes, since a running service can look healthy while predictions degrade.

For language-model and agent revisions, the same discipline applies but task outcomes and stochastic runs need their own evaluators. The agent iteration section continues that problem with tool contracts, traces and reviewed cases.
interpretation: A revision is easier to improve when we can reconstruct what changed and why we thought it would help.

options: Hold because of a group regression

practice.title: Can the repair learn the night effect without seeing the evaluation answers?
practice.question: Can the repair learn the night effect without seeing the evaluation answers?
task: Implement compare_revision(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y). Input matrices have two columns in order: heater setting, night indicator. Outcome arrays have one value per row. Require nonempty finite arrays with those shapes and a full-rank candidate training design [1, heater, night]; otherwise raise ValueError.

Fit a baseline [1, heater] and candidate [1, heater, night] by NumPy least squares using training data only. Return (baseline predictions, candidate predictions, baseline MAE, candidate MAE). Predictions must be NumPy arrays in test-row order.
Print predictions rounded to four decimals and the two rounded MAEs. The exact fixture is for learning the procedure, not claiming a deployed model has zero error.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
def compare_revision(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y):
    raise NotImplementedError

train_x = [[0,0],[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]]
train_y = [10,12,14,16]
old, new, old_mae, new_mae = compare_revision(train_x,train_y,[[2,0],[2,1]],[14,18])
print(old.round(4).tolist())
print(new.round(4).tolist())
print(round(old_mae,4), round(new_mae,4))
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
def compare_revision(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y):
    x, y = np.asarray(train_x,dtype=float), np.asarray(train_y,dtype=float)
    z, truth = np.asarray(test_x,dtype=float), np.asarray(test_y,dtype=float)
    if x.ndim != 2 or z.ndim != 2 or x.shape[1] != 2 or z.shape[1] != 2 or not len(x) or not len(z):
        raise ValueError("Use nonempty matrices with heater and night columns")
    if y.shape != (len(x),) or truth.shape != (len(z),):
        raise ValueError("One outcome per row")
    if not all(np.isfinite(a).all() for a in (x,y,z,truth)):
        raise ValueError("Use finite values")
    old_train = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x[:,0]])
    new_train = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    if np.linalg.matrix_rank(new_train) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Training data must identify all candidate coefficients")
    old_w = np.linalg.lstsq(old_train,y,rcond=None)[0]
    new_w = np.linalg.lstsq(new_train,y,rcond=None)[0]
    old_pred = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(z)),z[:,0]]) @ old_w
    new_pred = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(z)),z]) @ new_w
    return old_pred, new_pred, float(np.abs(truth-old_pred).mean()), float(np.abs(truth-new_pred).mean())

train_x = [[0,0],[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]]
train_y = [10,12,14,16]
old, new, old_mae, new_mae = compare_revision(train_x,train_y,[[2,0],[2,1]],[14,18])
print(old.round(4).tolist())
print(new.round(4).tolist())
print(round(old_mae,4), round(new_mae,4))
hints: Build training and evaluation design matrices separately, with the same column order.
Fit coefficients with training outcomes only. Use test outcomes only after matrix multiplication produces predictions.

title: What Does an Alarm Tell Us?
blurb: An alarm may catch most faulty sensors and still be wrong surprisingly often. We need to know how common faults are before deciding what an alarm means.
openingTitle: The Alarm Works. Why Are So Many Checks Unnecessary?
opening: Botie has a warning light that usually turns on when a greenhouse sensor is faulty. That sounds useful. But when he checks the sensors that triggered it, many are working normally. Has the warning light stopped working?

Before answering, we need to ask two different questions. How often does a faulty sensor trigger the light? And, among sensors that trigger the light, how many are faulty? Those questions describe different groups. Let's follow the sensors through both groups before reaching for a formula.

history.title: Working Back From What We Observed

sources.title: Bayes, communicated by Price: An Essay Towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)

blocks: Calculating what might happen under a known rule is one problem. Inferring something about that rule after seeing outcomes is another. Bayes's essay, communicated by Richard Price in 1763 after Bayes's death, addressed this reverse direction: what repeated successes and failures could tell us about an unknown chance.

Our alarm example is invented and uses a simpler finite table. Its useful connection to that history is the direction of reasoning. We observe the alarm, then update how plausible each possible cause is. We must account for both how well a cause explains the alarm and how common that cause was to begin with.

intuition.title: Start with all the sensors
intuition.explanation: Suppose exactly 10 of these 1,000 sensors are faulty. The other 990 work. These counts describe our invented report, not an estimated industry fault rate.

intuition.title: Follow the alarms from both groups
intuition.explanation: Nine faulty sensors trigger the alarm. So do 99 working sensors. A small fraction of a large group can contribute many alarms.

intuition.title: Now look only at the alarm group
intuition.explanation: Botie's question concerns the 108 alarms. Only nine of them came from faulty sensors. The group in the denominator has changed.

intuition.title: The same alarm can mean more when faults are common
intuition.explanation: Keep the detection and false-alarm rates fixed, but imagine a population with more faulty sensors. A larger share of the alarms now comes from real faults. The alarm's meaning depends on the starting population as well as the detector.

scene.caption: Invented populations of 1,000 sensors, with 90% detection and 10% false alarms.

parts.title: 1. Say Which Group We Are Talking About
paragraphs: A probability needs a reference group. In this report, the fault rate describes all sensors. The alarm rate among faulty sensors describes only the faulty ones. Once we are told that a sensor raised an alarm, our reference group becomes the sensors that raised alarms.
Conditioning means restricting our attention using information we know. The vertical bar in a conditional probability reads as 'given'. Its position matters.
parts.calculation:
P(alarm | faulty) = 9 / 10 = 0.9
P(faulty | alarm) = 9 / 108 ≈ 0.0833
interpretation: Both statements can be true at the same time. Catching most faults does not establish that most alarms are faults.

parts.title: 2. Count Every Way the Alarm Could Happen
paragraphs: An alarm can come from either a faulty sensor or a working one. We need both contributions. If we count only the faulty sensors that triggered, we have a numerator but no complete denominator.
The fault rate before reading the alarm is the prior probability. The alarm rate within each group tells us how compatible the alarm is with that group.
parts.calculation:
P(faulty and alarm) = 0.01 × 0.9 = 0.009
P(working and alarm) = 0.99 × 0.1 = 0.099
P(alarm) = 0.009 + 0.099 = 0.108
interpretation: These are shares of all sensors. They become expected counts if we multiply by a proposed population size; expected counts need not be whole numbers.

parts.title: 3. Turn the Contributions Into an Updated Probability
paragraphs: To find the faulty share of the alarm group, divide its contribution by the total alarm contribution. This is the posterior probability, meaning the probability after incorporating this observation.
Bayes' rule writes the same bookkeeping for named events. The denominator accounts for all the ways the observed evidence can occur.
parts.calculation:
P(faulty | alarm)
  = P(alarm | faulty) × P(faulty) / P(alarm)
  = 0.009 / 0.108
  ≈ 0.0833
interpretation: This updates a probability. Choosing whether to send a technician is another question, involving the cost of a missed fault and an unnecessary visit.

parts.title: 4. Change the Starting Population
paragraphs: Now move the same warning system to sensors with a much higher fault rate. Even if its behaviour within the faulty and working groups stays the same, an alarm can become more convincing.

That is why we should not carry a positive predictive value from one population to another without checking the assumptions. The new population might also change the alarm's behaviour within each group.
parts.calculation:
New prior: P(faulty) = 0.2
Faulty alarm contribution = 0.2 × 0.9 = 0.18
Working alarm contribution = 0.8 × 0.1 = 0.08
Updated faulty probability = 0.18 / 0.26 ≈ 0.6923
interpretation: The hardware did not improve in this calculation. We changed how common each possible cause was.

parts.title: 5. Keep the Assumptions Visible
paragraphs: Our two causes cover every sensor and do not overlap. Their prior probabilities must therefore sum to one. The alarm rates are conditional on those causes; they do not have to sum to one.

An event assigned zero probability by every cause cannot be used in this calculation because there is no alarm group to condition on. Repeating the update with another alarm also needs a model of dependence: two copies of the same report are not two independent pieces of evidence.
interpretation: Botie's workshop asks you to form the contributions and normalise them. It leaves the final inspection decision to a later lesson.

examples.title: Calculate both updated shares
paragraphs: Keep the two possible causes in the same order in both arrays.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
prior = np.array([0.01, 0.99])
alarm_rate = np.array([0.9, 0.1])
joint = prior * alarm_rate
posterior = joint / joint.sum()
print(np.round(posterior, 4).tolist())
interpretation: The first entry concerns faulty sensors. The second concerns working sensors. They now describe the alarm group.

parts.title: 6. Follow People through the Groups Before Dividing
paragraphs: A warning system can catch most faults while producing many false alarms. To see why, start with a population rather than a percentage. Separate faulty sensors from working sensors, then ask how many in each group trigger the light.

Only after counting those two routes should we restrict attention to the sensors whose lights are on. The denominator has changed from all sensors, or all faulty sensors, to all alarms. That change of group is the reason the two conditional probabilities differ.
parts.calculation:
1,000 sensors: 10 faulty, 990 working
80% of faulty sensors trigger: 8 alarms
10% of working sensors trigger: 99 alarms
Faulty among alarms = 8 / (8 + 99) ≈ 0.0748

parts.title: 7. Carry the Same Test into a Different Population
paragraphs: Now suppose Botie checks a batch that may have been damaged in transit. Faults are more common in this batch. Even with the same sensitivity and false-alarm rate, the warning light now means something different: a larger share of the alarms can come from faulty sensors.
So, before using a probability attached to a test result, we need to know which population it describes. A result from ordinary deliveries may not apply to this damaged batch.

examples.title: Change only the starting failure rate
paragraphs: The two entries represent ordinary stock and a damaged shipment.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
prior = np.array([0.01, 0.20])
sensitivity, false_alarm = 0.8, 0.1
alarm_fault = prior * sensitivity
alarm_working = (1 - prior) * false_alarm
print(np.round(alarm_fault / (alarm_fault + alarm_working), 4).tolist())
interpretation: The mechanism of the warning light did not improve. The evidence began from a different proportion of faulty sensors.

quiz.prompt: Which denominator answers 'What share of alarms came from faulty sensors?'
quiz.because: We have restricted the question to sensors that raised an alarm, so both sources of alarms belong in the denominator.

given.data:
Faulty sensors: 10; working sensors: 990.
Alarms from faulty sensors: 9; alarms from working sensors: 99.

quiz.prompt: The chance of a fault given an alarm is also 0.9.
quiz.because: Reversing the condition changes the reference group. We must include how common faults and false alarms are.

given.data:
P(alarm | faulty) = 0.9
P(faulty) = 0.01
P(alarm | working) = 0.1

quiz.prompt: Which pair should we normalise after observing an alarm?
quiz.because: Each cause contributes its prior multiplied by its conditional alarm rate.

given.data:
Faulty and working priors: [0.2, 0.8]
Alarm rates in the same order: [0.9, 0.1]

quiz.prompt: The copied report does not provide a second independent observation.
quiz.because: The copy repeats the same evidence. Treating it as independent would exaggerate what we learned.

build.problem: Botie sees an alarm. Combine the faulty and working groups' starting shares with their alarm rates, then calculate the updated shares.
build.challenge: Build the two joint contributions and divide each by their total. Keep faulty first and working second.
build.why: Weighting accounts for how common each cause is and how likely it is to produce the alarm. Dividing by the total changes the reference group to alarms.
build.limitation: These invented rates are known inputs. This calculation neither estimates their uncertainty nor decides whether an inspection is worth its cost.

title: Which Rule Could Have Produced These Observations?
blurb: A probability rule predicts possible observations. Likelihood holds the observations fixed and compares the rules that might have produced them. That distinction connects probability to fitting a model.
openingTitle: We Have the Results. Which Setting Explains Them?
opening: Botie tests a batch of seeds and records whether each one germinates. A proposed germination probability tells us how plausible each outcome would be. But the outcomes have already happened. What Botie wants to choose is the probability used by his model.

Let's try several proposed germination probabilities against the seeds we actually observed. Which setting makes that sequence most likely? Once we can calculate the comparison, we can ask how much it tells us about seeds we haven't tested.

history.title: Choosing a Model From Its Observed Consequences

sources.title: Fisher: On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

blocks: Statisticians needed ways to estimate a population's unknown settings from a finite sample. Fisher's 1922 treatment distinguished likelihood from probability when discussing that estimation problem. The observations are known; the proposed population settings vary.

The distinction matters because comparing how well settings explain data does not automatically assign probabilities to those settings. Our seed example makes the comparison visible with only one unknown parameter. It is a teaching model, not a reproduction of Fisher's data.

intuition.title: Record what happened
intuition.explanation: One means germinated and zero means did not. We will compare exactly this ordered sequence under each setting.

intuition.title: Try two rules
intuition.explanation: A very high germination probability favours the successes but makes the failure surprising. Both kinds of observation matter.

intuition.title: Look between the candidates
intuition.explanation: The observed successful share is two thirds. For this independent Bernoulli model, it maximises the sequence likelihood.

parts.title: 1. Define One Trial Before Combining Trials
paragraphs: A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, encoded here as one and zero. Its parameter is the probability of one. Once we choose that parameter, the probability of zero is its complement.

Our model assumes each seed has the same germination probability and that outcomes are independent given that probability. Shared damage or different seed varieties could make those assumptions unsuitable.
parts.calculation:
If p = 0.8:
P(germination) = 0.8
P(no germination) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2
interpretation: The parameter describes the proposed process. A short batch does not have to reproduce that fraction exactly.

parts.title: 2. Multiply the Probabilities of the Observed Outcomes
paragraphs: Under the independence assumption, the sequence probability is the product of its outcome probabilities. A germinated seed contributes the proposed probability; a seed that did not germinate contributes its complement.
The sequence contains two successes and one failure. Neither can be ignored just because one candidate fits the successes well.
interpretation: These numbers compare candidate rules on the same observations. They do not say there is a 12.8 percent probability that the parameter is 0.8.

parts.title: 3. Separate a Sequence From a Count
paragraphs: The particular sequence success, success, failure is only one ordering. If we instead ask for exactly two successes in any order, there are three possible arrangements. A binomial count probability includes that extra factor.
For this fixed batch and fixed success count, the factor is the same for every proposed probability. It changes the reported probability but does not change which parameter maximises it.
parts.calculation:
P(exactly two successes | p = 0.8)
  = 3 × (0.8² × 0.2)
  = 0.384
interpretation: Say which observation your likelihood describes. Do not compare a sequence probability from one model with an aggregated count probability from another.

parts.title: 4. Find the Setting and Connect It to a Loss
paragraphs: For this model, the maximum-likelihood estimate is the successful share. A longer list of probability factors can become extremely small, so we often add their logarithms instead. Logarithms preserve which positive likelihood is largest.

Negating that sum turns maximisation into minimisation. Averaging by the number of trials gives the familiar binary negative log-likelihood used in classification. Predicting a separate probability for each example is a later extension.
parts.calculation:
p̂ = successes / trials = 2 / 3
log L(p) = 2 log(p) + log(1 - p)
mean negative log-likelihood = -log L(p) / 3
interpretation: A logarithm is not a probability conversion. The log-likelihood can be negative and need not sum to one across settings.

parts.title: 5. A Best Fit Is Still an Estimate
paragraphs: An all-successful batch has its maximum at a probability of one in this simple model. That does not establish that failure is impossible in the wider population. Small samples can put the fitted setting at an extreme.

A prior distribution supports a different question about parameter uncertainty after seeing the batch. Held-out outcomes test whether the fitted rule predicts new observations. Neither uncertainty nor generalisation is settled by the training likelihood alone.
interpretation: The workshop compares candidate settings rather than claiming to have run a general optimiser.

examples.title: Compare a short grid of candidates
paragraphs: NumPy broadcasts one candidate per row against the same observed sequence. The product along each row combines that candidate's three factors.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
y = np.array([1, 1, 0])
factors = np.where(y[None, :] == 1, p[:, None], 1 - p[:, None])
print(np.prod(factors, axis=1).tolist())
interpretation: The best point on this small grid need not be the best point among all possible probabilities.

parts.title: 6. How Much Evidence Separates Two Germination Rates?
paragraphs: Botie observes three germinated seeds and one that did not germinate. Both a moderate rate and a high rate can produce that outcome. Likelihood compares how well candidate rates account for the observations; it does not assign those candidates posterior probabilities.

Working with log likelihood turns products into sums and avoids tiny products for long records. When a count is zero, its log term contributes zero. Do not calculate an undefined logarithm and hope multiplying it by zero will repair it.

examples.title: Compare candidate rates on the same seeds
paragraphs: These interior candidates avoid zero-probability boundary cases.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rates = np.array([0.25, 0.50, 0.75])
log_likelihood = 3 * np.log(rates) + np.log1p(-rates)
relative = np.exp(log_likelihood - log_likelihood.max())
print(np.round(relative, 4).tolist())
interpretation: The best candidate is used as a reference of one. These relative likelihoods do not sum to one and are not posterior probabilities.

parts.title: 7. All Successes Do Not Establish Certainty
paragraphs: If every seed in a small batch germinates, the maximum-likelihood rate is one. That is where this batch's likelihood is greatest. It does not establish that failure is impossible in future batches.

Keep the number of trials beside the estimate. A posterior distribution or an interval procedure addresses uncertainty that the single optimum omits. Also examine the trial model: seeds from one shared tray can be dependent, and combining them as independent trials may exaggerate the evidence.

quiz.prompt: Which expression is the likelihood of this sequence?
quiz.because: Independent outcomes contribute multiplicative probabilities, including the failure.

given.data:
Observed ordered outcomes: [1, 1, 0]
Candidate p: 0.8
Trials are independent given p.

quiz.prompt: This alone assigns probability 0.128 to the claim that p is 0.8.
quiz.because: Likelihood compares parameter settings for fixed observations. Parameter probabilities require an additional probabilistic model, including a prior.

given.data: The ordered sequence [1, 1, 0] has likelihood 0.128 under p = 0.8.

quiz.prompt: What is the maximum-likelihood estimate for their shared success probability?
quiz.because: For independent Bernoulli trials with one shared parameter, the fitted probability is the successful share.

given.data: Four independent trials have outcomes [1, 0, 1, 1].

quiz.prompt: For fixed counts, including all three orderings does not change which p maximises the likelihood.
quiz.because: The count probability multiplies every candidate's sequence likelihood by the same positive factor.

given.data: Exactly two successes out of three trials can occur as [1,1,0], [1,0,1], or [0,1,1].

practice.title: Which candidate best explains this batch?
practice.question: Which candidate best explains this batch?
task: Calculate the likelihood of the ordered outcomes under each candidate. Print the likelihoods as a list, then the winning candidate with two decimal places.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
candidates = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
outcomes = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1])
# Use every observed outcome.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
candidates = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
outcomes = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1])
factors = np.where(outcomes[None, :] == 1, candidates[:, None], 1 - candidates[:, None])
likelihoods = factors.prod(axis=1)
print(likelihoods.tolist())
print(f'{candidates[np.argmax(likelihoods)]:.2f}')
hints: Give candidates a column dimension and observations a row dimension.
Multiply within each candidate's row, then use argmax to recover the candidate index.

practice.title: Can you calculate the loss without multiplying tiny factors?
practice.question: Can you calculate the loss without multiplying tiny factors?
task: The model assigns probability 0.6 to success on every trial. Print the mean negative log-likelihood with four decimal places, then the fitted successful share with two decimal places.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1, 1])
p = 0.6
# Add log probabilities and calculate the observed share.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1, 1])
p = 0.6
loss = -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log1p(-p))
print(f'{loss:.4f}')
print(f'{y.mean():.2f}')
hints: A success uses log(p); a failure uses log(1 - p).
The negative mean of those terms is the average loss.

build.problem: Botie has observed which seeds germinated. Each candidate rule gives a probability for one seed, but he needs the likelihood of the whole ordered batch.
build.challenge: Calculate each candidate's sequence likelihood, find the largest likelihood's position, and retrieve the candidate at that position.
build.why: Each candidate is judged against the same observed sequence. The index of the largest likelihood selects the best supplied candidate.

title: Naive Bayes
blurb: A warm casing and an unstable reading may each suggest a faulty sensor. We need a way to combine those clues, while being explicit about what we assume about their relationship.
openingTitle: What If Several Clues Point to the Same Cause?
opening: The warning light was only one clue. Botie can also inspect whether a sensor's casing is warm and whether its readings fluctuate. A faulty sensor might produce both signs, but a working sensor can sometimes produce them too.

We could count every possible combination of signs in each group. As the list of signs grows, many combinations would have very few examples. Let's start with a simpler proposal: learn how often each sign appears within each group, then combine those contributions. We need to understand the assumption that makes that possible.

history.title: Classifying Without a Table for Every Combination

sources.title: McCallum and Nigam: A Comparison of Event Models for Naive Bayes Text Classification (1998)

blocks: Text classification made the combination problem particularly visible: a vocabulary can contain thousands of word features, and possible documents cannot be exhaustively tabulated. McCallum and Nigam's 1998 comparison examined different event models for naive Bayes, including binary word occurrence and word counts.

That paper did not invent Bayes' rule or every naive Bayes model. It demonstrated why the way we represent observations matters even within this apparently simple family. We will use invented binary sensor signs, then distinguish that model from counting repeated words.

intuition.title: Keep the causes separate
intuition.explanation: These probabilities concern seeing both observed signs, one sign at a time within each cause.

intuition.title: Combine within each cause
intuition.explanation: Assume the signs are independent once the cause is known. Their products give the proposed likelihood of seeing both.

intuition.title: Include how common the causes were
intuition.explanation: Faulty sensors start with a smaller prior share. Combining the prior and the likelihood, then normalising, gives the updated shares.

parts.title: 1. Learn Separate Rates Within Each Labelled Group
paragraphs: A training record contains the observed signs and a known class. For our sensor, a sign is either present or absent. Within the faulty group, count how many sensors show a warm casing; repeat for unstable readings. Then do the same within the working group.
The class frequencies supply priors. Each feature's frequency within a class supplies a conditional probability. Keep the feature order and class order fixed when these values become arrays.
parts.calculation:
Class order: faulty, working
Feature order: warm, unstable
Priors: [0.2, 0.8]
P(sign present | class):
  faulty  [0.8, 0.7]
  working [0.1, 0.2]
interpretation: These are supplied illustrative rates. Estimating them from labelled observations belongs entirely inside the training split.

parts.title: 2. Name the Independence Assumption
paragraphs: Let's make an assumption we can calculate with. Within each class, the model treats the features as conditionally independent. Once we specify faulty or working, learning that the casing is warm does not change the model's probability of an unstable reading. Across the whole population, the two signs can still be related because both may be more common in faulty sensors.

With that assumption, we can multiply the feature likelihoods for each class. Bayes' rule then brings in the prior class probabilities and lets us normalize the results. Later we will look at what happens when the signs are related even within a class.
parts.calculation:
Faulty contribution = 0.2 × 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.112
Working contribution = 0.8 × 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.016
Faulty posterior = 0.112 / (0.112 + 0.016) = 0.875
interpretation: Correlated clues can be counted too strongly. A classifier can still rank classes usefully while giving probabilities that are too confident.

parts.title: 3. An Absent Sign Also Supplies Evidence
paragraphs: In the Bernoulli version, every feature has a present-or-absent outcome. If the casing is warm but the reading is stable, use the warm probability and the complement of the unstable probability. Simply dropping absent features changes the model.
A multinomial text model instead describes counts of events such as word occurrences. It does not reuse the Bernoulli formula unchanged.
parts.calculation:
Observed signs: warm = 1, unstable = 0
Faulty likelihood = 0.8 × (1 - 0.7) = 0.24
Working likelihood = 0.1 × (1 - 0.2) = 0.08
interpretation: In the workshop, the supplied table already contains the probabilities of the outcomes actually observed. You combine its rows rather than guessing which features were present.

parts.title: 4. Keep One Unseen Event From Erasing Everything
paragraphs: A feature absent from a small class-specific training sample would otherwise receive a zero estimated rate. One such factor can erase that class's entire likelihood. Smoothing adds a small count to each possible outcome before dividing.

For a binary feature with one added count for presence and one for absence, both the numerator and denominator change. This is an explicit estimation choice, not evidence that the unseen event really occurred.
parts.calculation:
Present count = 0; class examples = 4
Smoothed present rate = (0 + 1) / (4 + 2) = 1/6
interpretation: With many features, add log likelihoods to avoid multiplying very small numbers. Fit smoothing choices on training and validation data, not the final test.

parts.title: 5. Check Whether the Simplification Helps
paragraphs: Compare this classifier with a simple class-frequency baseline. Inspect mistakes on new sensors, including cases where the two signs come from the same underlying measurement. Duplicating a feature can amplify its influence without adding information.
If we need reliable probabilities for inspection decisions, evaluate calibration as well as classification. A high posterior from an independence approximation is not a guarantee of correctness.
interpretation: The calculation remains useful because every contribution is inspectable. Its simplicity also makes its assumptions visible.

examples.title: Include a missing sign in the calculation
paragraphs: The observation is warm but stable. Each row describes one possible cause.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
prior = np.array([0.2, 0.8])
present = np.array([[0.8, 0.7], [0.1, 0.2]])
x = np.array([1, 0])
terms = np.where(x == 1, present, 1 - present)
scores = prior * terms.prod(axis=1)
print(np.round(scores / scores.sum(), 4).tolist())
interpretation: The stable reading changes the balance. The prior still matters after combining the signs.

parts.title: 6. Keep Fitting and Prediction as Separate Procedures
paragraphs: Fitting produces a class prior and a table of feature probabilities. Prediction receives a new sign vector and reads those saved tables. It must not count the new batch to redefine what a faulty sensor looks like.

For binary signs, every coordinate contributes either the probability of presence or the probability of absence. Add log probabilities to form one score per class. Subtract the largest score before exponentiating and normalising, just as we did for stable probability calculations in NumPy.

parts.title: 7. Fit Two Classes, Then Inspect a New Sensor
paragraphs: The training table below uses warm casing and unstable readings as its two columns. Labels zero and one mean working and faulty. We add one count for each binary outcome inside each class.
The example shows both learned tables and a new prediction. Inspect those tables before trusting the label: a feature order error can preserve every shape while changing the meaning of the evidence.

examples.title: A complete Bernoulli prediction
paragraphs: The four sensors are an invented training set, too small to establish real diagnostic performance.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[0,0], [1,0], [1,1], [1,1]])
y = np.array([0,0,1,1])
rate = np.array([(X[y == label].sum(axis=0) + 1) / ((y == label).sum() + 2) for label in [0,1]])
prior = np.array([(y == label).mean() for label in [0,1]])
new = np.array([1,1])
score = np.log(prior) + (new*np.log(rate) + (1-new)*np.log1p(-rate)).sum(axis=1)
probability = np.exp(score-score.max())
probability /= probability.sum()
print(rate.tolist())
print(np.round(probability, 4).tolist())
interpretation: Both signs favour the faulty class under the fitted approximation. These probabilities depend on the class priors, smoothing and conditional-independence assumption.

parts.title: 8. Copying a Clue Can Make the Model Overconfident
paragraphs: If the unstable-reading feature is copied into a second column, the model multiplies its evidence twice. It treats the copy as another conditionally independent observation even though no new measurement occurred.

Try that change and compare probabilities before labels. The predicted class may stay the same while confidence becomes more extreme. This is why a useful classifier can still need calibration, and why a high probability is not a substitute for inspecting the feature construction.

quiz.prompt: What likelihood does the model assign to both signs being present?
quiz.because: Conditional independence lets the model multiply the two class-conditional probabilities.

given.data:
Within the faulty class: P(warm)=0.8 and P(unstable)=0.7.
The model assumes conditional independence.

quiz.prompt: Treating those columns as conditionally independent can count one clue twice.
quiz.because: The duplicate supplies no independent observation, even though multiplication can make the result appear stronger.

given.data: Two feature columns contain identical copies of the same sensor reading.

quiz.prompt: Which factor belongs in that class's likelihood?
quiz.because: The probability of absence is the complement of the probability of presence.

given.data:
A Bernoulli feature has present probability 0.7 within a class.
Its observed value is absent.

quiz.prompt: That sample proves the feature is impossible in the class.
quiz.because: A small sample can miss possible outcomes. Smoothing is one explicit way to avoid treating that absence as certainty.

given.data: A feature is absent in all four labelled training examples of one class.

practice.title: Can you estimate smoothed sign rates from labelled sensors?
practice.question: Can you estimate smoothed sign rates from labelled sensors?
task: Rows are sensors and columns are two binary signs. For each class in order 0, 1, estimate each sign's present rate with one added present and one added absent observation.
Print the resulting two rows as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1,1], [1,0], [0,0], [0,1]])
y = np.array([1,1,0,0])
# Estimate rates separately within each class.

X = np.array([[1,1], [1,0], [0,0], [0,1]])
y = np.array([1,1,0,0])
rates = []
for label in [0, 1]:

title: Support Vector Machines and Margins
blurb: Several lines may separate the same labelled examples. We need a reason to prefer one, and a way to handle examples that cannot all be separated cleanly.
openingTitle: Which Separating Line Leaves Us Room to Be Wrong?
opening: Imagine two groups of inspected parts plotted by their measurements. We can draw a line between the groups, but we can also slide or rotate that line and still classify every training part correctly. Which line should we choose?

Measurements are not perfectly stable. A boundary pressed against one part leaves little room for a slightly different reading. Let's look for space between the boundary and the nearby examples, then decide what to do when a few observations intrude into that space.

history.title: Separating Examples That Do Not Cooperate
blocks: A separator that makes no training mistakes may still sit unnecessarily close to observations. Maximum-margin methods made the distance from a boundary part of the fitting problem. Real datasets then posed another difficulty: measurement error and overlapping classes can make perfect separation impossible.

Cortes and Vapnik's 1995 support-vector networks paper allowed the classifier to handle data that could not be separated perfectly. A point could violate the margin, but doing so carried a cost. The model could then balance a wider margin against those violations. We will use small geometric examples to understand that choice; the paper's experiments concerned optical character recognition.

intuition.title: Many lines separate these groups
intuition.explanation: The left points have label -1 and the right points label +1. A vertical boundary anywhere in the gap separates this sample.

scene.caption: Invented observations. Distances use the displayed coordinates.

intuition.title: Move the boundary away from the nearest points
intuition.explanation: The centred boundary leaves equal room on both sides. The nearest observations limit how wide that empty strip can become.

scene.caption: Invented observations. Distances use the displayed coordinates.

intuition.title: Allow a cost when observations enter the margin
intuition.explanation: Correct classification alone is not enough for zero hinge loss. An example also needs a sufficiently large signed score.

intuition.title: Two correct predictions can satisfy the margin differently
intuition.explanation: Both of these labelled points are on the correct side. One is still close to the boundary, so it contributes hinge loss; the other lies beyond the requested margin. Correct classification alone does not capture that distinction.

scene.caption: Supplied signed scores for two correctly classified observations.

parts.title: 1. Give the Boundary a Score
paragraphs: A linear score multiplies each measurement by a weight and adds a bias. The zero-score locations form the boundary. For this binary model, use class labels minus one and plus one. The score's sign chooses the side.
Multiplying the score by the known label makes a positive value mean correct-side placement for either class. This product is the functional margin.
parts.calculation:
score = w · x + b
signed score = y × score
For y = -1 and score = -0.5:
  signed score = (-1) × (-0.5) = 0.5
interpretation: A positive signed score is on the correct side. Its numerical size still depends on how the weights and bias are scaled.

parts.title: 2. Separate Score Size From Geometric Distance
paragraphs: Doubling every weight and the bias preserves the zero boundary while doubling all scores. It has not moved any observation. Dividing by the weight vector's length removes that arbitrary scale and gives signed perpendicular distance.
The conventional margin boundaries have scores minus one and plus one. Once we use that convention, a smaller weight norm means a wider strip.
parts.calculation:
signed distance = y(w · x + b) / ||w||
width between score -1 and score +1 = 2 / ||w||
interpretation: The distances depend on the feature units. Fit a scaler using training data before comparing features with incompatible scales.

parts.title: 3. Charge for Violating the Margin
paragraphs: An observation with signed score at least one lies on or beyond its margin boundary and receives zero hinge loss. A correctly classified observation inside the strip still receives a positive loss. A wrong-side observation receives a still larger loss.
Hinge loss measures this shortfall. It does not represent the probability of a class.
parts.calculation:
hinge = max(0, 1 - signed score)
signed score 1.5 → loss 0
signed score 0.5 → loss 0.5
signed score -0.5 → loss 1.5
interpretation: The workshop calculates these violations for supplied weights. It lets you inspect an objective component without pretending the weights were learned there.

parts.title: 4. Balance a Wider Margin Against Violations
paragraphs: The soft-margin objective combines a weight penalty with hinge losses. In the sum convention below, a larger C makes violations more expensive relative to widening the margin. Some formulations average losses and rescale the regularisation parameter; compare conventions before copying settings.

An optimiser chooses weights and bias to reduce the combined objective. Examples on or inside the margin can matter to the solution. The examples with nonzero dual coefficients are the support vectors.
parts.calculation:
Objective = (1/2)||w||² + C × Σ hinge_i
If ||w||² = 0.25, C = 0.5, and Σ hinge_i = 1:
  objective = 0.125 + 0.5 = 0.625
interpretation: This objective tolerates overlap. It does not promise that a linear boundary can express every useful pattern.

parts.title: 5. Connect the Boundary to Richer Representations
paragraphs: If a straight boundary is unsuitable in the measured coordinates, transformed features may help. Kernel support-vector machines express comparisons through kernel evaluations. The kernel lesson explains how such comparisons can correspond to a more useful representation.
Choose the penalty, kernel, and scaling through validation. A classifier's raw decision score is not automatically a calibrated probability, and increasing flexibility can fit accidental patterns.
interpretation: We now have a reason to choose a boundary, an explicit cost for exceptions, and a connection to the kernel machinery already in the course.

parts.title: 6. Which Observations Push the Boundary?
paragraphs: A point outside its margin already satisfies the hinge requirement, so that loss contributes no gradient there. A point inside the margin, including a correctly classified one, pushes the boundary toward a larger signed score. The weight penalty simultaneously pulls the weights toward zero.

The bias is not penalised in the convention used here. We average hinge losses and multiply them by C. This differs by a dataset-size factor from a sum-loss convention, so a copied numerical C need not represent the same tradeoff.

parts.title: 7. Repeat the Update Until the Boundary Can Be Checked
paragraphs: Begin with zero weights, calculate every signed score, collect only margin violations and make a small subgradient step. Repeat that procedure, then examine classifications and margin values separately.

Hinge loss is not differentiable exactly at its corner. The code uses zero contribution when the margin is exactly one, an allowed subgradient choice. A fixed step size can oscillate near the optimum; this small demonstration is not a replacement for a production solver.

examples.title: Train a one-feature separating rule
paragraphs: Negative and positive measurements belong to different inspected classes.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([-2., -1., 1., 2.])
y = np.array([-1., -1., 1., 1.])
w, b, C = 0., 0., 2.
for step in range(1000):
    active = y*(w*x+b) < 1
    dw = w - C*np.mean(np.where(active, y*x, 0.))
    db = -C*np.mean(np.where(active, y, 0.))
    rate = 0.1 / np.sqrt(step+1)
    w -= rate*dw
    b -= rate*db
print(np.sign(w*x+b).astype(int).tolist())
print(bool(w > 0), bool(abs(b) < 1e-10))
interpretation: The symmetric data produce a boundary at zero. Correct labels alone do not establish that the margin objective is fully optimised.

parts.title: 8. A Wide Margin Still Depends on the Ruler
paragraphs: Changing a feature from metres to millimetres changes its coefficient scale and the geometry of the weight penalty. Standardise using training statistics when that matches the feature meaning, and use the same transform for validation and prediction.

Inspect sensitivity to C on held-out records rather than choosing the setting with the widest-looking training strip. Overlapping classes, measurement errors and nonlinear relationships can all make a perfect separating line an unsuitable target.
