title: Learning From a Node and Its Neighbours Together
blurb: A graph convolution combines node features, self-connections, degree scaling, and learned weights. Work through these pieces before calling the result a layer.
openingTitle: How Can the Network Learn Which Shared Measurements Matter?
opening: Neighbour means gave Botie context, but a useful prediction may need to combine several features and retain the node’s own reading. Different connections also belong to nodes with different degrees.
A common graph-convolution layer first mixes features through a degree-normalised adjacency matrix, then applies shared learned weights and an activation. Each piece has a separate role.

history.title: A Simple Shared Layer on a Graph

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

blocks: Kipf and Welling proposed a computationally efficient graph-convolution approach for semi-supervised node classification. Their propagation rule combines self-loops, symmetric degree normalisation, learned feature transforms, and nonlinearities.

The construction here reproduces one forward layer with supplied weights. Training would require a loss on labelled nodes and an explicit split protocol; the forward calculation alone has not learned a classifier.

quiz.prompt: What are the resulting degrees?
quiz.because: Each node gains a self-loop.

given.data: A=[[0,1],[1,0]]. Add identity before calculating degrees.

quiz.prompt: Every resulting row must sum to one.
quiz.because: This is not generally a row-stochastic matrix.

given.data: Symmetric degree normalisation is applied to an irregular graph.

quiz.prompt: Which expression gives one linear propagation?
options: W @ S @ X in every shape
quiz.because: The multiplication order respects dimensions.

given.data: S mixes nodes, X stores node features, W mixes features.

quiz.prompt: That alone does not demonstrate training.
quiz.because: Learning requires a loss and parameter updates.

given.data: Only a forward pass with supplied W is performed.

build.title: Pass measurements through one graph layer
build.problem: Botie has an undirected adjacency matrix, node features, and supplied feature weights.
build.challenge: Add identity, calculate symmetric degree scaling, mix features, apply weights, then ReLU.
build.why: Graph mixing and learned feature mixing operate on different axes.
build.limitation: This is one forward layer with supplied weights. Symmetric scaling assumes a non-negative undirected graph.

intuition.title: Include self explicitly
intuition.explanation: The two connected nodes now each have two incoming contributions.

intuition.title: Scale both ends of each connection
intuition.explanation: Equal degrees here give one-half weight per contribution.

intuition.title: Transform the mixed feature
intuition.explanation: Both nodes receive the average before the shared weight and ReLU.

parts.title: 1. Add Self-Loops as a Modelling Choice
paragraphs: Start with an undirected non-negative adjacency matrix and add an identity matrix. This lets each node send its own feature into the aggregation. Compute degrees after adding those self-loops.
If the original matrix already contains self-weights, decide whether adding another identity is intended. Our inputs have zero diagonals.
interpretation: Self-loops are part of the propagation rule, not an accidental data duplication.

parts.title: 2. Normalise at Both Ends
paragraphs: A connection joins nodes that may have very different numbers of neighbours. Symmetric normalization scales its weight using both endpoint degrees, dividing by the square root of their product. Dividing only by the receiving node's degree would give a different operation.

On an irregular graph, the symmetrically normalized rows may not sum to one. We are using this matrix to propagate features, so we should not automatically interpret its entries as transition probabilities.
parts.calculation:
A_tilde = A + I
S[i,j] = A_tilde[i,j] / sqrt(degree[i] × degree[j])
interpretation: Adding self-loops ensures positive degree for every node in this non-negative graph.

parts.title: 3. Mix, Transform, and Activate
paragraphs: Let X contain node features and W contain shared learned feature weights. Multiply S by X to gather graph context, then multiply by W to transform feature channels. Apply an elementwise activation such as ReLU.
The graph dimension and feature dimension are different axes. W mixes features, while S mixes nodes. Both operations must respect their shapes.
parts.calculation: H = ReLU(S @ X @ W)
interpretation: One layer reaches immediate neighbours; stacking layers extends the receptive neighbourhood.

examples.title: Separate neighbourhood mixing from the learned feature change
paragraphs: With two connected nodes and self-loops, each node receives equal contributions from both. A supplied negative feature weight then changes the mixed value before ReLU.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
mixing = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]])
features = np.array([[1.], [5.]])
weight = np.array([[-1.]])
mixed = mixing @ features
weighted = mixed @ weight
print(mixed.tolist())
print(weighted.tolist())
print(np.maximum(weighted, 0).tolist())
interpretation: The graph first shares information, the weight changes its feature contribution, and the activation clips negative outputs. Practice constructs the normalised mixing matrix as well.

parts.title: 4. Keep Evaluation Boundaries Honest
paragraphs: A transductive protocol may expose the full graph and unlabelled test-node features during training while withholding their labels. An inductive protocol evaluates on unseen nodes or graphs. State which task you are testing.
Prevent held-out labels or future edges from entering feature construction. More layers do not automatically help: excessive mixing can make node representations too similar.
interpretation: The workshop uses a valid undirected graph and supplied weights to inspect one forward pass.

parts.title: 5. One Layer Reaches One Neighbourhood
paragraphs: One message-passing layer lets a node use its immediate neighbours. A second layer can bring information from neighbours of those neighbours because their first-layer representations already contain context.

The receptive field therefore grows with depth, but the number of distinguishable signals does not necessarily grow with it. Repeated mixing can wash out differences, and a narrow representation may compress many distant messages into very few coordinates.

parts.title: 6. Separate Graph Mixing from Feature Learning
paragraphs: The normalised adjacency determines which nodes exchange information and how it is scaled. The weight matrix determines how feature coordinates are combined. These are different axes of the calculation.
Check the graph operator on an unequal-degree example before adding learned features. Self-loops and degree normalisation should use the same augmented adjacency.

examples.title: Normalise a three-node chain
paragraphs: The graph is undirected. We add one self-loop to every node before computing degrees.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0.,1.,0.],[1.,0.,1.],[0.,1.,0.]])
augmented = A + np.eye(3)
degree = augmented.sum(axis=1)
S = augmented/np.sqrt(degree[:,None]*degree[None,:])
print(np.round(S, 4).tolist())
print(bool(np.allclose(S, S.T)))
interpretation: Symmetric normalisation remains symmetric, but its rows are not required to sum to one. It is not the same operator as a random-walk transition matrix.

parts.title: 7. A Whole-Network Prediction Needs a Readout
paragraphs: Node embeddings give one representation per node. To predict a property of an entire pipe network, combine them into a graph representation. A sum retains a dependence on graph size; a mean removes that direct count effect.

Choose the readout to match the target. Total capacity and average condition need different information. Keep separate graphs separate during batching so nodes from one installation do not exchange messages with another.

parts.title: 8. Define What the Test Nodes Are Allowed to Reveal
paragraphs: In a transductive task, the graph and unlabelled test-node features may be available during fitting while their labels are held out. In an inductive task, the method must handle previously unseen nodes or graphs under a stated information boundary.

Neither protocol is automatically dishonest, but they answer different questions. Do not report a transductive result as evidence of transfer to an unseen installation. For link prediction, remove held-out edges before building the message-passing graph.

practice.title: Can you build one graph-convolution layer?
practice.question: Can you build one graph-convolution layer?
task: Add self-loops, symmetrically normalise, apply the shared weight and ReLU. Print the output matrix.

X = np.array([[2.],[4.]])

Every row must sum to one

questions.because: Symmetric degree normalisation differs from row-stochastic random-walk normalisation. Both endpoint degrees use the augmented graph.

title: Scoring Connections We Have Not Observed
blurb: Node representations can score possible links, but missing links are not guaranteed negatives. Design the split and candidate set before evaluating.
openingTitle: Which Connection Might Be Missing From the Map?
opening: Botie’s network map is incomplete. Some connections were recorded, while others have not yet been inspected. He wants a useful order in which to check possible missing links.

We can score a possible connection using the representations of its two endpoints. But how were those representations obtained? If they already used the connection we supposedly held out, the test would reveal its own answer. We will calculate a simple pair score and follow which edges are available at each stage.

history.title: Learning Representations That Support Pairwise Questions

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Variational Graph Auto-Encoders (2016)

blocks: Variational graph auto-encoders combined graph-based representations with a decoder for reconstructing links. An inner-product decoder provides a simple way to turn two node representations into a link score.

Our exercise uses supplied vectors and the same basic dot-product decoder. It does not implement variational training, and its output should not be assumed calibrated merely because a sigmoid lies between zero and one.

quiz.prompt: What is their inner-product logit?
quiz.because: Only matching coordinates interact.

given.data: Node vectors [1,0] and [2,1].

quiz.prompt: Its structure can leak into the representation.
quiz.because: Messages can pass along the target edge.

given.data: A held-out edge remains in the graph encoder’s adjacency.

quiz.prompt: Can it distinguish u-to-v from v-to-u by that operation alone?
quiz.because: The dot product is symmetric.

given.data: A decoder uses dot(u,v).

quiz.prompt: It is guaranteed to be a genuine negative.
quiz.because: It may be an unobserved positive.

given.data: A pair was never recorded as connected.

build.title: Score a possible connection
build.problem: Botie has supplied representations for two candidate nodes.
build.challenge: Take their dot product and pass the logit through sigmoid.
build.why: The decoder turns pair compatibility into a bounded score.
build.limitation: Supplied embeddings must be learned without held-out target edges. The score is not automatically calibrated.

intuition.title: Choose a candidate pair
intuition.explanation: Both embeddings use the same learned coordinates.

intuition.title: Calculate compatibility
intuition.explanation: The inner product is a symmetric pair score.

intuition.title: Map to a bounded output
intuition.explanation: A sigmoid gives a score between zero and one.

parts.title: 1. Define What Counts as a Candidate
paragraphs: An undirected graph usually needs each pair only once and may exclude self-links. A directed graph needs an orientation. A symmetric dot product cannot distinguish one direction from the reverse.
Observed non-links can be confirmed absences or simply missing records. Sampling unobserved pairs as negatives creates a training convention, not certainty that every sampled pair is impossible.
interpretation: Record candidate and negative-sampling rules alongside the model.

parts.title: 2. Decode a Pair of Representations
paragraphs: Take the dot product of the two node vectors to obtain a logit. A sigmoid maps that value to a bounded score. In supervised binary training, a suitable loss compares these outputs with link labels.
interpretation: Ranking can use logits directly because sigmoid preserves their order.

parts.title: 3. Remove Held-Out Edges Before Encoding
paragraphs: If a graph encoder passes messages along a supposedly hidden test edge, it has already seen structural information about the answer. Build the training graph without held-out target edges, including reverse copies in an undirected representation.
Time-based link prediction must also exclude edges that appear only later. State whether node features and node identities were available when the prediction would have been made.
interpretation: Hiding an edge label is insufficient if the edge still remains in adjacency.

examples.title: What score does a zero dot product produce?
paragraphs: The two supplied node vectors are perpendicular. Calculate their compatibility score before applying the sigmoid decoder.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
first = np.array([1., 0.])
second = np.array([0., 2.])
logit = first @ second
print(float(logit))
print(float(1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))))
interpretation: A zero logit maps to one half. That is a property of this decoder, not evidence that half of all unobserved links really exist.

parts.title: 4. Evaluate What an Inspection Would Find
paragraphs: Rank eligible candidate pairs, inspect precision at an operational cutoff, and compare with simple common-neighbour or degree-based baselines. Report performance for new or isolated nodes separately.
High scores may reflect popularity or recording habits. They do not prove a physical connection exists, and a symmetric decoder is inadequate when direction is essential.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop scores a pair; the coding exercises also compare candidate rankings.

parts.title: 5. Remove Both Directions of a Held-Out Undirected Edge
paragraphs: An undirected connection is often stored twice, once in each direction. Holding out only one stored direction leaves the same connection visible to the encoder through the other entry.

Split unique physical edges first, then construct the training adjacency. Recompute graph-derived features from that training graph too. Removing an edge from the target list alone does not prevent degree counts, paths or embeddings from revealing it.

parts.title: 6. A Dot Product Cannot Distinguish Two Directions
paragraphs: A dot-product decoder gives the same score to a pair in either order. That can suit an undirected connection task. It cannot express that flow from A to B is likely while flow from B to A is unlikely.
A directed relation needs an order-sensitive decoder or separate source and destination representations. Choose that representation from the relation, not from whichever scoring formula is shortest.

examples.title: Check the symmetry of a pair score
paragraphs: The embeddings are supplied to isolate the decoder.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.,2.])
b = np.array([3.,1.])
print(float(a@b), float(b@a))
W = np.array([[0.,1.],[0.,0.]])
print(float(a@W@b), float(b@W@a))
interpretation: The bilinear example can distinguish order because its matrix is asymmetric. Whether that flexibility is useful requires training and evaluation.

parts.title: 7. An Unrecorded Pipe May Still Exist
paragraphs: A missing edge is not necessarily a verified absence. Negative sampling chooses unrecorded candidate pairs for a training or evaluation task, and some may be genuine undiscovered connections.

State candidate restrictions, time boundaries and how negatives were obtained. Easy random pairs can inflate scores compared with plausible inspection candidates. Evaluate the ranking against the inspection process the model is intended to support.

title: Separating a Useful Prediction From a Causal Claim
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Plants receiving extra water may grow poorly because they were already struggling. Compare the question a prediction answers with the question an intervention asks.
openingTitle: Did Extra Water Hurt the Plants?
opening: Botie notices that plants given extra water grew less. It would be easy to conclude that watering caused the poor growth. But the gardener may have watered the struggling plants more often.
The treatment groups began differently. We need to understand that selection before asking what would happen if we changed the watering rule.

history.title: Making the Intervention Question Explicit
blocks: Causal modelling distinguishes observing a choice from intervening to set it. Pearl’s graphical framework makes assumptions about common causes and pathways explicit, allowing us to ask when observational comparisons identify an intervention effect.
Our plant example is invented. Its purpose is to expose why a common cause of treatment and outcome can distort a comparison, not to establish an agricultural recommendation.

quiz.prompt: What causal role can dryness have?
options: A common cause of treatment and outcome
quiz.because: It influences selection and outcome.

given.data: Soil dryness affects both extra watering and later growth.

quiz.prompt: Changing that variable must improve growth.
quiz.because: Predictive association is not an intervention effect.

given.data: A variable predicts growth accurately.

quiz.prompt: What is the pooled treatment mean?
quiz.because: Use the treatment group’s proportions.

given.data: Treatment stratum means [4,9], weights [0.9,0.1].

quiz.prompt: We still need causal assumptions before interpreting the stratum comparison as an effect.
quiz.because: The reversal exposes composition, not identification by itself.

given.data: A pooled comparison reverses within strata.

build.title: Compare the observed group mixtures
build.problem: Botie has means within dry and moist beds and each group’s own proportions.
build.challenge: Calculate each weighted group mean, then subtract control from treatment.
build.why: The calculation makes each group’s composition visible.
build.limitation: This is an observed difference. A causal interpretation requires additional design and assumptions.

intuition.title: Notice unequal starting conditions
intuition.explanation: Extra water is given more often to dry plants.

intuition.title: Compare within starting conditions
intuition.explanation: The hypothetical treatment mean exceeds control in each stratum.

intuition.title: Inspect the mixture
intuition.explanation: Different group proportions can reverse the pooled comparison.

parts.title: 1. State the Two Different Questions
paragraphs: A prediction asks what outcome is likely among records with certain measurements. A causal question asks how the outcome would change under a specified intervention. A variable can help predict an outcome without being a useful lever to change it.
Define treatment, outcome, population, and observation window. Extra water needs a quantity and schedule before it becomes a well-defined intervention.
interpretation: The example studies a comparison procedure, not a claim that more water always helps.

parts.title: 2. Identify a Common Cause
paragraphs: Starting soil condition could influence both the gardener's watering choice and the plant's growth. That makes it a possible confounder: the groups may differ for a reason that existed before treatment.

A correlation alone does not establish that role. We need knowledge of how the measurements and decisions arose, including their timing. A feature that predicts growth well is not automatically something we should adjust for.
interpretation: Measuring a variable after treatment can give it a very different role.

parts.title: 3. Inspect Group Composition
paragraphs: Calculate pooled means by weighting stratum means with each group’s own stratum proportions. Then compare the same stratum across groups. A reversal shows that the pooled association depends strongly on composition.
parts.calculation:
Treatment mean = 0.9 × 4 + 0.1 × 9 = 4.5
Control mean = 0.1 × 3 + 0.9 × 8 = 7.5
Pooled difference = -3
Within-stratum differences = [1,1]
interpretation: A reversal does not itself prove the adjusted comparison is causal. The relevant assumptions still need support.

examples.title: A benefit within each group can reverse after pooling
paragraphs: The treatment outcome is higher within both starting conditions. However, the treatment group contains mostly the harder condition and the control group mostly the easier one.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
treatment = np.array([2., 8.])
control = np.array([0., 6.])
treatment_mix = np.array([0.8, 0.2])
control_mix = np.array([0.2, 0.8])
print((treatment - control).tolist())
print(f'{treatment @ treatment_mix:.1f}')
print(f'{control @ control_mix:.1f}')
interpretation: The pooled treatment average is lower despite both within-condition differences being positive. Group composition changes the comparison we are making.

parts.title: 4. Choose Evidence That Matches the Claim
paragraphs: Random assignment can remove systematic treatment selection under a valid experiment. Observational adjustment can be justified when measured variables suffice to block confounding and other identification conditions hold.
More predictive features do not automatically produce a better causal estimate. Conditioning on an effect of treatment or on a collider can create a different bias.
interpretation: The next lessons establish experimental comparisons and then a carefully stated observational adjustment.

parts.title: 5. Compare Like Starting Conditions before Combining Them
paragraphs: If the new watering schedule is used more often on dry beds, its overall growth average mixes treatment differences with differences in starting soil. Compare schedules within the same pre-treatment soil group first.
Then combine those comparisons using one shared target population. Giving each treatment its own soil mixture recreates the original imbalance rather than removing it.

examples.title: Separate group effects from group composition
paragraphs: Both soil groups gain two units under the new schedule, but treated beds are mostly in the harder dry group.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
old = np.array([2.,8.])
new = np.array([4.,10.])
old_mix = np.array([.2,.8])
new_mix = np.array([.8,.2])
target_mix = np.array([.5,.5])
print(round(float(new_mix@new-old_mix@old), 2))
print(round(float(target_mix@(new-old)), 2))
interpretation: The unadjusted difference reverses the within-group comparison in this invented table. The adjusted arithmetic has a causal interpretation only under the required assumptions.

parts.title: 6. Do Not Control for a Variable Merely because It Predicts the Outcome
paragraphs: A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome. A mediator lies on a pathway through which treatment affects outcome. Adjusting for a mediator changes the effect being estimated and can introduce other problems.

A collider is affected by two variables. Conditioning on it can create an association that was absent before. Draw the assumed directions from the problem before selecting adjustment columns. Predictive usefulness alone does not identify an appropriate adjustment set.

parts.title: 7. An Adjustment Cannot Repair an Unmeasured Common Cause
paragraphs: Soil condition may be recorded too crudely, or the gardener may use unrecorded plant health when assigning extra water. Comparing recorded soil groups does not guarantee comparable treatment groups within them.

State what would need to be measured and what remains uncertain. Use domain knowledge, study design and sensitivity analysis to examine those assumptions. A clean numerical difference is not proof that every relevant cause was controlled.

reading.experimentIntro: Inspect the outcome within each starting condition, then change the proportions of dry and moist beds in the two groups. The pooled comparison can move without any within-condition result changing.
reading.connectionTitle: Group composition can change the conclusion of a pooled comparison
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Expose a Reversal and Compare a Shared Population

title: Making a Fair Comparison by Assignment
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Random assignment separates a treatment decision from the reasons a gardener might otherwise choose it. Estimate an average effect while keeping the experiment’s unit and uncertainty clear.
openingTitle: Can Botie Choose the Watering Schedule Before Seeing Which Beds Struggle?
opening: The previous records mixed treatment with the gardener’s judgement. This time Botie can assign a schedule by a random procedure before observing outcomes.

That procedure makes the groups comparable in expectation. It does not guarantee identical groups in one small experiment, so we still need to calculate an estimate and describe its sampling uncertainty.

history.title: Defining Effects Through Alternative Outcomes

sources.title: Rubin: Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies (1974)

blocks: Rubin’s 1974 paper described treatment effects using the outcomes a unit would have under different treatments, and considered both randomised and nonrandomised studies. Randomisation supplies a known assignment mechanism for comparing groups.
We observe only the outcome under the assignment actually received. The example therefore estimates an average difference; it cannot reveal both possible outcomes for an individual bed.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference in means?
quiz.because: Subtract the control mean from the treatment mean.

given.data: Treatment outcomes [6,8,7], control [4,5,6].

quiz.prompt: Every realised small group must be perfectly balanced on all variables.
quiz.because: Balance holds in expectation, not exactly in every sample.

given.data: Assignment was random.

quiz.prompt: Which unit matters for independent assignment?
quiz.because: The randomisation unit defines the assignment structure.

given.data: Treatment was assigned by greenhouse.

quiz.prompt: No-interference assumptions need reconsideration.
quiz.because: Outcomes can depend on other units’ treatments.

given.data: One treated bed affects a control bed through shared water.

build.title: Compare randomly assigned groups
build.problem: Botie recorded outcomes after assigning schedules under the stated independent-unit design.
build.challenge: Average each group and subtract control from treatment.
build.why: Random assignment supports a comparison whose grouping was not chosen from predicted outcomes.
build.limitation: This estimates an average assignment effect under the design assumptions, with finite-sample uncertainty.

intuition.title: Assign at a defined unit
intuition.explanation: Each bed receives one schedule.

intuition.title: Compare group averages
intuition.explanation: Both groups use the same outcome and follow-up window.

intuition.title: Retain uncertainty
intuition.explanation: The difference is an estimate from a finite experiment.

parts.title: 1. Define the Unit and Assignment
paragraphs: What receives the random assignment: a plant, a bed, or a greenhouse? Choose a unit that fits how the watering is actually applied. If water runs from one bed into another, treating one bed can affect the other's outcome, so the no-interference assumption may fail.

Record the assignment probabilities and measure outcomes consistently. If whole greenhouses received the assignments, treating every plant as an independent experiment would overstate how much independent evidence we have.
interpretation: The examples assume independent units and no spillovers.

parts.title: 2. Compare Outcomes by Assignment
paragraphs: For an intention-to-treat comparison, group units by assigned treatment, even if some do not fully follow the schedule. Changing groups after seeing adherence can undo the benefit of randomisation.
Take the treatment mean minus the control mean. Under the experiment’s assumptions, random assignment supports interpreting this as an estimate of the average assignment effect.
parts.calculation:
Treatment outcomes = [6,8,7]; mean = 7
Control outcomes = [4,5,6]; mean = 5
Estimated difference = 2
interpretation: This is a group average, not the effect on every individual bed.

parts.title: 3. Measure Sampling Variation
paragraphs: Different random assignments can give different estimates. For independent groups, a common standard-error estimate combines each sample variance divided by its sample size, then takes a square root.

Use sample variance with the stated degrees-of-freedom correction. Small samples and unusual designs may need randomisation-based or other design-appropriate inference rather than a casual normal approximation.
parts.calculation: Estimated SE = sqrt(s_treated²/n_treated + s_control²/n_control)
interpretation: The exercise calculates the standard error but does not claim a precise interval from three units per group.

examples.title: Calculate the outcome difference before its uncertainty
paragraphs: These are outcomes from an illustrative random assignment of independent units. Inspect each assigned group's mean before forming the difference.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
assigned_treatment = np.array([5., 7.])
assigned_control = np.array([4., 4.])
means = np.array([assigned_treatment.mean(), assigned_control.mean()])
print(means.tolist())
print(float(means[0] - means[1]))
interpretation: The observed contrast is two outcome units. Its causal interpretation depends on the assignment design; its sampling uncertainty requires more than quoting this difference.

parts.title: 4. Protect the Experiment’s Meaning
paragraphs: Specify the outcome and analysis before inspecting results. Repeatedly testing many outcomes or stopping at the first favourable result changes error rates unless accounted for.

Missing outcomes, nonadherence, spillovers, and changes in measurement can undermine interpretation. Report them alongside the estimated effect instead of letting randomisation stand in for every design check.
interpretation: The workshop compares group means; the second coding task adds uncertainty.

parts.title: 5. Randomise the Unit That Can Receive Its Own Treatment
paragraphs: If neighbouring beds share irrigation, assigning each plant independently may not create independent treatments. Water delivered to one can affect another. Randomise beds or larger groups when that matches how treatment is delivered, and analyse uncertainty at the appropriate unit.

Random assignment balances starting conditions in expectation, not perfectly in every small run. Record the assignment procedure before outcomes arrive and inspect whether the intended procedure was followed.

parts.title: 6. Keep Assignment Separate from Compliance
paragraphs: A bed assigned extra watering may miss a scheduled visit. Comparing beds by what they actually received can reintroduce selection: the missed visits may happen on particular kinds of beds.

An intention-to-treat comparison groups outcomes by original assignment. It estimates the effect of the assignment policy under the experiment's conditions, including its compliance behaviour. It is not automatically the effect of receiving the treatment exactly as intended.

examples.title: Compare the assigned groups
paragraphs: Assignment is random in the imagined study; the arrays below are its supplied observed record.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
assigned = np.array([0,0,1,1])
received = np.array([0,0,1,0])
growth = np.array([4.,6.,9.,5.])
itt = growth[assigned == 1].mean()-growth[assigned == 0].mean()
received_difference = growth[received == 1].mean()-growth[received == 0].mean()
print(float(itt))
print(float(received_difference))
interpretation: The two comparisons use different groups. The received-treatment comparison no longer inherits randomisation simply because the study began randomly.

parts.title: 7. A Difference Needs an Uncertainty Assessment
paragraphs: Four beds are enough to demonstrate the calculation, not enough to establish a stable agronomic effect. Variation among units makes the estimated difference change across possible assignments and samples.

Choose a sample-size plan, outcome definition and analysis before inspecting results. A randomisation test can compare the observed statistic with assignments allowed by the actual design. Its permutations must respect blocks or clusters when those were part of assignment.

parts.title: 8. Repeated Peeking Changes the Experiment
paragraphs: Stopping the first time an ordinary significance threshold is crossed does not have the same error properties as one preplanned analysis. Nor does trying many outcomes and reporting only the most favourable one.

Use a fixed analysis plan or a suitable sequential design. Report effect size and uncertainty alongside the practical cost of the intervention. A small p-value alone does not establish that the effect is large enough to matter.

import numpy as np

practice.title: Can you estimate the standard error?
practice.question: Can you estimate the standard error?
task: Assume independent units. Use sample variances with ddof=1 and print the standard error to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
treated = np.array([4.,6.,8.,10.])
control = np.array([3.,5.,7.,9.])

title: Comparing Treatments in the Same Population
blurb: When starting conditions affect treatment choice, standardisation can compare both treatments using one target population, if the measured conditions suffice to control confounding.
openingTitle: Can We Make the Dry and Moist Beds Count Equally in Both Groups?
opening: Botie cannot rerun an old season as a randomised experiment. He does have starting soil measurements and outcomes under both schedules in each soil group.

We can calculate an outcome mean for each schedule within each group, then average both using the same target-population proportions. Whether that adjusted number is causal depends on what the measurements and causal assumptions leave out.

history.title: Choosing Variables by Their Causal Role
blocks: Causal diagrams provide a way to reason about which observed variables should be adjusted for. The back-door criterion addresses common-cause paths that can create association between treatment and outcome without representing the treatment’s effect.

The important step is deciding whether an adjustment set is justified. A numerical standardisation can always be computed from a complete table; a causal interpretation cannot be obtained from arithmetic alone.

quiz.prompt: What is the standardised difference?
quiz.because: Weight each stratum’s difference using the shared target.

given.data: Treatment means [4,9], control [3,8], target weights [0.6,0.4].

quiz.prompt: Adjusting for it can remove part of the total effect.
quiz.because: The adjustment changes the estimand.

given.data: A variable occurs after treatment and mediates its effect.

quiz.prompt: What is the issue?
quiz.because: That comparison lacks observed support.

given.data: No control observations exist in one target stratum.

quiz.prompt: That proves it adjusted for all confounding.
quiz.because: Prediction accuracy does not establish causal identification.

given.data: An outcome regression predicts accurately.

build.title: Standardise the schedule comparison
build.problem: Botie has both outcome means for each starting condition and one target population.
build.challenge: Subtract control stratum means from treatment stratum means, then take their weighted average using target proportions.
build.why: Both interventions are compared in the same target mixture.
build.limitation: Causal interpretation requires a sufficient adjustment set, consistency, overlap, and the other stated design assumptions.

intuition.title: Compare within starting soil groups
intuition.explanation: Both schedules have observations in each group.

intuition.title: Choose the target population
intuition.explanation: Use the same group proportions for both schedules.

intuition.title: Standardise both outcomes
intuition.explanation: Their difference now refers to the shared target mixture.

parts.title: 1. Specify the Causal Assumptions
paragraphs: Assume measured starting soil condition blocks the relevant common causes of schedule and outcome. Also require well-defined treatments, consistency between observed and specified treatment, no relevant interference, and positive chances of both treatments in the target strata.
These conditions are not established merely because a model fits outcomes well. Unmeasured plant health could still confound the comparison.
interpretation: The example states identification assumptions so readers can see exactly what the arithmetic depends on.

parts.title: 2. Select a Target Population
paragraphs: Suppose we want the effect for a particular mix of dry and moist beds. The target weights record the proportions of those starting conditions. They must be nonnegative and sum to one.

Use that same mix to average the outcomes under both schedules. If we instead use the treated group's proportions for one average and the control group's for the other, differences in starting conditions enter the comparison again.
parts.calculation:
Target weights = [0.6,0.4]
Standardised treatment = 0.6 × 4 + 0.4 × 9 = 6
Standardised control = 0.6 × 3 + 0.4 × 8 = 5
Difference = 1
interpretation: Changing the target population can change an average effect when stratum effects differ.

parts.title: 3. Do Not Adjust for Every Available Column
paragraphs: A mediator is affected by treatment and lies on a pathway to the outcome. Adjusting for it can remove part of the total effect. A collider is a common effect; conditioning on it can open an otherwise blocked association path.
Use the causal story and measurement timing to decide roles. A feature-selection algorithm designed for prediction cannot decide this from predictive usefulness alone.
interpretation: Our adjustment uses a pretreatment common cause, not a later moisture measurement caused by the schedule.

examples.title: Apply one target population to the condition-specific effects
paragraphs: The schedule's difference is not the same in the two starting conditions. Give both schedules the same target mixture so the final comparison answers one population's question.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
treatment = np.array([3., 8.])
control = np.array([1., 7.])
target_mix = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
effects = treatment - control
print(effects.tolist())
print(float(target_mix @ effects))
interpretation: The adjusted contrast lies between the two condition-specific differences. Changing the target mix changes whose average effect is being described, under the lesson's identification assumptions.

parts.title: 4. Inspect Empty and Sparse Strata
paragraphs: If one schedule never occurs in a soil group, its outcome mean there cannot be estimated directly from those observations. A regression may still return a value, but it is extrapolating.
Report overlap, sample counts, model dependence, and sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. More elaborate fitting does not create missing treatment comparisons.
interpretation: The workshop assumes all supplied stratum means are estimable; the limitations remain part of the result.

parts.title: 5. Both Treatments Must Describe the Same Target Population
paragraphs: Within each pre-treatment group, estimate the outcome mean under each treatment. Then average both sets of means using the same group weights. Subtracting those standardised outcomes answers what the difference would be for that target mixture under the identification assumptions.

The target could be the study population or another specified population. Changing the weights changes the estimand. Keep their source explicit rather than letting whichever group has more records decide the question.

parts.title: 6. Carry Group Means into Two Target Populations
paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ between soil groups. In that case, two target populations can have different average effects even when every group-specific estimate is unchanged.
This is a reason to report the group estimates and support, not only one overall adjusted number.

examples.title: Change the target mixture deliberately
paragraphs: The supplied group means concern dry and moist beds.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
untreated = np.array([2.,7.])
treated = np.array([6.,8.])
effect = treated-untreated
for weights in [np.array([.5,.5]), np.array([.8,.2])]:
    print(round(float(weights@effect), 3))
interpretation: The target with more dry beds has a larger average effect because that group benefits more in this supplied table.

parts.title: 7. An Empty Treatment Cell Requires Extrapolation
paragraphs: If every dry bed received treatment, we have no untreated dry-bed mean to compare. An outcome model can produce a numerical prediction there, but it extrapolates beyond observed treatment overlap.

Inspect the counts behind every estimated group mean. Combining sparse groups or restricting the target population changes assumptions or the question. State the change. More flexible modelling does not create observations of a treatment that was never used in that group.

practice.title: Can you standardise both schedules?
practice.question: Can you standardise both schedules?
task: Print standardised treatment mean, control mean and difference with one decimal.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

mc = np.array([3.,8.])
target = np.array([.6,.4])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

mc = np.array([3.,8.])

print(f'{target @ mt:.1f}')
print(f'{target @ mc:.1f}')
print(f'{target @ (mt-mc):.1f}')

Causal meaning still depends on the stated assumptions.

practice.title: Can a different target change the average effect?

Heterogeneous effects make composition relevant.

title: Reweighting Records Without Inventing Missing Evidence
blurb: Inverse-probability weighting changes which records count most. Understand the treatment probabilities and overlap assumptions before interpreting the resulting contrast.
openingTitle: How Can Rarely Treated Beds Represent Similar Untreated Ones?
opening: Some types of bed rarely received the new schedule. If one of those beds did receive it, its outcome carries information about a group underrepresented among treated records.

Inverse-probability weighting gives more weight to such records. That idea is useful only when treatment probabilities are credible and both schedules remain possible for the population being studied.

history.title: Making Observed Groups Represent a Shared Population

sources.title: Hernán and Robins: Causal Inference: What If
Rubin: Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies (1974)

blocks: The potential-outcomes framework defines an average effect as a comparison of outcomes under two interventions. Hernán and Robins develop identification and estimation methods, including weighting, while making exchangeability, positivity, and consistency assumptions explicit.
Our supplied propensity scores are part of a teaching model. Estimating them from observations adds uncertainty and model dependence; weighting does not automatically remove unmeasured confounding.

quiz.prompt: What is its inverse-probability weight?
quiz.because: Invert its observed treatment probability.

given.data: A treated record has propensity 0.25.

quiz.prompt: Observed data contain control outcomes for that group under the model.
quiz.because: There is no control overlap.

given.data: A group’s propensity is exactly one.

quiz.prompt: What is its denominator?
quiz.because: This is the stated unnormalised estimator.

given.data: The supplied method averages weighted contributions over all units.

quiz.prompt: Weighting may leave confounding.
quiz.because: The assignment model does not recover unmeasured information.

given.data: A propensity model omits a common cause of treatment and outcome.

build.title: Calculate an inverse-probability contrast
build.problem: Botie has outcomes, binary treatment assignments, and valid supplied propensities.
build.challenge: Weight treatment and control outcomes by their respective probabilities, subtract contributions, then average over all units.

sources.e: Propensities strictly between zero and one

build.why: Weighting changes how observed outcomes represent the target population under the identification assumptions.
build.limitation: This uses the unnormalised all-unit mean. Positivity and no unmeasured confounding cannot be established by the arithmetic.

intuition.title: Record assignment probabilities
intuition.explanation: A propensity is the probability of treatment given pretreatment covariates.

intuition.title: Weight the observed branch
intuition.explanation: Treatment uses its own probability; control uses the complement.

intuition.title: Inspect extreme values
intuition.explanation: Very small observed-branch probabilities create large weights.

parts.title: 1. Name the Missing Outcomes
paragraphs: For each bed, imagine its outcome under the new schedule and its outcome under the control schedule. We observe only the one corresponding to what it received. The average treatment effect concerns the average difference between those potential outcomes, even though we usually cannot measure an individual bed's difference directly.

The propensity e(X) describes the probability of receiving treatment given pretreatment measurements. It says how the schedule was assigned. It is not a predicted growth outcome or a confidence score for that prediction.
interpretation: A propensity model predicts assignment, while an outcome model predicts the response.

parts.title: 2. Calculate Weights for the Observed Branch
paragraphs: A treated unit receives inverse propensity. A control unit receives inverse one minus propensity. Under the identification assumptions, these weights can make the groups represent a shared covariate distribution.

The unnormalised Horvitz-Thompson-style difference averages weighted outcome contributions over all n units. A normalised group-weight estimator is a related but different finite-sample calculation. State which one is used.
parts.calculation:
Contribution_i = T_i × Y_i / e_i - (1-T_i) × Y_i / (1-e_i)
ATE estimate = mean(Contribution_i)
interpretation: The exercises use the unnormalised all-unit mean, not separately normalised weighted group means.

parts.title: 3. Require Overlap Before Trusting the Estimate
paragraphs: If a relevant covariate group always receives one treatment, the other potential outcome has no observed support there. Propensities near zero or one can also produce highly variable estimates from a few large weights.
Inspect weight distributions and covariate balance. Trimming or clipping weights changes the estimation procedure and can change the target or introduce bias. It is not a silent numerical repair.
interpretation: Exact zero or one propensities are rejected in the workshop.

examples.title: Inspect the weighted contributions before averaging
paragraphs: One treated record had a treatment propensity of one quarter. One control record had a treatment propensity of one half. Use the probability of the treatment each actually received.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
treatment = np.array([1., 0.])
outcome = np.array([4., 2.])
propensity = np.array([0.25, 0.5])
contributions = treatment * outcome / propensity - (1 - treatment) * outcome / (1 - propensity)
print(contributions.tolist())
print(float(contributions.mean()))
interpretation: The first record has much greater influence. This is why a final weighted contrast needs an overlap check as well as correct arithmetic.

parts.title: 4. Keep Causal and Statistical Uncertainty Separate
paragraphs: A precise numerical estimate can still be biased by an omitted common cause, ill-defined treatment, interference, or a misspecified propensity model. Sampling uncertainty does not account automatically for these identification failures.

Use domain knowledge, design checks, overlap diagnostics, and sensitivity analysis. If the assumptions cannot be defended, report an association or restricted comparison rather than presenting a causal answer as established.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop exposes weighting arithmetic without claiming that supplied propensities prove identification.

parts.title: 5. A Large Weight Is a Warning about Thin Evidence
paragraphs: If a kind of bed rarely receives the new schedule, a treated bed of that kind represents many similar beds under inverse-probability weighting. Its outcome can therefore dominate the estimate.

Inspect propensity ranges and weight concentration separately for treated and untreated records. A fitted probability near zero or one may reflect genuine lack of overlap, model misspecification or a small sample. None is fixed merely by printing more decimal places.

parts.title: 6. Measure How Concentrated the Weights Are
paragraphs: The effective sample size below describes how uneven weights reduce the information represented by a weighted average. It is a diagnostic, not a complete uncertainty calculation.
Compare it with the raw number of records. A large dataset whose result depends on a few enormous weights may still provide fragile evidence for the target population.

examples.title: Four records with one dominant weight
paragraphs: These are supplied nonnegative weights for one comparison group.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
weight = np.array([1.,1.,1.,9.])
effective = weight.sum()**2/(weight@weight)
print(len(weight))
print(round(float(effective), 3))
interpretation: Four records have the weight concentration of far fewer equally weighted records under this diagnostic.

parts.title: 7. Normalising Weights Changes the Finite-Sample Estimator
paragraphs: One estimator averages inverse-weighted outcomes over the full sample size. Another divides each group's weighted outcome sum by that group's weight sum, then takes the difference. The latter is often called a normalised or Hájek form.

These estimators can differ in finite samples even under the same propensity model. State which formula is used. Clipping large weights also changes the procedure and can trade variance for bias; it is not a neutral numerical repair.

parts.title: 8. Overlap Is Necessary but Not Sufficient
paragraphs: Even well-behaved weights do not establish that all treatment-outcome common causes were measured. Identification also depends on consistency and the stated exchangeability assumptions, with interference considered where relevant.

Report the target population, assignment model, balance checks and remaining causal assumptions. A predictive model of treatment assignment can help estimate propensities, but its classification accuracy is not the causal objective.

practice.title: Can you calculate the stated weighted contrast?
practice.question: Can you calculate the stated weighted contrast?
task: Use the all-unit mean formula. Print the estimate to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
T = np.array([1.,0.,1.,0.])
y = np.array([6.,4.,8.,5.])
e = np.array([.5,.5,.5,.5])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
T = np.array([1.,0.,1.,0.])
y = np.array([6.,4.,8.,5.])
e = np.array([.5,.5,.5,.5])
contribution = T*y/e-(1-T)*y/(1-e)
print(f'{contribution.mean():.3f}')
hints: T selects the observed treatment branch.
Average over all four records.

practice.title: Can you identify a dominant weight?
practice.question: Can you identify a dominant weight?
task: Calculate each observed-branch inverse probability. Print weights and the index of the largest.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
T = np.array([1,0,1,0])
e = np.array([.5,.8,.02,.3])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
T = np.array([1,0,1,0])
e = np.array([.5,.8,.02,.3])
observed_probability = np.where(T==1,e,1-e)
weights = 1/observed_probability
print(np.round(weights,3).tolist())
print(int(np.argmax(weights)))
hints: A control’s probability is one minus propensity.
A very large weight signals weak support.

reading.experimentIntro: A treatment received despite a very small propensity can receive a large weight. Change a valid propensity and inspect its influence before trusting the final contrast.
reading.connectionTitle: Weighting cannot replace evidence where overlap is missing
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Calculate a Weighted Contrast and Inspect Large Weights

title: Saving the Whole Prediction Procedure
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: Weights alone do not reproduce a prediction. Botie also needs feature order, fitted preparation, and the rules connecting them.
openingTitle: Why Did the Saved Model Give a Different Answer?
opening: Botie saves a model’s weights and loads them tomorrow. The code runs, but predictions change because the new process prepares inputs differently.

Suppose we save the model weights but forget the training mean used to centre its inputs. We can reload the weights and still get different predictions. We need to save the fitted preparation alongside the model, with a description of the expected features. Then we can check whether the loaded procedure reproduces known examples.

history.title: The Model Is One Part of the System

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Sculley and colleagues described dependencies and maintenance costs around machine-learning models, including the surrounding data and configuration. Those dependencies explain why copying only fitted coefficients is often insufficient.

Persistence documentation also distinguishes numerical model state from its execution environment. Our small JSON example makes the state explicit; it does not promise that arbitrary model objects can be safely or portably loaded.

quiz.prompt: What is the prepared row?
quiz.because: Subtract and divide coordinate by coordinate.

given.data: Saved mean [10,20], scale [2,5], new row [12,25].

quiz.prompt: Refitting its mean before prediction preserves training preparation.
quiz.because: It changes the transformation and can erase the input.

given.data: A request contains one record.

quiz.prompt: What must loaded records preserve?
quiz.because: Coordinates carry specific meanings.

given.data: Weights expect [temperature,humidity].

quiz.prompt: Loading it can execute code.
quiz.because: Deserialisation is not necessarily passive data reading.

given.data: A pickle artifact comes from an untrusted source.

build.title: Reproduce the saved predictor
build.problem: Botie has raw feature values and every fitted quantity used during training.
build.challenge: Subtract training means, divide by positive training scales, apply weights, and add bias.
build.why: The same retained transformation and model state produce the same numerical procedure.
build.limitation: Feature order and units must match the saved contract. This example is a linear predictor, not arbitrary model serialisation.

intuition.title: Retain training preparation
intuition.explanation: The feature order is temperature, then humidity.

intuition.title: Prepare one new record
intuition.explanation: Use saved values without refitting.

intuition.title: Apply saved model state
intuition.explanation: Weights and intercept complete the procedure.

intuition.title: Saved coefficients also need saved feature names
intuition.explanation: A model can accept the right number of values while receiving them in the wrong order. Save the feature order with the numerical state, then assemble every later row by those names.

scene.caption: Both arrays have two entries, but only one follows the saved order.

parts.title: 1. List Every Fitted Quantity
paragraphs: A standardising linear predictor needs feature names and order, training means, positive scales, weights, and intercept. A categorical pipeline may also need vocabulary, unknown-category rules, and imputation values.
Distinguish fitted values from configuration. Both matter for reproducibility, but fitted values must come only from the training partition.
interpretation: Keep units and preparation order with the state rather than relying on memory.

parts.title: 2. Apply Preparation Without Learning Again
paragraphs: On a new record, subtract the saved training mean and divide by the saved scale. Do not calculate a fresh mean from each request. That would make the prediction depend on what other records arrived in the batch.
parts.calculation:
x = [12,25]
Saved mean = [10,20]; scale = [2,5]
Prepared x = [1,1]
Prediction = dot([1,1], [3,-1]) + 2 = 4
interpretation: Inference transforms with retained state; fitting estimates that state.

parts.title: 3. Serialise a Small Inspectable Artifact
paragraphs: For this simple model, JSON can store lists, numbers, feature names, and a schema version. Convert lists back to arrays when loading and validate their shapes and finiteness.

For larger arrays, an array format can be more suitable. Do not load untrusted pickle-based objects: deserialisation can execute code. An artifact format and runtime compatibility policy are part of the system design.
interpretation: The example round-trips an in-memory JSON string so no filesystem or service setup is needed.

examples.title: A coefficient expects the scale it was trained on
paragraphs: This one-feature rule was fitted after centring and scaling. Compare its prediction with the result of mistakenly applying the coefficient straight to the raw reading.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
raw = 12.0
saved_mean, saved_scale = 10.0, 2.0
weight, bias = 3.0, 1.0
prepared = (raw - saved_mean) / saved_scale
print(prepared)
print(prepared * weight + bias)
print(raw * weight + bias)
interpretation: Saving the coefficient without its preprocessing would silently change the numerical procedure. Practice saves and restores the complete two-feature state.

parts.title: 4. Check Predictions Before and After Loading
paragraphs: Retain several representative input-output examples, including boundary cases. Compare the original and loaded procedures within a declared tolerance. Also check feature order, runtime versions, and any unsupported operations.
Exact agreement on fixtures does not prove identical behaviour for every input, but it catches common omitted-state and ordering failures before deployment.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop shows the full numerical pipeline from raw record to prediction.

parts.title: 5. Save What Was Learned and What Was Assumed
paragraphs: A linear predictor may need a feature order, units, imputation values, category vocabulary, scaling statistics, weights and an intercept. Some came from fitting; others came from the input contract. Both affect the answer.

Give the artifact a schema version. A loader should know which fields that version requires and reject unsupported versions explicitly. A model name alone does not specify how an incoming record becomes the array the weights expect.

parts.title: 6. Reload in a Fresh Object and Compare Predictions
paragraphs: Serialising a model is not finished when a file is written. Load the saved representation into a new object, reconstruct its numerical arrays and run fixtures that exercise more than one input.
Keep these fixtures separate from the training objective. They test that storage and loading preserve the procedure, not that the model generalises.

examples.title: Round-trip a centred linear predictor
paragraphs: The feature order is temperature then humidity, with a saved mean for each.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import json
artifact = {'schema': 1, 'features': ['temperature','humidity'], 'mean': [10.,50.], 'weight': [2.,.1], 'bias': 3.}
restored = json.loads(json.dumps(artifact))
X = np.array([[12.,60.],[10.,50.]])
def predict(model, X):
    return (X-np.array(model['mean']))@np.array(model['weight'])+model['bias']
print(predict(restored, X).tolist())
print(bool(np.allclose(predict(artifact,X), predict(restored,X))))
interpretation: The comparison includes the fitted centring step. Saving weights alone would not reproduce these predictions.

parts.title: 7. An Artifact Needs a Compatible Runtime
paragraphs: A saved representation may depend on library conventions, numerical precision or custom preprocessing code. Record the runtime and code version needed to interpret it. Test a fresh process rather than relying on imports and variables left in a notebook.

For the small model here, an inspectable JSON schema is sufficient. More complex models may require another format. Only load trusted executable serialisations; plain numerical formats reduce that need but still require schema and size checks.

title: Checking What Arrives at the Model
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: A model can produce a number from the wrong columns or units. Define and validate the request before trusting its arithmetic.
openingTitle: What If Temperature Arrives in the Humidity Column?
opening: Botie’s service receives two numbers, just as expected. Yet they are in the wrong order. A shape check passes while the model interprets humidity as temperature.
An input contract states names, order, types, units, allowed missingness, and shape. Validation turns malformed requests into clear errors before they produce misleading predictions.

history.title: Treating Data Expectations as Testable Rules
blocks: Production guidance draws attention to training-serving differences and data dependencies. Data-validation pipelines make expectations about incoming records explicit rather than waiting for a model failure to reveal a changed input.
The tiny contract here checks names, shape, and finite values. A real schema also needs units and domain-specific constraints that cannot be inferred from an array’s dtype.

quiz.prompt: Which array is correct?
quiz.because: Read names in saved order.

given.data: Saved feature order [temperature,humidity]; record contains named values humidity=25, temperature=12.

quiz.prompt: Its units and feature meanings must therefore be correct.
quiz.because: Shape does not encode semantics.

given.data: An array has the expected width.

quiz.prompt: What should this lesson’s strict contract do?
quiz.because: The declared missing-value policy is rejection.

given.data: A required temperature field is absent.

quiz.prompt: Finiteness needs a separate check.
quiz.because: Numeric dtype alone does not rule out non-finite values.

given.data: NaN can enter a float array successfully.

build.title: Validate an incoming numerical batch
build.problem: Botie must check record width and finiteness before using the model.
build.challenge: Send the table through the finite-width validator, then calculate its column means to confirm the same accepted values pass through.
build.why: Validation checks the data boundary before downstream operations run.
build.limitation: This numerical check cannot infer feature names or units. The request parser must enforce those separately.

intuition.title: Read named fields
intuition.explanation: Named values can arrive in any object order.

intuition.title: Apply the saved order
intuition.explanation: The model’s feature list determines coordinates.

intuition.title: Reject malformed data
intuition.explanation: A missing field is different from an explicit zero.

parts.title: 1. Write the Contract Before the Parser
paragraphs: Let's decide what the service accepts before converting a request to an array. Is it one record or a batch? Which fields must be present, and what happens to unfamiliar fields? The numeric type is not enough to describe a measurement: a float could be Celsius or Fahrenheit.

Categorical fields need a rule for unknown categories. A missing measurement needs either a clear rejection or the saved imputation procedure. Quietly inserting zero would give the model a value with a meaning the caller never supplied.
interpretation: The examples reject missing or extra fields and non-finite numbers.

parts.title: 2. Build Arrays From Names
paragraphs: Read each field in the saved feature order rather than trusting object insertion order. Convert to a declared numeric dtype, then check the resulting shape.
Reject booleans if the field is a measured quantity rather than a flag. Some languages treat booleans as numbers, so an apparently successful conversion can hide a malformed request.
interpretation: A correct array shape is necessary but not sufficient for a correct input.

parts.title: 3. Check Values Before Model Arithmetic
paragraphs: NaN and infinity can propagate through calculations and make later failures difficult to interpret. Reject them at the boundary. Bounds should reflect a justified domain rule, not arbitrary clipping that disguises a broken sensor.
Separate validation from scoring. A request that fails validation should not return a normal-looking prediction.
parts.calculation:
Required shape = (number_of_records, 2)
Feature order = [temperature_c, humidity_percent]
All values must be finite
interpretation: Units must be supplied correctly even when a wrong-unit value happens to fall within accepted numeric bounds.

examples.title: Use feature names to restore the expected order
paragraphs: The record arrived with keys in a different order from the model's saved feature list. Index by the saved names instead of relying on dictionary insertion order.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
features = ['humidity', 'temperature', 'pressure']
record = {'pressure': 1000., 'temperature': 18., 'humidity': 60.}
row = np.array([record[name] for name in features])
print(row.tolist())
interpretation: The model receives humidity first because that is its saved convention. Practice adds explicit checks for missing or unexpected fields and non-finite values.

parts.title: 4. Test Failure Paths as Carefully as Success
paragraphs: Include swapped fields, missing values, unexpected strings, NaN, empty batches, and wrong widths. Check that the error identifies the failed rule without exposing private record contents.
A schema change is a versioned change to the prediction interface. Coordinate it with preparation and model artifacts so a valid old request is not silently reinterpreted.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop validates a numerical table, then lets the same data pass downstream.

parts.title: 5. A Number Needs a Name and a Unit
paragraphs: Temperature and humidity can both be valid floating-point values while being assigned to the wrong columns. A parser should build arrays from declared names in a fixed order, rather than trusting the order of keys supplied by the caller.

Units also belong to the interface. Celsius and Fahrenheit values can both look plausible numerically. Either accept one documented unit or perform an explicit conversion before model preprocessing. Do not infer units from the magnitude alone.

parts.title: 6. Construct the Model Row from Names
paragraphs: Validate required fields before calculating a prediction. Missing fields, unknown fields and explicit null values need declared policies. Rejecting unknown fields can reveal a caller's typo; accepting them may be appropriate when a versioned envelope carries other metadata.
This small parser rejects both missing and extra fields and requires finite numerical values. It demonstrates the contract independently of any web framework.

examples.title: Preserve feature order despite dictionary order
paragraphs: The incoming dictionary lists humidity first, but the model contract lists temperature first.
interpretation: The caller's key order cannot swap the model's feature meanings. A complete contract can add valid ranges and explicit unit fields.

parts.title: 7. An Error Response Should Identify the Broken Promise
paragraphs: Distinguish a missing measurement from an unsupported unit, a wrong shape and a non-finite value. A caller can correct a specific contract error; a generic failed prediction provides little help.

Keep validation separate from a learned missing-value rule. If the model was trained to impute an allowed missing field, apply that saved policy. If it was not, silently filling zero invents behaviour the model was never evaluated to handle.

import numpy as np

record = {"humidity":25.,"temperature":12.}

hints: Dictionary insertion order must not choose feature order.
Check finiteness after conversion.

title: Keeping a Prediction Consistent Across Requests
blurb: The same input should have the same preparation and result whether it arrives alone or in a batch. Keep prediction free of accidental fitting and mutable shared state.
openingTitle: Why Should a Prediction Change When Another Request Arrives?
opening: Botie can run a model in a notebook. Serving it means other code supplies inputs, expects an output shape, and may call the predictor many times.
We will isolate a deterministic prediction function and check single-record and batch agreement. A network endpoint can call that function later; the mathematical contract should already be clear.

history.title: Reducing Differences Between Training and Serving
blocks: Production experience collected in Rules of Machine Learning includes checking differences between training and serving features. A model can behave unexpectedly even when its parameter file is correct if the surrounding computation changes.
Our browser exercise does not deploy a server. It tests the core prediction procedure that an API could call, separating numerical correctness from network transport and operational concerns.

quiz.prompt: What is the prediction shape?
quiz.because: One scalar prediction belongs to each row.

given.data: X has shape (5,2), w has shape (2,), scalar bias.

quiz.prompt: Its outputs can depend on unrelated companion records.
quiz.because: The preprocessing state changes with the batch.

given.data: A prediction request refits the scaler on its own batch.

quiz.prompt: Which response ordering is required here?
quiz.because: Responses must remain associated with requests.

given.data: Two requests arrive in a batch.

quiz.prompt: This alone proves the HTTP service meets latency requirements.
quiz.because: Transport and load behaviour need separate checks.

given.data: Numerical predictions pass fixture tests.

build.title: Predict a batch in order
build.problem: Botie receives a validated feature table and fixed model parameters.
build.challenge: Multiply each row by the weight vector, then add the same bias to each result.
build.why: Row order is preserved and all requests use the same parameter state.
build.limitation: Inputs must already satisfy the saved feature and preprocessing contract.

intuition.title: Receive a batch
intuition.explanation: Rows are requests and columns are features.

intuition.title: Apply one saved rule
intuition.explanation: Every row uses the same weights and intercept.

intuition.title: Return one result per row
intuition.explanation: Preserve request order.

parts.title: 1. Separate Fitting, Prediction, and Transport
paragraphs: The prediction function should use the fitted state as it stands. It should not relearn a mean from the current request or overwrite a parameter. Otherwise one caller could change another caller's answer.

Keep fitting separate from this calculation. The transport layer can then parse the request, call the prediction function, and serialize its result. We can test the numerical procedure before adding the endpoint around it.
interpretation: Our function receives only validated arrays and immutable model state.

parts.title: 2. Choose an Output Shape
paragraphs: For scalar regression, a batch of n records returns a vector of n predictions in the same order. A single record can be represented as a one-row matrix and still receive a one-element vector.
Avoid arbitrary squeezing of all singleton dimensions, which can make output type depend on batch size. Classification may need class order and separate scores, probabilities, and labels.
parts.calculation:
X shape = (n, feature_count)
w shape = (feature_count,)
Prediction shape = (n,)
prediction = X @ w + bias
interpretation: Shape is part of the public interface, not an implementation accident.

parts.title: 3. Check Batch and Single-Record Agreement
paragraphs: Apply the same prediction function to a whole batch and to its rows individually. Concatenated individual outputs should agree with the batch outputs within a stated tolerance.
Use evaluation mode for models with training-dependent layers. Batch normalisation and dropout must follow their inference rules rather than learn from each request.
interpretation: The example is deterministic linear inference, so the agreement should be straightforward.

examples.title: Keep the prediction rule separate from the request
paragraphs: A validated request supplies two features. The already fitted coefficients determine how to combine them; serving the request does not fit new coefficients.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
features = np.array([2., 4.])
saved_weights = np.array([1., 0.5])
saved_bias = 0.0
contributions = features * saved_weights
print(contributions.tolist())
print(float(contributions.sum() + saved_bias))
interpretation: Both features contribute to one answer. Practice packages this rule for a batch and checks that the same row gets the same answer when served alone.

parts.title: 4. Distinguish Numerical Failure From Service Failure
paragraphs: A valid mathematical function can still sit behind a service that times out, overloads, or returns inconsistent versions. Measure latency, throughput, error rates, and resource use separately from model accuracy.
Preserve request-to-response ordering when batching. Include a model version with results so later investigations can identify which state produced them.
interpretation: The workshop computes a batch prediction; the next lesson identifies the state responsible for that prediction.

parts.title: 5. A Batch Should Not Change the Meaning of One Record
paragraphs: A deterministic fitted predictor should return the same answer for a record alone or beside other records, unless the model explicitly uses batch context. Recomputing a batch mean during serving breaks that property.
Keep the fitted transform fixed, preserve output order and return one result or a documented error for each requested record. Test a short final batch and an empty batch according to the contract.

parts.title: 6. Check Single-Record and Batch Agreement
paragraphs: The same prediction function can serve both forms by representing one record as a one-row matrix. That keeps the feature axis in the same position and avoids special-case arithmetic.
The service wrapper can then handle request parsing and response formatting without changing the mathematical rule.

examples.title: Use one numerical path for both request sizes
paragraphs: Two features are transformed with saved training means.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
mean = np.array([10.,50.])
weight = np.array([2.,.1])
def predict(X):
    return (X-mean)@weight+3.
X = np.array([[12.,60.],[15.,40.]])
batch = predict(X)
single = np.array([predict(X[i:i+1])[0] for i in range(len(X))])
print(batch.tolist())
print(bool(np.array_equal(batch,single)))
interpretation: This verifies batch consistency for the supplied rule. The surrounding service still needs to preserve those rows and their request identifiers.

parts.title: 7. Limit Work before Starting Expensive Computation
paragraphs: A valid shape can still request an unreasonable amount of memory or compute. Define supported batch sizes, input dimensions and time budgets. Measure end-to-end latency, including parsing and feature preparation, rather than only a matrix multiplication.

Batching can improve throughput while increasing waiting time for an individual request. Choose that tradeoff for the application. Avoid retaining unbounded request arrays while waiting for a larger batch.

parts.title: 8. A Timeout Is Not a Numerical Prediction
paragraphs: Keep service failures separate from model outputs. A timed-out request should not quietly return a zero prediction, which downstream code may treat as a valid estimate.

Include the model version with successful results and retain request identifiers for later outcome matching. Retries should follow a documented policy, especially if a prediction also triggers an external action. The example predictor is pure; a production action workflow needs its own duplicate-handling rules.

Broadcast the same bias to each row.

practice.title: Do batch and individual predictions agree?
