title: Whose Pump Is Botie Allowed to Inspect?
blurb: The tool name is allowed, but its arguments point at another customer’s asset. Build the service-side checks that connect the caller, operation and stored record.
openingTitle: A Valid Pump ID Belongs to the Wrong Customer
opening: Botie now asks for an allowed tool: read_manual. The request contains a real asset ID, and the service can find a record for it. There is still a problem. The record belongs to a different customer.

We cannot settle that by asking Botie whether the caller seems trustworthy. The service needs the identity established by login and the permissions attached to that identity. Then it must compare those permissions with the particular object being requested.

history.title: Permission Had to Follow the Object Being Accessed
blocks: Shared computers had to keep one user’s programs from freely using another user’s files. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 paper describes design principles including least privilege, fail-safe defaults and complete mediation. The recurring problem is deciding whether a particular operation on a particular object is allowed.

An agent introduces a new way to propose that operation, but the service still has the same responsibility. In our invented workshop, the model proposes an asset operation while application-owned records establish the caller’s tenant and grants.

reading.experimentTitle: Does this caller have this permission on this asset?
reading.experimentIntro: Build separate tenant, asset and operation comparisons. Then change the stored asset’s tenant without changing its visible ID.
reading.connectionTitle: An allowed tool still needs an authorised object

intuition.title: The handler checks the object it actually loaded
intuition.explanation: Resolve the model-supplied ID inside the authorised tenant, then enforce the operation policy before returning data or making a change.

scene.caption: Use application-owned identity fields. Model arguments are requests, not authenticated claims.

parts.title: 1. Separate identity from permission
paragraphs: Authentication establishes which account is making the request, under the assumptions of the login system. Authorisation decides what that account may do. A signed-in technician may read manuals for assigned assets and still be unable to create jobs or access another site.

The service should derive the principal from the verified session or token, not from a field Botie supplies. Here principal means the application’s representation of that caller. Our small dictionary stores a tenant and two grant lists. A real application may query a policy service or database instead.
interpretation: A model-generated role such as administrator has no effect on the authenticated principal.

parts.title: 2. Check the object before returning its contents
paragraphs: Our service stores P7 under tenant north. A caller from north still needs a grant for P7. Checking the tenant alone would grant access to every asset in that organisation. Checking only the short ID would confuse two tenants that both use P7.

In the workshop, Match the tenant and Check this asset grant are separate components so their results remain visible. In a database, a scoped query can require both tenant and object ID before it returns the row. Keep a clear policy for objects shared across tenants rather than quietly removing the tenant condition.
interpretation: The example’s policy denies cross-tenant access. Sharing would require an explicit additional rule.

parts.title: 3. Deny requests that have no matching rule
paragraphs: The operation list contains read. A request to export, delete or schedule has no matching grant and is denied. That is a default-deny policy: absence of permission does not become permission. Missing or malformed principal fields must also fail the check.

Use exact identifiers from a controlled operation vocabulary. Substring matches are dangerous here: read is contained in some longer names without meaning the same operation. An unchecked wildcard can expand a narrow role into authority over future capabilities.
interpretation: This is a deterministic decision over server records. A second language model is unnecessary.

examples.title: Look up the owner before considering an operation
paragraphs: A dictionary can use a tuple as a compound key. Include the tenant in the lookup instead of searching by the short ID alone.
examples.code:
records = {("north", "P7"): "North pump manual", ("south", "P7"): "South pump manual"}
caller_tenant = "north"
requested_id = "P7"
print(records.get((caller_tenant, requested_id)))
print(records.get((caller_tenant, "P8")))
interpretation: The absent row remains absent. This lookup illustrates tenant scoping; operation and assignment checks still belong beside it.

parts.title: 4. Enforce the check where the action happens
paragraphs: Hiding an export button or removing a tool from a model prompt helps guide normal use. Neither prevents a caller from reaching an exposed service route another way. The service that reads or changes the asset must enforce the policy for each request.

For writes, keep the authorisation decision and the relevant state change together closely enough that an intervening ownership or permission change cannot silently invalidate the check. A database transaction, version comparison or policy revision check may be needed. The right mechanism depends on where those records live.
interpretation: This is the reason to test the handler directly, without a model or the website interface in the path.

parts.title: 5. Give the tool less authority than the whole service
paragraphs: A maintenance assistant that only reads manuals should use a scoped read capability. It should not receive a general database administrator credential or an unrestricted command runner. Credentials belong in the service environment and should stay out of model-visible arguments and results.

The application must account for both the user’s authority and the service’s own authority. A powerful service account does not mean every user who can ask Botie a question may exercise all of its permissions. Check the caller before using that service account on their behalf.
interpretation: Least privilege makes a mistaken request less consequential, while per-request authorisation decides whether that request may proceed.

parts.title: 6. Bind approval to what will actually be executed
paragraphs: An approved inspection for P7 does not authorise an inspection for P8. Preserve the action identity, arguments and revision that the reviewer saw, then compare them again at execution time. Recheck the reviewer’s current authority and the caller’s current access when your policy requires it.

Approval and authorisation answer different questions. A permitted caller may still need a human decision for a consequential write. A human saying yes does not give the application permission to cross a tenant boundary. Keep both checks in the execution path.
interpretation: The earlier approval workshop supplied an exact-action match. This lesson adds the object-access boundary around that action.

parts.title: 7. Make access failures observable without revealing the record
paragraphs: A denied caller should not receive the protected manual inside an error message. Depending on the application, even revealing whether an asset exists may disclose information. A consistent external response can hide that distinction while a protected audit record retains the internal reason.

Test a permitted read, another tenant’s matching ID, an unassigned object in the same tenant, and a forbidden operation. Add a case where permissions change before execution. These cases catch different mistakes; one successful read says little about the deny paths.
interpretation: The construction is correct only if it preserves the permitted case while closing the gaps exposed by the changed records.

title: How Much of the Maintenance Record Does Botie Need?
blurb: A manual lookup needs an asset and a symptom, but the original record also contains private contact details. Build the smaller payload and control where it can go.
openingTitle: The Lookup Works Without the Technician’s Phone Number
opening: Botie needs the pump model and reported symptom to find the right inspection notes. Our application has those fields, but they live in a larger maintenance record alongside a technician’s contact details and a building access code. Passing the whole record to the model would be convenient. What would the extra fields help it do?

If they do not help with this job, we can leave them out before making a request. That is easier to reason about than sending everything and hoping the model never repeats the wrong part. We also need to control the destination, because a small payload can still be sent to the wrong service.

history.title: Managing Data Meant Following It Beyond the Database
blocks: Keeping a database private does not settle what happens when an application copies its contents to another system. NIST’s January 2020 Privacy Framework organised privacy risk around data processing and the organisations involved in it. That gives us a useful question for an agent: which information leaves each boundary, for what purpose, and under whose controls?

Tools such as Presidio address a narrower part of that problem by identifying and transforming sensitive entities in text and other data. Its documentation explicitly warns that automated detection cannot find every sensitive item. Our workshop begins earlier, with a new record containing only the fields this lookup needs.

reading.experimentTitle: What actually leaves the maintenance record?
reading.experimentIntro: Project the necessary fields, inspect their application-owned release labels, and check the configured destination before releasing the payload.
reading.connectionTitle: A useful context is smaller than the source database row
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Prepare only the approved lookup payload
reading.exampleNote: All records are invented. The construction produces a local value; it sends nothing to a service.

intuition.title: Give each field a reason to travel
intuition.explanation: The manual lookup has a narrow purpose. Classify and select its inputs before serialization.

scene.caption: These values are invented. In a deployed service, field policy belongs to the application.

intuition.title: A destination is another independent decision
intuition.explanation: The selected fields must be approved for release and sent only to a configured service.

rows.label: Release
items: The checked payload or an empty withheld result

scene.caption: This model does not inspect free text for hidden secrets or implement a network firewall.

parts.title: 1. Choose inputs from the job backwards
paragraphs: Start with the lookup we want to perform. It needs an asset identifier and a controlled symptom code. A controlled code is a value from a vocabulary the application defines, such as VIBRATION. It is not an unrestricted note field.

Now create a new payload containing those fields. This operation is often called projection: select named columns or fields from a larger record. Keeping the source record intact is useful because another authorised operation may need its contact field later. It does not follow that this model request needs it now.
interpretation: Ask what each field helps this particular request accomplish.

parts.title: 2. Separate the right to read from the right to send
paragraphs: The technician may be permitted to view a contact number inside the maintenance system. That does not automatically permit sending it to an external model provider or logging platform. Destination, purpose and retention matter independently of the original read permission.

For the exercise we use a deliberately simple release label: approved. Every selected field needs that exact label. An unknown label or missing classification withholds the payload. Real classifications may depend on the tenant, destination, jurisdiction or contractual arrangement, and the application must resolve that policy before release.
interpretation: Our label is trusted metadata for this teaching example. A model-generated approved field would have no authority.

parts.title: 3. Inspect the smaller record before encoding it
paragraphs: A dictionary comprehension can select fields into a new dictionary. We iterate over the fields chosen by the application, rather than copying every key and trying to remember what to remove afterwards.

Do not silently ignore a requested field that does not exist. The resulting payload might still look valid while missing the information needed for the task. The workshop stops on that configuration error. A field added to the source record, however, stays excluded unless the application deliberately selects it.
interpretation: An allowlist of needed fields survives an unrelated source-schema addition more predictably than a list of known secret fields.

examples.title: A new internal field stays out of a summary payload
paragraphs: The source contains an internal note, but this summary only needs two named fields. The comprehension creates a separate dictionary.
interpretation: The payload has the selected keys. The original record still retains the internal note for authorised uses.

parts.title: 4. Constrain the destination before any network request
paragraphs: Our workshop chooses a service ID such as manual-index from an application allowlist. Server configuration resolves that ID to a known connection. Letting the model supply an arbitrary URL would introduce more decisions: scheme, hostname, port, resolved address and redirect behaviour.

A request to a permitted-looking hostname can redirect elsewhere, and DNS resolution can produce an address the service must not reach. Server-side request forgery is the problem of making a server request a destination it should not access. Use a narrow egress policy and a network client that enforces it. Revalidate redirects or disable them, and block inappropriate internal and metadata endpoints.
interpretation: An exact service-ID comparison is only one part of controlling egress. The workshop intentionally does not claim to validate URLs.

parts.title: 5. Treat a sandbox as a set of enforced limits
paragraphs: If Botie can run code, ask what that process can read, write and contact. Giving it a separate working directory is useful but does not establish isolation from the host, environment variables or network. A sandbox needs an actual enforcement mechanism and a defined threat model.

Restrict filesystem mounts, avoid inherited credentials, run without unnecessary privileges, and place limits on execution time, memory and output. Network access should follow the task’s egress policy. Review the isolation technology’s documented guarantees and patch it. A container can help package these controls, but its default settings are not a complete policy.
interpretation: The coding worksheet here is for learning. It is not a template for executing arbitrary model-written code inside your production service.

parts.title: 6. Use PII detection where the source really is free text
paragraphs: Sometimes a technician’s note is needed, and personal information can appear inside a sentence rather than a dedicated field. Presidio separates identification from transformation: recognizers locate possible sensitive entities, then an anonymisation step can replace, mask or otherwise transform the detected spans.

Evaluate recognizers on the languages and formats your application sees. A missed entity remains in the text; an incorrect detection can remove useful maintenance information. NeMo also exposes integrations for detecting or masking sensitive information at different points in a conversation. Choose where the check runs by following the actual data flow, including retrieved material and final answers.
interpretation: Redaction after a provider request cannot undo data already sent to that provider. Minimise and inspect before the relevant boundary.

parts.title: 7. Check logs, traces and saved conversations too
paragraphs: The model request is only one copy. Debug traces may store prompts, responses and tool results. Checkpoint storage can preserve the same fields for later runs. An error report may include an entire failed payload.

Define what each store needs, who can read it and when it should be deleted. Prefer identifiers and decision categories when full content is unnecessary. Apply redaction before export to a telemetry service. If you need protected sample traces for investigations, make that a controlled collection with its own access and retention policy rather than the default for every run.
interpretation: A redacted user interface tells us nothing about whether a raw request was copied into an observability tool.

parts.title: 8. Make the unknown case visibly withhold
paragraphs: The changed workshop case adds contact to the selected fields but leaves its release label restricted. The destination is still approved. Only the field-classification branch should explain why the result is withheld.

Then try an approved payload with an unapproved destination. This exposes a construction that checks only the fields. An empty result here is intentional: the output does not carry the disallowed payload along with a warning that a downstream component might ignore. A production audit record can separately retain a protected reason code.
interpretation: Do not let a convenient fallback resend the full original record after the minimised request fails.

parts.title: 9. Keep the teaching boundary honest
paragraphs: This construction checks field names and trusted classifications. It does not inspect the meaning of values. If a free-text symptom contains a password, labelling its field approved will not remove that password. If an asset identifier is itself sensitive, it also needs an appropriate policy.

Use realistic test fixtures for those cases in the actual application. The controlled symptom codes here let us study selection and routing without pretending to have built a complete privacy classifier. Keep that assumption in the test description when comparing implementations.
interpretation: A passing release test means this stated policy passed for these records. It is not a general privacy guarantee.

title: Can We Safely Use the Answer Botie Returned?
blurb: A response can be valid JSON and still name the wrong pump or contain unwanted markup. Check its structure, its relationship to the request, and the context that will consume it.
openingTitle: A Valid Answer for the Wrong Pump
opening: Botie returns a neat record with an asset, a citation and an inspection note. Every field is a string. The interface can read it. Then the technician notices that the answer concerns P8, while the request was about P7.

There is another boundary after generating an answer. We have to decide whether the record means what this request requires and how the next program will use its contents. A string that belongs in a text panel should not quietly become executable markup or a command.

history.title: A Correct String Can Become an Instruction to Another Program
blocks: Web applications have long had to distinguish text supplied by a user from markup interpreted by a browser. Cross-site scripting demonstrates what happens when that distinction is lost. Generated text introduces another source of untrusted content; the consuming browser still applies its own parsing rules.

Typed validation libraries help applications reject malformed records, while guardrail libraries organise additional checks and their failure actions. Our teaching example keeps the questions visible: are the fields usable, do their identifiers match this request, and will the display treat the content as text? These checks leave the correctness of the inspection advice for a separate review.

parts.title: 1. Begin with the contract the next component needs
paragraphs: The draft panel expects exactly asset, citation and text. Require those fields to contain nonblank strings and reject unexpected fields. This prevents a hidden execute flag from being accepted merely because the visible note looks ordinary.

Schema validation deals with representation. It can describe types, required properties and some value constraints. Provider-supported structured generation can help produce that representation, but the application should still validate what it receives. A truncated response, changed configuration or different producer can reach the same boundary.
interpretation: A valid structure makes the next check possible; it does not make the content correct.

parts.title: 2. Compare identifiers with this request’s evidence
paragraphs: The asset field must equal the requested asset. The citation must appear in the evidence supplied to this run and refer to that asset. These are semantic constraints because they concern relationships between the record and its surrounding data.

Our workshop stores a citation-to-asset map to make the comparison visible. It is deliberately incomplete as an evidence check. A citation can refer to the correct pump while the sentence contradicts its manual. Content support needs examination of the actual excerpt, possibly with domain rules, a reviewer or a separately evaluated model judge.
interpretation: Avoid a success label that claims more than was checked. We call the surviving record a draft for review.

parts.title: 3. Use strict types deliberately
paragraphs: Validation libraries may convert values into the declared type. Coercion is useful in some interfaces, but a boundary may need to reject a value supplied in the wrong representation. Pydantic provides strict validation controls for that choice.

The local recipe declares strict string fields, rejects extra keys and checks for whitespace-only values. It validates a Python dictionary with model_validate. Other input modes and types have their own rules, so test the actual entry point used by the application. A type annotation alone does not run a check over arbitrary incoming data.
interpretation: Keep this structural recipe separate from the request-specific evidence checks.

references.title: Declare the draft shape with Pydantic
description: Run this structural check in your own Python environment. The later asset and citation comparisons still belong in application code.
setup: Install a compatible Pydantic 2.x release in a local virtual environment and record the resolved version in your lockfile.
This example validates invented local data. It needs no model provider or credential.
interpretation: Strict fields and forbidden extra keys establish the record contract. This program has not checked permissions, citation support or how the text will be rendered.

parts.title: 4. Render text according to where it will appear
paragraphs: An HTML parser gives angle brackets a meaning beyond ordinary text. If the draft contains Inspect, a text panel should show those characters as text unless the product intentionally supports that markup. Use a text-content API or the framework’s normal escaped interpolation.

The offline example uses Python’s html.escape to demonstrate encoding before insertion into an HTML text node. Encoding is specific to the destination context. It does not make a string safe as JavaScript, a shell command, SQL or an arbitrary URL. Do not pass this encoded string to another interpreter and assume the same protection applies.
interpretation: If the frontend already escapes text, pass it raw text and let that boundary encode once. Double encoding would show the escape sequences themselves.

examples.title: Keep markup characters visible as text
paragraphs: This standard-library program encodes a short draft for an HTML text context. It does not execute or render HTML.
examples.code:
from html import escape

note = "Inspect <coupling> & mounting."
encoded = escape(note, quote=True)
print(encoded)
print(note)
interpretation: The source string stays unchanged. The encoded version is suitable for the stated HTML text context only.

parts.title: 5. Treat links, rich text and executable requests separately
paragraphs: If the interface allows Markdown, decide which features it needs. A remote image can cause a network request when rendered, and a link can point to an unwanted scheme or destination. Disable raw HTML when it is unnecessary, restrict URL schemes and destinations as appropriate, and use a maintained sanitizer for the rich content the product intentionally supports.

If the result is meant to query a database, use parameterized queries and application-owned query structure. If it proposes a tool call, return to the authorisation and argument checks before execution. Never use an LLM’s output as an unrestricted command just because it passed a text-quality filter.
interpretation: Every consumer introduces its own interpretation rules. Name the actual consumer when choosing the protection.

parts.title: 6. Choose what a failed validator does
paragraphs: Guardrails AI validators define criteria and report a pass or failure. Configured failure actions determine what happens next. A retry may request a different answer; a failure can also stop processing or trigger another application path. Inspect the outcome and use only a result that passed the required checks.

Automatic repair is appropriate only when changing the value preserves the intended task and policy. Silently replacing an invalid asset with the requested asset could attach a note about P8 to P7. For this lesson, inconsistent fields return repair draft with empty display text. A bounded retry can ask for a new candidate, which must pass every check again.
interpretation: A repaired string is a new candidate, not an exemption from validation.

parts.title: 7. Hold streamed content until its required checks finish
paragraphs: Streaming makes an interface feel responsive, but a final output check cannot take back text already shown or a tool already executed. Decide which parts can be displayed before full validation. A typing indicator or progress state can be useful while a protected result is withheld.

If validation operates on chunks, test content that spans a chunk boundary and check the final assembled message as needed. Structured output may be incomplete until the stream finishes. Keep cancellation, truncated output and validator errors distinct from successful completion.
interpretation: The workshop uses complete records so its validation order is visible. A streaming application needs additional tests for that order.

parts.title: 8. Test misleading success cases
paragraphs: Keep a correctly shaped draft for the wrong asset in the suite. Add a citation from the right evidence collection but for another asset. Then supply markup characters in an otherwise matching draft and verify that the output remains text.

A correct implementation should preserve ordinary drafts while repairing invalid relationships. Separately test whether the note is supported by the excerpt and whether a technician finds it useful. This separation gives a failure a location: representation, request relationship, display handling or advice quality.
interpretation: A single overall guardrail score would hide which of those responsibilities failed.

title: Did Botie Create the Inspection, or Did the Reply Get Lost?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: A request times out after Botie submits an inspection. Work out what the service may already have done before sending another request.
openingTitle: One Approved Inspection Has Become Two Jobs
opening: The technician approves an inspection of P7. Botie submits the request, but the connection closes before the reply arrives. He tries again. The service now shows two inspection jobs for the same request.

From Botie’s side, the first attempt failed to produce a reply. From the service’s side, it may have succeeded. We need to keep those facts separate. This lesson builds a recovery decision that can reuse a recorded result, wait for a pending operation, or stop when another attempt would be unsafe.

history.title: A Lost Reply Was a Problem Before Models Called Tools

sources.title: Amazon Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
Amazon Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

blocks: Distributed services have long faced the problem of a request whose effect succeeds while its reply is lost. Amazon’s Builders’ Library describes how client request identifiers let a service recognise repeated intent; its idempotent API article was announced in January 2021. An agent calling a work-order service inherits this same communication problem.

The practical idea is to give the intended inspection a stable identity. A repeated delivery of that operation can then recover its earlier result within the receiving service’s documented contract. Our receipt ledger is a teaching model. It does not implement a distributed transaction or promise that every request eventually succeeds.

reading.experimentTitle: What should happen after the missing reply?
reading.experimentIntro: Keep the receipt lookup, retry safety and run deadline visible on separate branches. Then combine them into one recovery action.
reading.connectionTitle: Recover an operation without inventing another one
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Decide the next recovery action
reading.exampleNote: No work-order service is called. Receipt records and clocks are supplied fixtures.

intuition.title: A timeout describes the caller’s observation
intuition.explanation: The effect and the reply happen at different points. A broken connection can separate them.

rows.label: Work-order service
items: Create WO-41 and store the operation receipt

rows.label: Botie
items: Sees a timeout; cannot infer that no work occurred

scene.caption: The service receipt answers a question that the missing reply cannot.

intuition.title: Look at what the receiver knows
intuition.explanation: Use the same operation key and compare the complete action payload.

records.label: Completed, same payload
cells: The intended effect has a recorded result

records.label: Pending, same payload
cells: Query status within a bounded policy

records.label: Same key, different payload
cells: The caller changed the intended action

records.label: No receipt
cells: Apply retry safety and deadline checks

scene.caption: An absent receipt is usable evidence only within the service’s consistency and idempotency contract.

parts.title: 1. Classify the failure before choosing another attempt
paragraphs: A permission denial or invalid asset identifier will not improve because the same request is sent again. Route those permanent failures to repair or review. A temporary overload or interrupted connection may justify a retry, but the tool’s contract must establish whether repeating the operation is safe.

Keep unknown outcomes distinct from known rejections. For a write, a timeout can mean the service completed the effect without delivering a reply. For a read, another request usually avoids duplicate business effects, though it still consumes resources and can return changed data. Our fixture labels outcomes success, transient, permanent or unknown; real adapters map their documented error codes into those categories.
interpretation: The model does not get to reinterpret a permission denial as an invitation to try different arguments until something works.

parts.title: 2. Give the intended operation an identity
paragraphs: Create an operation key when the application accepts the approved intent. Persist it before sending the write. Reuse it when delivering that same operation again. A genuinely new inspection needs a new key, even if its asset and other fields match an earlier inspection.

The receiver binds the key to the caller’s scope and the relevant payload. The same key with a different pump or schedule must be a conflict. Avoid relying on the model to invent or remember this identity. It belongs to application state alongside the approved action revision.
interpretation: A key in a request header is only useful if the receiving service enforces the contract.

parts.title: 3. Recover the receiver’s answer before scheduling more work
paragraphs: A completed receipt can return the earlier work-order ID. A pending receipt tells us the operation is already under way. A status query or a bounded wait is appropriate; launching a second operation is not.

This requires an authoritative ledger. A stale cache or an unavailable status endpoint cannot prove that the operation never happened. When the receiving service offers neither an idempotency contract nor a reliable reconciliation path, retain the ambiguous outcome for review. Do not turn it into an automatic new write. The workshop’s absent receipt assumes a trustworthy snapshot within the stated service contract.
interpretation: Approval answers whether we may perform the action. A receipt answers what happened when we tried. Neither replaces the other.

parts.title: 4. What the idempotency boundary has to store
paragraphs: The service needs a unique operation identity, a fingerprint or canonical representation of its payload, a processing state, and a stored result. Concurrent deliveries of the same operation must compete at an atomic boundary so both cannot decide they are the first.

The exact transaction depends on where the effect happens. A database write and its receipt may share a transaction. An external email or another service cannot automatically join that transaction; outbox delivery and downstream idempotency may be needed. Receipt retention also matters. Once a receiver forgets a key, a late replay may be treated as new work. Read the actual API contract and keep retries inside its scope and retention window.
interpretation: Our Python dictionary lookup demonstrates the decision only. It is not a concurrency-safe store.

examples.title: Recover a known operation result
paragraphs: A dictionary indexed by operation key makes a completed receipt easy to find. This example performs no write.
interpretation: The result belongs to the earlier operation. The full challenge will also reject a reused key whose payload changed.

parts.title: 5. Give every attempt a timeout and the whole run a deadline
paragraphs: A per-attempt timeout bounds how long the caller waits for one operation. A run deadline bounds the whole recovery process, including delays and repeated attempts. Starting a fresh timeout after each failure can otherwise keep the run alive far longer than intended.

Count attempts that have actually started, including the first. Before scheduling another, check the remaining attempt allowance and whether its delay plus timeout fits the remaining deadline. Use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time accounting in a real process. Pass the remaining deadline to downstream calls where supported. Timing out locally does not roll back an effect already accepted elsewhere.
interpretation: The supplied fixture clock is an integer millisecond counter so every branch can be tested without sleeping.

parts.title: 6. Spread retries without letting them continue forever
paragraphs: Repeated immediate requests can worsen an overloaded service. Exponential backoff increases the upper delay after successive attempts, and a cap prevents unbounded waiting. Jitter chooses a delay within a range so many clients do not all retry at the same instant.

Our full-jitter demonstration supplies a fraction between zero and one rather than drawing randomness during a test. We multiply that fraction by the capped upper delay and round down to whole milliseconds. In production, draw the random value per attempt and honour the service’s documented Retry-After guidance. Keep a separate total deadline; a capped delay alone allows infinitely many retries.
parts.calculation:
upper_delay = min(cap_ms, base_ms * 2 ** max(attempts_started - 1, 0))
delay_ms = floor(upper_delay * jitter_fraction)
next_attempt_fits = now_ms + delay_ms + timeout_ms <= deadline_ms
interpretation: Equality is allowed in our scheduling fixture. Actual transport scheduling and cancellation are not precise guarantees that a remote operation finishes at that instant.

parts.title: 7. Choose one place to own automatic recovery
paragraphs: A provider SDK may already retry a request. A framework may retry a model response that fails validation. A tool adapter may retry its service call. If each surrounding layer also repeats the whole operation, the actual number of requests can grow much faster than the visible loop count.

Inspect the layers and give each failure one deliberate recovery owner. Count transport attempts separately from model turns and tool proposals. Record the operation key, attempt number, error category and final outcome without leaking sensitive request bodies. A validation retry asks for corrected content; a transport retry resends delivery. They have different purposes and may consume different budgets.
interpretation: An agent’s friendly message that it is trying again should correspond to a recorded recovery decision in the application.

parts.title: 8. Let a cancellation leave an honest outcome
paragraphs: If the user cancels after submission, stop scheduling new work and request cancellation of any supported in-flight operation. The receiver may already have committed the effect. Preserve its operation identity and reconcile the final state before reporting that nothing happened.

For a workflow with several external effects, recovery may involve a compensating action such as cancelling a created appointment. That compensation is a separate authorised operation with its own possible failure. It does not erase the fact that the original effect occurred. Make partial outcomes visible to the person responsible for the request.
interpretation: The next lesson will keep budget reservations for unresolved work rather than pretending a cancelled caller immediately receives its resources back.

parts.title: 9. Trip the retry loop with a completed write
paragraphs: Begin with the missing-reply case whose service supports a stable key. The recovery rule can permit another delivery within the deadline. Then load the completed receipt. The same construction should return its stored work-order ID immediately.

Change the payload under that key and check that the result becomes a conflict. Finally, remove the idempotency guarantee and leave the result unknown. Time remaining is no longer enough to justify another write. These cases test different reasons for stopping, so a single retry-until-success loop cannot satisfy them.
interpretation: The result of this lesson is a recovery decision. Executing that decision still requires the live service contract and current authorisation checks.

practice.title: Which recovery action can Botie safely take next?
practice.question: Which recovery action can Botie safely take next?
task: Write next_action(command, receipts, outcome, schedule, state), returning a dictionary with route, delay_ms and result. Match a receipt by command.key and compare the complete payload. A conflict returns "reject changed payload". A matching completed receipt returns "return stored result" and its result; pending returns "query operation status". Otherwise success returns "done", permanent returns "repair request", and a write without receiver-enforced idempotency returns "reconcile outcome".

For other transient or unknown outcomes, calculate capped full-jitter delay as shown in Part 6. Permit "retry same operation key" only when attempts is below max_attempts, now_ms is before deadline_ms, and delay plus timeout fits. Otherwise return "stop at run limit". Non-retry routes have delay_ms 0; result is None except for stored completion. Inputs use the displayed dictionary fields. Each completed receipt must include result, which may explicitly be None. Compare nested payload values with JSON type semantics: True is different from 1, while numeric 1 and 1.0 match. Reject missing or malformed fields, duplicate receipt keys, negative integer counters, zero timeout, and jitter outside [0,1] with ValueError. Do not mutate inputs. This exercise makes no network calls.
Print the recovery dictionary for the supplied request after an unknown outcome.
hints: A matching receipt takes precedence over the retry schedule. Check the complete payload, not only the asset.
Do the safety decision before the timing decision. An unsafe duplicate write remains unsafe even with plenty of time.

title: Can Two of Botie’s Calls Spend the Same Remaining Budget?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: Two proposed lookups each appear affordable until they start together. Reserve shared resources before dispatch and keep the whole run within its operating limits.
openingTitle: Both Calls Saw Enough Budget, and Together They Spent Too Much
opening: Botie wants to summarise a manual and compare it with the repair history. The application checks both proposals against the same remaining allowance. Each fits on its own, so both begin. Their combined work exceeds the allowance.

Checking the balance was only part of the job. We also needed to reserve the resources when admitting each call. We will build that decision, then see what changes when the user cancels, a dependency starts failing, or the next request cannot finish before the deadline.

history.title: An Agent Run Inherits the Resource Problems of a Service

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Circuit Breaker pattern
Pydantic AI: Usage limits and cancellation

blocks: Services already needed ways to stop failed dependencies from consuming every available worker. Circuit breakers record a dependency’s health and temporarily prevent new calls when repeated failures make more work unhelpful. The pattern belongs to distributed-service design; adding a model-controlled loop makes its resource consequences easier to overlook.

A model can propose more work than the application can afford to execute. Current agent libraries expose run limits, but their counters and enforcement moments differ. Our lesson uses an explicit reservation ledger so the reader can inspect what was spent, what is still in flight, and what another call would require.

reading.experimentTitle: Reserve work before allowing parallel calls
reading.experimentIntro: Subtract settled usage and in-flight reservations first. Check cancellation and circuit state on a separate branch, then admit calls in the declared queue order.
reading.connectionTitle: A proposed call still needs an execution slot
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Reserve a batch of proposed calls
reading.exampleNote: All amounts are invented. Cost units are integer accounting units, not provider prices.

intuition.title: The allowance has three different states
intuition.explanation: The application must count work that started but has not yet reported final usage.

records.label: Limit
cells: Maximum reserved or settled work for this run

records.label: Settled usage
cells: Usage already reported by completed work

records.label: Still reserved
cells: An earlier call is in flight

scene.caption: A reservation represents a bound used by the admission policy. Real usage is reconciled when the operation ends.

intuition.title: Reserve before the next proposal reads the balance
intuition.explanation: Both proposed calls need a reservation of 300 tokens. Queue order is deliberate in this fixture.

scene.caption: A real shared ledger needs an atomic check-and-reserve operation. Two workers cannot safely check separate stale copies.

parts.title: 1. Name the work that each limit counts
paragraphs: A model request is one interaction with a provider, but an agent framework may count a model turn differently from transport attempts. A tool proposal is a request to use a capability; a tool execution is the actual work performed by its handler. Decide whether your operational counters count attempts, successes or both.

Token usage counts input and output processing. Money depends on prices and provider accounting, so equal token totals can have different costs. Elapsed time measures what the user waits for. These quantities cannot substitute for one another. The workshop carries separate tokens, cost_units, model_requests and tool_calls fields, with a wall-clock deadline checked separately.
interpretation: Document counter semantics at the boundary that enforces them. A limit whose name is ambiguous will be hard to test.

parts.title: 2. Keep one request small enough to send
paragraphs: A run can stay below its total allowance while one request exceeds the model’s context window or your application’s input-size limit. Measure the request after assembling its instructions, evidence and conversation state. Reserve room for the response according to the provider’s actual context rules.

The workshop supplies input_tokens and checks it against max_input_tokens. Its token reservation includes that input plus a chosen output allowance. This is a teaching contract, so a reservation smaller than the input is rejected as malformed. Real systems need a tokenizer or provider counting interface appropriate to the model, including any special messages and tool definitions.
interpretation: A cumulative token cap and a per-request context cap protect different boundaries.

parts.title: 3. Count work still in flight
paragraphs: Settled usage records operations whose accounting has arrived. A reservation records work already admitted whose final usage is not known. Subtract both when deciding what remains.

If an operation finishes below its reserved bound, move actual usage to the settled ledger and release only the unused remainder. If accounting is missing, keep an unresolved entry and reconcile it. Treating missing usage as zero creates fictional capacity. Where provider behaviour can exceed an estimate, choose conservative limits and enforce output caps where supported. Application reservations are only as reliable as their bounds and the accounting contract.
parts.calculation: available = limit - settled_usage - in_flight_reservations
interpretation: Never subtract a reservation from one run and charge its result to an unrelated run. Keep the request and operation identities with both entries.

parts.title: 4. The second proposal must see the first reservation
paragraphs: Our two calls each request 300 tokens. The shared remainder is 500. Checking them independently against that initial value admits too much work. Checking the first, reserving it, then checking the second produces a different outcome.

We use queue order as a transparent admission policy. Other schedulers may prioritise urgent work or maximise useful work under a budget, but they still need a shared atomic reservation step. In a multi-worker service this commonly belongs in a transaction or another concurrency-safe store. Our single-process dictionary calculation only demonstrates the policy.
interpretation: A reservation is an execution decision made by the application. The model’s belief that a call is affordable does not reserve anything.

parts.title: 5. Represent each proposed call as an inspectable record
paragraphs: Each proposal has an id, input_tokens, timeout_ms and a reserve dictionary. The reserve dictionary names the same four resources as the run limits. A list preserves the queue order. A dictionary stores the remaining amount for each named resource, so tokens cannot accidentally be compared with tool calls.

The admission function validates every proposal, including one it will later refuse. It returns accepted IDs, rejected IDs with reasons, and the remaining budget. It does not perform network work or mutate the input ledger. That separation makes a test able to inspect the decision before any actual expense or effect occurs.
interpretation: The caller must commit the returned reservations atomically before dispatching accepted calls.

examples.title: Subtract a reservation on a copy of the ledger
paragraphs: A dictionary copy keeps the supplied starting allowance intact while we inspect one proposed reservation.
interpretation: The copied result shows the proposal’s effect. The original record remains available for a transaction or a failed-decision comparison.

parts.title: 6. Carry the run deadline into every branch
paragraphs: Parallel calls spend resources at the same time. Their elapsed durations do not simply add, but each must respect the run’s remaining deadline. The fixture admits a call only if its full timeout fits before deadline_ms. It uses a shared now_ms snapshot because it is making one batch decision.

A live dispatcher must recheck remaining time immediately before each launch. Waiting in a queue consumes the same deadline. Downstream operations need the remaining budget rather than a new full timeout at every hop. Reserve time for combining results and returning a response, especially if the calls are only an intermediate stage.
interpretation: The timeout is a bound on local waiting, not proof that a remote effect will be undone when the clock expires.

parts.title: 7. Cancellation stops new work before it frees old work
paragraphs: When the user cancels, stop admitting proposals and signal cancellation to supported in-flight operations. Keep each in-flight reservation until the operation’s final usage or an authoritative cancellation outcome is known. A closed local stream may still leave provider work running or an external write committed.

The workshop’s cancelled flag blocks the batch and leaves its supplied reservations in place. It does not simulate a remote cancellation protocol. A production UI should distinguish requested cancellation, confirmed cancellation, and an unresolved effect. Partial output also needs a clear status so it is not mistaken for a completed answer.
interpretation: Returning early to the user and stopping all downstream work are separate events.

parts.title: 8. Stop feeding a failing dependency
paragraphs: A circuit breaker watches failures associated with a dependency. In its closed state, calls can proceed subject to other limits. When the configured failure policy opens the circuit, new calls fail promptly rather than repeatedly spending the request budget on the same unavailable service.

After a recovery interval, a half-open state can allow a limited probe. A successful probe can support closing the circuit; another failure can reopen it. Our fixture receives the current state and an application-granted probe slot. It admits at most one proposal while half-open. It does not compute failure windows or recovery transitions, which need service-specific policy and tests.
interpretation: An open circuit should describe the dependency that is failing. It should not silently turn every unrelated tool off.

parts.title: 9. Read the library’s limit contract before relying on its name
paragraphs: Pydantic AI documents usage limits for requests, tool calls, tokens and cost. Its current tool_calls_limit counts successful tool invocations. Its request_limit counts model responses acted on by the agent loop, rather than every provider transport attempt. Provider retries and some continuation or fallback requests can therefore make transport activity differ from the turn count.

The enforcement moment matters too. Output-token and cost checks can occur after a response, and cancelled-stream usage may be incomplete. These controls do not all provide a pre-dispatch spending guarantee. Read the installed version’s documentation and test the cases your application relies on. Add application reservations or provider-side limits where the requirement calls for them. Keep unknown prices or usage visible as unknown.
interpretation: The workshop’s queue policy is our own teaching design. It does not claim to reproduce a particular framework’s scheduling policy.

parts.title: 10. Use limits at more than one scope
paragraphs: A per-run allowance protects one request. It does not stop thousands of permitted requests from exhausting a shared provider quota. A service may also need per-user rate limits, organisation spend controls, concurrency limits, and a bounded queue. Decide which boundary owns each limit.

A queue is a promise of future work. Bound it and provide a clear overload response instead of accepting an unlimited backlog. Reserve capacity for essential recovery and status work where appropriate. Otherwise an exhausted task budget might prevent the very reconciliation needed to discover whether a write completed.
interpretation: Fallbacks need permissions and accounting too. Switching providers or launching a helper agent should not reset the original run’s allowance.

parts.title: 11. Test contention, cancellation and recovery as different cases
paragraphs: The first fixture exposes two proposals competing for one remaining allowance. The next gives the second call enough room by changing the existing reservation; the same construction should then admit both. A cancelled run must admit neither, regardless of its apparent budget.

The half-open fixture tests a different rule: only one probe can run even when resources are plentiful. Additional cases isolate the context cap and the deadline. Keep refusal reasons visible so a learner can explain which boundary acted. When a real service refuses work, those same reasons help distinguish expected limits from faulty accounting.
interpretation: The next observability lessons will follow these decisions through traces and outcomes instead of reducing every stopped run to one generic error.

task: Write reserve_calls(proposals, limits, used, reserved, control, clock). Subtract used and reserved from limits for tokens, cost_units, model_requests and tool_calls. Each is a nonnegative integer and booleans are invalid. An overdrawn ledger raises ValueError. Process proposals in list order without mutating inputs.

Each proposal has a unique nonblank id, nonnegative input_tokens, positive timeout_ms, and a reserve dictionary with those four resource fields. Reserved tokens must cover input_tokens. Validate all input records. control contains boolean cancelled, circuit (closed, open or half-open), and boolean probe_granted. clock contains nonnegative integer now_ms, deadline_ms and max_input_tokens.

Refusal precedence is cancelled; circuit unavailable for open or ungranted half-open; probe slot used after one accepted half-open call; request too large; deadline; resource budget. An accepted call reserves every resource before the next call is checked. Return {"accepted": IDs, "rejected": [{"id": ID, "reason": reason}], "remaining": resource dictionary}. Reject malformed input with ValueError. Print the supplied example’s result.
hints: Store available resources in a fresh dictionary. Deduct a reservation immediately after accepting it.
Keep the refusal checks in the declared order, and count accepted proposals when enforcing the one-probe rule.

title: Which Examples Should We Put in the Prompt?
blurb: Botie keeps making an inspection sound mandatory. Show what a supported answer looks like, then check that the examples teach the distinction we intended.
openingTitle: Our Example Accidentally Teaches “Always Inspect”
opening: We give Botie an example: a noisy pump, a manual excerpt, and an answer recommending inspection. The next technician asks what a warning light means. Botie recommends an inspection again. Perhaps it copied the most obvious pattern in the example.

An example shows more than the desired format. It also shows which evidence led to which decision. We need cases that make the distinction visible, including a question the supplied evidence cannot answer. Then we need questions that were never used to choose those examples.

history.title: Showing a Task Inside the Input
blocks: The 2020 GPT-3 paper studied tasks presented through instructions and a small number of demonstrations in the model’s input. In that setting, adapting to the task did not require gradient updates during inference. This made the contents of the prompt part of how the task was specified.

For our maintenance desk, that means we can show a supported answer and a request for clarification side by side. It does not guarantee that a model will infer the intended rule. We still have to test what it does with unfamiliar questions.

reading.experimentTitle: Choose examples without peeking at the exam
reading.experimentIntro: Select relevant development examples, then fit them into the reserved prompt space.
reading.connectionTitle: Selection comes before packing
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Turn demonstrations into message pairs
reading.outputLabel: Selected example IDs and remaining allowance
reading.exampleNote: These are invented, recorded examples. The browser runs your construction without calling a language model. Passing them checks the surrounding program, not the quality of a live model.

intuition.title: Give the decision a reason
intuition.explanation: These are abbreviated teaching examples, not complete maintenance advice.

records.label: Meaning of a warning; manual explains it
Whether inspection is due; revision missing
cells: Do not fill an evidence gap

records.label: Request to book; no approval
cells: An answer is not authority to act

scene.caption: The differences matter more than repeated phrasing.

intuition.title: Keep a question out of the selection pool
intuition.explanation: Examples A and B were written while developing the prompt. C is a held-out test.

scene.caption: Even when C fits more easily, using it as a demonstration would compromise this test’s independence.

parts.title: 1. Write the rule before choosing a demonstration
paragraphs: Our rule is to answer from the supplied approved evidence and ask for missing information when that evidence is insufficient. Start there. Then choose examples in which the evidence changes what a good answer can say.

If every example ends in inspection, the prompt leaves an important boundary unexplained. Include a supported explanation that needs no proposed action. Avoid real customer details; synthetic examples can teach the structure without exposing private records.
interpretation: Examples illustrate the written instruction. They do not grant access or override the tool’s permission checks.

parts.title: 2. Keep input and response together
paragraphs: A demonstration has an input and a reviewed response. The input should include the evidence available at that moment. The response should show only claims that evidence supports. A polished answer without its source passage teaches a less useful relationship.

Use the message format your provider supports. A common representation alternates user and assistant messages after the system instructions. Keep the current user request last and label retrieved material as data.
interpretation: Do not mix an example answer into the current user’s request as though the user supplied it.

examples.title: Inspect the structure before adding more examples
paragraphs: Each dictionary is one message. The role tells the API how that message participates in the conversation.
examples.code:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Use the supplied manual. Ask if evidence is missing."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "P7: which revision applies? Evidence: none."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Which revision is listed on P7?"},
]
print([message["role"] for message in messages])
interpretation: The example response belongs to an assistant turn. The programming challenge will append a separate current request.

parts.title: 3. Reserve space before selecting examples
paragraphs: The request also needs instructions, tool definitions, retrieved material and room for the output. Decide how much of the context allowance examples may use. Measure costs with the provider’s tokenizer or usage tools, including message overhead where applicable.

Our workshop supplies recorded costs for complete examples. It selects the requested kind from the development split, then scans in order and accepts each example that fits. This first-fit rule is easy to inspect. It does not find the most informative combination.
parts.calculation:
Example allowance: 80 tokens
A costs 40 → select A; 40 remain
B costs 55 → skip B; 40 remain
interpretation: The recorded costs are teaching fixtures, not token counts calculated by the browser. A production request needs a full context check after assembly.

parts.title: 4. An example can be correct and still be a poor choice
paragraphs: Two nearly identical supported answers may use the space that would have shown a missing-evidence case. An example may also depend on information absent from its input, or contain an obsolete policy. Review content as well as length.

For a small task, begin with a few deliberately contrasting demonstrations. Compare their order and selection on development cases. If dynamic retrieval chooses demonstrations, test that selector too: a relevance score does not enforce privacy or keep held-out questions out of the pool.
interpretation: Longer prompts are not automatically better. The evaluation must justify the added examples and their cost.

parts.title: 5. Leave the test answers outside the prompt
paragraphs: Keep development cases separate from the held-out set used to assess the chosen prompt. Near duplicates can leak the answer just as easily as exact copies. Split by the unit that matters, such as asset family or customer conversation, when related records would otherwise cross the boundary.

Once you inspect held-out failures and use them to change the prompt, those examples have become development evidence for the next revision. Retain them as regression tests and collect fresh cases for another independent assessment.
interpretation: Record the example IDs, their order and the prompt version with the run. A changed demonstration is a changed experiment.

parts.title: 6. Test the distinction the example was meant to teach
paragraphs: Try a new warning with sufficient evidence, then remove the decisive passage. The expected behaviour should change. Also try a different asset whose manual uses different wording. This checks whether the candidate learned a useful task pattern rather than simply repeating our sample answer.
A test double can verify message assembly. Only runs against the intended model can provide evidence about its responses, and those responses may vary across repetitions.
interpretation: The next lessons will keep this distinction between testing our program and evaluating the model visible.

practice.title: Can we assemble the examples without confusing them with the current question?
practice.question: Can we assemble the examples without confusing them with the current question?
task: Implement messages_for(instruction, examples, question). Each example dictionary contains input and output strings. Return a system message, a user/assistant pair for each example in order, and the current user question last. Leave the supplied list unchanged.
practice.starter:
def messages_for(instruction, examples, question):
    pass
practice.solution:
def messages_for(instruction, examples, question):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": instruction}]
    for item in examples:
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": item["input"]})
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": item["output"]})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": question})
    return messages

print([m["role"] for m in messages_for("Use evidence.", [{"input":"P7?", "output":"Need revision."}], "P8?")])
hints: Start a new list for the messages.
Append both turns for an example before moving to the next one.

title: Why Did Botie Take So Long?
blurb: An answer arrives late, but the text cannot tell us where the time went. Follow one maintenance request through retrieval, tool calls and the final response.
openingTitle: The Answer Is Right. The Technician Is Still Waiting.
opening: A technician asks Botie which inspection procedure applies to pump 7. He finds the manual and gives a useful answer, but it takes much longer than yesterday. Was the manual search slow? Did a tool fail and retry? Did Botie keep asking the model for something he already had?

The final answer has thrown away most of that story. We need a record of the operations that produced it, with their relationships and timings still attached. Then we can change the part that actually caused the delay.

history.title: Following a Request Across Machines
blocks: A slow response was already difficult to explain in distributed services before language-model agents. A request could cross many machines, while each machine kept only its own local record. Google’s 2010 Dapper paper described a tracing system that connected work across those boundaries using related spans.

OpenTelemetry supplies shared instrumentation and propagation conventions for this kind of record. Our assistant has the same practical need: connect a manual search and a model call to the request that caused them. The invented timings below illustrate that relationship; they are not measurements from a deployed assistant.

reading.experimentTitle: Which span measures the technician’s wait?
reading.experimentIntro: Select one request, find its root span, and measure its elapsed time. Compare that result with the child intervals when two tools overlap.
reading.connectionTitle: Keep the cause attached to the operation
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Measure one request
reading.exampleNote: Invented spans use a shared clock. Short trace names stand in for real trace identifiers.

intuition.title: Start with the whole request
intuition.explanation: The request begins before retrieval and ends after the answer has been assembled. Its interval contains the work the technician is waiting for.

scene.caption: The two lookups overlap. The answer call waits until both have finished.

intuition.title: Two kinds of duration answer different questions
intuition.explanation: Child time can count the same wall-clock interval twice when work runs in parallel. The root interval gives the elapsed request duration.

records.label: Child durations
cells: Sum of the selected operation durations

scene.caption: These invented spans also leave time outside the child operations. Do not silently call every uninstrumented interval model time.

parts.title: 1. Write down an operation while it happens
paragraphs: A span is a record for one operation. Give it a useful name, a start time and an end time. A manual lookup might also record which document version it searched and whether the service returned an error.
A log line tells us that something happened at a moment. A span gives the operation a duration. Both can be useful, provided we can connect them to the same request.
interpretation: Begin with boundaries you can act on: the request, a retrieval call, a model call and any tool whose failures matter.

parts.title: 2. Give related work an identity
paragraphs: A trace groups the spans belonging to one request. Each span has its own ID, and a child records the ID of the operation that started it. The request span has no parent in our complete fixture.

Two technicians can call the same tool at the same time. A tool name and timestamp alone cannot reliably tell us which request produced which call. The trace and parent IDs preserve that relationship.
interpretation: A parent describes causal context. It does not imply that siblings ran one after another.

parts.title: 3. Keep concurrent work on the same clock
paragraphs: Botie can request the manual and equipment details concurrently. On our table, both operations are active for part of the same interval. Adding their durations counts that shared time twice.

For the technician’s elapsed wait, measure the root request. To investigate its slow path, examine when dependencies actually finished and what the next operation was waiting for. Adding every descendant also double counts nested spans.
parts.calculation:
Request duration = end − start
Request duration = 900 − 0 = 900 milliseconds
interpretation: A sum of span durations is not automatically CPU time, either. An operation can spend much of its duration waiting on a network.

parts.title: 4. A retry needs its own visible attempt
paragraphs: Suppose manual search times out and succeeds on the second attempt. Recording only the successful call hides the first delay and its failure. Keep an enclosing operation and separate attempts, or otherwise record attempt numbers and errors clearly.
Marking an HTTP call successful only says it returned normally under that call’s definition. A model response can still cite the wrong manual. Later lessons will attach quality judgements separately.
interpretation: The trace should let us distinguish a slow successful call from a quick failure followed by a second call.

parts.title: 5. Carry the context across the tool boundary
paragraphs: When Botie calls another service, that service needs the current trace context if its work is to appear in the same trace. Instrumentation can inject that context into a request and extract it at the receiver. OpenTelemetry commonly uses the W3C traceparent header for this.

If propagation is lost, the receiver may create a new root. The work still happened, but the picture becomes disconnected. For queued or fan-in work, span links can express relationships that do not fit one parent.
interpretation: Do not infer that missing spans mean no work occurred. First check instrumentation, propagation and sampling.

parts.title: 6. Read a recorded span with Python
paragraphs: A dictionary keeps a timestamp beside its meaning. A list contains several span records. Selecting a trace should happen before choosing the root; otherwise another technician’s request can supply the duration by accident.
interpretation: This small program inspects recorded data. It does not install a tracer or send telemetry.

examples.title: Find the operation with no parent
paragraphs: The two records describe one request and a lookup inside it. None marks the root’s absent parent.
examples.code:
spans = [
    {"id": "request", "parent": None, "start": 10, "end": 210},
    {"id": "manual", "parent": "request", "start": 20, "end": 170},
]
roots = [s for s in spans if s["parent"] is None]
print(roots[0]["id"])
print(roots[0]["end"] - roots[0]["start"])
interpretation: The child describes part of the interval. The challenge adds selection between traces and rejects ambiguous root data.

parts.title: 7. Instrument the same boundaries in OpenTelemetry
paragraphs: A tracer creates spans. An SDK provider collects them, and an exporter sends them somewhere we can inspect. Start with the console exporter so we can see a small record without configuring a hosted dashboard.

The nested context manager below establishes the parent relationship for a local lookup. A real remote client also needs propagation. Use instrumentation suited to that client instead of assuming a Python with block follows an HTTP request into another process.
interpretation: This example records a real local function execution. Its tiny in-memory manual is still a fixture, and it performs no model inference.

references.title: Record a local lookup with the OpenTelemetry SDK
description: Run as a separate Python script. The SDK prints spans with generated identifiers and measured timestamps, so there is no fixed output to copy.
references.code:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor, ConsoleSpanExporter

provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter()))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer("fitlab.maintenance")

with tracer.start_as_current_span("maintenance-request"):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("manual-lookup") as lookup:
        manual = {"P7": "Request inspection before restart."}.get("P7")
        lookup.set_attribute("manual.found", manual is not None)

provider.shutdown()
setup: Install opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-sdk in your own Python environment.
Run once in a new process; applications normally configure their provider once at startup.
interpretation: Inspect the child’s parent ID and the common trace ID. Console export is a first check, not a production storage policy.

parts.title: 8. Count tokens where they were consumed
paragraphs: Record usage on the model generation that consumed it. Input tokens and output tokens can have different prices, and caching or other provider categories may change the bill. Keep the model identifier and the pricing assumptions with a cost estimate.

A parent summary may already include its children’s usage. Summing that summary with those same children charges the work twice. A retry that reached the provider may add usage even if the application later discarded its answer.
parts.calculation:
Illustrative input cost = (1200 / 1000000) × 2 = 0.0024 currency units
Illustrative output cost = (300 / 1000000) × 8 = 0.0024 currency units
Estimated generation cost = 0.0024 + 0.0024 = 0.0048 currency units
interpretation: These rates are invented to show the calculation. Use the actual provider’s pricing categories and usage records for accounting.

parts.title: 9. Keep useful evidence without copying private records
paragraphs: A technician’s request can contain names, internal equipment locations or secrets pasted by mistake. Logging every prompt verbatim creates another copy of that information. Decide which fields are necessary before exporting them.

For our maintenance flow, a document version and a controlled error code may answer the debugging question without retaining the full manual. Redact before export, restrict access, and set retention deliberately. Do not put credentials or personal information in tracing baggage that may travel to other services.

Record boundary decisions where the application makes them: the policy revision, the resource identity and an access-controlled reason code for an allowed or denied action. Link the decision to its action ID so a later investigator can distinguish a blocked attempt from a write that actually happened. Do not copy secrets or hidden model reasoning to explain that decision.
interpretation: A redacted trace should still preserve operation identities and relationships. Redaction that removes every useful distinction makes diagnosis harder.

parts.title: 10. Use traces beside rates and distributions
paragraphs: One trace explains one recorded execution. Metrics can tell us whether slow requests are becoming common, while logs can retain details of a particular error. Correlating them lets us move from a rising error rate to an example of the failing path.

Sampling reduces the stored trace volume. A sampled set can miss rare failures, and selecting only slow traces biases latency summaries. Record the sampling policy and compute service-wide metrics from appropriate observations.
interpretation: A missing failure in the viewer is weak evidence if the relevant request was never retained.

parts.title: 11. Repair the part the trace points to
paragraphs: If retrieval dominates the elapsed time, changing the answer prompt may barely change the wait. If repeated model calls dominate, inspect the loop’s stopping rule and what each call receives. If the root has a large unexplained gap, instrument that gap before guessing.

Compare the repaired request with fresh requests under similar conditions. Keep quality checks beside timing so an answer that arrives quickly but ignores the manual does not look like a successful repair.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop measures the root of a chosen trace. The changed case introduces overlap, and the fresh case mixes in another request to test whether the construction still follows the right technician.

quiz.prompt: Which fields let us attach a lookup to the correct request?
options: Its trace ID and parent relationship
The order in which log lines reached storage
quiz.because: Transport and storage can reorder events. The identifiers retain the intended relationship.

given.data: Two requests call manual-lookup concurrently. Their trace IDs differ, and each lookup records its parent span ID.

quiz.prompt: This record fully explains the request’s latency.
quiz.because: The failed attempt and any retry wait are missing from the explanation.

given.data: A retry succeeds after the first attempt times out. Only the successful attempt is stored.

practice.title: How long did the selected technician wait?
practice.question: How long did the selected technician wait?
task: Write request_duration(spans, trace_id). Each span has trace, parent, start and end. Return the selected trace’s root duration in milliseconds.

Require exactly one selected span with parent=None. Raise ValueError for missing or multiple roots, nonnumeric or nonfinite root times, Boolean times, or an end before its start. This function measures the root; it does not validate every child relationship.
Use the supplied two-trace fixture and print the duration for A.
practice.starter:
def request_duration(spans, trace_id):
    pass

spans = [
    {"trace": "A", "parent": None, "start": 20, "end": 470},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 30, "end": 310},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 50, "end": 330},
    {"trace": "B", "parent": None, "start": 0, "end": 900},
]
print(request_duration(spans, "A"))
practice.solution:
import math

def request_duration(spans, trace_id):
    selected = [s for s in spans if s["trace"] == trace_id]
    roots = [s for s in selected if s["parent"] is None]
    if len(roots) != 1:
        raise ValueError("Expected exactly one request span")
    root = roots[0]
    start, end = root["start"], root["end"]
    if (isinstance(start, bool) or isinstance(end, bool)
            or not isinstance(start, (int, float))
            or not isinstance(end, (int, float))
            or not math.isfinite(start) or not math.isfinite(end)
            or end < start):
        raise ValueError("Invalid root timing")
    return end - start

spans = [
    {"trace": "A", "parent": None, "start": 20, "end": 470},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 30, "end": 310},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 50, "end": 330},
    {"trace": "B", "parent": None, "start": 0, "end": 900},
]
print(request_duration(spans, "A"))
hints: Select trace A before looking for its root.
A root has parent=None. Subtract its start from its end; do not add child durations.

questions.because: The request boundary measures the whole wait. The child intervals overlap and omit some surrounding work.

given.data: A request spans 0–900 ms. Its children span 50–350, 100–500 and 500–850 ms.

questions.prompt: The shared parent alone does not establish a sequential execution order.
questions.because: Parentage records context, while timing and dependencies determine execution order.
